Reorganization can require work. The book's hysteresis discussion associates different forward and return paths with the work invested in changing structure. Once the conditions retreat, the organization need not simply trace an identical reversible course. Calling this memory identifies a dependence on prior change. [WME-W001, 48–49, figs. 11–12]

Jantsch connects an established regime with economy of operation and a transition with expenditure on restructuring. That is a useful distinction between using an arrangement and making another arrangement possible. His novelty/confirmation and entropy-production diagrams organize the conceptual story; they are not calibrated accounts in one unit of lifecycle cost. [WME-W001, 42–53, figs. 12–14]

The book's schematic contrasts between maximum and minimum entropy production extend beyond the conditions under which those principles hold. They do not establish an optimizing law across physical, biological and social regimes. [WME-W001, chs. 2–3]

### Co-evolution changes the surrounding possibilities

Co-evolution changes the surrounding possibilities

Jantsch's macro–micro narrative makes organisms and their surroundings participants in a connected history. The environment supplies conditions for local processes, while the accumulated effects of those processes alter the environment encountered by later participants. Adaptation to a fixed setting is therefore only one part of the account. The rules and opportunities of further evolution can also change. [WME-W001, chs. 4–8]

The value of this claim lies partly in its causal direction. A feature that appears economical inside one organism may be possible because other processes now supply what it no longer produces. The account of reduced internal biosynthetic capability, illustrated through vitamin supply, locates a corresponding environmental dependence. Its relevant point is that missing internal production and independence are different things. [WME-W001, ch. 7, 133–138]

The architect's plan provides an especially accessible illustration. A plan sent to a distant building site is effective only if local conditions permit realization: materials must be available or obtainable, skills must exist, and infrastructure and environmental relations must support construction. Sending the plan does not transport the completed building or create skilled masons. Jantsch uses the example in explaining the transfer of process programmes rather than all the material conditions of their execution. [WME-W001, 133]

He also discusses the other side of adaptation. Acquired ecological information and an established way of life can increase present capability while narrowing later possibilities. A relation that once opened opportunities can become a dependency. Autonomy and flexibility do not therefore increase together in every step of the evolutionary narrative. The book's changing levels and criteria prevent its account from being reduced to monotonic improvement on one scale. [WME-W001, 141–142]

The biological and cosmic chapters range widely. Their original dates, evolutionary reconstructions, particle-physics models and neurobiological frameworks are historical premises of the 1980 account. [WME-W001, chs. 5–9, 11]

<!-- PDF page 33 -->

### A record becomes useful through selective activation

A record becomes useful through selective activation

Jantsch distinguishes ongoing processes from relatively conservative storage. DNA, books, tools and representations can preserve possibilities, yet preserved form becomes effective only through its use in an active context. His term “epigenealogical” describes the relation between stored information and its selective retrieval in living, changing processes. The book's diagram makes both the record and its interpreting context visible. [WME-W001, ch. 11, 195–202, fig. 38]

The musical score illustrates the point. Its marks preserve an ordered possibility, while a performance involves learned conventions, interpretation and present activity. A book likewise does not make its knowledge available independently of readers and their purposes. Selection changes which stored possibilities become operative. Storage can support reuse without executing itself. [WME-W001, 202; ch. 18, 286–296]

This is more than a claim that a container holds information. Jantsch places novelty and confirmation in relation: prior patterns can guide activity, while a changed context can activate them differently. His evolutionary learning process has no permanently fixed school-like target. Existing histories and traditions channel what can happen, but a channeled process is not the same as a sequence directed toward a single externally supplied goal. [WME-W001, 202]

The account also retains implementation work in cultural creation. Vision must acquire rational form, and form must be interpreted and realized through learned and manual capabilities. A notation or representation can make an intention transportable and repeatable while depending on the skills and materials of performance. [WME-W001, ch. 18]

### Interaction, communication, symbiosis and fusion

Interaction, communication, symbiosis and fusion

Jantsch distinguishes several kinds of relation rather than treating all coupling as one thing. Interaction names exchange with an environment not organized as a comparable participant at the selected level. Communication involves one organized process evoking activity in another. Symbiosis involves the mutual use of products or services, while fusion describes the limiting case in which the former participants lose their separate autonomous organization. These distinctions concern the processes and autonomy retained, not merely the number of connecting arrows. [WME-W001, 203–207, fig. 39]

In his communication account, the recipient must be capable of the activity evoked. A description of a sunset works through a listener's experience and capacity to form meaning; it does not transfer the sunset itself. A stimulating signal also does not provide all the recipient's energy. Jantsch explicitly retains each system's responsibility for its own structural problems and energy flow. [WME-W001, 203–205]

Dialogue can in turn reorganize knowledge rather than merely exchange already completed packages. The claim is that mutual stimulation can change the participants' cognitive domains. That remains a conceptual account of generative communication. [WME-W001, 205–206]

Symbiosis introduces a different dependency. Participants use one another's transformation products or services. Each can relinquish some individual autonomy while participating in a larger organization with capabilities at another level. The lower-level processes do not necessarily vanish. This is why Jantsch distinguishes a partially autonomous relation from complete fusion. His own account also allows excessive mutual dependence, in which the relation narrows possibilities without producing the anticipated novelty. [WME-W001, 206–207]

His application of “co-operative” to whole ecological processes needs its stated viewpoint. A predator– prey relation may contribute to an ecosystem's pattern while destroying particular prey. Organization at the larger level does not imply benefit to each individual. Jantsch explicitly recognizes that affected

<!-- PDF page 34 -->

participants might not experience the relation as cooperation. The qualification matters whenever larger-system persistence is used as a criterion. [WME-W001, 135–136, 206]

### Multiple levels retain different tests and responsibilities

Multiple levels retain different tests and responsibilities

The book's account of emergent levels includes distinct criteria: energetic penetration, error correction, variety, flexibility, consistency and connectedness. These are not interchangeable numerical forms of one variable. Jantsch describes higher-level openness supported by more settled lower-level activities, but that construction does not make the lower levels inert or eliminate their conditions of existence. [WME-W001, ch. 12, 218–230, figs. 41–43]

His time- and space-binding account relates stored experience, present interactions and anticipation. A present organization can employ records of the past and images of a possible future. [WME-W001, ch. 13, 231–238, fig. 44 and table 5]

Stratified autonomy is his alternative to a picture in which information merely travels upward and orders travel downward. Each organized level can maintain some direct relation with a wider environment. A cell's surroundings, in his illustration, include more than adjacent cells. In the proposed social extension, local participants retain contact with their own circumstances while a broader level performs synthesis. The practical issue is the distribution of initiative and integration. [WME-W001, ch. 14, 239–250]

Jantsch's formulation of decentralized initiative and centralized synthesis therefore retains a management role. The manager as catalyst is an assigned activity, not an absence of organization. He also argues that an institutional pattern can suppress novelty at precisely the levels where broader changes need consideration. These are the author's organizational proposals and criticisms. Jantsch quotes Mesarović in discussing control hierarchies and relative frequencies. [WME-W001, 248–250]

The argument about intermediate organizational levels supplies a further distinction. A choice between very large and very small units can omit forms that connect local capability with wider provision. His machinery illustration, attributed to Schumacher, describes technical development reinforcing an expected disappearance of small producers. It is a historical reported example of the relation between technological options and organizational scale. [WME-W001, 249]

### Planning can change what counts as satisfactory

Planning can change what counts as satisfactory

Jantsch separates tactical planning for an already recognized output from strategic, policy and value questions. At the tactical level, efficient realization within a relatively stable structure can be a reasonable aim. At the strategic level, alternatives are imagined, examined and prepared. Policy places the organization's activity in a wider social context, while values influence which futures deserve pursuit. The planning task changes as the level changes. [WME-W001, ch. 16, 266–274, table 6]

It follows within his account that a more open planning process can deliberately introduce options, uncertainty and complexity. Minimizing immediate effort or maximizing short-term profit does not settle whether a new social function should be developed or a harmful one discontinued. He distinguishes the survival of a particular organization from continuity of the social processes it serves. The book thus contains a substantive challenge to using organizational survival as the only criterion. [WME-W001, 266– 267]

The evolutionary proposal is not simply enthusiasm for destructive discontinuity. Jantsch recognizes that large transitions can damage the biological and cultural substrate on which further life depends. His proposed “gliding” evolution imagines partially overlapping changes and plural paths instead of requiring an entire civilization to change through a single rupture. [WME-W001, ch. 15, 251–262]

<!-- PDF page 35 -->

Part IV explicitly offers perspectives rather than solutions to every problem. Its ethical account places several levels of obligation and experience in tension. The passage on Antigone illustrates conflict between personal moral commitment and the law of the larger social order, not a method that automatically reconciles them. Jantsch's wish to ground an evolutionary ethics is a normative and philosophical proposal. Biological or social survival does not by itself establish a moral duty. [WME-W001, ch. 16, 263–274]

The technology discussion also limits a direct transfer from ecology to human economy. Exosomatic tools, restructuring of environments and increased energy use change the conditions of the comparison. A human arrangement can become more capable by expanding its material dependencies. [WME-W001, ch. 17, 275–285]

### Connected descriptions without a supermodel

Connected descriptions without a supermodel

Near the end, Jantsch explicitly rejects one supermodel combining all autonomous levels into a single description. He favors an account of the web of relations among descriptions. His contrast between macroscopic and microscopic approaches returns here: descriptions may be complementary because they answer different questions, rather than waiting to be replaced by one all-purpose vocabulary. [WME-W001, ch. 19, especially 303]

Jantsch brings maintenance, transformation, environmental capability, stored forms, communication and changing purposes into a connected evolutionary account. The epilogue extends his inquiry to meaning. [WME-W001, ch. 19 and epilogue 307–311]

### The earlier dissipative-structures excerpt

The earlier dissipative-structures excerpt

An excerpt from Jantsch's earlier Design for Evolution (1975) proposes the extension from physical to human systems as a hypothesis. Its examples concern a freeway changing urban activity, a newcomer stimulating a bureaucratic office, and a revolution followed by new structures and restrictions. In each, an initial alteration is followed by reorganization and a more established regime. [RGC-W001, excerpt and linked figure]

The freeway example is particularly informative because the new regime can become congested again. Opening capacity changes activity rather than permanently removing every source of congestion. The office example likewise makes the surrounding condition decisive: colleagues can absorb and exclude the newcomer, or existing tensions can permit a wider change. These are illustrative mechanisms and conditional stories, not controlled evaluations of road building or office reform. [RGC-W001]

The revolution example connects initial participation with the later consolidation of power and narrowing of permitted contributions. Jantsch uses entropy, power and rigidity in explaining that trajectory. Those social correspondences are not measured thermodynamic equalities. The examples help identify the proposed sequence and the retained costs of restructuring. [RGC-W001]

### Greene's later reconstruction and intellectual reception

Greene's later reconstruction and intellectual reception

Herman Greene's 2018 review reads Jantsch from an ecozoic perspective and traces a connection with Brian Swimme and Thomas Berry. He explains the book through process, self-organization, exchange and co-evolution, and relates those terms to differentiation, interiority and communion in the later writers. This is substantive evidence of a sympathetic intellectual reception. [WME-W002, 363–372]

Greene quotes and interprets Swimme and Berry as well as Jantsch. Their expanded use of autopoiesis and subjectivity belongs to Greene's account of the relationship among these authors; he points to The Universe Story in support. [WME-W002, especially 363–364, 370–372]

<!-- PDF page 36 -->

## S20 Gharajedaghi: purposeful organizations and the work of redesign

S20   Gharajedaghi: purposeful organizations and the work of redesign

### A connected organizational account

A connected organizational account

Jamshid Gharajedaghi's Systems Thinking: Managing Chaos and Complexity, third edition, connects holistic inquiry, operational dynamics, purposeful social activity and interactive design. His organizational synthesis examines how interdependence, decision criteria, modularity, competence, incentives and governance affect performance. [WME-W003, 2011, preface]

### Purpose and choice change the description

Purpose and choice change the description

In 1984, Gharajedaghi and Russell Ackoff argued that treating a social system as a machine or an organism was an inadequate guide to decisions about it. [RGC-W002]

Gharajedaghi distinguishes passive mechanical systems, organisms treated as having a unified purpose, and social systems composed of purposeful participants. In the last category, participants can choose ends as well as means. A procedure can consequently fail even when it is technically feasible: people may reject its purpose, interpret it differently or pursue another interest. The relevant organizational problem includes choice, rather than only transmitting commands to interchangeable components. [WME-W003, ch. 1, 9–22; ch. 2, 29–37]

Control, influence and context are correspondingly different relations. An actor's ability or authority to determine something differs from an ability to affect it, and both differ from conditions that the actor must accommodate. The boundary is relative to the actors and their capabilities. Describing a supplier, regulator or customer as part of an environment does not make its choices disappear. [WME-W003, 29– 37]

The book also distinguishes information about what, knowledge of how and understanding of why. Shared instructions and shared reasons are therefore different accomplishments. A member who understands only an immediate instruction can still require repeated direction when circumstances change. The account of purposeful actors makes the development of relevant understanding an organizational activity in its own right. [WME-W003, ch. 2]

Gharajedaghi's criticism of biological and cybernetic models, including Beer, is part of his argument. His own later foundation diagram acknowledges Beer alongside Ackoff, Forrester and Boulding. [WME-W003, chs. 1, 4; diagram preceding ch. 5]

### Inquiry joins structure, function, process and context

Inquiry joins structure, function, process and context

The book rejects a simple one-to-one inference from structure to outcome. The same implement can perform different functions depending on its use and setting. Conversely, one function can be realized through different structures. Process explains how an arrangement produces an outcome, while context supplies enabling and limiting conditions. Gharajedaghi therefore proposes iterative inquiry among structure, function, process and context. [WME-W003, ch. 5, 89–93]

Iteration involves examining each perspective and revisiting its relations with the others. His expanding view places the focal activity within progressively wider surroundings until further enlargement ceases to add useful insight. The practical claim is that inquiry should expose assumptions and missing relations. Gharajedaghi proposes the four perspectives as mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. [WME-W003, 92–93, fig. 5.4]

<!-- PDF page 37 -->

His five social dimensions—wealth, power, knowledge, beauty and values—likewise organize the inquiry. Generation and distribution, rational and emotional commitments, and present and future effects can conflict. The dimensions direct attention toward matters that a purely financial account can omit. [WME-W003, chs. 2, 5]

Multidimensionality seeks alternatives beyond a forced choice between two unsatisfactory extremes. An arrangement might improve both production and distribution, or permit local discretion together with broader consistency. That is a design ambition and a question to investigate. The book itself recognizes difficult differences in worldviews and the need to protect minorities. [WME-W003, 38–55, 103–108]

### Shared criteria can support local decisions

Shared criteria can support local decisions

The contrast between two managers makes the proposed mechanism concrete. A manager can promise autonomy while retaining unspoken preferences; unexpected decisions then provoke intervention, and a subordinate starts seeking permission for everything. Another manager repeatedly explains why decisions are made. As the subordinate learns the relevant criteria, locally proposed action can become acceptable without detailed direction on every occasion. The illustration concerns shared reasons and judgments, not the announcement of decentralization alone. [WME-W003, 98–99]

Gharajedaghi proposes nested learning and design cells that connect a manager, board, superior and direct reports. Their task is to develop common understanding of purpose, cultural defaults and decision criteria. This institutionalizes the conversations rather than expecting every individual to acquire an identical understanding through private contact with the leader. [WME-W003, 99–100, fig. 5.8]

Effective criteria must leave a degree of freedom. If they prescribe every decision, they cease to support meaningful choice. They also need internal consistency, explicit assumptions and expected consequences, and a basis for collective commitment. A production cost target and a sales revenue target can create structural conflict if each rewards conduct that makes the other's task harder. The work of aligning the criteria precedes any claim that local decisions will fit together. [WME-W003, 100–101]

Consensus is described as an agreement to act, rather than majority rule or a requirement that every person privately agree. Leadership remains necessary when discussion does not resolve the issue. The leader can formulate an explicit default, or parties can agree on an experiment with performance criteria and conditions that would count against their positions. The process retains authority, design of tests and judgment about timing. [WME-W003, 101]

### Culture and learning reproduce the arrangement

Culture and learning reproduce the arrangement

Shared images and default assumptions help reproduce an organization even when individual members change. Improvement within an existing rule and learning that questions the rule are different activities. Gharajedaghi's second-order learning asks how the organization can examine the frames and criteria through which it identifies a problem. Training in an established process is therefore insufficient when that process itself produces the difficulty. [WME-W003, ch. 3, 57–68]

Information-mediated integration requires people who can interpret and use what is communicated. Knowledge can be shared without disappearing from its original holder. Gharajedaghi also draws physical analogies involving entropy, quantum phenomena and attractors; his organizational arguments can be distinguished from those extrapolations. [WME-W003, chs. 2–3]

Development is distinguished from growth. A larger organization need not be more able or willing to serve its members and environment. Differentiation can increase specialized capability while making integration more demanding. Gharajedaghi's concern is the relationship between these changes, rather

<!-- PDF page 38 -->

than an assumption that scale, output or specialization alone measures development. His sweeping historical classifications remain his interpretations. [WME-W003, ch. 4, 69–85]

### Operational models make delays and incentives visible

Operational models make delays and incentives visible

The stock-and-flow models describe accumulations, rates, feedback and delays. A policy can improve a local indicator while worsening the condition that later drives the same indicator. Modeling is intended to make those interactions available for discussion and testing. The book explicitly makes the usefulness of a model depend on the validity of its underlying equations and assumptions. [WME-W003, ch. 6, 109–131]

The telephone-company example joins several causes. Demand had consumed spare lines previously retained for failures. A repair could then appropriate another active line, briefly satisfying one customer while generating another complaint. Different departments controlled interdependent activities, records deteriorated as more people worked on the plant, and volume-based rewards encouraged activity and overtime. The problem was not described as a shortage of worker effort alone. [WME-W003, 128–129, fig. 6.24]

The reported redesign groups related work in neighborhood units, changes rewards toward results and customer satisfaction, gives managers authority to limit new installations when plant condition and slack require it, and directs expansion toward the limiting parts of the system. Capacity, maintenance, records, local responsibility and incentives change together. The author reports resolution within three months. [WME-W003, 128–129]

The account is particularly informative about spare capacity. Eliminating an apparently idle reserve can increase later interdependence and repair traffic. Its value depends on the disturbances and demand it supports. The book also proposes preserving assumptions and expectations in a read-only log so later experience can be compared with what was expected. [WME-W003, 128–131]

### Modularity groups dependencies and maintains competence

Modularity groups dependencies and maintains competence

Gharajedaghi defines a module through strong internal interdependence and relatively weak external dependence. A platform supplies a predesigned relation through which a class of modules interacts with the rest of the arrangement. The aim is to integrate related activities inside a unit while making its external interactions simpler and more explicit. [WME-W003, ch. 7, 138–140]

The proposed multidimensional architecture distinguishes inputs, markets and outputs. Input modules hold resources and competencies, including knowledge and shared services, and must renew them through research and education. Market modules identify needs and opportunities. Output modules combine external opportunities with internal capabilities in products, projects or programmes of differing duration. Their authority over work and money need not include ownership of all the capital they use. [WME-W003, 139–140, fig. 7.4]

Capability maintenance is therefore deliberately separated from the life of a particular project. The book does not propose that every temporary team independently own every specialist resource. Members of a knowledge bank also need design competence in addition to functional expertise. A simpler interface for an output group can depend on continuing work elsewhere in the architecture. [WME-W003, 139–140]

### Cross-functional water-system design

Cross-functional water-system design

The custom water-purification design example contrasts sequential passage through functional hierarchies with a cross-functional module. In the original reported process, chemical, process, electrical and mechanical engineering each passed work up and down their own chains before transferring it

<!-- PDF page 39 -->

onward. Costing and customer negotiation followed. The author estimates six to eight months and roughly $500,000 for the prior process. [WME-W003, 140–141]

The proposed experiment formed a learning cell of four junior engineers, a cost accountant and a sales engineer. Each taught the others the essential concerns and variables of the work. This preparation took three months, on the members' own time, with a promised $10,000 salary increase for each participant if the shared learning and project were successful. The team then met the customer together, rather than relying on a distant serial interpretation of requirements. [WME-W003, 141]

The book reports a completed design in six weeks at $120,000 and says the experiment was repeated twice with similar results. Shared understanding and concurrent contact with the customer replaced repeated hierarchical handoffs. [WME-W003, 141]

### Design and realization are separate tasks

Design and realization are separate tasks

Idealized design is constrained by technical feasibility and operational viability, while being capable of learning and adaptation. It changes the available alternatives instead of only optimizing the inherited arrangement. [WME-W003, 133–150]

Gharajedaghi describes realization as potentially the most resource-intensive phase. It involves preparation, monitoring of constraints, trust and ownership of the change, following the inquiry and design process. [WME-W003, 144–150]

Measurement and reward are part of the arrangement being designed. Local financial centers can pull against one another, while incompatible present incentives can burden future members. The proposed social calculus incorporates chosen coefficients for need, scarcity and strategic importance. Those choices require continuing revision. They are normative and managerial decisions, not discovered physical constants. [WME-W003, 150–157]

### Service, authority and internal markets

Service, authority and internal markets

The multidimensional design combines horizontal customer–supplier relations with vertical authority. Hiring, promotion and formal accountability do not disappear because units also purchase services. The internal market is intended to make demand and service performance visible, while the authority relation addresses matters it cannot settle. Gharajedaghi presents the two relations as complementary. [WME-W003, ch. 9, 181–207, especially 198]

Centralization requires a specific justification: indivisible functions, common measurement and information arrangements, scale effects or development of a core technology. The benefits must outweigh the disadvantages for the whole. Shared-service provision should not be confused with control, because mixing them can compromise both useful service and legitimate oversight. The control work remains assigned elsewhere. Some redundancy is also deliberately retained for flexibility. [WME-W003, 191, 195]

In his 1984 article on multidimensional modular design, Gharajedaghi argues that narrow specialization leaves an organization with too few ways to respond when conditions change. His proposal builds some redundancy into a modular design so that units can adapt and redefine their functions. [RGC-W003]

Inside–outside purchasing choices are intended to discipline internal providers, but a higher authority can override a choice by accepting the corresponding cost or loss. The account therefore retains governance even where price-like relations organize demand. Its broad assertions that an internal market eliminates bureaucratization are proposals for expected behavior, not universal effects established by the framework's definition. [WME-W003, 198]

<!-- PDF page 40 -->

The COM/Energy design supplies a particularly concrete cost distinction. Buying an external service does not make corporate fixed costs vanish if the organization still incurs them. The design requires the purchasing unit to bear a proportional internal charge until those costs can actually be eliminated. The comparison is between outside supply plus retained costs and the relevant internal alternative, rather than an allocated-cost figure that moves when the accounting changes. [WME-W003, ch. 13, 309–310]

Measurement itself also costs something. Gharajedaghi says its cost should not exceed the information's value and warns that overhead allocations can be mistaken for causal costs, inducing harmful cuts. The value-added coefficients of his performance centers reflect chosen strategy. These passages specify both a practical accounting issue and the limits of treating a managerial measure as a neutral description. [WME-W003, 202–206]

### The cases have different evidential status

The cases have different evidential status

“Mess formulation” gathers interacting difficulties into an intelligible pattern. The proposed process searches, maps and tells a story to support recognition and action. It is presented as early warning rather than prediction. The utility named XYZ is expressly fictitious, and its exaggerated scenario is a design aid. [WME-W003, ch. 8, 159–179]

The Part IV cases are selected consultant/client design synopses. Oneida is described as an ongoing fifth iteration; the Butterworth account condenses a much longer design after six iterations, acknowledging losses or misrepresentations in compression. Their detail is valuable for understanding intended arrangements. It does not convert all the proposed activities into implemented and sustained outcomes. [WME-W003, introductions to chs. 10–11, 211, 245]

Oneida's design retains dedicated expertise, boards and membership cells, together with support for meetings, material preparation, minutes and facilitation. Consensus is explicitly time-consuming. Self-reliance differs from doing everything internally: outside contractors can participate while training local  counterparts, and outsourcing should avoid excessive vulnerability. Multiple employment possibilities may be desirable redundancy. The account shows how participation and local capability require supporting organization. [WME-W003, ch. 10, 211–243]

The Butterworth health-care design combines community modules with shared specialist, capital-intensive capabilities. It recognizes risk, quality and rights, and the limits of reversible experimentation.  Core knowledge is maintained beyond temporary projects. The professional as learner, designer and practitioner is an integrative role that can broaden the competence required of a person. These are features of a proposed organizational design. [WME-W003, ch. 11, 245–279]

The book explicitly associates integration there with cooperation, attention from the president and cultural transformation. Flexible learning can sometimes be less immediately efficient than a perfected routine. A decision to preserve that learning has a purpose different from minimizing all overhead. [WME-W003, 273–279]

The Marriott design combines regional autonomy with shared components, core knowledge, training and maintenance. Initial subsidies may be needed. Policy teams establish criteria; where policy is absent, a local decision can become material for later learning. This is an account of how discretion and common capability are intended to fit together. [WME-W003, ch. 12, 281–289]

COM/Energy distinguishes a regulated core from entrepreneurial platforms and retains technical expertise, alliances, planning and learning networks. Its expectation of automatic or self-administered coordination is conditional on those continuing networks. Confidential supporting reports are not reproduced in the book. [WME-W003, ch. 13, 291–315]

<!-- PDF page 41 -->

Carrier is even more clearly bounded. The chapter says that implementation was not attempted because corporate circumstances and strategy changed. The architecture is a tentative idealized design produced by a team, not a realized success case. Its content is still informative: purchased components leave a requirement for whole-system design capability, and make, buy and alliance choices each retain relevant knowledge in different relations of control or influence. [WME-W003, ch. 14, 317–332]

The Carrier proposal further includes cross-disciplinary training, technical partnerships, models, shared design capability and policy teams. Revenue shares are proposed strategic allocations informed by benchmarks, alternatives, history and negotiation. [WME-W003, 321, 328–332, fig. 14.5]

<!-- PDF page 42 -->

## S21 Miller: process allocation, adjustment and purpose-relative costs

S21   Miller: process allocation, adjustment and purpose-relative costs

### Processes, structures and adjustment

Processes, structures and adjustment

James Grier Miller's living systems framework connects material and informational flows with structures, functions, regulation and costs. Miller asks how allocating processes to structures changes dependencies, communication, control, vulnerability and the effectiveness of adjustment.

Miller develops these concepts in the Basic Concepts excerpt from Living Systems and in his 1970 paper The Nature of Living Systems. Later author accounts and scholarly reconstructions develop and assess the framework. [RGC-W004; WME-W004; SG-W008]

### Matter-energy, markers and meaning

Matter-energy, markers and meaning

Miller treats living systems as concrete organizations existing in physical space and time. They process matter-energy and information, but information travels through physical markers. A message's pattern, its material carrier and its meaning to a recipient are related aspects, rather than one interchangeable quantity. Communication requires some physical realization and a system capable of receiving and interpreting it. [SG-W008, printed 1–9; WME-W004, §§1–4]

The distinction prevents a particular omission. A brief signal can influence a large activity without supplying all its energy, but the receiver still requires energy and the relevant capability. Information processing also involves channels, transformations, memory and other activities. Describing a message in informational terms does not remove those processes from the system's resource requirements. [SG-W008, 6–9; WME-W004, §§3–4]

Miller expressly separates Shannon information from meaning. Measures defined over alternatives and probabilities do not automatically measure significance, usefulness or agreement. Miller also connects information with negative entropy and develops speculative optimizing extensions. [WME-W004, §§3, 13]

Formal identities also require compatible dimensions, units or specified transformations. A curve drawn in one coordinate system can look different after a change of scale, while superficially similar curves can concern different relations. Miller's cross-level ambition therefore needs more than a visual resemblance. An asserted identity requires the measurement relation as well as a shared name for the process. [SG-W008, 23–25; WME-W004, §§1–4, 8]

### Structure, process and history differ

Structure, process and history differ

Structure describes spatial organization at a selected instant; process describes changes in matter-energy or information through time. History includes changes in the structure and functioning of the system. Its explanatory question includes how the organization changes, not only how flows pass through an unchanged diagram. [WME-W004, §§5–8]

The distinction between a component and a subsystem is equally important. A component is an identifiable structural unit. A subsystem is identified by the process it carries out and can span several components. One component can perform several processes, and several components can jointly perform one. The mapping between structures and functions is many-to-many. Counting departments, persons or physical parts is therefore different from identifying the activities they perform. [WME-W004, §11]

The discussion of organizational roles makes this concrete. A role specifies demands and activities, but the characteristics and needs of the person filling it also affect what happens. Adjustments can involve compromises between the member and the larger system. A formal position does not by itself establish

<!-- PDF page 43 -->

who actually leads or decides. Miller's distinction asks the investigator to examine the process rather than infer it directly from a title or shape. [WME-W004, §11]

He also distinguishes a system level from a decision echelon. Levels concern the organization of cells, organs, organisms, groups and further forms. Echelons are steps within a decider's organization, at which different decisions may be made. They need not coincide with levels, and some deciders are not arranged in echelons. [WME-W004, §§8–9]

Cross-level comparison requires both identities and “disidentities.” Similar functions can coexist with differences in mobility, duration, transferability of processes, boundaries and other characteristics. Miller's programme seeks quantitative similarities and relevant differences together. [WME-W004, §8.2]

### Allocating a function changes dependencies

Allocating a function changes dependencies

Miller's allocation patterns include localization in one component, combination with other processes, lateral distribution across components, upward or downward provision within a hierarchy, and outward provision by other systems. The allocation determines which parts depend on which other parts. Two systems can carry out similar functions while distributing the work differently. That difference belongs in an explanation of their performance. [SG-W008, 28–34; WME-W004, §11]

The framework explicitly proposes studying effectiveness and costs under alternative allocations. Distance over which material or messages must move, the number of participating components, difficulties of integration and duplicated capabilities can all matter. These are presented as candidate general principles and research questions. [WME-W004, §11]

Redundancy supplies an important countervailing consideration. A duplicate component capable of the same process can maintain function when another is disabled. Whether that possibility improves survival or just adds an unnecessary cost depends on the failures, capacities and other conditions. Miller offers a proposed relationship between allocation and vulnerability. [WME-W004, §11]

Outward provision is especially relevant. A function absent inside a system may still be carried out by a provider with which it exchanges resources or services. The absence of internal production does not mean the life function is unnecessary. It creates a relation to another system, potentially with exchange costs, asymmetric dependence or parasitism. [WME-W004, §11 and dispersion discussion]

The framework also describes differentiation or “shred-out,” in which increasingly specialized components take on processes previously combined. It supplies a way to ask how specialization changes structure without assuming that the function itself has newly come into existence. More differentiated parts can still depend on communication and integration. [WME-W004, §§8, 11]

### Critical processes and the decider condition

Critical processes and the decider condition

The earlier architecture names nineteen critical subsystems. They include the boundary and reproducer, matter-energy ingestion, conversion, production, distribution, storage and output, and information transduction, channels, decoding, association, memory, deciding, encoding and output. The list identifies required kinds of activity in the framework. [SG-W008, subsystem table; WME-W004, §11]

A system can lack an internal instance of a critical process if another system effectively supplies it. Miller makes an exception for deciding: an independently existing living system must retain its own decider. If that function is wholly transferred upward, downward or outward, he treats the focal unit's independent system identity differently. This is a substantive condition of his theory. [WME-W004, §11.8]

An artifact can participate in a critical function without itself becoming a living system. Living and nonliving components can be included in a larger organization. Thus the capability to store, filter or

<!-- PDF page 44 -->

transmit something is not sufficient on its own to establish living-system status. The decider requirement and living-system scope limit transfer to passive devices or decentralized formal arrangements that are described under different definitions. [WME-W004, §11]

This distinction also shows where an organizational decision remains. Miller permits variations in the internal distribution of deciding but requires an account of that process. Describing an organization as decentralized does not answer who settles conflicts, establishes comparison values or changes the allocation. Those activities must be located rather than assumed absent. [WME-W004, §§9, 11, 13]

### Adjustment can change more than the immediate response

Adjustment can change more than the immediate response

Adjustment maintains relevant variables within a range despite stress. Negative feedback uses information about actual performance to compare an outcome with a desired condition and alter activity. Timing matters: feedback arriving after the effective opportunity for correction can fail its purpose. A label saying “feedback” does not supply adequate speed, accuracy or action capacity. [SG-W008, 41–44; WME-W004, §13]

Miller's adjustment repertoire also includes learning or reorganization, changing the environment, withdrawal and changing targets. Not every difficulty is answered by exerting more force within an unchanged structure. A system can alter its relations or the condition it seeks. The range of alternatives makes its selected purpose and boundaries essential to evaluating the result. [WME-W004, §§12–13]

Equifinality is correspondingly bounded. Different starting conditions or routes may lead to a similar condition, but only within relevant ranges and with essential inputs available. The text explicitly notes histories and conditions that alter or destroy an organization. [WME-W004, §13.2.4]

### Costs are tied to purposes and time

Costs are tied to purposes and time

Miller's cost discussion is unusually direct. Adjustment uses material resources, energy, information and time; social systems also use money, which he discusses as information conveyed through markers. Any of these can be scarce. Costs differ between processes and can be immediate or delayed, short-term or long-term. The framework therefore explicitly reaches beyond the visible effort of the current act. [SG-W008, 45–46, §13.2.4; WME-W004, §13.2.5]

Efficiency is defined in relation to success at a known purpose and the costs involved. An operation can be active without being useful in the larger system. One must know what it is expected to achieve before judging whether its resource use is effective. Miller uses programme budgeting to illustrate separate accounts for the components or programmes carrying out distinct activities. [WME-W004, §§13.2.4– 13.2.5]

Different performances and resource dimensions can require different comparisons. Miller's claim that economic decisions improve performance and decrease costs expresses the account's optimizing orientation. [SG-W008, 45–46; WME-W004, §13.2.5]

Information itself has a place on both sides of the decision. Relevant information can improve selection among adjustments, but obtaining it costs resources. Reliability, distortion, accuracy, whether the inquiry concerns an act or a policy, and how it is acquired affect its value. The account thus includes information acquisition as work. More messages or more measurement are not automatically an improvement if they do not help the selected performance enough to justify their cost. [WME-W004, §13.2.5]

These passages connect allocation, dependence, regulation, information and performance within Miller's own account.

<!-- PDF page 45 -->

### Hammond and Wilby: a substantive reconstruction with objections

Hammond and Wilby: a substantive reconstruction with objections

Hammond and Wilby's 2006 article reconstructs Miller's effort to connect behavioral science, cybernetics and an organismic hierarchy through material and informational processes. It traces his research institutions and quantitative ambitions, while examining the implications of his categories. The article is adapted from a chapter of Hammond's 2003 book. [RGC-W005, 429–435]

The decider is a central issue in their account. They describe its role in forming intentions, coordinating activity and allocating power, and ask how that model works as the levels become socially more complex. The existence of a category called deciding does not by itself settle the relation between individual purposes and collective control. They preserve the tension between integrating members and supporting their needs. [RGC-W005, living-systems section]

They also report Boulding's criticism: an essentially physiological template can be too elaborate for lower levels and insufficiently complex for higher ones. This criticism is mediated through Hammond and Wilby. It challenges the adequacy of the cross-level template while leaving open whether particular relations or questions are useful. Their discussion of measurement limits is likewise a critical interpretation. [RGC-W005, concluding living-systems discussion and reflections]

### Ruscoe: a schema does not supply its own instruments

Ruscoe: a schema does not supply its own instruments

Gordon Ruscoe's response to Miller's editorial shares the aspiration to inquiry beyond artificial disciplinary boundaries but questions the proposed strategy. He distinguishes a conceptual system, an empirical theory and a research paradigm. A classificatory arrangement can contain useful concepts without itself supplying empirically testable statements and the instruments needed to examine them. [WME-W005, printed 11–12]

His operative objection is the chain from process to variable to indicator. The investigator needs reasons for selecting a variable, connecting it to the process and deciding that an indicator measures it. Those inferential steps require methodological justification beyond placing the study within a living-systems box. A formally similar label is insufficient to establish a valid cross-level measurement. [WME-W005, 12]

Ruscoe also distinguishes generating a fruitful empirical question from retrospectively fitting completed research into a schema. Both can be useful, but the second does not prove the first. His letter is a methodological challenge to the warrants for the research programme. [WME-W005, 11–12 and editorial note]

### Later applications and the status of their evidence

Later applications and the status of their evidence

Miller and Miller's Applications of Living Systems Theory (1992) reports that the 1978 book contained 173 cross-level hypotheses and discusses studies of overload, communication networks and conflicting commands. Some model applications are explicitly described as compatible with the framework rather than derived from it. Completed and proposed studies remain distinguishable. [RGC-W006]

The overload account reports measurements at several levels, from neural preparations to individuals, small groups and laboratory organizations. It proposes a response in which increasing input initially increases output, then exceeds capacity and can produce deterioration. The later account also stresses compatible units and dimensions for a formal cross-level comparison. [RGC-W006, basic-research section]

The conflicting-command game offers a more specific organizational example. Individuals or groups receive instructions from several nominal superiors, and the account reports slower deciding as commands differ. That result belongs to the reported experimental setting. The biased-network study

<!-- PDF page 46 -->

similarly concerns specified communication probabilities and reported predictions. [RGC-W006, cross-level tests]

The organizational application describes a three-year study of forty-one Army battalions with more than five thousand participants. It reports relationships between information-processing characteristics and effectiveness, including meaning, lag, volume, cost and distortion. The same account initially lists objective process data but later says only subjective data were collected in that study. [RGC-W006, Army and industrial-project sections]

The later proposed industrial study includes objective measures, computerized responses, voluntary location badges and expert-system analysis. These are plans for a study, not results. [RGC-W006]

The Swanson–Miller EOLSS chapter introduces a later eight-level, twenty-subsystem form. It distinguishes conceptual and concrete systems and retains limitations on measuring meaning. This differs from the earlier seven-level, nineteen-subsystem architecture. [RGC-W007]

Swanson's 2007 proceedings abstract for Living Systems Theory and Entity-Systems Theory raises questions about dispersed subsystems, conceptual systems and emergence. [RGC-W008, abstract]

<!-- PDF page 47 -->

## S22 Beer and viable systems: autonomy, coordination and contested purposes

S22   Beer and viable systems: autonomy, coordination and contested purposes

### Viability and organizational functions

Viability and organizational functions

Stafford Beer's viable system model concerns an organization's continuing existence in a changing environment. It locates activities among local units, coordination, resource allocation, audit, attention to future conditions, and the articulation of identity and policy.

In The Heart of Enterprise, Beer develops the viable system model. John Brocklesby, Stephen Cummings and John Davies's 1991 reconstruction draws on Heart, Brain of the Firm and Diagnosing the System. J. P. van Gigch's book review and Michael Jackson's critique offer distinct judgments. Beer's later methodological account and Raul Espejo's 2022 development extend the discussion. [W101; RGC-W009; RGC-W010; RGC-W011; RGC-W012; UX-W007]

The Italian Viable Systems Approach, whose authors acknowledge Beer, appears below. [SG-W014]

### Variety is relative to the distinctions and purpose being considered

Variety is relative to the distinctions and purpose being considered

The reconstruction begins with the problem of maintaining a separate existence while circumstances change, including circumstances not foreseen when an organization was designed. It distinguishes responding within established operating norms from reconsidering those norms. A procedure can correct deviations toward a target while leaving untouched the question of whether that target or procedure remains appropriate. Brocklesby and colleagues use this contrast to explain why viability is more demanding than repeating a previously successful routine. [RGC-W009, printed pp. 3–5]

Their account of variety concerns distinguishable states relevant to a system's purposes. A producer's relevant circumstances include customers, suppliers, regulations, and conditions bearing on what it is trying to do. Different operational activities encounter different local environments, which may overlap. The choice of system and purpose therefore enters the identification of what differences matter. [RGC-W009, pp. 5–7]

Ashby’s variety counts distinguishable possibilities within a specified set, as explained in S03. Brocklesby and colleagues use “absorbing local variety” to describe how local circumstances relate to an organization’s capacities for action. [W001; RGC-W009, pp. 5–7]

Brocklesby and colleagues describe two ways of changing the relation between demands and response capacity. Amplification increases what a system can bring to bear; attenuation reduces the variety with which it must contend. Their examples include improving a response capability and avoiding an exposure, rather than merely collecting more data. The usefulness of either depends on what the system seeks to accomplish. Avoiding a demand by abandoning the relevant purpose would describe a different accomplishment. [RGC-W009, pp. 6–7]

### The original Heart passage: ignorance is also a filter

The original Heart passage: ignorance is also a filter

The selected original passage of The Heart of Enterprise gives an unusually sharp qualification to the language of attenuation. Beer argues that the variety reaching an operation or management can be reduced through ignorance: the operation recognizes only some environmental features, while a manager recognizes only what the manager's existing model makes perceptible. Such reduction can produce an apparently manageable world without competent management. He explicitly distinguishes this from designing effective amplifiers and attenuators. The existence of filtering is therefore not evidence that the right distinctions have been preserved. [W101, pp. 96–97]

<!-- PDF page 48 -->

His first principle of organization calls for designing the relationships among managerial, operational, and environmental varieties with attention to damage to people and cost. The passage also criticizes the automation of an inherited information arrangement whose relevant design questions have not been addressed. A computerized filter can preserve an inadequate selection while losing the flexibility of the earlier manual system. A capacity to process more data does not decide what distinctions the organization must be able to act upon. [W101, pp. 97–98]

Beer then considers amplification of managerial influence through meetings, communications, staff, and the development of policies. Their appropriateness depends on the variety of the situation; a managerial style is not assigned a constant effectiveness independent of the circumstances. This selected passage describes design judgments and their possible costs. It also directs attention away from an immediate argument about what a manager wants to know and toward the design of regulation. [W101, pp. 98–99]

### System 1: put local response where local knowledge exists

System 1: put local response where local knowledge exists

In the 1991 reconstruction, System 1 consists of the operational activities through which the system in focus does what it exists to do. The system in focus is the entity and activity boundary selected for the analysis. For an automobile producer, different model-producing units can be System 1 activities; for a university considered through teaching and research, academic units can occupy that role. These are examples of identifying primary activities from a stated purpose, rather than deriving them from the appearance of an organization chart. [RGC-W009, pp. 10–11]

The operational units are expected to have local management and enough autonomy to deal with their own circumstances. Senior university officers, in the authors' example, cannot keep abreast of every academic field in the way specialists can through journals, conferences, and professional communities. Moving all the relevant decisions upward would move work away from the people who encounter and understand those distinctions. Their account predicts overloaded higher management, weak sensing of local conditions, and inadequate responses. It connects autonomy to the location of knowledge and action. [RGC-W009, pp. 11, 14–16]

“Local” need not mean geographically small. An academic field's environment can be international. Nor does the model's use of an autonomous unit imply a unit without dependence on other people or resources. The reconstruction's criterion concerns potential independent existence and management of its activities, within the chosen account. [RGC-W009, pp. 10–11]

The boundary can also change the classification. A university computer-support service may be a supporting activity when the whole university is the focus. If the focus is a support system whose purpose is to provide that service, computer support can become a primary operational activity, with the rest of the university now part of its environment. The authors use this example to warn against treating corporate boundaries and departmental names as the only possible analytical divisions. A change of focus must remain visible, because it changes what a label such as System 1 refers to. [RGC-W009, pp. 10–11]

### Systems 2, 3, and 3*: autonomy keeps coordination and accountability

Systems 2, 3, and 3*: autonomy keeps coordination and accountability

Autonomous operational units can interfere with one another. They may seek the same scarce resource, create incompatible standards, or withhold something whose shared use matters to the whole. The reconstruction gives System 2 the coordination function that reduces harmful interference or oscillation. This is not a second layer that performs every local task. It concerns relations among tasks whose individual pursuit can create trouble for one another. Scheduling, shared guidance, and the communication necessary for decentralized action are among the relevant activities. [RGC-W009, pp. 9, 12–13]

<!-- PDF page 49 -->

System 3 concerns internal cohesion and the present conduct of the organization. Resource bargaining connects what operational units undertake with what they receive and with the expectations under which they act. Allocation is one outcome of that bargain, rather than the whole relation. The reconstruction also gives this function a role in implementing policy and establishing criteria of accountability. Coordinating potentially conflicting activities and deciding how the organization uses its resources are consequently related but distinguishable responsibilities. [RGC-W009, p. 13]

The audit function, System 3*, examines operational performance rather than relying entirely on routine representations reaching management. The authors use “audit” more broadly than an occasional accounting review: it includes ways of questioning whether activities are being performed within the agreed guidelines. Their discussion includes both checking what has occurred and a continuing capacity for examination. [RGC-W009, pp. 13, 15]

In the reconstruction's critical case, System 3 tries to occupy the local management role, generating transmissions and interventions until it becomes overloaded and loses capacity for its own tasks. The proposed alternative retains coordination, resource relationships, and audit while allowing operational managers to address the circumstances for which they hold better knowledge. [RGC-W009, pp. 14–16]

Training, induction, and shared guidance are important parts of the alternative. People can respond without seeking a senior decision at every step when they understand the broad expectations. Yet those expectations should leave room for judgment in circumstances that cannot be exhaustively anticipated. A highly elaborate rule network providing a supposed answer to every possible local situation would defeat the use of local knowledge that the account seeks to preserve. These passages locate an enabling arrangement and the continuing competence needed to use it together. [RGC-W009, pp. 15–16]

The guidelines must also be open to challenge. An operational unit may learn that an established way of acting no longer suits its environment, and the communication with coordinating functions must allow proposed changes. The authors further retain an accessible direct connection between operational and higher management for exceptional situations. Being free from constant interference is not the same as being unable to obtain guidance. Their account includes the social possibility of making contact, not just the existence of a line on a diagram. [RGC-W009, p. 16]

### Systems 4 and 5: operating now while considering what should change

Systems 4 and 5: operating now while considering what should change

The reconstruction distinguishes System 3's present, internal concern from System 4's attention to the wider environment and future. Intelligence here can involve research, development, planning, and interpretations of emerging conditions. Its purpose is not simply to produce a larger information store. It must bring the implications of those conditions into a relation with the organization's actual capacity and conduct. [RGC-W009, p. 18]

The authors' automobile example gives this relationship an ordinary managerial form. Market research may favor producing six models, while current operations favor four because of the resources and reorganization required. Both positions bear on the undertaking, and neither alone determines the appropriate decision. A claim about future demand has to meet a claim about present productive capability. [RGC-W009, p. 18]

System 5 concerns identity and policy: what purposes hold the undertaking together and how competing interpretations are resolved. In the example, a policy about a broad range of family cars at a reasonable price admits disagreement over both range and price. Policy is therefore not a substitute for every operational decision, but neither is it a decorative statement unrelated to them. The reconstruction gives it a role in balancing the present and future concerns represented by Systems 3 and 4, and in providing the context for guidelines used elsewhere. [RGC-W009, pp. 18–19, 21]

<!-- PDF page 50 -->

The performance discussion makes a related distinction among actuality, capability, and potentiality. Actuality concerns what is achieved under existing resources and constraints; capability concerns what could be achieved with those resources and constraints; potentiality concerns possibilities through developing resources and removing constraints. These are different comparisons, rather than three names for a current output measure. The source proposes ratios among them. Their explanatory relevance is the distinction between doing better with what is already available and changing the conditions of what becomes possible. [RGC-W009, p. 17]

### A communication link must carry usable distinctions

A communication link must carry usable distinctions

In Brocklesby and colleagues' account, having each of the five functions present is insufficient if the relationships among them do not work. Channels must be established and maintained. Messages must arrive in a form that recipients can understand. They use transducer for the means by which information is carried across a boundary in usable form. The term does not make interpretation disappear; it identifies a function whose adequacy must be examined. [RGC-W009, p. 19]

Their computer-system example concerns departments whose specialists express different requirements in different technical languages. A message's transport does not show that the receiving group can interpret its significance. The authors make this issue explicit through a passage in which Beer distinguishes a translator's linguistic competence from grasp of the intended possible states. They acknowledge that perfect conveyance is an ideal rarely achieved in practice. Thus the reconstructed model retains both communication capacity and the understanding required at the boundary. [RGC-W009, p. 19]

### Recursion is a claim about organization at selected boundaries

Recursion is a claim about organization at selected boundaries

The model is recursive in the reconstruction's account: an operational unit can itself exhibit the functions needed for viability, and the system in focus can be an operational unit within a wider system. The five labels are therefore not five fixed departments at the top of a corporation. The local operational unit has its own management and relevant internal relationships. Repeating the logical organization is how the model describes relations among selected levels. [RGC-W009, pp. 10–11, 21–23]

The selection of levels remains an analytical act. The authors' automobile example permits different wider systems to be drawn, and they acknowledge interpretive choices in higher-level boundaries. The activity, environment, capacities, and relationships claimed for it still have to be identified. [RGC-W009, pp. 21– 24]

The reconstruction itself ends with a warning against the attraction of a tidy diagram. A model does not provide a complete picture of people and their interactions, and its appearance does not make participants committed to changing an organization. The authors offer it as a language and framework for examination, sometimes alongside other models. It also preserves the work of application: empirical understanding, judgment, and participation are not supplied by the diagram alone. [RGC-W009, p. 24]

### Van Gigch's review: an explanation still needs practical mastery

Van Gigch's review: an explanation still needs practical mastery

J. P. van Gigch's 1981 review of The Heart of Enterprise reconstructs the five functions and their variety relationships while raising objections about how the account can be put to work. He finds important insights in the book but considers the presentation difficult to master. His criticism is more precise than saying that the model has no relevance: an uninitiated reader may not acquire the knowledge and practice needed for application simply by reading the book. He also questions the presentation of rules as maxims, principles, theorems, axioms, and laws without the mathematical derivations he expected in that volume. [RGC-W011, pp. 128–129]

<!-- PDF page 51 -->

The review further distinguishes identifying obvious mismatches from calculating calibrated entropy exchanges in a real organization. Van Gigch describes practical measurement of the relevant entropy as extremely difficult, including attempts to compare mental effort across degrees of mechanization. The review leaves the reader with both an account of what the book illuminates and a concrete reason why conceptual clarity is insufficient for competent implementation. [RGC-W011, p. 129]

### Jackson's dispute: structural constraints or an interpretive instrument?

Jackson's dispute: structural constraints or an interpretive instrument?

Michael Jackson's 1992 research note rejects a simple reading in which an analyst finds an objective organization and rearranges it to fit an idealized chart. He then distinguishes two more serious interpretations. His preferred structuralist reading allows observers to select identity and purpose, while maintaining that the organization pursuing that purpose faces real structural constraints. On this view, the model seeks underlying relationships that explain operational difficulties; the analyst's task is more than facilitating whichever account participants already favor. [RGC-W010, pp. 561–562]

Jackson contrasts this with the interpretive use he attributes to Harnden and Espejo, where a model supports conversations among different perspectives about emergent organizational forms. The dispute becomes sharp when a cybernetic diagnosis conflicts with participants' beliefs. Jackson asks which should guide action and argues that the existence of cybernetic constraints cannot be settled merely by choosing a preferred conversation. [RGC-W010, pp. 563–564]

The note is relevant to gambits engineering because it makes the status of an organizational explanation consequential. A claim about a constraint, a proposal for collective interpretation, and a participant's agreement are different grounds for action. Jackson argues for one reading. [RGC-W010, pp. 561–564]

### Beer on modeling, identity and informational economy

Beer on modeling, identity and informational economy

The reproduction of Beer's account of the VSM's provenance and methodology distinguishes literary analogy from more precisely specified mappings. Beer argues that a model selects relationships and invariances, and that the context and boundaries of its application must be nominated. His account of internal regulation, attenuation, and amplification remains connected to that modeling program. The reproduction also lists applications, while acknowledging the absence of a systematic archive and reliance on records and recollection at hand. [RGC-W012, pp. 4–8, 16–17]

Within that account, Beer uses “intrinsic control” for a relation in which a common influence delimits environmental circumstances and evokes a response converging on an adaptive outcome. The described ordering need not be understood only as a rule imposed by a separately identified manager. This is his explanation through Sommerhoff and Ashby, whose positions are mediated through this particular passage. [RGC-W012, p. 5]

Identity is also explicitly difficult in the later text. Beer asks who “we” are when a manager asks what business an organization is in: shareholders, employees, managers, customers, and other interested people can offer different answers. His account recognizes an observer's imputation of purpose and reports disagreement about the purpose of a health system. The source therefore makes the choice of an organizational identity visible rather than treating it as an automatically shared fact. [RGC-W012, p. 10]

Appendix 1 gives a concrete connection between informational economy and lost explanatory power. Beer describes combining the outputs of three shifts into one total. The resulting representation handles fewer distinctions, but calculations within it cannot recover which shift produced what. He treats this as a choice to give up some modeling power for economy in recording and handling data, acceptable only when deliberate and remembered as a limitation. The appendix also distinguishes this known

<!-- PDF page 52 -->

simplification from aspects of a large system that the modeler has failed to recognize at all. This extract is reproduced from The World, the Flesh and the Metal. [RGC-W012, appendix 1, pp. 13–14]

### Espejo's later account: residual variety depends on local organization

Espejo's later account: residual variety depends on local organization

Raul Espejo's 2022 article develops an explicitly retrospective account of Cybersyn and his subsequent work. One relevant distinction concerns information systems and organizational transformation. He reports that some later clients possessed substantial computing resources and programming capability but sought help understanding their organization and developing meaningful performance indicators. The difficulty in his account was not merely a lack of software. It concerned how activities, purposes, and communications were understood and arranged. [UX-W007, “Real-time management and variety engineering”]

The article's central illustration concerns residual variety. Local self-organization and self-regulation handle much of what occurs before every matter reaches a separate managerial decision. The organization then faces a remaining range of circumstances, and management a further residual. Espejo explicitly calls the lines used to show these reductions impressionistic. They are not measured ratios demonstrating that a particular number of units of effort or information has been eliminated. His argument concerns the response demands that reach particular relationships after other activities have already occurred. [UX-W007, fig. 3 and accompanying discussion]

His account retains the means through which such an arrangement operates. Information filters, communication devices, skills, learning, collaboration, and wider cultural or regulatory conditions remain relevant. Reducing the variety reaching a manager can depend on activities taking place among people and within the surrounding institutions. His political and ethical preferences about how these relations should be formed remain part of his argument. [UX-W007, “Real-time management and variety engineering”]

Espejo also distinguishes two descriptions. A black-box description examines relations among an organization, its environment, and regulation under an assumed agreement about purpose. An operational description examines the interactions through which people construct the organization, its purposes, and coordinated action. He argues that the descriptions are complementary. The second description matters because the agreement presupposed in the first is itself something people have to produce and sustain. [UX-W007, figs. 4–5 and accompanying discussion]

The operational relationships include performance, cohesion, policy, inclusion, and organizational citizenship. Policy involves conversations between present operations and those attending to future circumstances. Inclusion concerns to whom policy makers are accountable; wider normative contexts also enter the account. Espejo contrasts authoritarian and more mutually respectful forms of cohesion and raises questions of power, ownership, and stakeholder participation. These are explicit concerns in this later formulation. [UX-W007, fig. 5 and accompanying numbered relationships]

His discussion of VIPLAN adds a methodological example. Naming the transformation, suppliers, actors, customers, owners, and interveners is a way of making the selected organizational description explicit. Later methodological development attends to communications and interactions through which problematic situations are addressed. The article traces this development through his own projects and collaborations. They supply the source's own account of how governance and meaning enter its organizational method. [UX-W007, “From the Viplan method to the Viplan methodology”]

<!-- PDF page 53 -->

### A distinct Italian programme: structure, interaction, and compatibility

A distinct Italian programme: structure, interaction, and compatibility

Sergio Barile, Jaqueline Pels, Francesco Polese, and Marialuisa Saviano introduce the Italian Viable Systems Approach as a methodological framework for business and social phenomena, including marketing. They acknowledge Beer as part of its background while drawing on a broader set of systems traditions. Their text explicitly describes the approach as a meta-level orientation, rather than a ready set of operative models for each problem. [SG-W014, printed pp. 62–63]

Their structure–system distinction separates a description of components and organized relations from the dynamics of their actual interaction. The account also identifies decision-making and operations, selective openness to resources, and dependence on other actors. The relevant context includes actors whose resources and influence bear on the undertaking's viability. Their broader propositions about all viable systems are premises of their approach. [SG-W014, pp. 63–65]

Consonance and resonance make one selected distinction particularly concrete. Consonance refers to potential compatibility among entities that might interact. Resonance concerns the harmonious interaction that actually develops. A favorable structural possibility is consequently distinguished from its realization in activity. The source relates this distinction to selecting relationships and engaging actors who control relevant resources. [SG-W014, pp. 65–66]

### Viability, identity and organizational purpose

Viability, identity and organizational purpose

The central VSM account is connected: local units respond using local knowledge; coordination addresses interference; cohesion and resource bargaining relate activities to the undertaking; audit supplies examination; intelligence brings changing wider conditions into view; policy addresses identity and direction. Channels and interpretation connect these functions.

These sources ask whose identity an organization preserves, how purposes are agreed, and what its measurements support. They locate decisions and responsibilities among participants with different information, capacities and authority.

<!-- PDF page 54 -->

## S23 Le Moigne: purposeful modeling and organized activity

S23   Le Moigne: purposeful modeling and organized activity

### A theory of modeling and its changing layers

A theory of modeling and its changing layers

Jean-Louis Le Moigne's La théorie du système général: Théorie de la modélisation develops a connected account of contextual purpose, representation, organized processes, memory, coordination and adaptation. The relevant material concerns both how a model can economize inquiry and how a modeled arrangement can change the demands on its participants.

The 2006 presentation of the 1994 edition includes earlier layers, later rereadings, a postface and appendices. [UX-W027]

The 2006 preface positions the enterprise as a theory of systemic modeling rather than a universal ontology declaring what every natural system really is. The model is constructed for a project in a context. Ends, means, representations and reasoning can recursively revise one another. Finalization therefore includes the ongoing formation of purposes, rather than merely execution toward an eternally fixed goal. Choosing those purposes remains an epistemic and ethical responsibility. [UX-W027, PDF 13–15, 35–47]

The book does not present this as a finished formal calculus. It acknowledges incomplete tools for organization and memory, borrows extensively and permits plural methods.
