## S55 Numerical fidelity and computational cost

S55   Numerical fidelity and computational cost

A numerical computation can use different amounts of arithmetic precision in different places. The accounts below explain how programmers and numerical analysts select those places, check the returned result and pay for correction or monitoring. Their tasks range from solving a specified linear system to accepting a measured change in an application’s output. The required answer and the means of judging it enter the procedure alongside the available arithmetic.

S35 develops conditioning, stability and preparation of numerical problems. Here the focus is the allocation of fidelity during computation: what work can become cheaper, what must remain accurate and what happens when the initial allocation proves insufficient.

### Buttari and colleagues: a cheap factorization with more accurate correction

Buttari and colleagues: a cheap factorization with more accurate correction

Buttari and colleagues divide the work of solving a dense linear system, Ax = b, between two arithmetic formats. They convert the matrix and right-hand side to single precision, factor the converted matrix and obtain an initial solution. They preserve the original double-precision matrix. Each subsequent correction begins by calculating the residual, b − Ax, using that original matrix in double precision. The existing single-precision factors are then reused to solve for a correction, which is added to the solution in double precision. The analogous procedure uses Cholesky factorization for a symmetric positive-definite system. [CG-W001, §1.1, Algorithms 2–3]

The procedure places the cubic-cost factorization in the faster arithmetic while retaining more accurate residual calculation and solution updates, whose cost per refinement step is quadratic. It also retains two matrix representations and conversions between them. Single precision therefore describes a particular part of the computation; it does not replace the accuracy required of the returned answer. The paper's error analysis makes the result conditional on a sufficiently well-conditioned matrix relative to the correction arithmetic and an adequately stable correction solver. Low-precision errors must still permit refinement to make progress. [CG-W001, §1.1 and Appendix A]

Their implementation comparisons show why the size and architecture matter. On the conventional processors tested, the reported gains reach approximately 1.8 for the nonsymmetric solver and 1.5 for the positive-definite solver when problems are sufficiently large. For small systems, even a few correction steps can outweigh the cheaper factorization. The Cell results use a different comparison: the mixed-precision solver's achieved throughput is compared with the processor's double-precision peak, giving  the reported factors of seven and eleven. The experiments provide implementation evidence for this division of arithmetic work; the graph labels and processor configurations specify what was compared. [CG-W001, §1.2, Table 2 and Figures 1–8]

### Carson and Higham: correction accuracy and convergence are different requirements

Carson and Higham: correction accuracy and convergence are different requirements

Carson and Higham make three arithmetic roles independently adjustable: factorization, storage of data and solution, and residual calculation. Their general analysis also distinguishes the effective accuracy with which a correction equation is solved. This fourth parameter is useful when a low-precision factorization supports a more accurate iterative correction. An algorithm can thus store its answer in single precision, factor in half precision and compute residuals in double precision. Their conditions distinguish the rate at which errors decrease from the accuracy eventually attainable. More accurate residuals can lower the final forward-error level without repairing a correction process that fails to converge. [CG-W002, Algorithm 1.1, §§2–4 and 7]

<!-- PDF page 121 -->

Their GMRES variant uses the low-precision factors as a preconditioner, rather than relying on their triangular solves alone to supply each correction. This can extend the class of systems for which the solution reaches working-precision accuracy. The procedure still needs the original matrix and accurate applications of the preconditioned operator. Half precision's narrow numerical range also requires attention to scaling; when the initial solve overflows, the authors describe starting refinement from zero instead. [CG-W002, §§6 and 8, Algorithm 8.1]

The experiments expose a limit that a count of outer refinement steps would miss. For one generated 100-by-100 system, three outer steps contain 91, 92 and 92 GMRES iterations. A different family, with one small singular value, reaches the required error level with seven GMRES iterations in total despite a very large condition number. Every inner iteration performs additional accurate work. The authors accordingly distinguish successful numerical correction from an economical implementation: enough inner iterations can erase the benefit of a cheaper factorization. These tests use MATLAB, including emulated half precision, to examine error and iteration behavior. The paper's potential speed advantage remains conditional on hardware and correction cost. [CG-W002, §§10–11, Figures 10.7 and 10.9]

### Precimonious: search against an explicit acceptance test

Precimonious: search against an explicit acceptance test

Rubio-González and colleagues turn precision allocation into a search over program variants. The programmer supplies a program, test inputs and an accuracy requirement. Precimonious identifies floating-point variables whose types can change and, where alternatives are supplied, calls that can use another mathematical-function implementation. It generates candidate programs, compiles and runs them, and retains changes only when the results pass the accuracy and exception checks and the program satisfies the performance requirement. Their modified delta-debugging procedure tests groups of changes and progressively refines them. It seeks a locally minimal retained set of higher-precision variables rather than exhaustively finding the best possible allocation. [CG-W003, §§2–3, Figures 3–4]

The acceptance test compares a candidate's output with the original program's output on the supplied inputs. This provides a practical engineering contract, but its reference is the original implementation rather than an independently established mathematical answer. The authors' additional summation example makes the distinction consequential: truncating an infinite series and accumulating roundoff introduce different errors. Arithmetic precision can also change the number of iterations before a program stops, so apparently changing only a variable type can change the amount of work actually performed. [CG-W003, §§3.4 and 4.3]

Their experiments connect precision choices to execution cost. In the arc-length program, the reported speedup reaches 41.7% at two selected error thresholds. Several other programs improve less, while three produce no accepted faster configuration at the tested thresholds. The conversion instructions introduced between formats can outweigh savings elsewhere. A more permissive accuracy threshold consequently need not lead this search to a faster program. The FFT case with the strictest tested threshold explores 663 configurations and takes 116 minutes and 51 seconds. At publication, the suggested changes also required manual mapping back into source code, although transformed intermediate code was generated automatically. [CG-W003, §4.2, Tables 1–3; §5]

The authors test the limits of their input selection directly. They tune the NAS benchmarks using Class A inputs and subsequently try Classes B and C. Several allocations that pass the original test fail these new cases; for the EP benchmark, failures remain even at the most relaxed tested threshold. Its EP performance figure also has a specific scope: the 33.2% headline concerns the Gaussian-deviate phase that was tuned, while the reported improvement for the whole program averages 14%. [CG-W003, §4.2, Table 4 and footnote 6]

<!-- PDF page 122 -->

### FPTuner: allocate precision under a conservative expression-wide bound

FPTuner: allocate precision under a conservative expression-wide bound

Chiang and colleagues require a precision allocation to meet an error target throughout a declared input domain. Their object is a real-valued expression with a fixed computational structure, not an arbitrary program. They model rounding at operations and conversions, use symbolic Taylor expansions to relate these errors to the expression's output, and obtain conservative bounds over the input intervals. The allocation is then an optimization problem: maximize a weighted count of lower-precision operations while satisfying the error constraint. [CG-W004, §§2–4]

The procedure includes a further check. Its allocation search initially uses first-order error terms. FPTaylor then checks the generated allocation with higher-order effects included. If the candidate violates the target, the procedure can add an allowance for those effects and repeat the search. The authors report that the candidates in their experiments passed this check immediately. Thus the fast search approximation and the conservative acceptance check perform different jobs. Bounds on conversion error are included, and conversion counts can also be constrained. Groups of operations can be assigned the same precision to support vectorization. [CG-W004, §§4.1–5, Figure 4]

Their measurements show why a rigorous accuracy constraint does not make the cost objective exact. The objective's weighted operator count is a guide to allocation, not a direct measurement of execution time or energy. On a Jetson TK1 board, the authors measure single/double-precision versions using current and voltage instrumentation. Four selected benchmarks save energy on average when moved from all-double to one mixed allocation, but other configurations consume more energy or take longer. In the jetEngine expression, mixing formats increases register pressure and causes constants to be spilled and reloaded. The executed instructions defeat an apparent saving visible in the arithmetic allocation alone. [CG-W004, §6.3, Table 5 and Figures 7–8]

A separate timing comparison replaces some software-implemented quadruple-precision work with hardware-supported double precision. Those results have a different baseline from the Jetson comparison, where both formats have hardware support. The all-double version is also insufficient for the stricter error contracts used in the quadruple/double study; its faster time cannot be treated as an accuracy-matched alternative. Tuning itself can take seconds or, in one reported case, twenty minutes, followed by the final verification. [CG-W004, §§6.1–6.3 and 7.1]

The scope of the conservative result remains explicit. FPTuner treats straight-line expressions over bounded input domains. The paper does not implement general treatment of branches and loops: rounding can change a branch decision, and bounding the resulting difference is a separate problem. The contribution is a developed allocation and checking procedure for its stated expression model, accompanied by measurements that reveal when the intended resource gain survives compilation. [CG-W004, §§7.2–7.4]

### Green: calibrate the effect on the output and restore accuracy when needed

Green: calibrate the effect on the output and restore accuracy when needed

Baek and Chilimbi's Green system supports two deliberate approximations: replace an expensive function with a supplied alternative, or stop a loop before its original end. The programmer supplies an output-quality measure, a target and calibration inputs. Calibration relates the approximation to both its output  effect and its performance and energy costs. Generated code then selects among function versions according to input ranges or determines when a loop can stop. In the adaptive loop policy, it also observes whether further iterations continue to improve the chosen quality measure. [CG-W005, §§2–3, Figures 1– 3]

The reference computation remains part of the operating arrangement. During sampled recalibration, Green records the quality that an early termination would have produced and then continues the precise

<!-- PDF page 123 -->

computation so that the difference can be assessed. It can increase the work retained, select a more accurate function version, or relax an approximation that is more accurate than the target requires. For a function input range where no available approximation meets the criterion, it uses the precise function. These comparisons and changes have a sampling cost. [CG-W005, §§2.2.3 and 3.2, Figures 3 and 5–7]

Local acceptance also has to survive combination. In the option-pricing benchmark, the locally selected exponential approximation and logarithm approximation do not together meet the application's target. Green changes the logarithm choice from one polynomial approximation to a more accurate one. The resulting combined version has less than 0.8% loss under the chosen output measure, with reported performance and energy improvements of 28.5% and 28%, respectively. The authors retain the application-level comparison rather than assuming that acceptable individual substitutions add up to an acceptable program. [CG-W005, §§3.4 and 4.4, Figures 8 and 23–24]

The search-engine experiment specifies a different output criterion. It counts queries whose ordered top results differ from the precise backend's results; it does not measure human judgments of relevance. Tests use a production index and query logs, with crawling and index updates disabled. One adaptive configuration improves throughput by 21% and reduces joules per query by 14%, while 0.27% of queries produce a different ordered result. Whole-system energy is measured from the main power cable. [CG-W005, §§4.1–4.3, Figures 10–12]

An intentionally inaccurate calibration model exposes the time required for restoration. The chosen target allows 2% differing queries, but the initial cutoff typically produces about 10%. After each 10,000 queries, Green runs the next 100 precisely and uses their comparison to increase the retained search work. In this experiment it reaches the target after 180,000 queries. More frequent monitoring could accelerate adaptation while consuming more resources. The paper's claims about statistical quality rest on calibration and observed target tracking; this experiment makes the delay visible rather than establishing a bound on every query. [CG-W005, §4.3, Figure 14]

### EnerJ: protect the part that must remain precise

EnerJ: protect the part that must remain precise

Sampson and colleagues distinguish permission to approximate from the requirement to preserve precise computation. EnerJ extends Java with types that mark data as approximate or precise. Approximate values can use less reliable storage or operations, and approximate objects can select a supplied alternative algorithm. Unannotated data remains precise. The type system prevents approximate information from flowing into precise state without an explicit endorsement by the programmer. [CG-W006, §§2.1–2.5]

That protection includes indirect routes. An approximate condition cannot silently determine a branch that changes precise state. Array indices and lengths remain precise, and the implementation does not approximate pointers. An endorsement permits a selected approximate value to cross this boundary. It does not repair or recompute the value; the programmer accepts responsibility for how the receiving computation uses it. A checksum, for example, can be calculated precisely over data whose earlier production was approximate. Precisely encoding or storing that data preserves the selected value rather than proving it was the right value. [CG-W006, §§2.2, 2.4, 2.6 and 5.1]

The paper states a noninterference property for a core language without endorsements: changing approximate values does not change its precise state. This is an isolation property. Approximate values themselves have no quantitative accuracy guarantee. The conference article develops the language rules, states the properties and describes the implemented checker. [CG-W006, §3]

Their resource study uses a simulated approximation-aware architecture. It combines reduced floating-point mantissas, less reliable operations and storage, and reduced memory refresh. The energy model  counts instruction execution and SRAM and DRAM storage; instruction fetch and decode retain their cost.

<!-- PDF page 124 -->

Its parameters combine earlier measurements with values explicitly identified as estimates. The model omits implementation and switching overheads, including voltage-scaling latency. The article reports potential CPU/memory energy savings ranging from 7% to 38%, not measurements from constructed approximate hardware. [CG-W006, §§4–5 and 6.1, Table 2 and Figure 4]

Application quality varies independently of that range. Means over twenty simulated runs show relatively small losses under mild approximation, while FFT and SOR lose substantial fidelity at stronger settings. The programmer also has work beyond adding declarations. For the barcode reader, the authors changed an out-of-bounds image-coordinate response to return a white pixel, then endorsed approximate coordinates where they became array indices. This adaptation made the computation more tolerant of errors; it was not performed automatically by the type system. EnerJ's developed contribution is the explicit protected boundary, with application-specific approximation and acceptance still supplied around it. [CG-W006, §§6.2–6.3, Figure 5]

The mandatory and optional task portions in S57 address another way of reducing computational work: stopping a refinement or choosing a shorter procedure while still delivering an acceptable result. That account concerns task execution and scheduling; the procedures here specify arithmetic roles, output comparisons and protected computation.

## S75 Algorithm selection, adaptive sorting and computing only what is needed

S75   Algorithm selection, adaptive sorting and computing only what is needed

### Choosing a method for an instance

Choosing a method for an instance

Lars Kotthoff's 2012 survey organizes algorithm selection around problem instances, descriptive features, a set of candidate algorithms and a performance measure. Its account of the earlier Rice framework makes the selection problem explicit: map information about an instance to a method expected to perform well on it. The desired result might be a short running time, a high-quality solution within a budget, or success on a difficult search problem. An algorithm's favorable average over one collection of instances need not make it the best choice for every member. [TD-W024]

The survey distinguishes choosing one algorithm before execution from scheduling a portfolio and from responding to observations during execution. A static selector might use instance features measured in advance. A schedule can allocate time among solvers, while an online approach obtains further information as work proceeds. These arrangements offer different ways to use uneven performance. They also require decisions about which features to compute, how expensive those computations may be, and when to use a default instead. [TD-W024]

Feature computation is itself work that can be budgeted. A predictor that needs an expensive search to describe an instance may consume the time that its choice was supposed to save. Kotthoff discusses selection and feature costs as part of assessing the system, along with the chosen algorithm's performance. The engineering question is consequently concrete: what can be learned economically about this instance, and which decision can still be changed by learning it? The histories of numerical preparation and precision in S35 and S55 concern other ways in which the representation and conduct of a computation affect its performance. [TD-W024]

### Different kinds of partial order

Different kinds of partial order

Vladimir Estivill-Castro and Derick Wood's 1992 survey shows why “nearly sorted” needs a specified meaning. Straight insertion sort maintains an ordered prefix and inserts each new item by moving larger predecessors aside. Each such shift removes one inversion: a pair whose earlier item is greater than its later item. If there are I inversions among n items, the work is O(n + I). A sequence with only O(n) inversions can therefore be sorted in linear time by this method. The relevant quantity is the number of inverted pairs, rather than simply how many items look displaced. [TD-W025]

Consider two explanatory inputs. The sequence [2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5, 8, 7] has four inversions and four adjacent descents. Straight insertion needs four shifts of larger predecessors. The sequence [5, 6, 7, 8, 1, 2, 3, 4] has only one adjacent descent, but sixteen inversions: every item in the first half exceeds every item in the second. It consists of two ascending runs, which a merge can combine with linear work. Generalizing the second construction to two equal sorted halves gives n²/4 inversions even though only two runs need merging. [TD-W025]

A linear scan can find adjacent descents and run boundaries. That does not make it a linear-time count of all inverted pairs. Different measures expose different opportunities: few inversions suit ordinary insertion, while a few long runs favor merging. The survey develops adaptive sorting through explicit measures of disorder and bounds relative to the number of inputs compatible with a given amount of disorder. It reports Mannila's formalization and examples of algorithms designed to meet such bounds. [TD-W025]

This analysis does not contradict the worst-case comparison bound for unrestricted sorting. If a comparison procedure must distinguish all n! orders of distinct keys, its decision tree needs enough

<!-- PDF page 126 -->

leaves to represent them, requiring Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. A restricted class can contain fewer possibilities, and an adaptive algorithm can do less work on favorable inputs while retaining a larger worst case elsewhere. Sortedness is itself recognizable in linear time by checking neighbors. The useful distinction is between the task's worst case and the work justified by the particular order already present. [TD-W025, TD-W026]

### Using the key representation

Using the key representation

MIT's 2011 linear-time sorting notes contrast comparison sorting with methods that inspect keys as data. Counting sort assumes integer keys in a range of size K. It allocates positions or buckets for those keys, scans the n records to count or distribute them, and visits the key range in order. The time is Θ(n + K); a record-carrying bucket implementation also uses Θ(n + K) space. If keys represent ages from zero through one hundred, K is small. If two keys are zero and a trillion, the same direct range allocation is unattractive despite the small number of records. [TD-W026]

Least-significant-digit radix sort instead represents a key by d digits in base b and performs a stable counting pass for each digit, from least to most significant. Stability preserves the order established by earlier passes among records sharing the present digit. For an explanatory example, sorting 21, 12, 11 by units gives 21, 11, 12, retaining the order of the two records ending in one; a stable tens pass then gives 11, 12, 21. The bound is Θ(d(n + b)). It becomes linear in n under suitable restrictions on d and b. A small key range, a bounded digit representation and a favorable probability distribution are different assumptions, each supporting different methods. [TD-W026]

### Making radix sorting practical

Making radix sorting practical

Peter McIlroy, Keith Bostic and M. Douglas McIlroy's 1993 engineering study treats string sorting as a problem of using the bytes already present in keys. A most-significant-byte distribution forms piles by the next byte and recursively sorts each unfinished pile. Strings sharing a prefix then advance together to the next position; a completed string need not continue through later characters. This avoids repeatedly rediscovering a long common prefix through whole-string comparisons. [TD-W027]

The bookkeeping matters. Clearing or scanning every possible byte pile can dominate when only a few piles are occupied, so the authors examine ways to track the occupied range or piles. Small piles can be finished by an insertion method rather than paying the full distribution overhead again. Their “American flag” method counts pile sizes, computes their destination ranges, and cycles misplaced string descriptors into the appropriate ranges in place. Once a descriptor is placed, the displaced descriptor supplies the next item to move. This yields an in-place distribution without requiring a separate full array of descriptors, although the permutation is not stable. [TD-W027]

Recursion order also affects storage: leaving the largest pile until last limits the stack needed for the remaining work. The article combines these details with tests on actual workloads and attention to the sorting interface. Its performance gains belong to those implementations and data. The enduring substance of the account is visible in the connected construction: use a key's next byte, group a shared prefix, avoid empty-pile work, move descriptors through counted ranges, and switch methods where a smaller routine is preferable. [TD-W027]

### Sampling and equal-key blocks

Sampling and equal-key blocks

Jon Bentley and M. Douglas McIlroy's 1993 account of a library sort began with inputs that defeated existing implementations. Organ-pipe patterns and arrays containing only zeros and ones exposed quadratic behavior. The replacement was developed for a general interface in which a caller supplies the comparison operation and records may be expensive to exchange. Comparisons, swaps and partition

<!-- PDF page 127 -->

bookkeeping therefore had different costs from those in an abstract count of unit-time operations. [TD-W028]

Pivot sampling varied with size: a middle element for small inputs, a median of three for larger ones, and a pseudomedian assembled from nine samples for still larger ones. The authors chose thresholds empirically rather than presenting a single sampling rule as costless at every size. Their partitioning also gathered equal keys so that, after rearrangement, the middle block contained items equal to the pivot. Only the less-than and greater-than blocks required recursive sorting. With an all-equal input, one partitioning scan could finish the problem. [TD-W028]

For an explanatory zero/one input, choosing zero as pivot collects the zeros into the equal block and leaves only the ones on the greater side. Sorting need not repeatedly partition the zeros as if they still had unknown relative ranks. The authors' split-end partitioning implements this treatment of equals while supporting the general library interface. The paper supplies an engineering account of robustness across troublesome inputs; it should not be conflated with later introspective sorting methods that add a worst-case fallback. [TD-W028]

### Choosing which runs to merge

Choosing which runs to merge

Natural mergesort discovers ordered runs, but it still must decide which adjacent runs to combine and in what order. A merge of runs of lengths a and b costs in proportion to a + b. Repeatedly merging a long run with each small arrival can scan its contents many times. A suitable merge tree limits how often an item travels through successive merges while preserving the adjacency needed for stable sorting. This is the problem addressed by J. Ian Munro and Sebastian Wild's 2018 peeksort and powersort algorithms. [TD-W029]

Peeksort finds the run around the middle of an interval and recursively organizes work around the resulting boundaries. Powersort processes runs from left to right and assigns a power to the boundary between neighboring runs. The power records the first binary subdivision depth that separates their normalized midpoints. It represents where the boundary belongs in a nearly balanced tree without requiring the entire run sequence in advance. When a new boundary has a shallower power than a pending one, the deeper work is merged first. A stack retains the unfinished adjacent pieces. [TD-W029]

For run lengths L₁ through Lᵣ totaling n, the authors use the entropy H = Σ(Lᵢ/n) log₂(n/Lᵢ). It reflects the distribution of run lengths: one long run and several tiny ones need not require the merge work of many equally sized runs. Their powersort analysis bounds total merge cost M by nH + 2n. The additive linear term makes the result nearly optimal in this cost model. The measured runtime also depends on the implementation of a merge, memory traffic and comparisons. [TD-W029]

Vincent Jugé's 2020 account of adaptive ShiversSort develops another economical policy. It uses levels derived from the integer parts of the base-two logarithms of run lengths and examines only the top three runs on its stack when deciding the next merge. Run-size comparisons determine whether an older pair should be combined before the newest run is allowed to remain pending. This small local view is used to control the larger merge structure. The paper separates the merge policy from preparation of short runs and from optimizations inside a merge. [TD-W030]

Number the pending runs from the stack's top, so R₁ is newest, and let each level be the floor of log₂ of its length. If either of the top two levels is at least the third, the policy merges R₂ with R₃. Otherwise, if the top level is at least the second, it merges R₁ with R₂; otherwise it admits another run. At the end it merges the remaining stack. For an explanatory stack with lengths 8, 4, 4 from bottom to top, the levels are 3, 2, 2. The two top runs merge to length eight, after which the two eights merge. The older eight is not scanned once for each arriving four. [TD-W030]

<!-- PDF page 128 -->

Jugé states an nH + O(n) merge-cost bound for the adaptive policy and compares it with earlier guarantees. A better coefficient in an entropy bound concerns accumulated merge work, not an identical percentage reduction in execution time on every machine or input. The account shows how a compact rule operating on a few stack entries can be the subject of a substantial global guarantee. It also preserves a distinction between the historically described TimSort merge policies and later implementations adopting powersort. [TD-W030]

### Adaptation during the work

Adaptation during the work

The sorting design notes shipped with CPython 3.14.0, released in October 2025, connect run discovery with the work of sorting itself. The implementation detects natural runs, normalizes descending runs, extends short runs with stable binary insertion, and uses powersort to organize their merges. Its treatment of equal-key subruns allows normalization while preserving stability. These are details of this frozen release, which incorporates developments after the original introduction of TimSort. [TD-W031]

For example, [3, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 0] begins with a descending stretch. Reversing its first three items produces [1, 2, 3], after which the scan can extend the ordered run across the following 3, 4, 5. Recognizing order and acting on it are interleaved. There need not be a separate, completed diagnosis of the whole input before sorting begins. If a run is too short for efficient merging, binary insertion brings it to the desired working length. [TD-W031]

During a merge, galloping responds to a sustained winning streak by one run. Exponential search followed by binary search finds a block that can be copied together rather than comparing each item against the other run's next item. The threshold adapts so that useful streaks encourage further galloping and unsuccessful attempts discourage it. The implementation therefore uses information at several scales: runs in the input, their lengths and merge positions, and temporary dominance during a particular merge. [TD-W031]

### A rank without a full order

A rank without a full order

Manuel Blum, Robert Floyd, Vaughan Pratt, Ronald Rivest and Robert Tarjan's 1973 selection paper proved that the item of a specified rank can be found with a worst-case linear number of comparisons. Their PICK construction sorts fixed-size columns, selects representatives, recursively finds a representative of controlled rank, and uses it to partition the original candidates. The representative is chosen so that a guaranteed fraction can be discarded. If the sought rank lies above the discarded lower part, its rank is adjusted within the remaining part; if below, the upper part becomes irrelevant. [TD-W032]

The original construction develops its guarantee through column sizes and representative positions, including a basic analysis with columns of twenty-one. Its result is about finding a rank, not arranging all items in order or necessarily supplying the fastest practical routine for a tiny requested subset. Once a cutoff rank is known, the relevant side of a partition can be retained without sorting the other side. Ordering the retained items is a further task whose size may be much smaller than n. [TD-W032]

### Keeping a small extreme subset

Keeping a small extreme subset

CPython 3.14's heapq implementation gives a practical streaming alternative for a small requested k. To retain the largest k items, a min-heap of k candidates exposes the smallest retained item at its root. Each new item is compared with that boundary. If it cannot enter the retained set, it is discarded; if it can, it replaces the root and the heap is repaired. After the scan, only k candidates remain. The worst-case work is O(n log k), with O(k) retained storage, followed by O(k log k) if the retained set is sorted for presentation. For a fixed ten candidates, the scan is linear in n. [TD-W031]

<!-- PDF page 129 -->

The release's nlargest and nsmallest functions include useful boundary cases: a request for one uses an extremum operation, and a request at least as large as a known input size can use a full sort. The functions return their retained results in order. Their heap entries also carry an order field, preserving a defined treatment of equal keys. A custom routine that only needs the set can leave its heap unordered; it should not assume that a library function returning ordered results omitted the final sort. [TD-W031]

Local top-k results also admit a simple merge. Under a consistent total ordering, an item excluded from a partition's top k already has at least k items ahead of it in that partition, so it cannot enter the global top k. The global answer is therefore contained in the union of the local answers; another top-k selection over that union suffices. Equal keys require a shared tie rule if exact membership matters. This is a direct consequence of the retained-set rule, illustrated by disjoint candidate partitions, rather than a separate empirical performance claim. Scanning a filesystem can involve additional work to compute directory totals or identify shared files; selecting the largest measured candidates is the part explained by this algorithm. [TD-W031]

## S37 Morphology, embodiment and physical computation

S37   Morphology, embodiment and physical computation

### The body changes the control problem

The body changes the control problem

The sources in this section examine how a body's shape, materials and dynamics affect behavior, perception and control. They disagree about when such contributions should be called computation.

### Hoffmann and Müller: a design tradeoff, not an automatic transfer

Hoffmann and Müller: a design tradeoff, not an automatic transfer

Hoffmann and Müller's 2014 paper considers a design space extending from relatively simple bodies with model-based control to complex, compliant bodies with distributed or model-free schemes. Conventional rigid-robot engineering often simplifies the body dynamics that a controller must manage. A soft or highly compliant body supplies richer dynamics that can help produce useful behavior, but can also be difficult to model faithfully. The contribution of morphology therefore cannot be evaluated solely by counting fewer instructions in an otherwise unchanged controller. [W007, relevant definitions and body–control discussion]

The paper distinguishes exploiting physical properties to simplify control from performing a computation. It also asks whether a model is required and how difficult that model is to construct. A body well suited to a task can make the task easier, while its high dimensionality and nonlinearity make accurate modeling harder. The proposed tradeoff includes the design and knowledge problem.

Their criticism of proposed morphological-computation measures is particularly pertinent. A measure that rewards little influence by the agent's actions can favor a system that is difficult to control. A measure that rewards strong natural dynamics need not favor the body that makes the intended task easy. The authors distinguish these properties from engineering usefulness. Physical dynamics can resist a controller as well as assist it, and the desired balance depends on the task and environment. [W007]

### Müller and Hoffmann: control, perception and computation are distinct contributions

Müller and Hoffmann: control, perception and computation are distinct contributions

The 2017 article examines characteristic cases including passive walking, self-stabilization and gecko adhesion, task-shaped visual sensing and physical reservoir computing. Its classification separates morphology that facilitates control, morphology that facilitates perception and morphology that performs computation under a defensible account of physical computation. A useful foot or leg does not necessarily calculate an output merely because its properties reduce a controller's difficulty. [W008, characteristic cases and conceptual analysis]

In a passive walker, the movement can result from the physical dynamics without an abstract computational level. In a sensing arrangement, geometry or the distribution of receptors can make task-relevant distinctions available before later processing. These mechanisms deserve explanation in their  own terms. Calling them all offloaded computation can obscure what the arrangement actually does and what sensing or action remains.

Reservoir examples offer a more specific computational use of rich dynamics. Inputs perturb a physical system, and a trained readout extracts an output useful for a task. The article discusses a tensegrity body used to classify terrain, as well as arrangements with feedback and a readout producing a periodic command pattern. The trained readout, input coupling and interpretation of the output remain parts of these examples. [W008, physical-reservoir discussion]

<!-- PDF page 131 -->

### Miłkowski: when physical assistance counts as computation

Miłkowski: when physical assistance counts as computation

Miłkowski's abstract and opening passages argue that physical implementation matters to computation generally, and that morphology facilitating control need not itself constitute computation. A special label should not suggest that ordinary physical computing is independent of its material substrate. This challenges the language of outsourcing computation to a body. [W054, abstract and opening]

### Liu and colleagues: behavior generation and morphology-based intelligence

Liu and colleagues: behavior generation and morphology-based intelligence

The opening sections of Liu, Guo, Sun and Zhang's 2023 review place body, brain and environment in interaction. They organize a broader research area around behavior generation through morphology, learning-based morphology control and learning-based morphology optimization. The early sections are especially useful because they distinguish resembling an organism from actually exploiting a body's dynamics in control. A biomimetic shape can enable a new capability while still requiring a complex controller. [W011, printed pp. 1132–1137, §§1–2.2.2]

Their account of morphology uses shape, material and dynamic properties to affect behavior. The examples include passive walking and physical interaction that produces movement, with an emphasis on implicit physical processes rather than merely wearable or implanted digital devices. The review's vocabulary is broad: it often calls this contribution morphological computation. That choice is reported as the review's usage, alongside the stricter distinctions in the preceding papers.

The review also keeps learning and morphology in a two-way relation. Behavior can gather samples that support learning; learning can alter control; control can alter morphology; and optimization can change the designed body. These are different routes, not a single completed method. The wider device literature is mediated through the review. [W011, conclusion, printed pp. 1148–1149]

### Chen and colleagues: controllability depends on the arrangement

Chen and colleagues: controllability depends on the arrangement

Chen, Yu, Zhang and Su analyze vibration controllability in an underactuated flexible manipulator. Their example separates two questions. First they examine state controllability of the corresponding rigid system under different actuator placements, disregarding elastic deformation. Then they investigate structural vibration controllability of the flexible system. The operative variables include both joint configuration and where actuation is supplied. [W009, model, analysis and conclusion, printed pp. 391– 398]

Their conclusion makes controllability conditional on configuration, placement and the vibration-controllability matrix. It also uses a minimum singular value and a modal-reachability indicator to  distinguish configurations and relative difficulty. Thus fewer actuators or a flexible link do not by themselves determine whether a particular motion can be controlled effectively. The arrangement matters within the approximated model.

The paper's simulation supports comparisons within its planar manipulator example and associated generalization. The informative contribution is the explicit dependence of control capability on how physical degrees of freedom and inputs are connected. [W009]

### Montúfar, Ghazi-Zahedi and Ay: capacity for embodied behavior

Montúfar, Ghazi-Zahedi and Ay: capacity for embodied behavior

A Theory of Cheap Control in Embodied Systems provides a more formal meaning of cheap control than a general appeal to simplicity. Its main finite, reactive sensorimotor-loop model has fixed body and world channels. A policy maps sensor states to action distributions; the induced behavior also depends on the embodiment. Distinct policies can consequently be equivalent at the level of behavior. A controller need

<!-- PDF page 132 -->

not represent every possible policy distinction when those distinctions have no effect on the specified embodied behavior. [UX-W041, methods, lemma 1 and main theorem]

The authors exploit this reduction to give a sufficient approximation result for a model class of conditional restricted Boltzmann machines. The main theorem bounds a sufficient number of hidden units using the relevant sensory support and the dimension of embodied behavior. It establishes representational capacity to approximate the specified behavior, rather than a universally exact minimum controller size. The fixed channels, finite variables and reactive policy setting are part of the result.

The experimental treatment shows why estimating the relevant support is itself a substantive task. The authors sample a target behavior, estimate frequencies and prune the data before estimating support and a behavior dimension. They acknowledge that support estimation is a research problem in its own right and state that their pruning choice preceded the reported experimental outcomes. The controller-capacity calculation therefore relies on empirical estimates and a declared treatment of sampling noise.  [UX-W041, experimental support estimation and discussion]

The result supplies an explanation of how an embodiment can restrict the behavior space a controller must cover. Representational capacity does not establish how quickly a learning algorithm can find the corresponding policy. [UX-W041]

### Langer and Ay, 2021: a controller measure need not measure behavioral importance

Langer and Ay, 2021: a controller measure need not measure behavioral importance

In their 2021 study, Langer and Ay use simple simulated agents moving on a racetrack without touching its walls. Changing sensor length changes the relation between the body and environment. They optimize policies and analyze information flows among environment, sensors, controller and actions. This provides a controlled setting for asking how the complexity of a task is distributed across interacting parts. [UX-W022, abstract, §1.1 and §4 discussion]

Their discussion points out that the integrated-information quantity in a controller can be high even when that quantity has no behavioral relevance. Information flowing into and out of the controller must also be considered. An internal measure cannot, by itself, establish what the controller contributes to the task. The optimization can converge to different local optima depending on its starting distribution, yielding more than one reasonably successful strategy.

The discussion separates directly optimizing a policy from learning an adequate world model. A result about a prepared policy does not settle how the agent would acquire the knowledge needed to behave that way. This limitation motivates the later study. [UX-W022]

### Langer and Ay, 2024: learning can temporarily require more controller complexity

Langer and Ay, 2024: learning can temporarily require more controller complexity

The later paper makes the acquisition problem explicit. Again using simulated racetrack agents and information-theoretic measures, it adapts an em-algorithm that alternates improvement of goal-directed behavior with updating an internal world model. It compares agents whose world model is supplied with agents that must learn one, and includes split-controller arrangements that cannot integrate information in the same way. [UX-W015, selected v3 introduction, learning results and conclusion]

In the reported internal-world-model agents, successful learning is associated with initially higher controller complexity, followed by a decrease as useful body–environment interaction increases. Agents supplied with an ideal world model do not face the same prediction-learning demand. The comparison locates a possible earlier burden behind an apparently simple eventual controller.

The split internal-world-model agents predict the next sensory state less well and, on average, perform only marginally better than random movement, with relatively few successful agents. The authors take

<!-- PDF page 133 -->

this as support for the importance of integrated controller processing during world-model learning. They also recognize alternative explanations associated with the simplicity of the task, including the possibility that a single wall-avoidance problem demands little once an appropriate policy is available. [UX-W015, selected PDF pp. 14–18]

The paper supplies evidence about this sensorimotor loop, prediction task and learning scheme. [UX-W015; UX-W022]

### Wang and colleagues: responsiveness is not sufficient for their physical-computing definition

Wang and colleagues: responsiveness is not sufficient for their physical-computing definition

The selected opening of Wang, Zhou, Kahak and Li's 2026 Perspective defines a physical-computing kernel in which encoded inputs evolve through physical interactions into decoded outputs, with the possibility of programming the input–output evolution. It distinguishes analog and algorithmic forms and names analog oscillators, physical reservoirs and physical algorithmic computing as strategies for soft robots. The paper explicitly treats its framework as a proposed definition rather than universal agreement. [W098, published PDF pp. 1–2]

A responsive material can change shape or properties under heat, light, magnetic fields or other stimuli. Such a response can help adaptation or simplify operation while failing to satisfy the paper's computing definition. The distinction gives a concrete test of terminology: material responsiveness alone does not establish encoding, decoding and programmability. [W098]

### Xie and colleagues: count persistence as well as task achievement

Xie and colleagues: count persistence as well as task achievement

The energy-accounting discussion in Xie and colleagues' article argues that task scores alone can conceal important embodied costs. Their reserve-based formulation tracks an internal energy stock, expenditure during a time step and energy intake. It treats remaining above an admissible energy boundary as a persistence condition. Energy is the accounted physical quantity; viability is a condition assessed through that account, rather than a synonym for energy. [W099, selected Energy as a Common Currency section]

The source points to search, movement, docking, processing, conversion and storage as possible demands associated with obtaining energy. Maintenance and persistence costs can also distinguish agents that achieve the same immediate task. Environment structure can change intake or dissipation. The proposal is consequently a call for explicit comparable accounting.

In their illustrations and discussion of open challenges, the authors expressly avoid claiming one universal energetic model for organisms and robots. [W099]

### Co-design of morphology and control

Co-design of morphology and control

Rosendo, von Atzigen and Iida built two-module robots and tested how closely they could move toward a target. Their joint search varied the orientation and offset of the modules along with the amplitude and angular offsets of their motion. In a second set of trials, they froze the body design at several points in the search and used the remaining time to tune only the controller. Controller tuning improved several of the poorer body designs. For the same design time, continuing to search both body and controller produced the higher best scores later in the trials. [W034, figs. 2–5]

### Mechanical assistance, perception and control

Mechanical assistance, perception and control

These sources provide detailed accounts of mechanical assistance, task-shaped perception, physical computation, controller-capacity bounds, learning and physical accounting.

How a surface flaw enters the fracture question

A. A. Griffith introduces his 1921 paper through a question about filing, grinding and polishing machine parts subjected to repeated loads. Properties of a particular processed material

Chen, Zhang and Ritchie tested a silicon carbide ceramic whose grain boundaries were initially glassy. In the as-processed material, measured fracture toughness was 6.2 MPa√m at 25 °C and 4.3 MPa√m at 1300 °C. After annealing for 85 hours at 1300 °C, the corresponding values were 7.2 and 5.2 MPa√m. Microscopy showed that most grain-boundary films had crystallized. In the authors’ account of fatigue, cracks extend between grains while intact grains bridging the crack behind its tip oppose its advance. ## S46 General physical principles and cross-domain proposals

S46   General physical principles and cross-domain proposals

### Physical and explanatory quantities

Physical and explanatory quantities

The sources propose physical accounts and connections across physical, biological and cognitive domains. Physical free energy, variational free energy, entropy production, assembly index and reduced descriptive dimension concern different objects and operations.

### Prigogine: thermodynamic openness and internal production

Prigogine: thermodynamic openness and internal production

Prigogine's Nobel lecture connects thermodynamics, kinetics, spatial and temporal structure, fluctuations and microscopic irreversibility. Its physical Helmholtz free energy is F = E − TS, using energy, temperature and entropy. This quantity belongs to the thermodynamic account; it is not introduced as a generic cost function for organizations or as the variational quantity in a later cognitive theory. [SG-W045, lecture opening, equation 1.1]

The entropy balance distinguishes exchange with the environment from nonnegative internal production. An open system can maintain or increase internal organization while exchanging matter and energy. That does not suspend the entropy balance over an appropriate boundary. A visually ordered structure is not enough to determine the whole balance, and an internal decrease cannot be treated as a global disappearance of entropy.

The expression of production through fluxes and forces uses local-equilibrium assumptions. The minimum-entropy-production result requires narrower conditions, including a near-equilibrium linear regime with appropriate constant coefficients. The lecture does not justify extending that result to every open steady state or every self-organizing process. These distinctions are central to what the physical source can contribute. [SG-W045, opening thermodynamic development]

### Structure can appear while entropy production increases

Structure can appear while entropy production increases

The Bénard-convection discussion provides an explicit countercondition to the idea that self-organization always minimizes production. Beyond a threshold, the system develops macroscopic flow structure while entropy production increases. The order of the pattern and the direction of the production change therefore answer different questions. [SG-W045, convection example, PDF p. 5]

Near equilibrium, thermodynamic stability arguments can use a restricted relation between fluctuations and restoring behavior. Farther away, kinetics and the sign of excess-production terms become important. An autocatalytic reaction can supply a necessary feature for instability in the setup being discussed without being sufficient for it. Naming positive feedback does not establish that a transition occurs or that its result is beneficial. [SG-W045, PDF pp. 6–9]

The relevant lesson is source-specific: the operating regime and reaction mechanism determine which result applies.

### The Brusselator retains maintained reservoirs and reaction conditions

The Brusselator retains maintained reservoirs and reaction conditions

Prigogine's chemical-clock model makes its supporting arrangement explicit. In the stated simplified reaction scheme, external species are held constant and rate constants are normalized. The homogeneous stationary concentrations are X = A and Y = B/A. Under the model's conditions, the threshold B > 1 + A² marks instability of that branch and the emergence of oscillatory behavior. [SG-W045, selected connected chemical-instability development]

<!-- PDF page 136 -->

These equations do not describe an isolated chemical device sustaining itself without resources. Maintaining the external species is part of the model. Adding diffusion introduces possibilities of spatial pattern, with system size, shape and boundary conditions affecting what occurs. A repeating chemical pattern can be generated through the arrangement and kinetics without a central agent specifying every oscillation, while its material and energy provision remain.

The lecture also distinguishes behavior along a branch from selection among branches near a bifurcation. Fluctuations and history can matter to which continuation occurs. Its discussion of relative fluctuations retains the conditions behind large-number approximations; nonlinear reaction behavior and critical correlations need not follow the simplest independent-particle picture. [SG-W045, PDF pp. 10–15]

### Irreversibility is an argument with restrictions and open questions

Irreversibility is an argument with restrictions and open questions

The later lecture examines the relation between reversible microscopic descriptions and irreversible macroscopic behavior. Prigogine discusses alternatives involving representation and coarse-graining, then develops his own operator-based approach. The proposed transformation is conditional on properties of the dynamics and is not claimed to be possible for every periodic motion. [SG-W045, PDF pp. 16–21]

One apparent printed sign error in equation 7.8 conflicts with the nonnegative quantity defined earlier. The conclusion retains open questions and a proposal for relating levels of temporality. [SG-W045]

### Bruers, Maes and Netočný: the variable and reversal symmetry matter

Bruers, Maes and Netočný: the variable and reversal symmetry matter

The selected 2007 preprint studies entropy-production principles in linear electrical circuits through Langevin descriptions and dynamical fluctuation theory. It relates minimum and maximum principles to the close-to-equilibrium structure of fluctuations, including the parity of the relevant observable under time reversal. The choice between a current-like odd variable and an even variable is not an interchangeable labeling choice. [W079, selected setup and §§2.2–3.3]

The discussion explains a known counterexample and qualifications concerning unequal temperatures. Its conclusion questions exact extension beyond the linear regime and argues that dynamics, not thermodynamics alone, must justify further generalizations. These are results and interpretations within the selected circuit analysis. [W079, selected conclusion]

### Bejan and Lorente: flow access is their proposed general principle

Bejan and Lorente: flow access is their proposed general principle

Bejan and Lorente's selected constructal account proposes that finite flow systems persisting over time evolve configurations offering greater access to their currents. It treats branching flow arrangements across animate, inanimate and engineered settings as instances of a design phenomenon. The authors distinguish the proposal from a fixed final optimum or an inevitable end configuration. [W082, selected §§1–4]

Their engine-and-brake discussion also resists reducing every case to maximizing or minimizing one entropy-production quantity. Flow can involve useful delivery and dissipation in different parts of an arrangement. Their proposed generality therefore differs from the claim that nature always chooses the least resistance.

Bejan and Lorente extend their proposed law through scaling arguments. [W082, selected passages and conclusion]

### Friston: variational free energy concerns a model of observations

Friston: variational free energy concerns a model of observations

The opening and Box 1 of Friston's 2010 review present variational free energy in relation to a generative model and an approximate density over hidden causes. The formulation provides a tractable bound related to the surprise of observations, with perception and action interpreted through changes affecting that bound. Its energy and entropy terms are defined in that probabilistic construction. They are not simply the E and TS of the thermodynamic equation above. [W052, opening and Box 1]

Biehl and colleagues, and the response: a scoped mathematical dispute

Assembly theory: a construction measure with specified building blocks

Sharma and colleagues define an assembly space through elementary building blocks and permitted recursive joining operations. Previously assembled motifs remain available for reuse. Wilson and Flack: a coarser description can have a specific explanatory role

Wilson's renormalization-group lecture examines rescaling, fixed points and universality near critical conditions.
