## S28 Development, plasticity and constructed environments

S28   Development, plasticity and constructed environments

### Arrangements have developmental and evolutionary histories

Arrangements have developmental and evolutionary histories

These selected sources explain how stable responses, variable responses and environmental modifications arise or persist. Development within an individual, evolutionary change across generations and immediate ecological effects remain different processes.

### Waddington: buffered development is conditional

Waddington: buffered development is conditional

Waddington's 1942 article proposes canalization: a developmental reaction can produce a fairly definite outcome despite minor variation in the conditions along its course. The account includes tissue differentiation and the comparative constancy of wild-type outcomes. Such buffering is not absolute. Large abnormalities, late disturbances and pathological conditions can defeat it. [W032, 563–564]

He distinguishes an environmental influence that selects a developmental path from an influence participating in the processes that maintain it. These are conceptual alternatives rather than a rigid description of every real organ. Depending on how the alternatives are specified, the same influence can appear as a switch or as a modification within a path. The organism's developmental organization is part of the explanation of a response to the environment. [W032, 564]

The ostrich-callosity illustration supports a proposed evolutionary argument. If an environmental stimulus initially elicits a useful response, selection can favor the genetically influenced capacity to respond appropriately. If a relatively definite result is advantageous across variation in stimulus, canalization can develop. A different trigger, including a genetic one, can later activate the path. This is not inheritance of an acquired bodily change by assumption; it is a proposed sequence involving selection on developmental responsiveness. [W032, 563–565]

Timing and prior capability remain necessary. A replacement trigger needs to act before the environmental stimulus has already done the work for it. The developmental path must also be available and able to produce the response. Waddington's “normal” or “optimum” outcome belongs to this historical selection argument. [W032, 565]

### Niche construction can leave a usable environmental legacy

Niche construction can leave a usable environmental legacy

Odling-Smee and colleagues' selected practical guide distinguishes alteration of the environment from subsequent evolution in response to the altered conditions. Nests, burrows, webs, decomposition and changes to nutrient or other material flows can modify what later organisms encounter. Ecological inheritance names a legacy that persists and affects descendants' conditions, rather than genetic transmission alone. [TA-W020, PDF 3–8]

The distinction makes persistence and boundaries important. A constructed feature can decay, be counteracted or affect other organisms as well as the constructor. It can alter population dynamics without causing the evolutionary response attributed to it. Conversely, a lasting environmental change can modify selection after the original constructor has gone. The passages describe resource types, signatures and durability as matters to investigate. [TA-W020, PDF 3–8, 13]

The authors advocate recognizing niche construction as an evolutionary process in its own right. That is their theoretical position, not a settled conclusion established by the mere existence of environmental modification. Construction can also reduce fitness or produce effects negligible for the evolutionary question. A changed environment is not necessarily a better one for every participant. [TA-W020]

<!-- PDF page 141 -->

### Outsourcing memory: a specified trade-off model

Outsourcing memory: a specified trade-off model

Lee, Flack and Krakauer's selected revised model balances noisy present observations against memory that can become outdated. Their environment has a specified binary structure and persistence time. Longer memory can improve an estimate during a stable period while making adjustment after a switch slower. A useful memory duration consequently depends on the modeled environment and sensing conditions. [TA-W019, revised v2, model and results 1–2]

In the slow-environment regime examined, the authors derive a sublinear relation between optimal memory duration and environmental persistence under stated approximations. The result concerns their model and objective. Their separate metabolic estimate adds assumptions relating neural tissue, memory burden, size and lifespan. It is a model-based estimate. [TA-W019, results 2–3]

Active stabilization adds another option. Making the environment more persistent can reduce the new information required for adaptation. Their examples include persistent trails, caches, writing and maps. The relevant mechanism is that a maintained external regularity changes what an agent must continually estimate or encode internally. The construction and maintenance of that regularity remain activities. [TA-W019, result 4]

The model also exposes a distribution problem. Stabilizers pay for changing conditions, while other agents can enjoy the more predictable environment. Free riders can therefore exploit the benefit. The authors examine conditions involving monopolization and combine assumed costs of memory complexity, stabilization and sensing precision with adaptation error. The relative weights matter: changing them changes which strategy is favored. [TA-W019, result 4, equations 15–18]

Their local adaptive argument uses perturbative and convexity approximations. The discussion connects the model to institutions and social regularities as hypotheses about outsourced memory. [TA-W019]

### The niche-construction dispute is about implications

The niche-construction dispute is about implications

Scott-Phillips and colleagues' selected critical appraisal is an adversarial collaboration between an advocate and skeptics. The authors agree that organisms modify environments and that those effects can be consequential. They disagree about whether this requires a fundamental reformulation of evolutionary theory, how to define an evolutionary process and what explanatory role construction should receive. It is not a dispute over whether burrows or altered selection environments exist. [TA-W021, introduction and paired accounts]

Their dairy-farming example makes the distinction concrete. The standard account treats the changed nutritional environment as a source of selection on variation in lactose persistence. The niche-construction account emphasizes how the cultural practice generates and coevolves with that selective  setting. The paired explanations and summary identify differences in emphasis and causal framing. [TA-W021, case study and summary table]

For gambits engineering, the informative point is the source's distinction between a demonstrated environmental feedback and a stronger claim about the reconstruction of theory. An arrangement's practical consequences can be examined while the wider theoretical interpretation remains contested.

### Michod: group performance can constrain its members

Michod: group performance can constrain its members

Michod's selected 2003 account asks how a group becomes a new evolutionary individual with heritable variation in fitness at the group level. Cooperation can benefit the group while imposing costs on participating cells. That creates potential conflict between levels. A conflict mediator changes the

<!-- PDF page 142 -->

opportunity for selection within or between groups, rather than merely announcing that the cells have a common interest. [TA-W023, PDF 1–2]

The simple model uses cooperating and defecting alleles and a life cycle from propagule to adult group and further propagules. Group fitness depends on adult size and functionality; cell replication can increase one while impairing the other. These assumptions make the level of the measure explicit. A faster-replicating cell and a more effective multicellular group need not be the same success. [TA-W023, PDF 2]

Propagule size, reproductive specialization, mutation processes and policing provide different possible mediators. A small propagule can reduce within-group conflict but also directly reduce adult group size under the model's conditions. Germ–soma specialization constrains reproductive opportunity for many cells while supporting the larger organism's functioning. Policing can require cooperating cells to spend time and energy monitoring defection. Conflict control is an activity or developmental constraint, not an automatically costless outcome of membership. [TA-W023, PDF 5]

Michod also notes that a mediator can restrict later evolvability, illustrated by a nonreplicative soma in Volvox. Greater current individuality is therefore not a guarantee of unlimited future potential. Cooperation and conflict in multicellularity also frame the abstract of Michod and Roze’s earlier 2001 article. [TA-W023, PDF 2, 5; TA-W022]

### Costs of responsiveness require a careful comparison

Costs of responsiveness require a careful comparison

Van Buskirk and Steiner distinguish selection on the phenotype expressed in an environment from costs associated with the capacity for a plastic or canalized response. The mechanisms making a range of responses possible can have consequences even when a particular organism does not express the whole range. Plasticity and canalization can each be targets of cost comparisons; neither is presumed to be the cost-free baseline. [TA-W037, abstract and results/discussion]

Their meta-analysis reports twenty-seven studies and usually mild measured costs, with no simple general predominance of plasticity over canalization costs. Weak detected differences do not establish zero absolute costs. Shared costs, statistical detection and environmental stress remain relevant explanations in the account. [TA-W037]

The critical discussion in Auld, Agrawal and Relyea's article identifies another problem: correlation between trait values and plasticity can make estimated costs imprecise or biased. Bias can itself be environment-specific. They call for re-examining existing estimates, rather than concluding that all past estimates must be false. The passages also distinguish limits involving the range of developmental responses and the reliability of environmental information. [TA-W038, discussion of costs, bias and limits]

Its significant contribution here is a warning about what a comparison actually measures. The cost of producing one phenotype, the cost of retaining a response capacity and the failure to achieve an appropriate response are related but distinguishable questions. [TA-W038]

### Developmental resources extend beyond the conventional organism

Developmental resources extend beyond the conventional organism

Griffiths and Gray's selected introductory argument rejects a division in which genes form one fundamental kind of developmental cause and everything else forms another. Genes, cytoplasm and features of a learning environment are among interacting resources. Their proposed developmental unit comprises the resources producing outcomes stably replicated in a lineage, potentially extending beyond the conventional body boundary. [SG-W054, PDF 1–3, printed 277–278]

<!-- PDF page 143 -->

The parity claim is about reasoning and explanatory status, not equal numerical contributions from every resource or the absence of genetic specificity. Reproducing a developmental process still requires the relevant resources to be present and related appropriately. It identifies a broader boundary for asking how a recurring outcome is produced. [SG-W054]

<!-- PDF page 144 -->

## S40 Biological organization, closure and autopoiesis

S40   Biological organization, closure and autopoiesis

### Several meanings of closure

Several meanings of closure

The selected sources concern systems that produce, constrain or maintain conditions of their own activity. The term closure has different meanings in the sources: dependence among constraints, a production organization, closure of a reaction set and mathematical conditions for self-maintenance. None of these means that an organism or chemical system needs no external matter or energy.

### Montévil and Mossio: constraints and the processes they shape

Montévil and Mossio: constraints and the processes they shape

Montévil and Mossio distinguish thermodynamically open processes from constraints acting on them. A constraint is a contingent structure or dynamics that changes the process while relevant aspects of the constraint remain conserved over the time scale considered. Its presence alone is insufficient: the effect must differ from the unconstrained case. Their vascular-system example concerns oxygen carried through a structured transport system rather than simply diffusing in its absence. [W013; GL-W026, 2015 article, §§2–3, definition 1]

The time-scale qualification matters. Conservation of a relevant property during a constrained process does not mean the structure lasts forever or never needs repair. A relatively persistent arrangement can shape many faster events while its longer-term production and maintenance depend on other processes. This is how the framework avoids treating every constraint as a permanently external boundary condition.

The paper's example of an inclined plane clarifies the difference. The plane constrains a sliding object, but that sliding does not normally produce or maintain the plane. Biological organization, in their proposed account, involves constraints whose continued existence depends on processes constrained by others in the organization. The system uses constrained thermodynamic flows in maintaining the constraints themselves. [W013, §§3–5]

### Dependence, boundary and closure are specified rather than inferred from a cycle

Dependence, boundary and closure are specified rather than inferred from a cycle

The authors ask whether any circular chain is enough and answer by defining dependence more carefully. Their framework distinguishes direct dependence from an indirect contribution through a longer chain of processes. Strict closure requires the relevant mutual dependence among constraints, rather than merely reciprocal benefit in a broad environment. Constraints outside the closed set and specified boundary conditions can still be necessary. Closure is consequently contextual, while thermodynamic openness continues underneath it. [W013; GL-W026, §§4–6]

The upper and lower boundaries pose an explicit problem for the framework. Descriptions of actual organisms are incomplete. The authors propose considering maximally closed systems within the available description, then examining how interacting systems can retain distinguishable organization. Their hunting-and-cooking example treats some collective dependencies as indirect and warns that loose cooperation need not satisfy strict closure. A team doing mutually useful work is therefore not automatically a biological closed organization under their definitions.

The authors state that their purpose is to characterize general features rather than supply a model capturing all the complexity of real organisms. Their later discussion retains the relation between stability and variation. [GL-W026, §§5–7]

<!-- PDF page 145 -->

The abstract of Mossio, Montévil and Longo’s 2016 Theoretical principles for biology: organization proposes organization as a principle for making biological objects intelligible and relates it to variation. [GL-W091, abstract]

### Corti: causal conditions do not by themselves settle what ought to happen

Corti: causal conditions do not by themselves settle what ought to happen

The selected part of Corti's critique examines a counterfactual argument for biological normativity. In the organizational account as he reconstructs it, a constraint must perform its role or the mutually maintained system will cease to exist. A further inference assigns what the constraint ought to do. Corti questions whether the causal premise is sufficient for that normative conclusion. [W047, counterfactual argument]

His comparison with a simple dependence relation makes the issue concrete. A condition can be necessary for an outcome without thereby acquiring a normative obligation to produce it. He then asks whether making the conditions internally generated and mutually dependent changes that inferential step. He accepts that closure can mark an important descriptive difference while disputing that the difference, on its own, establishes intrinsic norms.

### Dittrich and Speroni di Fenizio: chemical closure is a property of a reaction set

Dittrich and Speroni di Fenizio: chemical closure is a property of a reaction set

Chemical Organisation Theory begins with molecules and reaction rules. A closed set contains the products generated by reactions available within it. This is a different meaning from a physical seal around a container. The theory also distinguishes semi-self-maintenance, in which consumed types can be produced, from the stronger quantitative condition needed to maintain amounts. [W077, author preprint dated 1 December 2006, §§2.2–2.3]

The authors' small reversible example is instructive. Two molecular types produce one another, but both also decay. Having a route that produces each type is not sufficient to keep either at positive concentration. A diagram of reciprocal production can therefore conceal net depletion. Their self-maintenance condition uses the stoichiometric matrix and the existence of a compatible flux vector for  which the relevant net production rates are nonnegative. The stipulated positivity of available reactions is part of that definition.

A chemical organization combines closure and self-maintenance in this formal sense. Its existence identifies a structural possibility under the reaction rules and flux conditions. It does not, without further kinetic information, establish that actual concentrations will approach a stable persistent state. An available feasible flux is different from the flux generated by a particular reaction-rate law and initial condition. [W077, definitions 5–11]

The later selected theorem relates fixed points of the specified dynamics to organizations under a mapping from concentrations to present molecular types. Threshold and reaction-positivity assumptions enter the construction. The direction reported is that the appropriately mapped stationary state is an organization, not that every formally feasible organization is a stable attractor. [W077, §3.2, definition 41 and theorem 42]

### Varela, Maturana and Uribe: a production organization that realizes its boundary

Varela, Maturana and Uribe: a production organization that realizes its boundary

The early sections of Varela, Maturana and Uribe's 1974 paper characterize an autopoietic system through a network of component-producing processes. The components participate in generating the network that produces them and in realizing the system as a unity in a domain. Its boundary is consequently part of an ongoing production organization, rather than merely a wall placed around a collection of parts. [W081, printed pp. 187–191, §§1–7]

<!-- PDF page 146 -->

The distinction between organization and a particular material realization allows turnover without making the system an unchanging stock of molecules. The selected model and figures illustrate the proposed organization. Their role is conceptual demonstration in a specified construction. Reproduction is also not identical to the maintenance of such an organization; a system can be described in terms of its organization without making reproduction the definition of each operation.

### Marletto: a recipe requires an executing and maintained constructor

Marletto: a recipe requires an executing and maintained constructor

Marletto's selected constructor-theoretic argument asks what tasks the laws of physics permit, including accurate construction and reproduction under laws that do not contain a ready-made design for the task. Possibility is defined through arbitrarily good approximate constructors short of perfection. This differs from asking how probable a task is under observed evolution, or how much a particular implementation costs. [W092, §§2–3.1 and selected conclusions]

Her car-factory example separates a task-specific recipe from a more general vehicle that carries out its constituent operations. The recipe can be decomposed into subtasks permitted by the laws, with a modular programme specifying their organization. The task-specific information must be instantiated and preserved; the executing machinery must also remain capable of carrying out the operations. A stored recipe is therefore part of an architecture, rather than an alternative to physical execution.

Marletto connects accurate constructors, replication and maintenance in an architecture that joins a reusable recipe to machinery capable of executing it. [W092]

### Hopfield: specificity can require an additional driven path

Hopfield: specificity can require an additional driven path

Hopfield's 1974 kinetic-proofreading paper asks how biosynthetic processes can discriminate more accurately than a simple equilibrium recognition scheme would suggest. In the model, correct and incorrect substrates differ in their dissociation behavior. An additional reaction stage, driven away from equilibrium, creates an effective delay before incorporation. The more rapidly dissociating incorrect complex has more opportunity to leave before the final product forms. [TA-W017, printed pp. 4135–4137, reaction schemes 1–10]

The driving is essential in his analysis. Within the equilibrium constraint, merely adding the intermediate does not supply the desired improvement. Coupling to an energy source, such as phosphate hydrolysis, changes the available kinetic organization. The effective delay is a physical reaction mechanism, not a decision by an external inspector. Reactions that appear superfluous in a simpler description can serve a discrimination function.

Hopfield relates the mechanism to reported biosynthetic examples. The model shows why fidelity can retain additional pathways and free-energy supply. [TA-W017]

### Galstyan and colleagues: spatial proofreading relocates part of the work

Galstyan and colleagues: spatial proofreading relocates part of the work

The selected spatial-proofreading account uses gradients and spatial separation to create a discrimination opportunity. A bound complex must persist long enough during movement or diffusion to reach the region where product formation occurs. Different dissociation rates can then yield different success probabilities. The arrangement supplies a spatially organized delay rather than requiring the same local chemical architecture as the classical scheme. [TA-W018, selected model and gradient-maintenance passages]

The authors make the boundary of energy accounting explicit. An initial reported power calculation concerns the additional cost caused by proofreading's tendency to homogenize a gradient; it excludes the baseline cost of creating that gradient. Appendix B separately examines the continuing power needed to

<!-- PDF page 147 -->

counter diffusion even without the proofreading enzyme. [TA-W018, energy-cost discussion and appendix B]

The more realistic model describes a membrane-associated kinase and a distributed phosphatase maintaining an active-substrate gradient. At low enough enzyme activity, the gradient can persist and support proofreading. If activity overwhelms the maintaining mechanism, the gradient flattens and proofreading is lost. The selected parameter examples use experimentally constrained ranges, but the study remains a conceptual model rather than a demonstration that every proposed biological implementation uses the mechanism. [TA-W018, gradient-maintenance model]

Spatial organization can alter where discrimination work occurs, while successful use still depends on maintaining the spatial difference.

### Synthetic Notch: a selected modular sensing–response account

Synthetic Notch: a selected modular sensing–response account

The summary and introductory material from Morsut and colleagues describe synthetic Notch receptors with replaced extracellular sensing and intracellular transcriptional modules. Binding an external ligand triggers release of a regulator, connecting a selected input to a selected cellular response. Their account reports pathways that do not share common signaling intermediates and can be combined to integrate cues, including Boolean response programmes. [GL-W060]

The engineered sensing interface uses receptor processing, transcriptional machinery and cellular resources to execute its response. [GL-W060]

### Hypercycles: cooperative organization with vulnerabilities

Hypercycles: cooperative organization with vulnerabilities

The selected 2016 PLOS Topic Page defines a hypercycle as a cyclic autocatalytic arrangement of self-replicating molecular types, each catalyzing a successor. Its historical motivation concerns an error  threshold: imperfect copying can prevent a long sequence from retaining the information needed for more accurate replication. Coupled shorter replicators were proposed as a way of organizing a larger informational capacity. [SG-W047]

The review retains difficulties in the traditional ordinary-differential-equation model, including parasites and limits to stable cycle size. It also distinguishes an experimentally reported cooperative ribozyme network from a hypercycle in the strict sense. [SG-W047]

### Maintained organization, productive closure and fidelity

Maintained organization, productive closure and fidelity

The constraint framework describes a conserved causal role and mutual maintenance; chemical organization adds reaction-set and feasible-flux conditions; autopoiesis concerns component production and realized unity; constructor theory examines task possibility and recipes; proofreading makes fidelity and supporting work concrete.

<!-- PDF page 148 -->

## S50 Biological circuits, cellular organization and intervention

S50   Biological circuits, cellular organization and intervention

### From components to cellular behavior

From components to cellular behavior

Biological circuits provide concrete cases of organization producing a capability: a temporary signal can leave a persistent expression state, a regulatory loop can generate repeated pulses, and the allocation of cellular machinery can change what an introduced construct achieves. Systems biology examines such behavior through molecular interactions, measurements and models. Synthetic biology also constructs circuits to investigate and use it. These traditions contain pertinent historical foundations for asking how a capability is produced, what sustains it, and what an intervention changes.

The accounts below move from experimentally investigated circuits to metabolic constraints, whole-cell modeling and selected recent computational approaches. Their objects include living cells, mathematical representations of cells, and the conduct of biological research. The experiments show particular realized behaviors; the models and reviews explain the questions, assumptions and methods through which those behaviors can be investigated.

### Kitano on structure, dynamics, control and design

Kitano on structure, dynamics, control and design

Hiroaki Kitano's 2002 overview identifies four aspects of system-level understanding: structure, dynamics, control and design. A list of components supplies a different kind of knowledge from a network of interactions, and an interaction diagram supplies a different kind from the behavior of that network over time. His road-map analogy makes the distinction tangible: the map helps locate possible routes, while explaining traffic requires information about movement and interaction. Control asks how a state can be changed or stabilized; design asks how systems with desired properties can be constructed. [BC-W001, p. 1662]

The research cycle he describes makes a model's assumptions available for testing. Competing explanations can guide the choice of an experiment that distinguishes them, and disagreement with observation can require revision of the model. The needed measurements depend on that purpose: broad coverage, adequate temporal sampling and simultaneous observation of different molecular properties can matter differently. Kitano's account thus joins modeling to the organization of experimental work. He presents expanded control and design capabilities as ambitions supported by continuing advances in measurement, analysis and software. [BC-W001, pp. 1663–1664]

### Alon on response time and persistence detection

Alon on response time and persistence detection

Uri Alon's 2007 review explains selected regulatory patterns through their dynamics and experimental investigation. Negative autoregulation occurs when a transcription factor represses production of itself. A strong promoter permits rapid initial accumulation; as the repressor approaches its threshold, it reduces further production. Relative to simple regulation reaching the same final concentration, the circuit can respond faster. The steady concentration and the route taken to reach it are separate properties. Alon also discusses reduced variation between cells and the possibility of noise amplification when feedback contains a long delay. [BC-W002, pp. 450–451]

A coherent feedforward circuit gives a different example. X activates Y, and both activate Z. When activation of Z requires both X and Y (an AND rule), it waits for Y to accumulate sufficiently. A brief input can disappear before that happens, whereas a persistent input permits expression. Turning X off can stop new Z production promptly even though Y remains. Alon describes experimental tests in the arabinose system and contrasts OR-like regulation in flagella, where either input can suffice and the delayed

<!-- PDF page 149 -->

transition changes. Timing therefore depends on the regulatory signs, the input rule and molecular kinetics as well as the wiring. [BC-W002, pp. 452–453]

### Gardner, Cantor and Collins construct cellular memory

Gardner, Cantor and Collins construct cellular memory

Gardner, Cantor and Collins constructed a toggle from two genes whose protein products repress one another's promoters. When one side dominates, it suppresses production of its opponent and thereby sustains its own predominance. A temporary inducer weakens the active repressor, allowing the opposing side to accumulate and establish the other state. After the inducer is removed, mutual inhibition can retain the selected expression state. Their experiment thus separates the signal used to change state from the continuing gene expression that maintains it. [BC-W003, pp. 339–340]

The two arrows are only part of the design. Their model requires sufficiently cooperative repression and appropriately balanced effective synthesis rates. Six constructs shared the same basic configuration, but one had only one stable expression state. In one construct, the two culture states persisted for twenty-two further hours without inducer, under the reported growth conditions. These particulars explain what has to be arranged for a temporary input to leave a persistent cellular response. [BC-W003, box 1 and figs. 2– 4]

### Elowitz and Leibler construct an oscillator

Elowitz and Leibler construct an oscillator

Elowitz and Leibler's 2000 repressilator connects three transcriptional repressors in a cycle: LacI represses tetR, TetR represses cI, and CI represses lacI. Their design model permitted either convergence to a steady state or sustained oscillation, depending on expression, repression and decay parameters. To favor oscillation, the construction used tightly repressible promoters and degradation tags that shortened repressor lifetimes. Cellular protein destruction participates in producing the temporal behavior. [BC-W004, pp. 335–337]

A separate fluorescent reporter allowed the researchers to follow individual cell lineages. They observed oscillations lasting longer than a cell-division cycle and substantial variation in amplitude and period, including skipped or delayed cycles. At least forty percent of cells met their oscillation criterion in each of three movies. A population average would conceal important aspects of this behavior as cells lost synchrony. The experiment supplied a working synthetic oscillator whose irregularity was itself a subject for further investigation. [BC-W004, pp. 335–338]

### Adaptation and a programmable sensing interface

Adaptation and a programmable sensing interface

The chemotaxis account in S05 supplies another relation between organization and response. Yi and colleagues reconstruct exact adaptation through integral feedback: an internal state associated approximately with total receptor methylation changes with the difference between a methylation contribution and activity-dependent demethylation. At a stable steady state, its rate of change is zero. Under the specified biochemical assumptions, activity returns to a value independent of the changed ligand level. The continuing receptor-modification reactions support that response. [W012]

S05 explains the four biochemical assumptions and the stability requirement in detail. This is a response that returns an activity measure after a changed input, whereas the toggle experiment selects and retains an alternative expression state. The distinction gives a reader two concrete behaviors to investigate without using persistence as a single undifferentiated outcome. Their mathematical descriptions identify different states and different conditions for the reported result. [W012; BC-W003]

The selected synthetic Notch account in S40 describes replaced extracellular sensing and intracellular transcriptional modules. Ligand binding can release a regulator and connect a chosen external cue to a

<!-- PDF page 150 -->

chosen transcriptional response. The sensing interface is engineered while receptor processing and cellular execution remain involved. S40 develops the sensing interface and combined-cue response programmes. This example places an intervention at the connection between a signal and an existing cellular apparatus. [GL-W060]

### Ceroni and colleagues measure the host's remaining capacity

Ceroni and colleagues measure the host's remaining capacity

Ceroni, Algar, Stan and Ellis examine the burden imposed by introduced gene-expression constructs. Their capacity monitor uses a gene integrated into the bacterial chromosome that produces a fluorescent protein without an inducing signal. Its production rate provides an indirect assay of expression capacity remaining as another construct draws on cellular resources. Construct output, the monitor's output and cellular growth can then be compared. An introduced function enters a cell that already has demands on its expression machinery. [BC-W006, supplementary figs. 1–3]

Their translational resource model represents ribosomes moving along transcripts and returning to a shared pool. Stronger recruitment and slower elongation can change how much machinery is occupied. In the selected supplementary analysis, changing coding-sequence length or ribosome-binding strength changes both predicted output and remaining capacity. Tests with shorter antibody-fragment constructs captured important trends, while the model overestimated burden in some conditions. The comparison makes the object of improvement explicit: obtaining a desired product while retaining more host capacity. Its diagnostic is a measured reporter response supported by a specified model, rather than a direct inventory of every resource in the cell. [BC-W006, supplementary note 4 and figs. 9, 13–15]

### Orth, Thiele and Palsson on feasible metabolic flux

Orth, Thiele and Palsson on feasible metabolic flux

Orth, Thiele and Palsson's 2010 primer explains flux balance analysis through a stoichiometric matrix S and a vector of reaction rates v. Each matrix column records what a reaction consumes and produces. At steady state, Sv = 0 balances the represented metabolites. Upper and lower reaction bounds restrict the allowable rates, including exchange with the environment. These conditions define a feasible set that can contain many flux distributions without requiring a kinetic rate constant for every reaction. [BC-W005, box 1 and figs. 1–2]

Selecting a growth or production objective adds another commitment. Linear programming chooses a feasible distribution maximizing or minimizing a specified linear combination of fluxes. Biomass production can be represented by a reaction consuming measured proportions of precursor materials. The primer illustrates environmental intervention by changing oxygen-uptake bounds, and discusses alternative optima when several pathways attain the same objective. Standard FBA describes steady-state fluxes; it does not determine metabolite concentrations or automatically include regulatory dynamics. Feasibility, the selected objective and the additional biology needed for prediction remain distinct elements of the method. [BC-W005, From constraints to optimizing a phenotype; The many uses of flux balance analysis]

### Karr and colleagues integrate a whole-cell model

Karr and colleagues integrate a whole-cell model

Karr and colleagues' 2012 model of Mycoplasma genitalium divided cellular function among twenty-eight process models. Different mathematics served different processes, including flux balance for metabolism and stochastic descriptions for degradation. Integration used shared cellular variables and an approximation of process independence over short intervals. Submodels advanced using values determined at the preceding step. The model's architecture therefore included an explicit computational means of reconnecting processes initially developed separately. [BC-W007, pp. 389–391, fig. 1]

<!-- PDF page 151 -->

The study also used discrepancies to direct experiments. In its examination of twelve gene-disruption strains, two-thirds of predicted growth rates were consistent with the measurements. The lpdA disruption was particularly informative: a colorimetric assay initially failed to detect growth, while an alternative doubling-time measurement indicated viability. The authors interpreted the combined evidence as severe but noncritical impairment of growth. The authors investigated such disagreements to refine parameters and functional assignments. Their whole-cell construction supplies a historical example of connecting heterogeneous representations to experimental correction. [BC-W007, Model-Driven Biological Discovery]

### Maintaining processes and realizing their relations

Maintaining processes and realizing their relations

The cellular-resource account has a useful neighboring question in the Rosen material in S26: how are the processes on which operation depends themselves produced and repaired? Louie's reconstruction distinguishes a transformation's output from production of the machinery performing that transformation. Siekmann examines the proposed closure of these productive relations and disputes what can be inferred about their biological realization from the abstract maps. The disagreement concerns an identified step between a formal construction and the organized material process it is intended to describe. [W104; W103]

S40 develops other source-specific accounts of maintained organization. Chemical organization uses closure and feasible-flux conditions for reaction sets. Hopfield's kinetic proofreading adds a driven intermediate stage that gives an incorrectly bound substrate another opportunity to dissociate. The spatial-proofreading account instead examines gradients and movement, including the work needed to maintain the spatial difference. These accounts locate particular requirements inside their mechanisms: productive closure, sustained chemical driving, or a maintained gradient. Their full expositions and qualifications remain in S40. [W077; TA-W017; TA-W018]

Development adds a further historical route. Waddington's canalization account in S28 concerns a fairly definite developmental outcome despite minor variations along its course. His argument distinguishes a trigger selecting a path from conditions participating in its maintenance. The niche-construction accounts consider changes to environments that can outlast the activity producing them. Those sources direct attention beyond an instantaneous input-output relation to the history and persistence of the conditions under which a biological response occurs. [W032; TA-W020]

### Zuidberg Dos Martires and colleagues on representing reaction conditions

Zuidberg Dos Martires and colleagues on representing reaction conditions

Zuidberg Dos Martires and colleagues' 2024 position paper argues that knowledge representation and automated reasoning can help connect molecular knowledge to system-level questions. Explicitly listing every combination of a protein's site states can generate an enormous microstate space; representing only whole components can omit distinctions that observations resolve. The authors favor descriptions separating reactions from the site-specific conditions on which they depend. The representation preserves locally meaningful detail without beginning by enumerating every complete configuration. [BC-W011, §§3–4]

Their signaling illustrations distinguish deterministic Boolean simulation from probabilistic reasoning. Adding probabilities can express uncertainty about reactions but introduces a harder inference problem. They propose knowledge compilation and related reasoning methods to address it, with model structure supplied by biological knowledge and parameters learned from data. Their claim that this integration is necessary for precision medicine is their position; the quantitative programme remains a proposed direction alongside the worked illustrations. S42 provides the separate Darwiche–Marquis account of choosing a compiled representation for the operations it must support. [BC-W011, §5; TA-W008]

<!-- PDF page 152 -->

### Soltani and colleagues distinguish an association graph from an assembly

Soltani and colleagues distinguish an association graph from an assembly

Soltani and colleagues' 2026 methodological review distinguishes several meanings of an edge in a protein-interaction network. Direct binding, recovery in the same purified complex, co-expression and shared localization supply different evidence. Proteins can be associated without touching, and interactions observed at different times can enter the same static graph. A dense cluster can therefore fail to describe a physically possible assembly. [BC-W010, §§2, 4]

Their proposed response brings cellular conditions and molecular interfaces into detection and validation. Compatible locations and binding surfaces qualify a candidate; a plausible pairwise interface still does not show that every proposed subunit can assemble simultaneously. They also identify a risk of circular evaluation when functional annotations help generate a prediction and are reused to validate it. Their recommendations concern evidence integration and comparable tests. [BC-W010, §§4.5–4.6, 6, 8, 11]

### Li and colleagues on learned flows and biological trajectories

Li and colleagues on learned flows and biological trajectories

The flow-matching survey by Zihao Li and colleagues describes learning a vector field that transports a simple probability distribution toward a distribution of biological data. In the continuous formulation, generation follows a learned ordinary differential equation from an initial sample. The flow parameter orders the generation process; its biological interpretation depends on the modeling task. Geometric choices can matter when ordinary straight-line interpolation passes through states unsuitable for the represented data. [BC-W009, Background; Flow Matching Methods]

Selected applications concern cell trajectories and spatial transcriptomics. The review discusses reconstruction from sparse, noisy observations and methods that retain aspects of expression geometry or tissue context. A generated path links modeled observations under learned assumptions; testing a biological transition requires evidence appropriate to that interpretation. The survey's evaluation discussion identifies heterogeneous tasks, datasets and constraints as obstacles to comparable assessment. These passages explain choices in building a computational representation, including the space in which movement is modeled and the conditions by which generated samples are judged. [BC-W009, Dynamic Cell Trajectory Prediction; Cellular Microenvironments from Spatial Transcriptomics;  Evaluation Tasks and Datasets]

### Li and colleagues on cellular predictors and research agents

Li and colleagues on cellular predictors and research agents

Krinos Li and colleagues' 2025 virtual-cell survey separates direct cellular predictors, called oracles, from agents organizing scientific tasks. Their cellular-modeling discussion includes representation, perturbation prediction and gene-regulation inference. The agent discussion concerns planning, tool use and the division of research work. A predictor of cellular response and an agent arranging an analysis occupy different places in the resulting research process. [BC-W008, §§2–3]

The distinction makes their unresolved questions concrete. Predictors must generalize to unfamiliar cellular contexts and make uncertainty intelligible. Agents must sustain coherent work across tool calls and experimental stages, with suitable evaluation of the completed task. In its single-agent architectures, one model manages the workflow, sometimes switching roles through prompts. Multi-agent architectures divide responsibilities among specialized planners, analyzers or executors that coordinate through dialogue or shared memory. Its taxonomy and surveyed examples concern selected approaches to virtual-cell research; the evaluations it calls for remain part of establishing what these approaches can reliably  accomplish. [BC-W008, §3.1 and Conclusions and Future Directions]

<!-- PDF page 153 -->

### Reading routes through the biological foundations

Reading routes through the biological foundations

For a reader interested in building a particular response, the switch and oscillator accounts supply constructions to study alongside Alon's timing mechanisms. The capacity-monitor account adds a way to examine effects on the host. The metabolic primer makes environmental supply and chosen objectives explicit, while the whole-cell model supplies a worked architecture for relating several processes and confronting their combined predictions with observations. The recent accounts address the representation of reaction conditions, evidence for assemblies, learned biological representations and the conduct of research with AI.

The neighboring sections retain further detail: S05 on adaptation and robustness; S26 on production, repair and realization; S28 on development and environmental legacies; S40 on closure, proofreading and synthetic Notch; S42 on representations and reasoning; and S47 on linked flow accounts. These routes allow the particular intervention or modeling question to determine which historical account the reader studies next.

## S43 Ecological resilience and environmental arrangements

S43   Ecological resilience and environmental arrangements

### Persistence and an acceptable outcome are different questions

Persistence and an acceptable outcome are different questions

The selected sources explain how ecological and environmental arrangements persist, how their behavior can be modeled and how physical or biological processes are used in practice. The accounts distinguish persistence from constancy and from desirability.

### Holling: resilience is not rapid return to equilibrium

Holling: resilience is not rapid return to equilibrium

Holling's 1973 argument begins with two different views of ecological behavior: whether relationships persist at all, and how constant the numbers of organisms remain. A system designed to operate narrowly around a target may be evaluated by fluctuations and correction speed. An ecological system repeatedly encountering external changes can require a different question: can its relationships continue despite changes in variables and parameters? [GL-W067, selected introduction and synthesis]

His synthesis distinguishes resilience, concerning persistence while absorbing change, from stability, concerning return toward an equilibrium after a temporary disturbance. Under these definitions a system can fluctuate substantially and remain resilient. A relatively constant population can be vulnerable to an unusual event outside the range it has experienced. The definitions are not interchangeable labels for generally good performance. [GL-W067, IIASA edition, printed pp. 17–18, PDF pp. 19–20]

Holling reports historical examples and model interpretations. His management discussion contrasts maintaining a predictable yield with preserving a domain within which the system can persist. Interventions that narrow variability can also change the conditions determining vulnerability. The argument concerns those conditions.

Persistence of a harmful state remains persistence under the definition.

### Response diversity includes differing reactions, not just a species count

Response diversity includes differing reactions, not just a species count

The Stockholm Resilience Centre synthesis distinguishes redundancy in a function from diversity in how contributors respond to disturbances. If several entities perform a similar function but fail under different conditions, their differing responses can help sustain it. Merely counting more entities does not show that they supply that property. [GL-W068, selected response-diversity and redundancy account]

The synthesis also recognizes management demands and costs. Diversity has to be understood in relation to the function, disturbances and boundaries considered.

### Cury and colleagues: remain within constraints rather than maximize one target

Cury and colleagues: remain within constraints rather than maximize one target

Cury, Mullon, Garcia and Shannon present viability theory as a modeling approach for ecosystem-based fisheries. Instead of choosing only a single quantity to maximize, the account asks which trajectories can remain within a set of constraints over time. The viability kernel identifies states from which admissible evolution is possible under the model and available controls. A state can satisfy today's limits yet fail to belong to that set if no permissible continuation can keep the constraints satisfied. [UX-W018, viability principle and modeling tools]

The source makes operational specification necessary. Relevant states, dynamics, indicators, reference values and available actions must be described, with data and computation adequate to the problem. In its fisheries discussion, agreement about avoiding collapse, extinction or displacement may be easier than

<!-- PDF page 155 -->

agreement about one ideal ecosystem target. The constraints still embody choices and can conflict. The southern Benguela application is presented as an initial attempt, not a completed universal solution.

A viable trajectory satisfies the modeled constraints; unmodeled disturbances can change whether those constraints remain attainable. Cury and colleagues apply Aubin's viability theory to the fisheries problem. [UX-W018]

### FAO precaution: objectives, limits and the ability to observe them

FAO precaution: objectives, limits and the ability to observe them

The selected FAO fisheries guidance distinguishes desired targets from undesirable outcomes that operational constraints should avoid. Such limits may concern stock, age or spatial distribution, ecosystem effects and bycatch. The document also relates these choices to what can be measured and to the time needed to adjust. Approaching a target too quickly can overshoot a limit. [GL-W055, selected chapter 3, paragraphs 19–44]

Data sufficiency, uncertainty, community alternatives, reversibility and wider effects remain relevant. A rule can be intelligible while its monitoring and adjustment still require institutions and skill. This is context-specific prescriptive guidance.

### Beven: predictive agreement can leave explanatory alternatives

Beven: predictive agreement can leave explanatory alternatives

Beven's equifinality essay questions the assumption that calibration identifies one uniquely correct environmental model. Multiple structures or parameterizations can fit available observations acceptably. Imperfect measurements, model inadequacy, scale and incomplete knowledge can leave several explanations or predictive representations in play. A good fit to selected data is therefore not identical to identifying the system's causal structure or parameters. [GL-W015, selected §2, PDF pp. 3–5]

Beven distinguishes a response adequate for a task and a uniquely determined explanation. Additional observations can constrain alternatives, but their relevance and the criterion of acceptability matter. The source proposes a more serious treatment of multiple acceptable models and developments of GLUE, while leaving research questions open.

Agroecology: a framework and a limited performance account

The FAO ten-elements framework brings diversity, synergies, efficiency, recycling and resilience together with knowledge, human values, culture, governance and economic relations. Controlled traffic: geometry must match equipment and remain usable

Constructed wetlands: the treatment medium still has to be established and maintained

### Targeting heat recovery before choosing equipment

Targeting heat recovery before choosing equipment

Truls Gundersen’s primer describes a history from process development through unit operations to attention to interactions between operations. ### Evolving a feasible network

Evolving a feasible network

The second paper begins with a feasible design, preferably one with maximum heat recovery, and examines changes that promote properties such as low cost or easier start-up. ## S47 Networks, flows and competing information measures

S47   Networks, flows and competing information measures

The sources examine support, connectivity and statistical dependence through accounts of maintained capacities, linked budgets, alternative paths and predictive relations.

### MuSIASEM: maintained funds and linked flow budgets

MuSIASEM: maintained funds and linked flow budgets

Giampietro, Mayumi and Ramos-Martin distinguish funds, whose identity is maintained during the accounting interval, from flows transformed during that interval. People, capital and land provide different kinds of fund; their continued availability requires maintenance and renewal. A rate of energy use per hour of human activity is consequently a relation between a flow and a fund, rather than an account of energy alone. Their account explains how descriptions at household, production and whole-society levels can constrain one another. What is feasible at one scale cannot be chosen independently of  the other accounts. [SG-W017]

The authors call this a “Sudoku effect”: linked totals and component allocations restrict the combinations that can consistently be entered elsewhere. Human time allocated to production is unavailable for other activities, while production must support the activities and maintained funds outside its immediate boundary. A locally attractive intensity or productivity figure can therefore conceal an allocation that cannot reproduce the larger system. This is a consistency argument, not a claim that the equations select one uniquely desirable future. The distinction matters when an apparent saving in one production compartment depends on maintenance or supporting work located in another. [SG-W017, accepted manuscript §§1–2]

Categories are chosen before calculation. The narrative about what a system is and does determines which funds, flows and levels enter the representation. The authors expressly allow this narrative to fail: a fund may be unable to handle its proposed flow, cannot be maintained throughout the interval, or requires flows inconsistent with boundary conditions. They treat such failures as reasons to revise the representation. A fixed taxonomy is especially problematic for a system becoming something different, rather than merely changing its quantities within unchanged categories. [SG-W017]

The paper extends the account toward ecological constraints through land-use funds and densities of energy and material flows. The paper distinguishes areas whose flows are controlled by human activity from areas represented through ecosystem self-organization, while acknowledging that it cannot fully develop that application there. The model constrains linked budgets. [SG-W017]

### Emergy: proposed accounting for paid and unpaid support

Emergy: proposed accounting for paid and unpaid support

Campbell, Brandt-Williams and Meisch’s West Virginia report proposes accounting for support that market payments can leave invisible. Its selected methodological pages define emergy as energy of one kind previously used, directly and indirectly, to produce a product or service. Transformity supplies a conversion factor between that accumulated supporting energy and a resulting quantity. The intended account includes ecological inputs as well as purchased inputs, so the production boundary extends beyond the immediate enterprise and its monetary accounts. [SG-W018, preface; §§1–2.2]

The proposed common basis depends on the specified transformations, system boundary, input data and treatment of co-products. An accounting convention does not, merely by assigning comparable numbers, demonstrate an equivalence among energy, knowledge and economic value. Allocation of shared inputs determines how co-products enter the supporting-energy account. The report itself calls its state account a first step because important subsystems remain outside the analysis. The report was published in 2005. [SG-W018]

<!-- PDF page 161 -->

### Q-analysis: connectivity at different dimensions

Q-analysis: connectivity at different dimensions

Smirnov, Kurkin and Hramov describe a Python package for Q-analysis and applications including network physiology. In the definitions, a simplex represents a set of incident elements. Two simplices are q-near when they share a q-dimensional face; q-connectivity extends the relation through a chain of such adjacencies. Increasing q makes the required overlap more demanding. The first structure vector records the number of q-connected components at successive dimensions. Connectivity is therefore a graded property of the chosen complex, rather than a single yes-or-no attribute of a graph. [SG-W022, selected definitions and discussion]

This representation can distinguish arrangements that simpler summaries obscure. A large complex connected through single shared vertices can fragment when the analysis requires shared edges or higher-dimensional faces. But the choice of incidence data and the construction of simplices determine what those differences describe. A clique extracted from pairwise observations does not itself demonstrate a causal interaction that requires the entire group. The authors characterize the core framework as exploratory and descriptive, useful for comparison and hypothesis generation. [SG-W022]

### Reconstructability analysis: a simpler predictive distribution

Reconstructability analysis: a simpler predictive distribution

Shervais, Kramer, Westaway, Cox and Zwick explain reconstructability analysis through decompositions of categorical probability distributions. Suppose A, B, C and D are inputs and Z is an output. A structure written ABCD:ABZ preserves the joint input distribution and the relation of A and B to Z, while not retaining every dependence in the saturated distribution ABCDZ. Maximum-entropy composition of the selected projections yields a reconstructed distribution. Its conditional distribution can then be used to predict Z. The question is whether a simpler specified structure retains useful information about that output. [SG-W053]

The authors express predictive information as uncertainty reduction, for example H(Z) − H(Z|AB), relative to a stated independence model. Normalizing by H(Z) gives a percentage uncertainty reduction when that denominator is appropriate. This is a defined statistical comparison, not a measurement of energy saved or an automatic causal interpretation of a gene–gene relation. “Independence” also depends on whether the model is directed toward an output or treats all variables symmetrically. The model’s statement must be recovered before its simplicity or information score is interpreted. [SG-W053]

The method passages distinguish loopless feature-selection structures from models with multiple predicting components and loops. Loopless calculations are simpler and faster; loops can require iterative computation. Exhaustive searches over candidate structures can become prohibitive. Thus the representation may reduce a prediction problem while leaving model search, estimation and validation as substantial work. [SG-W053]

### Ulanowicz and colleagues, 2009: what the flow identities say

Ulanowicz and colleagues, 2009: what the flow identities say

Ulanowicz, Goerner, Lietaer and Gomez begin with nonnegative directed flows Tᵢⱼ and total throughput T. Normalizing gives probabilities pᵢⱼ= Tᵢⱼ/T, together with sender and receiver marginals. Their joint entropy H describes uncertainty in the joint flow distribution; mutual information X describes statistical dependence between origin and destination. The remainder Ψ= H − X is the sum of the two conditional entropies, H(origin|destination) + H(destination|origin). It is not one conventional conditional entropy. These quantities require consistent support, a common logarithm base and the usual zero-probability conventions. [WME-W025, printed pp. 27–29]

Multiplying by throughput yields the paper’s extensive measures C = TH, A = TX and Φ= TΨ, with C = A + Φ. The authors call A ascendency and interpret it in terms of organized constraint or efficiency; Φ is

<!-- PDF page 162 -->

associated with overhead and reserve. The identity is an accounting decomposition of observed flows. An information-weighted throughput is not automatically a thermodynamic conversion efficiency, a stock of spare equipment, or a measured ability to recover after a disturbance. Those interpretations require further evidence about the system represented. [WME-W025]

The distinction between averages and individual events also matters. Independence maximizes expected joint entropy at fixed marginals. It does not maximize the surprisal of every possible joint event. An individual term log [pᵢⱼ/(pᵢ·p·ⱼ)] can be negative, although the average mutual information is nonnegative. Statistical symmetry between origin and destination is not a causal version of Newton’s third law. The paper’s discussion of absence, constraint and autocatalysis supplies an interpretation of the equations; these broader philosophical assertions are not all consequences of the entropy identities. [WME-W025, pp. 28–29; WME-W024]

### The food-web example and the conditions on fallback

The food-web example and the conditions on fallback

The 2009 article uses a simplified network involving prawns, turtles, fish, snakes and alligators. It isolates a small set of flows from a larger web and deliberately makes extreme changes for illustration. Concentrating modeled flow along fewer paths can increase the indicated throughput while removing an alternative route that would matter if fish failed. The example explains why a present flow arrangement and its apparent efficiency can fail to reveal a dependence on a particular intermediary. It is a didactic counterfactual, not an observed disturbance experiment. [WME-W025, p. 30]

The account retains the inputs, conversions and dissipation that sustain the organisms. Its reserve measure is expressly not a palpable stock. An alternative path is useful only if the organisms or facilities on it remain viable, have capacity, can perform a substitutable function, and can act within the disturbance’s time scale. Statistical diversity alone does not establish those properties. The authors also discuss autocatalytic concentration that entrains resources and can starve outsiders, so increased internal organization need not benefit everything affected by the network. [WME-W025; RGC-W042]

### The proposed optimum and the critical preprint

The proposed optimum and the critical preprint

The article proposes a family of fitness functions of relative ascendency α= A/C, with a positive chosen parameter β. In natural-log notation, the normalized form is F = −e α^ βln( α^ β); robustness also includes throughput. The maximum at α= exp(−1/ β) follows from that chosen curve. It is not a theorem identifying the fraction that maximizes actual survival in every network. The article acknowledges limited data, a heuristic balance, a nonuniversal β, an arbitrary bound used in its illustration, and sensitivity to resolution. It leaves transfer from ecology to economics open. [WME-W025, pp. 31–35]

Trancón y Widemann and Bogner’s critical preprint targets the formal presentation. The preprint was submitted in 2012 and posted in 2016; rejection without review is the authors’ report, not evidence of peer-reviewed acceptance. The critics identify the two-conditional-entropy issue, problems with maximum-surprisal reasoning, ambiguity between source and receiver, and confusion between intensive information measures and throughput-scaled quantities. They expressly do not infer that the ecological observations or philosophical possibilities should be rejected wholesale. [WME-W024]

One consequential problem is the original use of dimensional A and Φ as exponents in transformed connectivity and effective-size measures. The intensive X and Ψ, with compatible logarithm conventions, are required for that construction. A further numerical example does not produce the printed relative ascendency from its stated connectivity and size. Nonnegative conditional entropy also does not establish that an entire network is connected: disjoint deterministic branches can satisfy the same inequality. [WME-W024; WME-W025, pp. 31–32]

<!-- PDF page 163 -->

The critical source itself requires discrimination. Its conversion between bits and nats is printed in the wrong direction: one bit is ln(2) nats, about 0.693, while one nat is about 1.443 bits. Loose statements about the convexity of logarithms also do not replace the relevant entropy argument. Local derivatives with respect to independently varied flows present another limit: real interventions may have to preserve mass balance and satisfy capacity, timing and material constraints. A sensitivity formula is not a feasible redesign procedure or a convergence proof. [WME-W024; WME-W025, eq. 18]

### Goerner, Lietaer and Ulanowicz: the economic extension

Goerner, Lietaer and Ulanowicz: the economic extension

The related economic article argues that development depends on the organization and diversity of flows, not simply on aggregate economic throughput. It discusses enterprises at different scales, human capital, concentration, local circulation and the possibility that autocatalytic growth drains resources from surrounding participants. This is the authors’ proposed economic synthesis. [RGC-W042, pp. 76–81]

The transfer assumes that a flow framework can apply across matter, energy, information and money. The article does not supply a new measured economic network dataset with out-of-sample survival validation. Its comparisons of local spending and its historical interpretations of trade, banking, food control and empires remain attributed claims. Equity, human capability and the triple bottom line also involve normative commitments not derived from C = A + Φ.  [RGC-W042]

There are additional quantitative discontinuities. A footnote identifies sustainability with capacity C, rather than the earlier throughput-scaled fitness function. C alone does not have that function’s claimed interior optimum in relative ascendency. The article specifies natural logarithms while repeating numerical information values from the bit-based example without the corresponding conversion, and a redrawn flow differs while the stated total remains unchanged. Calling mutual information “efficiency” and overhead “resilience” does not by itself measure energy efficiency or recovery. These defects limit the promise of a single established economic sustainability metric while leaving the conceptual argument available for study. [RGC-W042, p. 78 and fig. 2]

### Ulanowicz, 2020: a narrower balance conjecture

Ulanowicz, 2020: a narrower balance conjecture

The 2020 article changes notation: A and Φ denote intensive quantities, and H = A + Φ. A reader carrying over the 2009 extensive meanings would misread the argument. The article reports 17 articulated networks clustering near relative ascendency 40 percent, selects an optimum of 0.401 with β= 1.0914, and explicitly expects optima in other domains to differ. This is a narrower empirical conjecture associated with a chosen fitness curve, not retrospective confirmation of a universal 46 percent rule. [RGC-W043, pp. 1–6]

Plotting networks on F( α) does not supply an independent measurement of their survival. Resolution, boundaries and which surviving systems entered the dataset matter. An oyster-reef example adds a hypothetical flow along a specified route; it is not an observed intervention. The printed derivative also loses a minus sign relative to the fitness function. Recommendations to adjust flows according to sensitivities still require a feasible physical intervention and do not establish dynamic convergence or real recovery. The article’s metaphysical claims about indeterminacy and life exceed what the entropy identities demonstrate. [RGC-W043]

These related articles and their criticism put explicit quantities behind a consequential structural proposal. [WME-W024; WME-W025; RGC-W042; RGC-W043]

Double contingency: expectations about expectations
