## S31 Chaos engineering and organizational learning

S31   Chaos engineering and organizational learning

### Connecting experiments with changes in practice

Connecting experiments with changes in practice

An experiment can identify an unexpected dependency without changing it. An organization can observe repeated failures without learning how to prevent them. The material selected in this section concerns the practices that connect intervention, observation, interpretation, and subsequent work.

### The practitioner principles: make a claim about observable behavior

The practitioner principles: make a claim about observable behavior

The Principles of Chaos Engineering formulation defines a discipline of experimentation intended to build confidence in a system's ability to withstand turbulent production conditions. Its problem is not limited to a failed component. Interactions among functioning services can produce unexpected outcomes, while unusual events can expose weaknesses in fallback settings, retries, capacity, and dependencies. These are examples of the systemic uncertainty that the formulation proposes to investigate. [AFC-W004, definition and opening discussion]

The proposed experiment begins with a measurable output that indicates ordinary behavior, then states a hypothesis that this behavior will continue in a control and an experimental group. The experimental change represents an event such as a server crash or severed connection. Investigators try to disprove the hypothesis by looking for a difference in the measured behavior. The formulation's “steady state” therefore concerns a selected observational description over a period, rather than an internal state of each component. Throughput, error rates, and latency percentiles are among its suggested outputs. [AFC-W004, “Chaos in practice”; “Build a hypothesis around steady state behavior”]

The distinction between output and internal attribute is consequential. The experiment is directed toward whether the service continues to work under the chosen conditions. Merely confirming that a disturbance was introduced does not answer that question. Conversely, finding a weakness supplies a target for further improvement. In this formulation, discovery is followed by the opportunity to address the weakness; a disturbance by itself is not a repair. The underlying choice of measurable output remains part of what the experiment asks. [AFC-W004, “Chaos in practice”; advanced principles]

The advanced principles retain the surrounding engineering work. They recommend choosing realistic events by likely occurrence or potential impact, including non-failure changes such as traffic surges. They prefer production experiments because environment and traffic affect behavior. They also call for automation of orchestration and analysis, partly because repeated manual experiments consume labor. At the same time, they explicitly recognize possible short-term customer harm and assign responsibility for containing the experiment's effects. [AFC-W004, advanced principles]

### Brier: connect stated probabilities with subsequent events

Brier: connect stated probabilities with subsequent events

Glenn Brier’s 1950 article begins with a practical objection to forecast verification: a scoring system can reward statements that serve the score better than the forecast’s users. A forecaster may learn to report something other than the probability they judge credible. Brier investigates a verification method for probability forecasts, asking how its incentives affect what the forecaster says. His categories must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive, with their assigned probabilities summing to one. The record therefore specifies both what outcomes count and how much confidence was assigned to them. [CG-W021, p. 1]

For each forecasting occasion, his score sums the squared differences between every category’s assigned probability and its observed indicator, one for the category that occurred and zero for the others. It then

<!-- PDF page 221 -->

averages those sums over the forecasting occasions. A perfect forecast scores zero; certainty in a category that does not occur scores two. His rain/no-rain example counts the errors for both categories. The article’s normalization consequently gives a range from zero to two. [CG-W021, pp. 1–2, equations 1–2]

The worked example links ten forecasts with the events that subsequently occurred. Their score is 0.19. A forecaster assigning the sample’s rain frequency, 0.3, on every occasion would score 0.42; using a climatological rain probability of 0.2 would score 0.44. The sample frequency is a benchmark calculated after observing the period, whereas a working forecaster must estimate such probabilities from available information. Brier uses the comparison to distinguish recognition of an average departure from climatology from discrimination among individual occasions. Both can contribute information. [CG-W021, p. 2, table 1 and equations 3–4]

Brier also groups a larger series of eighty-five forecasts by issued rain probability and compares those groups with observed rain frequencies. The relationship shows where the forecaster’s confidence needs adjustment. He says that this relationship alone does not establish usefulness: how often different probabilities are issued also matters. His closing account reports several months of experimental six-hour precipitation forecasts at the Weather Bureau. Some initial criticism concerned misunderstanding the method or disappointment at how little confidence the forecasts justified; he also leaves substantive questions about the scoring method for further investigation. [CG-W021, pp. 2–3, table 2 and conclusion]

### Nosek and colleagues: preserve the plan and make changes inspectable

Nosek and colleagues: preserve the plan and make changes inspectable

Brian Nosek and colleagues’ 2018 account concerns the relationship between research questions, analysis choices and observed results. They distinguish predictions tested by observations from explanations generated after seeing them. Both activities contribute to inquiry. The difficulty arises when an explanation discovered in the data is presented as though the same data had tested an advance prediction. Their account joins reasoning biases with research incentives and the many decisions available when analyzing a dataset. [CG-W023, “Mental Constraints on Distinguishing Predictions and Postdictions”; “Standard Tools of Statistical Inference Assume Prediction”]

Their proposed preregistration mechanism deposits the questions, design and analysis plan in an independent registry before outcomes are observed. The registry preserves the record and makes it discoverable, sometimes after an embargo. A later report can then be compared with the plan, distinguishing planned tests, amendments and newly generated questions. The authors describe the case for preregistration as theoretically strong and supported by some correlational evidence, while explicitly saying that sufficient experimental evidence establishing superiority for reproducibility was not yet available. [CG-W023, “Preregistration Distinguishes Prediction and Postdiction”]

The practical examples retain the work required when research departs from its plan. A study may recruit fewer participants than intended or reveal violated statistical assumptions. Researchers can report amendments, their reasons and what outcomes had already been seen. Other possibilities include staged registration, blinded datasets, decision trees and standing procedures. These methods have conditions: an earlier stage may reveal the outcome intended for a later test, and a decision tree can formalize a biased stopping rule. Recording that rule makes it inspectable without improving its statistical properties. [CG-W023, challenges 1–2]

For existing datasets, the relevant separation concerns information access. Data may already exist while remaining unseen by the analyst. Conversely, earlier summaries or knowledge of correlated variables can influence a nominally new analysis. The authors therefore ask who has seen what and what has been communicated. They also describe splitting a dataset: exploration develops a prediction using one part, and registration precedes testing on a sealed part. Fast experimental workflows can use a related

<!-- PDF page 222 -->

sequence, treating initial experiments as exploration and then repeating a selected experiment with its design and analysis recorded in advance. [CG-W023, challenges 3–5 and 7]

The record must also extend beyond the successful attempt. In their example of a research program producing one positive result in twenty tries, registering every attempt does not prevent misleading selection if only the positive result is reported. Preserved, accessible registrations and outcomes permit examination of that wider history. The authors distinguish ordinary registration from Registered Reports, which add methodological review and in-principle publication acceptance before results are known. They also retain a further difficulty: selective narrative emphasis can overstate a subset of results even when the planned quantitative outputs are all reported. [CG-W023, challenges 6 and 9; “Advancing the Motive for Preregistration”]

### Van den Akker and colleagues: compare expected benefits with published results

Van den Akker and colleagues: compare expected benefits with published results

Olmo van den Akker and colleagues tested several expected benefits in an article first published in 2023. They compared 193 published psychology studies earning preregistration prizes or badges with 193 related non-preregistered studies published in the same year. Registered Reports were excluded. Controls were selected from Web of Science’s related-publication lists, using shared references to match subject matter. This compared observed publication groups whose researchers had chosen their own practices. [CG-W024, pp. 5427–5428]

The comparison found almost the same proportion of positive results, 0.69 and 0.68. It did not support the expected reductions in effect sizes or gross statistical reporting inconsistencies. Preregistered studies more often reported power analyses, 55 percent against 23 percent, and had larger median samples, 216 against 116. The authors also disclosed a change to their planned positive-result analysis after recognizing an asymmetry in how hypotheses had been coded; they reported both versions, each giving an unsupported predicted difference. [CG-W024, p. 5430]

Assessing the results required choices about what counted as a hypothesis test. In preregistered studies, reported results were matched to recorded hypotheses. For controls, the researchers extracted reported statistical results while excluding identified exploratory tests and checks. They acknowledge that some remaining results might not have been intended as hypothesis tests. They also discuss self-selection into preregistration and the difficulty of making causal claims from the comparison. Their evidence supports particular differences in reported planning and sample size, while leaving the expected reductions in the selected bias indicators unsupported. [CG-W024, pp. 5429–5432]

### Microsoft's guidance: test a complete flow against its targets

Microsoft's guidance: test a complete flow against its targets

The Microsoft guidance distinguishes three levels of activity. Fault injection introduces a fault into a component, dependency, or system path. Chaos testing investigates a particular resilience hypothesis under disruption. Chaos engineering incorporates such testing into culture, engineering practice, and the development cycle. These definitions place a technical intervention within an experiment and the experiment within continuing organizational work. [AFC-W005, definitions]

Its full-flow account explains why component recovery is insufficient as the sole criterion. A component may recover within its target while the dependent service still takes too long to become usable. Detection, response, and the recovery of other dependencies matter to the observed result. Similarly, responsibility for testing depends on what a team controls in infrastructure, platform, and software services. A managed service can move some work to a provider while leaving the workload's interactions, fallback behavior, throttling response, and boundary assumptions to be examined. The source calls attention to these differing responsibilities rather than treating a purchased service as the end of the reliability question. [AFC-W005, scope by service type; end-to-end targets]

<!-- PDF page 223 -->

The guidance also keeps preparation and revision explicit. It recommends scenarios based on critical flows and failure modes, measured baselines, experiments with clear hypotheses, containment, and the ability to stop and restore. It favors beginning in lower-risk environments before proceeding to production with safeguards. Results feed new tests, recovery-plan changes, and remediation work; architectural changes can make earlier assumptions obsolete. [AFC-W005, critical flows and failure scenarios; fault injection and chaos engineering]

### Monperrus: improvement must occur in the software or its engineering process

Monperrus: improvement must occur in the software or its engineering process

Martin Monperrus's Principles of Antifragile Software, in the 2017 paper, asks how an error can become more than something to survive. His account distinguishes static fault tolerance from an adaptive mechanism that learns when errors occur. Static tolerance can preserve a result without becoming more capable afterward. In his proposed use of “antifragility,” learning and improvement are the distinguishing conditions. [AFC-W007, §§3.1–3.2]

His distinction between state repair and behavioral repair adds detail. A state repair changes the current program state, such as a data structure. Behavioral repair changes the program's subsequent conduct through a patch. The latter can leave a change in the code after the triggering failure, which is why he treats it as particularly relevant to improvement through encountered faults. The paper refers to existing repair research as examples. [AFC-W007, §3.2]

Fault self-injection in production enters his argument through its effect on the engineering ecosystem. Repeated disruption exercises recovery behavior, draws engineering attention to it, and creates opportunities to learn from observations. He explicitly says that the injected fault alone is not what improves the system: design principles, the engineers' thinking, and other surrounding practices matter. He also requires a balance between the dependability lost through introduced failures and gains from software improvements. Measuring that tradeoff is a problem for the proposed engineering program. [AFC-W007, §3.3]

The process discussion supplies two specific mechanisms. First, a regression test that reproduces a discovered bug can remain in the test suite after repair. The accumulated suite can support later changes by making some regressions easier to detect. Monperrus relates testing, refactoring, and frequent deployment through this retained aid. [AFC-W007, §4.1]

Second, he discusses dependency on indispensable individuals. Moving people among projects can distribute knowledge and reduce the consequences of losing one person, while producing immediate learning costs, delays, and frustration. Reducing concentrated key-person dependency can require repeated smaller costs. [AFC-W007, §4.2]

The broader relation between process and product remains expressly hypothetical. Drawing on Conway's law, Monperrus proposes that processes embodying his error-oriented principles may be better at producing software with the corresponding properties. His mention of Ariel Tseitlin's The Antifragile Organization identifies a related organizational argument. [AFC-W007, §4.3; AFC-W019, through Monperrus]

### Edmondson and Cannon: seeing failure is a different competency from analyzing it

Edmondson and Cannon: seeing failure is a different competency from analyzing it

The HBS Working Knowledge excerpt by Amy Edmondson and Mark Cannon explains why awareness of a failure may leave its causes unchanged. An error count can show that something is wrong without showing what to correct. Their examples include discussion forums in medicine and military after-action reviews, but the operative point is the work of inquiry: people need to disclose relevant knowledge, hear

<!-- PDF page 224 -->

different accounts, and examine the event deeply enough to alter their understanding. [AFC-W015, opening analysis discussion]

The authors identify organizational and personal obstacles to that inquiry. Revisiting a failure can threaten confidence and invite defensive explanation. Reward systems can favor rapid, decisive action over patient investigation. Habitual attribution can explain away a large failure as outside interference or a small one as an irrelevant fluke. The result can be repeated experience without corresponding learning. Their reported telecommunications case illustrates such rationalization. [AFC-W015, barriers to analysis]

Their proposed supports are correspondingly substantial. They describe forums, resources, incentives, technical expertise, diverse perspectives, and skill in managing group inquiry. Such arrangements are meant to make interpretations contestable and the findings usable elsewhere in the organization. A reported hospital example extends analysis to near misses and small errors, with formal studies, clinical teams, and logs that preserve information for further examination. These details matter to gambits engineering because learning depends on organized work and retained records, rather than on failure's occurrence alone. [AFC-W015, organizational forums and selected hospital example]

The excerpt expressly distinguishes identifying failures, analyzing them, and deliberate experimentation as relatively independent competencies, rather than a required three-step sequence. Different competencies can be inhibited by different social and technical conditions. Their treatment supplies reasons to investigate how an organization notices, understands, and acts on evidence, without making failure a necessary or sufficient cause of improvement. [AFC-W015, concluding distinction among competencies]

### The practice guide: experiment design and its supporting organization

The practice guide: experiment design and its supporting organization

The China Academy of Information and Communications Technology's 2021 Chaos Engineering Practice

Guide (《混沌工程实践指南》) presents experimentation as a core activity supported by strategy, people, culture, risk management, and assessment. It also describes subsequent improvements to architecture and development or operations procedures as extensions of the practice. This organization of the guide makes the relationship between an experiment and its surrounding institution explicit. [AFC-W014, printed pp. 9, 23–28]

The design account begins with a hypothesis about a possible stability weakness, informed by user feedback, test records, and understanding of the architecture. Probability, scope of effect, and seriousness enter the proposed prioritization. The system needs to be performing a business scenario for the experiment's effects to be observed; an oversimplified scenario can leave important tasks unexercised. The guide describes production traffic branches or canary versions as possible ways of limiting exposure, and suggests replaying production variables or using representative simulated data when working outside production. These are alternative arrangements for the experimental situation, each retaining work to make the scenario relevant. [AFC-W014, printed pp. 9–10]

Measurement is designed alongside the intervention. The selected passage recommends observing extremes as well as averages, supporting tasks as well as final outputs, and designated stopping indicators. Its categories include time, throughput, failures, resource use, and business feedback such as user retries or error reports. The choice of metrics is to depend on the object, scenario, and monitoring facilities. This connects what can be concluded to what the experiment is equipped to observe. The guide does not treat the introduction of a disturbance as a sufficient account of the resulting service condition. [AFC-W014, printed pp. 10–11]

Cost limits the proposed coverage. The guide says that simulating every disturbance is impractical and therefore requires selection. It proposes relevance to the hypothesis, frequency, representativeness, and

<!-- PDF page 225 -->

significant impact as selection considerations. Fixed and random injection are suited to different situations in its account: repeated automation is more suitable for comparatively contained, short-lived disturbances with lower recovery cost, whereas wider, longer, or more costly cases may call for designed exercises at specified times. It further distinguishes single from combined disturbances, with combinations able to expose cascading behavior missed by individual factors. [AFC-W014, printed pp. 11– 13]

The support discussion keeps possible losses visible. Production experiments can cause failure; a system with inadequate observability makes defects harder to identify and locate; a weak initial stability basis can make repeated exercises disruptive and demoralizing. The guide discusses containment and lower-risk environments as possible responses. Its culture account calls for exposing rather than hiding defects  and for habits developed through practice. [AFC-W014, printed pp. 23–24]

Return on investment is explicitly difficult to assess, partly because a prevented failure is less conspicuous than a realized incident. The guide proposes separate assessment of adoption, capabilities, and benefits, with the framework adapted to the organization's people, business, and architecture. Selected benefit indicators concern response efficiency, repeated defects, monitoring and detection, transparency, and experimental efficiency. Its architectural and procedural extensions ask whether discovered problems are actually resolved, including whether recurring lower-level errors warrant changes in development or operations discipline. The framework proposes what to examine when assessing benefits. [AFC-W014, printed pp. 24–28]

### Owotogbe and colleagues: what a review can tell us about the practice

Owotogbe and colleagues: what a review can tell us about the practice

Joshua Owotogbe and colleagues' v2 review manuscript, dated 19 June 2025, brings together 96 selected sources: 49 academic sources and 47 grey-literature sources. It reports on a chaos-centered body of material covering January 2016 through April 2024. [AFC-W011, §§3, 6, 8]

Its selection and analysis procedure helps define that scope. Searches covered four academic databases and grey literature, followed by eligibility screening and quality assessment. The eligibility requirements included English and accessible full text, while exclusions concerned short items and material outside the chosen chaos-engineering focus, among other conditions. The practice account distinguishes clear objectives, small initial experiments, automation, monitoring, stakeholder participation, and documentation. ### Verhulst: where the system boundary places improvement

Eric Verhulst proposes assured reliability and resilience levels distinguished by how components meet a contract in the presence of faults. A component may itself be a system within a larger system. He distinguishes preserving service through redundancy and repair from a wider process that updates the system, and describes aviation through a boundary including operating conditions, stakeholders, feedback, and authorities. If a technical artifact changes only through surrounding maintenance and institutional activity, the source account concerns that larger arrangement. ### Caulkin's account of Seddon: some recurring work is created by earlier failure

Caulkin's account of Seddon: some recurring work is created by earlier failure

Simon Caulkin's journalistic account of John Seddon's “failure demand” concerns a different relationship between failure and subsequent activity. A customer calls again because something was not done, was done incorrectly, or did not resolve the original need. The repeat contact is work that the service's own earlier conduct helped create. Caulkin contrasts this with the demand the service exists to meet. The distinction concerns the history and purpose of a request, rather than treating every arrival as an independent unit of useful output. [SG-W020]

His selected insurance example describes agents constrained by detailed contracts, repeated transactions to resolve one case, and a redesign intended to let an agent complete the case with appropriate access to expertise. A second example contrasts apparently successful project and activity indicators with whether distressed customers actually return to normal. These reported cases make the argument more informative than a general call for efficiency: the proposed change concerns the organization of the work that generates later demand. Caulkin does not identify the organizations. [SG-W020]

The relevant proposed reduction in work depends on meeting the original purpose more successfully. Refusing access, leaving a problem unresolved, or reclassifying a legitimate need out of the count would not establish the mechanism Caulkin describes. His argument is about reducing preventable return work through service design. [SG-W020]

## S42 Representations, standards and knowledge infrastructures

S42   Representations, standards and knowledge infrastructures

### Making something available differs from making it usable

Making something available differs from making it usable

Physical records, symbolic systems, programs, classifications, standards and assurance arrangements make information available for action. Their design shapes which operations a person can perform and which distinctions a representation preserves.

### Pattee: symbols require physical realization and interpretation

Pattee: symbols require physical realization and interpretation

Pattee's selected discussion relates dynamical laws, constraints, memory and symbolic control. He argues against accounts that detach symbols from physics and against accounts that assume real-time sensorimotor dynamics explain every aspect of life. A relatively persistent memory structure can affect a time-dependent process through physical mechanisms that read or respond to it. The symbolic description and the dynamics are distinguishable, but the connection needs an implementation. [UX-W012, discussion of laws, constraints and memory]

This account does not classify every useful physical constraint as a symbol. A structure can constrain motion without serving as a record interpreted within a symbolic-control system. Pattee's discussion of flexible mechanical constraints, switches and molecular mechanisms asks how stored alternatives can enter dynamic operation. The relevant material is the connection between a comparatively rate-independent record and rate-dependent execution, not a free-standing informational cause outside  physical processes.

Pattee’s epistemic-cut argument relates descriptions to operations and connects symbolic control with his account of biological origins. [UX-W012]

Etxeberria and Moreno’s reconstruction of Pattee’s hierarchical-control account [UX-W014] distinguishes structural hierarchies from control hierarchies and discusses constraints, records and symbols in that setting. Its usefulness is the distinction between assembling levels of material organization and specifying how a record controls a process. A higher descriptive level does not become a controller merely by being drawn above another level. [UX-W013, selected manuscript pp. 2–4 and concluding caveat]

### Darwiche and Marquis: choose a representation for the operations required

Darwiche and Marquis: choose a representation for the operations required

A Knowledge Compilation Map examines propositional theories compiled in advance into representations suited to later reasoning. Darwiche and Marquis compare languages along two dimensions: succinctness and the queries or transformations they support in polynomial time. A language can be convenient for one operation and unsuitable for another. The choice is therefore application-dependent rather than a contest to find one universally smallest or fastest representation. [TA-W008, printed pp. 229–236]

Their framework treats several classes as restrictions on directed acyclic representations in negation normal form. Conditions such as decomposability, determinism and smoothness impose different structures. Those restrictions affect which operations are tractable and how large a representation may need to be. A more concise language can leave an operation hard; a less concise compiled form can make repeated queries manageable.

The authors propose identifying the needed operations before choosing a target language. The relevant saving is not simply deleting information. An equivalent representation can reorganize the information so that a particular query is easier. Conversely, having a small equivalent representation in principle does not establish that it can be constructed efficiently from the original input. Compilation and representation size remain separate obligations.

<!-- PDF page 229 -->

### Jones, Gomard and Sestoft: move known computation to an earlier stage

Jones, Gomard and Sestoft: move known computation to an earlier stage

The opening of Partial Evaluation and Automatic Program Generation explains specialization using a program with some inputs already known. A partial evaluator produces a residual program for the inputs still unknown. When given those remaining inputs, the specialized program is intended to return the result the original would have returned from the complete input. The relation is semantic, while its efficiency depends on what can actually be evaluated in advance. [TA-W009, selected printed pp. 1–4 and staging passages pp. 6–9]

The authors' power-function example is concrete. Knowing the exponent in advance can allow recursive control and exponent-dependent work to be unfolded or precomputed. Knowing the base instead, while leaving the exponent unknown, need not yield a significant speedup in the same example. Advance information has to match the structure of the computation; any known input is not equally useful.

Their term binding-time engineering concerns changing when subcomputations occur. It retains the earlier computation, the specialized code and the circumstances in which the preparation remains valid. Correct specialization is not by itself proof of faster execution or lower total cost. [TA-W009]

### Necula and Rahul: a smaller oracle can guide a trusted checker

Necula and Rahul: a smaller oracle can guide a trusted checker

The selected 2001 oracle-based checking paper describes a variant of proof-carrying code. Trusted inference rules are represented as a logic programme, and a nondeterministic interpreter checks the property. A supplied bit stream resolves choices that would otherwise require search. The oracle guides the checker; it does not replace the rules that determine whether the proposed steps are acceptable. [TA-W011, PDF pp. 1–3]

The article contrasts this with carrying an explicit proof syntax for every inference. Its proposal can exploit directed or simple checking procedures without charging the full proof-size overhead of a very general representation. In the reported type-safety examples for code compiled from Java, the authors report oracle sizes averaging twelve percent of code size and a factor-of-thirty reduction relative to an earlier proof representation.

The retained trusted components are decisive: the policy, verification-condition generation, inference rules and checker must be appropriate. Cryptographic evidence of who supplied code differs from evidence about what the code does. A compact oracle can reduce transmitted proof information while verification still requires execution of the trusted procedure. Safety remains relative to the specified property, not unrestricted harmlessness. [TA-W011]

Necula introduced Proof-Carrying Code in 1997; the account above follows the later paper. [TA-W010]

### Edmonds: greedy choice depends on an independence structure

Edmonds: greedy choice depends on an independence structure

Edmonds considers finite linear-objective combinatorial optimization and asks why certain problems admit efficient algorithms. In a matroidal problem, feasible independent sets satisfy a structure that permits a greedy procedure to select weighted elements while preserving feasibility. A simple sequence of choices can be globally justified under these conditions, rather than relying on a general belief that local decisions are good. [TA-W012, printed pp. 127–130]

The representation of the feasible family matters: the source explicitly asks how membership is determined. An independence test or oracle is part of the algorithmic setting. Arbitrary constraints do not necessarily have the exchange property behind the characterization.

The selected characterization explains how an independence structure supports a computational method. [TA-W012]

<!-- PDF page 230 -->

### Liskov and Wing: an interface must preserve behavior over time

Liskov and Wing: an interface must preserve behavior over time

Liskov and Wing's selected account of behavioral subtyping asks when an object of a subtype can be used while reasoning with the supertype's specification. Matching method names or signatures is insufficient. Invariants and the allowed evolution of state matter. The source includes ways of preserving history properties directly through constraints or indirectly by explaining additional methods through operations already available at the supertype. [W087, selected §§1–2 and 5.2–5.3]

Aliasing makes the issue substantive. The same mutable object can be accessible through more than one name, with one user reasoning through the supertype and another invoking subtype methods. Effects of the additional method can later be visible through the first name. A contract that considers only an isolated call can therefore miss behavior that undermines the first user's reasoning. [W087, printed pp. 1811–1815]

The stack-and-bag discussion explains how an additional operation can preserve or violate what remains fixed in the abstract history. The account thus concerns substitution under a stated behavioral contract, not an absence of knowledge about implementation. The contract itself must specify the relevant guarantees and be justified against the implementation. Liveness and certain cross-object safety properties lie outside the stated scope. [W087, selected printed pp. 1822–1829 and 1836–1837]

### Tonet and da Paz: knowledge sharing continues after initial transmission

Tonet and da Paz: knowledge sharing continues after initial transmission

Tonet and da Paz propose four phases of workplace knowledge sharing: initiation, implementation, support and incorporation. Their account attends to the source, recipient, knowledge and context rather than treating sharing as the delivery of a detachable message. Support after initial transfer matters when the recipient encounters difficulties using what was received. [W088, selected four-phase model and support discussion]

The sequence helps distinguish access from incorporation into practice. A proposal can fail because participants lack the relevant understanding, opportunities or contextual support, even after information has been supplied. The model offers questions and guidance for examining the process.

### Buckland: stored things are not identical to knowledge

Buckland: stored things are not identical to knowledge

The conceptual discussion in Buckland's Information as thing distinguishes information as a process, knowledge and evidence treated as a thing. Storage and retrieval systems directly handle objects or representations: documents, records, data and other things regarded as informative. Calling them information does not guarantee that a user has learned from them or that their content is true. What counts as informative is situational and can depend on agreement about evidence. [GL-W020, situational information and the topography of information-related activities]

His topography of information-related activities distinguishes the constraints of museums, archives, printed libraries and coded-data systems. Selection, representation, identification, location and physical access are not the same task in each setting. A convenient representation can support one activity without preserving every physical or evidential property of its subject. The account is conceptual classification.

### Potts: conventions and context both contribute to meaning

Potts: conventions and context both contribute to meaning

Potts's exposition distinguishes conventional linguistic content from context-dependent interpretation. Indexicals require a setting to determine what is referred to; implicatures involve what a speaker conveys beyond a literal formulation. Compositional rules can support interpretation without eliminating the situation in which an utterance is used. [GL-W014, selected body on semantics and pragmatics]

<!-- PDF page 231 -->

This supplies a substantive qualification to any picture in which a message is wholly self-contained. The recipient's context and conventions can carry information not repeated in the words.

### Star and Lampland: standards coordinate while retaining local work

Star and Lampland: standards coordinate while retaining local work

The selected pages of Reckoning with Standards examine standards as arrangements embedded in activities, rather than neutral descriptions floating above them. A standardized category, measure or procedure can enable work across settings while fitting some local circumstances better than others. The chapter's account directs attention to classifications and their consequences for those who must use them. Uniformity can facilitate coordination and also obscure variation or make accommodations necessary.

Archives: context is part of description

### Internal control: separation, authorization and review remain different functions

## S39 Lafitte, Simondon and technical objects

S39   Lafitte, Simondon and technical objects

### Technical operation, its conditions and its human setting

Technical operation, its conditions and its human setting

Simondon's On the Mode of Existence of Technical Objects examines technical genesis, functioning and culture. Four scholarly articles reconstruct Lafitte's programme. Archaeology and conservation accounts address human dependence on things and the preservation of material objects.

### Simondon: understand an object through its genesis

Simondon: understand an object through its genesis

Simondon begins by arguing that technical objects are poorly understood when culture sees them only as useful tools, alien machinery or imagined robots. They embody human invention and natural processes. To understand them requires technical knowledge: neither owning a machine, operating it habitually nor knowing an isolated scientific law supplies the whole account. His proposed cultural integration of technical knowledge is normative as well as explanatory. [W020, introduction, pp. 15–21]

The first part favors the genesis of a technical type over classification only by use. Objects performing the same named function can have very different internal organizations and histories. A later object is not better in every setting. Simondon's comparison of engines notes that an older design can be more repairable, autonomous and tolerant of imperfect conditions in a particular use. The history is not simply a list of newer devices replacing worse ones. [W020, part I, printed pp. 25–29]

Concretization is his central account of technical development. In an abstract arrangement, parts are conceived as separately complete organs, each with a dedicated function, and must then be made compatible. Their residual interactions can create burdens or conflicts. A more concrete arrangement develops a mutually supporting organization in which a structure participates in several compatible functions. The change is not merely cosmetic simplification or a smaller number of components.

### Cooling fins that also reinforce an engine

Cooling fins that also reinforce an engine

The engine cylinder-head example makes the mechanism precise. Fins exchange heat with external air, while the same ribbed structure stiffens the head. Because ribbing supplies rigidity, the wall can be thinner than an equally rigid unreinforced shell; the thinner wall can also improve heat exchange. In Simondon's account, structural and thermal functions converge rather than simply competing for a compromise thickness. [W020, printed pp. 27–28; PDF pp. 39–40]

The best location of ribs for strength need not coincide with the best position for airflow and cooling. Simondon therefore describes designs that remain mixed or incompletely concrete.

Simondon connects internal coherence with material, construction-work and operating-energy economies in particular developments. An air-cooled design still needs heat transfer to its surroundings; a water-cooled system can retain useful thermal buffering even while adding pumps and other dependencies. Similarly, removing a manual starting action can create dependence on a battery. The examples are historically situated comparisons, not timeless rankings of all engines. [W020, printed pp. 29–33]

### Technical progress can reorganize the functions themselves

Technical progress can reorganize the functions themselves

Simondon distinguishes small improvements within an existing organization from a more substantial reorganization that changes the relation among functions. A previously troublesome effect can sometimes become a functional resource. The vacuum-tube sequence illustrates how electrode arrangement, feedback and electric fields are reorganized rather than handled as entirely separate problems. Changing

<!-- PDF page 235 -->

relative geometry can perform work otherwise assigned to an added specialized electrode, while another change can require an additional component. Concretization therefore has no general rule that fewer parts are always better. [W020, printed pp. 32–39]

The Crookes-to-Coolidge example concerns the separation of roles previously assigned to gas that was needed for one effect while obstructing another. The later arrangement retains a heated cathode, vacuum, fields, cooling and precise construction. Likewise Simondon's account of the diesel engine treats compression heat as useful while retaining more exact fuel-injection requirements. A structural gain can be accompanied by a narrower tolerance for some other condition. [W020, printed pp. 38–47]

Minor improvements can be useful without resolving an underlying antagonism. The rotating-anode discussion adds motion to spread heating while preserving a concentrated source. It also adds a new dependency: actual rotation must occur. An energized motor circuit is not the same fact as a rotating target, and a protective interlock can itself fail. [W020, printed pp. 39–43]

He treats complete concretization as a limiting condition, not an achieved property of every mature machine. Full knowledge of all relevant physical interactions is unavailable in practice, and experiments remain necessary.

### Hypertely: high performance can narrow the usable setting

Hypertely: high performance can narrow the usable setting

Simondon uses hypertely for overadaptation to determinate conditions of production, use or milieu. A highly specialized object may perform well locally while being less capable of functioning elsewhere. Dependence on another technical system is also relevant: a device fitted to one supply network inherits its constraints. Technical success in a narrow environment is consequently different from broad autonomy. [W020, printed pp. 53–58]

Simondon distinguishes adaptation to a given environment from creating a technical–geographical relation that helps sustain the object. This leads to the associated milieu.

### The Guimbal turbine: a mutually enabling environment

The Guimbal turbine: a mutually enabling environment

Simondon's Guimbal example places a turbine and a compact generator within a water conduit. Water supplies the driving energy and removes heat. Pressurized oil lubricates, insulates the windings, transfers heat toward the casing and prevents water entering through the shaft seals. The small generator becomes possible because the surrounding arrangement supplies the heat removal needed at that size. The environment is not an incidental container; its operation participates in making the architecture viable. [W020, printed pp. 57–62; PDF pp. 69–70]

Simondon calls this reciprocal operational relation self-conditioning. A generator designed to depend on water cooling cannot deliver the same power in air.

The associated milieu is partly constituted through natural processes and partly through the technical operating regime. Inventive anticipation represents a future compatible whole during design. Simondon extends this relation philosophically to life and thought.

### An ensemble can require separation rather than a common milieu

An ensemble can require separation rather than a common milieu

The audiometer discussion identifies the technical boundary by the conditions of functioning, rather than the manufacturer's enclosure. A supply, oscillators, an amplifier, headphones or a speaker, and the acoustic room can all matter. Stable frequencies and intensities require suitable temperature, voltage and noise conditions. In a relevant configuration, the room belongs to the complete apparatus even though it is outside the instrument's box. [W020, printed pp. 63–66]

<!-- PDF page 236 -->

Simondon distinguishes merely stabilizing a power supply from feedback that regulates a particular variable. If the supply does not respond to the oscillator's relevant deviation, it cannot be described as regulating that deviation. He also identifies beneficial and harmful common dependencies. Shared oscillator drift can cancel in a beat-frequency arrangement, while interactions with an amplifier can interfere with the intended behavior.

An ensemble can therefore require separate supplies, shielding and high-impedance connections. A common associated milieu is useful for a technical individual only when the coupled functions support one another appropriately. Making every component share a medium is not his criterion for a well-organized ensemble. The source's own example includes deliberate insulation against unwanted  interaction. [W020, PDF pp. 75–77]

This is also why element, individual and ensemble are not simply names for small, medium and large objects. Their distinction concerns relations of functioning and the associated milieu.

### Small objects can carry a large technical history

Small objects can carry a large technical history

Simondon describes technical inheritance through elements, individuals and ensembles. An element can carry properties developed in a much larger production setting. A spring, adze or needle embodies metallurgy, forging, treatment and skilled fabrication, even if the finished item looks simple. Its visible shape does not reveal all the knowledge and organized work needed to give it the relevant properties. [W020, printed pp. 67–76]

Simondon distinguishes synchronization of technical developments from complete historical determination. He asks the reader to consider the ensemble that manufactured an object's elements.

The discussion of tools and machine operation likewise retains cleaning, lubrication, sharpening, waste removal, belt adjustment and maintenance. The historical displacement of the human tool-bearing individual does not remove humans from technical ensembles. Their relation changes, and Simondon assigns importance to coordination, invention, interpretation and upkeep. [W020, printed pp. 77–81 and 129–140]

### Technical knowledge is neither mere habit nor a detached formula

Technical knowledge is neither mere habit nor a detached formula

The second part considers different modes of acquiring technical knowledge. Apprenticeship can transmit implicit practical skill; reflective engineering connects operation with more explicit scientific understanding. Simondon criticizes social rankings that separate learned culture from technical work. Some categorical historical and psychological claims in the discussion remain source idealizations rather than established findings about all children, adults or trades. [W020, printed pp. 103–127]

The encyclopedia supplies a concrete example of portable technical representation. Schematics communicate selected structure without reproducing every detail of an image or practical encounter. Simondon also warns that a simultaneous inventory can hide the inventions, failures and crises through which technical objects became possible.

His ambition for information theory is broad: it would mediate among sciences, techniques and learning. [W020, printed pp. 114–127]

### Timing, signals and the energy that an operation uses

Timing, signals and the energy that an operation uses

In discussing the governor and load changes, Simondon distinguishes reacting after speed has changed from receiving a separate signal about a disturbance soon enough to act. A faster information path can

<!-- PDF page 237 -->

matter because waiting for the output deviation can allow an undesirable event. [W020, printed pp. 142– 147]

The book distinguishes efficiency in energy conversion from fidelity in signal transmission. A narrow resonance useful for energy transfer can be poor for preserving a broader range of informational variation. Low carrier energy also encounters noise. Simondon discusses thermal and shot noise and the importance of bandwidth and signal conditions. [W020, printed pp. 145–150]

Metastability and relaxation explain how a small trigger redirects stored potential energy: the signal does not supply all the energy released. Synchronizing oscillators require compatible phase and frequency conditions. [W020, printed pp. 151–156]

### Openness, memory and the historical machine claims

Openness, memory and the historical machine claims

Simondon does not equate increasing fixed automation with greater technical perfection. He values a margin of indeterminacy through which a machine can receive information and enter relations with other machines. This can include earlier programming and configuration rather than a human supplying every instruction at the instant of action. [W020, introduction and printed pp. 135–163]

His contrasts between machine memory and lived human memory, and his claims concerning future-oriented invention, are historically situated philosophical positions from the 1958 work. His criticism of  the homeostat concerns a particular device and problem.

The culturally important claim is that technical understanding cannot be replaced merely by ownership or command. Both an owner and a worker can be separated from the machine's operation. Simondon's preference for a responsible technical relation is normative; it does not settle every conflict over property or labor.

### The philosophical third part: a proposed genesis, with plural values

The philosophical third part: a proposed genesis, with plural values

The third part explicitly advances a hypothetical genetic interpretation of technical and other modes of thought. Simondon describes an original unity differentiating into technical and religious phases, with aesthetic and philosophical mediation. These phases are not presented simply as a necessary chronological succession. Their role is to situate technicity within a wider human–world relation, rather than make technology the answer to every question. [W020, part III, printed pp. 167–190]

The relevant aesthetic examples depend on functioning and setting: a sail in wind, a pylon in a valley or a communications installation can be understood differently when their operation is known. Cosmetic appearance can obscure that relation. Yet aesthetic, ethical and technical judgments remain distinguishable. Simondon also warns that a premature apparent reconciliation can stop inquiry too soon. [W020, printed pp. 191–210]

Failure has an explanatory role. A suction pump's limit cannot necessarily be removed by more precise construction; an adequate account must incorporate pressure, material and environmental conditions. This is a source example of revising the conceptual problem rather than merely improving execution. [W020, printed pp. 211–216]

Simondon explicitly separates the value of ease from the value of efficiency. At printed p. 217 he denies an analytic link between them even while regarding their combination as desirable. An easy action is not automatically resource-efficient. Practical experience informs a plurality of values. The later chapters develop political, ethical and cultural proposals about mediation and responsibility. [W020]

<!-- PDF page 238 -->

### The material mold and the continued act of construction

The material mold and the continued act of construction

The conclusion returns to a technical operation obscured by descriptions that name only a worker, an intention and a result. In the clay-and-mold example, the worker prepares malleable clay and a material mold, brings them together and applies pressure. The coupled physical system then effects the taking of form. The mold is an actual prepared object, not an abstract shape floating independently of matter. [W020, printed pp. 247–253; PDF p. 261]

Simondon calls for knowledge of the operation itself, beyond the customary gesture that brings it about. The worker prepares the clay and mold, while their physical interaction effects the taking of form.

The following pages reject a once-for-all view of construction. Manufactured units realize the inventive schema imperfectly and require adjustment, repair and sometimes running-in. Maintenance continues construction. His claim that serviceable objects do not deteriorate is explained through replacement and repair, not literal immunity to wear. A technical object can carry knowledge and still require a competent recipient to interpret, maintain and adapt it. [W020, conclusion, PDF pp. 267–269]

The proposed response includes channels for technical information and worker participation following actual operations rather than only the social hierarchy. The conclusion also distinguishes a productivity number from the technical schema: different arrangements can produce the same output figure while functioning differently.

### Lafitte through Sandrone, Vaccari and Lawler

Lafitte through Sandrone, Vaccari and Lawler

Sandrone, Vaccari and Lawler reconstruct three connected dimensions of Lafitte's thought: how to study machines, what sort of organized bodies machines are, and how human life and machinery develop in relation. They distinguish the art of conceiving, building and ensuring operation from descriptive history or mechanography and from a proposed science of machines, mechanology. Physical events occur within machines, but a list of those events does not exhaust the organization of the machine as an object of inquiry. [UX-W023, especially PDF pp. 2–6]

Their account identifies passive, active and reflex or reflective machines. Passive cases such as columns or rafts can do useful work through resistance or support without an internally cycling transformation. Active machines transform, transmit or transport energy. Reflex machines regulate operation through sensitivity to their surroundings. These are Lafitte's categories as reconstructed by the authors. A passive object is not useless, and an active or reflex object is not automatically more economical. [UX-W023, PDF pp. 6–11]

The wider proposed organology includes natural and artificial organized bodies. It asks about relationships among machines, organisms and human organization without reducing them to a single physics formula. Human creation matters to the existence of machines, but their operating properties and lineages are not arbitrary consequences of an inventor's intention. The article relates this to ethical and political questions about living with machines. It expressly presents an early programme and germs of arguments, rather than a finished unified theory. [UX-W023, PDF pp. 9–14]

Sandrone, Vaccari and Lawler's account reconstructs Lafitte's Réflexions sur la science des machines (1932). [W074, through UX-W023]

### Guffroy and Bontems: a lineage is a historical problem

Guffroy and Bontems: a lineage is a historical problem

Guffroy and Bontems reconstruct the genealogy of mechanology while asking how a technical lineage can be identified. Their account distinguishes the 1932 work, Simondon's 1958 thesis, his mediated encounter with Lafitte through Jean Le Moyne in 1968, and later colloquia and continuators. The dates

<!-- PDF page 239 -->

prevent an easy assertion that Lafitte directly generated the argument of the 1958 book. Similarities and later acknowledgment do not establish that earlier influence. [UX-W024, printed pp. 255–280]

The article also treats the organization of machine science as unfinished. What counts as a lineage, branch or generation depends partly on the scale and criterion of comparison. Data collection, processing and representation need more stable methods. Its discussion of genetic diagrams includes abandonment, resurgence, saturation, branching and hybridization, rather than inevitable progress along a single line. Institutional failure is not taken to settle the worth of the questions, but neither is methodological ambition treated as a completed synthesis.

The authors report criticism of attempts to unite naturalist and formalist approaches in other scholarship. They also distinguish classification by function from classification through functioning in comparing Lafitte and Simondon. This distinction concerns functioning, while Sandrone and colleagues emphasize intrinsic organization. [UX-W024]

### Bontems: several aspects can coexist in the same object

Bontems: several aspects can coexist in the same object

Bontems's article reconstructs Simondon's classification and develops it through later material. It explains concretization through structural and functional synergy, while retaining hypertely and the associated-milieu criterion for element, individual and ensemble. The article notes ambiguities in early examples and the need to distinguish the 1958 text from later lectures and ethical work. [UX-W025, printed pp. 184–190]

The later passive, active and informational classification can identify different performance aspects within one object. Structural integrity, energy transformation and fidelity of information all matter, with their own supports: resistance to wear, energy supply, sensors, filtering or cooling. Bontems proposes a matrix crossing types and levels; it is his analytical proposal rather than a verbatim table from Simondon. [UX-W025, printed pp. 190–196; matrix, PDF p. 12]

His ChemCam example describes separate structural and thermal validation, optical and electronic validation, and later combination and compatibility checking. The point is not that separate tests make integration unnecessary. Different aspects must first be examined and then checked together. He also qualifies the idea that infrastructure, energy and communication technologies necessarily form one beneficial synergy. Network participation can impose dependencies and constraints.

A programme prepared earlier can reduce instructions supplied during action. Bontems connects stored programmes with later adaptation. [UX-W025]

### Marratt: resonance without a simple direct descent

Marratt: resonance without a simple direct descent

Marratt offers an architectural and historiographic reading of the relation between Lafitte and Simondon. It explores convergences, differences and multiple technical temporalities, including networks as encounters among natural structure, human need and invention. Its operative body recognizes the mediated later encounter, even where an abbreviated introductory account might invite a simpler genealogy. This is an interpretive account, not a finished formal mechanology. [UX-W026, printed pp. 203 –214]

Marratt's paired quotation and translation differ: the quotation says that machines cannot be defined any better than living beings, while the translation suggests that living beings define machines best. The latter wording changes the claim. [UX-W026, note 11 and associated body]

<!-- PDF page 240 -->

### Sigaut and related accounts of mechanology

Sigaut and related accounts of mechanology

Part IV of Sigaut's manuscript reconstructs a debate about machines, technology and human activity. It questions whether renaming a science of machines supplies a genuinely new undertaking, and it distinguishes the machine phenomenon from an account exhausted by physical sciences. It also locates proposals extending inquiry beyond objects toward human activity. [RGC-W035, PDF pp. 25–30]

The abstract of Hayward and Thibault's Ethics in Jacques Lafitte's Mechanology objects to a precursor-to-cybernetics reading that overlooks Lafitte's ethical and social purpose. [RGC-W033, abstract]

Sigaut comments on Lafitte's 1933 Sur la science des machines. [RGC-W034, through RGC-W035]

### Hodder: mutual dependencies and an unfinished integration

Hodder: mutual dependencies and an unfinished integration

The conclusions of Hodder's 2011 article describe human–thing entanglement through interdependent changes in material and social practices. His pottery discussion relates changes to houses, hearths, bricks and cooking, rather than explaining an artifact lineage solely by transmission or reproductive success. A trait's fittingness concerns how it works within those mutual dependencies. [GL-W012, printed pp. 172– 173]

Hodder explicitly acknowledges that his attempted integration has not fully brought the different theories together. He still argues for the value of a partial integrative account.

In Where Are We Heading?, Hodder asks where the wheel ends as an object of historical explanation. A wagon wheel needs an axle and a frame, as well as a source of motion. Making the wheel calls for tools and carpentry skills. Drawing the wagon with cattle calls for a yoke and trained animals. Where wheels serve road transport, road building and upkeep enter the account as well. Hodder argues that different answers about where the object ends lead to different accounts of its origin and use. [GL-W096, pp. 54– 55]

### Conservation: preserving information can constrain intervention

Conservation: preserving information can constrain intervention

The Canadian Association for Conservation of Cultural Property defines conservation around safeguarding culturally significant qualities with the least appropriate intervention. Its statement includes examination, documentation, prevention, preservation, restoration and reconstruction. Preventive action can be directed at an object's surroundings rather than repeatedly treating the object itself. [GL-W099, definition]

The source explains why more intervention can be worse: treatment can erase information about manufacture, use and prior history. Earlier repairs or wear may themselves be significant. Treatment materials should avoid future harm and, as far as possible, remain removable; documentation should distinguish an addition from original material. The degree of intervention involves trained judgment and consultation with the custodian. This is a professional purpose and set of principles.

The Canadian Conservation Institute's selected painting guidance gives more concrete material examples. An unstable support or inherent material problem can persist after a treatment. A controlled microenvironment can reduce environmental variation, while ongoing delamination can still require professional intervention. The account therefore distinguishes shielding an object from repairing every internal defect. [GL-W100, inherent vice and microenvironments]

In the documented Buffalo Stampede example, consolidation did not remove the painting's sensitivity to humidity because reactive glue remained in its structure. An enclosed frame was added to moderate the local environment. In Charlottetown Revisited, the account describes adding supportive inserts and a

<!-- PDF page 241 -->

protective back rather than removing the painting from its original strainer. These documented professional decisions retain historical material and improve support. [GL-W100, selected examples]
