## S09 Multilevel coordination: arranging local decisions to meet an overall requirement

S09   Multilevel coordination: arranging local decisions to meet an overall requirement

### Local decisions and overall performance

Local decisions and overall performance

Mihajlo Mesarović, D. Macko and Yasuhiko Takahara's Theory of Hierarchical, Multilevel, Systems concerns descriptions of complex systems, local decision problems and overall performance. Its publisher preview sets out a programme for arranging local decisions and higher-level intervention to meet a larger requirement without making the higher level solve the entire problem again. [W096, publisher preview; W097, pp. 23–26; SB-W008, pp. 3–5]

The 1969 coordination paper develops the formal mechanism. Richardson’s 1975 conference paper, Findeisen and colleagues’ 1980 book, and Abraham, Tribolet and Winter’s 2013 article examine practical control, modeling and organizational difficulties. [W097; SB-W006; SB-W007; SB-W008]

### Strata, layers and echelons ask different questions

Strata, layers and echelons ask different questions

Richardson describes three distinct hierarchy concepts in the 1970 programme. Strata concern levels of description or abstraction. Layers concern decision complexity. Echelons concern priority of action and organizational coordination. A coarser representation, a more complex decision and a superior organizational office are consequently different things. They may be related in an application without becoming interchangeable meanings of higher level. [W097, p. 24]

The distinction helps recover what has been delegated. A detailed model and an aggregate model can describe the same system differently. A local regulator can act within a setting selected by another decision process. An organization can assign intervention rights among offices. Calling all three hierarchical would conceal whether the relevant economy concerns representation, the division of computation or the allocation of authority. The sources deliberately provide several descriptions for these different relationships. [W097, pp. 24–26; SB-W007, hierarchy framework]

Richardson also describes the programme as combining heuristics for decomposing and representing large problems, mathematical theory, and methods for improving behavior. Satisfactory performance, rather than exact optimization, is included in his reconstruction. [W097, pp. 24–25]

### The 1969 paper: local success has to map into overall success

The 1969 paper: local success has to map into overall success

In Two Coordination Principles and Their Application in Large Scale Systems Control, the same three authors distinguish an overall control problem, local control problems and a coordination problem. Local units directly influence the controlled process. The higher or supremal unit acts indirectly by influencing those units. Its task is not defined simply as being above them: it has to make their decisions compatible with the overall requirement. [SB-W008, pp. 3–5]

The formal setup considers families of local problems indexed by intervention parameters. A transformation maps a joint solution of the local problems into a candidate solution of the overall problem. The crucial condition is that every relevant joint solution under the chosen intervention maps into an overall solution. Without such a condition, separately satisfactory local decisions need not constitute a satisfactory whole. A decomposition supplies multiple problems; it does not automatically supply their compatibility. [SB-W008, pp. 4–5]

The law of consistency constrains the coordinator's own problem. Solving that problem should be sufficient for the joint local results to meet the overall requirement. One trivial way to ensure this is to

<!-- PDF page 244 -->

make the coordinator solve the complete original problem. The authors explicitly recognize why that misses the intended advantage: the art is to find a simpler coordination problem while retaining consistency. [SB-W008, p. 5]

Coordinability adds an existence question. It concerns whether some intervention in the specified family can produce the required relation between local solutions and the overall solution. That differs from saying what follows if a suitable intervention is found. The paper itself distinguishes a principle's applicability from the existence of a parameter that meets its matching condition. [SB-W008, pp. 5, 8]

### Prediction and balance retain different work

Prediction and balance retain different work

Interaction prediction begins by specifying anticipated interface inputs for the local units. Each local controller optimizes with those predictions fixed. When their controls are applied to the connected process, actual interface inputs result. The coordinator compares actual inputs with predictions and changes the predictions to reduce the discrepancy. The architecture has separated local decisions by supplying information about their interfaces; it has retained a problem of making that information consistent with actual joint operation. [SB-W008, pp. 6–8]

Interaction balance instead modifies local performance functions. The local problems then optimize over their controls and desired interface inputs. Actual operation supplies interfaces that may differ from those desired. The higher level changes its intervention parameters to bring the desired and actual values into agreement. Local autonomy in this construction is conditional on the objective modifications and on the interfaces supplied by the connected system. [SB-W008, pp. 7–8]

The authors allow a mismatch measure to be minimized when exact zero error is not attainable. Such a formulation is a further problem definition. [SB-W008, p. 8]

### What the conditional optimality argument actually uses

What the conditional optimality argument actually uses

Theorem I in the 1969 paper supplies sufficient conditions for applying interaction balance. For every relevant intervention and feasible overall control, global cost must be expressible through an order-preserving aggregation of the modified local costs evaluated at actual interfaces. Local units must attain  minima over the stated local controls and freely chosen interface inputs. If their chosen interfaces then match those arising from the joint controls, the resulting overall control minimizes global cost. [SB-W008, pp. 9–10; appendix A]

The proof explains why all these premises matter. Each local minimizing pair is no worse in its local cost than the corresponding pair associated with an arbitrary feasible overall alternative. Order preservation carries these componentwise comparisons into a comparison of global cost. Matching allows the locally selected pairs to be interpreted as the actual interconnected result. The conclusion concerns that declared objective and feasible set, not every property a real system might be expected to have. [SB-W008, appendix A, proof of theorem I]

Theorem II provides an additive special case. Modifications can be introduced into local objectives while summing to zero at feasible interconnections. The overall cost is then preserved by those modifications, allowing the first theorem's reasoning to apply. The important feature is the verified relation among objectives, rather than an assumption that any collection of individually optimized goals will combine well. [SB-W008, p. 10; appendix A]

Existence results add further hypotheses about attained and unique local minima, convexity, lower semicontinuity, compactness and the relevant dual relation. These hypotheses cannot be suppressed when moving from the conditional matching argument to a claim that matching can be achieved. The

<!-- PDF page 245 -->

paper does not provide a general convergence algorithm, a response-time guarantee or a measured reduction in total computation. [SB-W008, theorems III–V and appendices]

In Example III of the 1969 paper, the printed parameter makes one local quadratic unbounded below despite the claimed minimum. Theorem V's compactness reasoning also requires appropriate space and attainment assumptions beyond an unrestricted normed-space reading. [SB-W008, example III, proof of theorem V and appendix B]

Four questions consequently remain separate in this account: whether matched local solutions satisfy the global criterion; whether a matching intervention exists; whether an actual procedure reaches it; and whether the procedure does so reliably and soon enough for the real application. An answer to an earlier question does not answer the later ones. Correct specification of the real objective and constraints is another obligation throughout. [SB-W008; SB-W006, ch. 1]

### Findeisen and colleagues: control must work on an operating system

Findeisen and colleagues: control must work on an operating system

The introductory chapter of Control and Coordination in Hierarchical Systems, by W. Findeisen, F. N. Bailey, M. Brdys, K. Malinowski, P. Tatjewski and A. Wozniak, develops the practical coordination problem. [SB-W006, introduction and ch. 1, pp. 4–74]

Its introduction identifies reasons to divide decision responsibility: limited individual capability, spatial separation, communication cost and delay, distorted information, and private local information. For control, it also insists that the system is operating under disturbances and that current information can be used to improve decisions. Models, real constraints, measurement and response horizons are therefore part of the subject from the beginning. [SB-W006, pp. 1–4]

The chapter distinguishes multilayer organization of different control tasks from multilevel decomposition and coordination of related local problems. Different horizons and kinds of information can justify different decision processes. Treating all units as copies of one static optimizer would hide what a faster regulator, a slower planning process or a model-updating function actually does. The architecture has to respect the process and the time available for action. [SB-W006, §§1.2–1.4]

The formulation of global performance has a consequential assumption: it is an order-preserving function of local performances. The authors say that this excludes gamelike situations among decision makers from their discussion. Their coordination results therefore cannot be carried directly into an organization with unresolved conflicting aims simply because its chart contains local units and a center. The required objective relationship has to be supplied, not inferred from the word hierarchy. [SB-W006, p. 36]

Direct coordination illustrates the feasibility problem. The coordinator prescribes outputs and allocates resources; local units then try to achieve those demands. Some demands may be impossible under local equations or constraints, and disturbance or model uncertainty can change the feasible region. Staying inside a known safe region can preserve feasibility but may require conservative decisions and substantial knowledge. Issuing a target is not proof that a local unit can produce it. [SB-W006, pp. 36–38]

The chapter also distinguishes solving local models offline from coordinating people or controllers acting on a real process. An optimization result computed from models becomes open-loop control if applied without correcting it from actual system behavior. In real interaction, separate decision makers can cause instability while each is attempting to do well locally. Even a mathematically convergent coordination scheme needs an appropriate relation to the process operating between its updates. [SB-W006, pp. 40– 41]

<!-- PDF page 246 -->

### An adverse case: decomposition can enlarge the central problem

An adverse case: decomposition can enlarge the central problem

The ammonia-plant example directly challenges an automatic saving from decomposition. The plant contains feed-forward and recycle relationships, including heat flows that contribute to its operation. Cutting it into subprocesses while representing all relevant cross-boundary quantities would require roughly forty coordination variables. Yet the original overall optimization concerned only twenty-two adjustable control variables. The result would be a larger coordination problem plus the added local problems. The authors call that version more complex and expensive than direct treatment. [SB-W006, pp. 42–45]

Their reported response uses engineering understanding and operating experience. Only five quantities were retained as essential coordination variables for an approximate solution; others were related to them, treated as nearly constant or judged less relevant to the objective. The reduction is not supplied by the drawing of the boundary. It depends on knowing which couplings can be compressed or neglected for the application. [SB-W006, pp. 44–45]

This motivates subcoordination: using fewer variables than a strict interface description would require. Its economy is bought through an approximation whose adequacy must be examined. Knowing a model exactly enough to encode a perfect low-dimensional prescription would be a different situation from controlling a process with model–reality differences. The source itself cautions against making that exact-knowledge assumption. [SB-W006, pp. 45–47]

The authors’ plant example provides significant adverse evidence within their account: hierarchical decomposition can increase work, and successful simplification can require more retained system knowledge than the abstract partition suggests. [SB-W006, pp. 43–47]

### Dynamic control, information and model revision

Dynamic control, information and model revision

The introductory chapter extends coordination to dynamic problems with states, time functions and finite horizons. Solving a steady-state problem repeatedly is not automatically an adequate dynamic controller. Actions influence later conditions, and the time spent measuring, communicating and computing can matter to the result. Decomposing a horizon or using a shorter horizon changes the problem unless its consequences are controlled. [SB-W006, ch. 1, dynamic control and information-structure discussions, pp. 49–63]

The information structure specifies who knows what and when. Local decision makers may have measurements unavailable to the coordinator, while the center may possess information about interactions unavailable locally. Feedback can help with model error, but measurements, transmission and interpretation are retained activities. A formally convenient hierarchy is therefore only part of the arrangement needed for actual control. [SB-W006, §1.4]

### Richardson: building and using integrated models

Richardson: building and using integrated models

Richardson's 1975 paper reports on the Multilevel Regionalized World Modeling Project and related work on Lake Erie pollution. Richardson is an insider describing a continuing research programme. His paper connects the earlier framework to later modelling practice and explicitly says that technical and organizational skills developed together. [W097, pp. 23–25]

His Lake Erie discussion uses strata to organize submodels associated with different disciplines. Partial decomposability permits some development and validation before final integration. The qualification is important: in crisis situations, couplings can become stronger. A decomposition useful under ordinary conditions may not preserve the same independence when the situation changes. Integration remains a task even when subgroups can make progress separately. [W097, pp. 25–27]

<!-- PDF page 247 -->

The regionalized world model differentiates regions by relevant economic and political conditions rather than treating the globe as one uniform aggregate. Trade, migration and other flows connect the regions. Within regions, causal, organizational and normative descriptions address different aspects of behavior. Values and beliefs affect the selection among satisfactory policies; allowing users to supply norms interactively is one response to the difficulty of simulating them completely. [W097, pp. 28–30]

This makes retained judgment concrete. Model builders must decide which regional differences matter, how decisions are represented and what belongs in the scenarios. The paper's food-policy example joins separately developed submodels whose detailed documentation is much larger than the conference exposition. Their existence and integration are reported facts about the project. The scenario curves remain historical model outputs under their stated policy assumptions. [W097, pp. 30–31 and figs. 10–12]

Richardson's agenda is unusually explicit about limits. He argues that difficulty quantifying social and value questions does not justify ignoring them. He emphasizes judgment and design in training, cooperation across disciplines and an institutional environment that supports integrated work. A framework for modelling cannot itself create the professional relationships and durable organizations required to use it. [W097, pp. 32–33]

He also questions whether fitting historical data is sufficient validation for long-term models when parameters and structures are changed to explore alternatives. Claims to decision makers should remain conservative relative to actual utility. Institutional pressures can favor short horizons even where a model asks long-term questions. [W097, pp. 33–35]

### Abraham, Tribolet and Winter: transformation as well as operation

Abraham, Tribolet and Winter: transformation as well as operation

Abraham, Tribolet and Winter's 2013 article applies distinctions among strata, layers and echelons to enterprise architecture management. It positions architecture management across these dimensions and proposes interlinked feedback loops for transformation. [SB-W007, hierarchy framework and reference 6]

The authors distinguish a functional understanding of an enterprise from an understanding of its construction. Principles can restrict design freedom and help coordinate planned change, but the relevant perspective is broader than a single place in an organization chart. An architectural model can describe different strata while transformation decisions and intervention responsibilities occupy other dimensions. [SB-W007, introduction and hierarchy discussion]

Their feedback model distinguishes routine optimization within an existing understanding, planned transformation that changes models and goals, and improvisation under severe unpredictable disturbance. The latter can require making sense of a new situation before returning to planned projects and routine operation. The categories are part of the authors' conceptual proposal. [SB-W007, feedback-loop model and fig. 4]

The model also makes continued activity visible. An enterprise must keep operating while it undertakes a transformation, and useful experience must enter its representations if it is to handle a formerly unfamiliar exception routinely later. Models, goals and practices do not update simply because a new diagram is available. The Portuguese Air Force case serves as an illustrative application in the article. [SB-W007, feedback and application sections]

The article’s assertion that observability is universally necessary for controllability is not a general control-theoretic result. Its enterprise-transformation proposal joins observation, modeling and intervention, whereas Mesarović and colleagues’ 1970 book also addresses dynamic control. [SB-W007; W096, contents; W097, p. 24]

### Interventions, objectives and interface compatibility

Interventions, objectives and interface compatibility

These coordination accounts connect local and overall problems through interventions, objectives, interface compatibility, measurement and revision. [SB-W008; SB-W006; W097; SB-W007]

## S13 Information, routines and organizations: Stinchcombe's connected account

S13   Information, routines and organizations: Stinchcombe's connected account

### The task determines which news matters

The task determines which news matters

Arthur Stinchcombe's Information and Organizations develops a connected sociological explanation of organizational structures through the information needed to handle uncertainty. The relevant unit is often a lasting part of an organization engaged with a particular task, rather than either a whole legal firm or an isolated individual decision. Different tasks expose people to different uncertainties, sources of news and opportunities for action. An arrangement that makes useful information available to competent decision makers can consequently have a different structure from an arrangement serving another task. [UX-W003, chs. 1, 10]

Stinchcombe asks where early, useful news about a task's constraints appears and what organizational structure makes a timely response possible. A department may need detailed information about an immediate production difficulty while corporate investment decisions require a different kind of summary over a longer period. Combining all information indiscriminately would obscure those differences. The question concerns what someone needs to know in order to do a particular job, with authority and practical capacity to act on it. [UX-W003, chs. 1, 3–4]

Uncertainty does not mean that no action is possible until everything is known. The book follows staged commitments and differences in the reliability of information. An exploration report, a first successful well and a more developed reserve estimate carry different degrees of uncertainty in its oil-industry example. A knowledgeable recipient can use them differently. Treating all three as equally established would damage the information system rather than simplify it usefully. [UX-W003, ch. 1, especially pp. 13– 15]

Trustworthy information therefore need not be error-free. It must avoid routinely misleading users about how uncertain its conclusions are. Evidence and qualifying information allow a user to go behind an assertion when that is necessary. Stable matters need not be reinvestigated at every use, while unsettled matters continue to receive scrutiny. The resulting economy depends on expert care and an intelligible assessment of uncertainty, not on an assumption that all communicated conclusions are certain. [UX-W003, ch. 1]

Incentives can corrupt this arrangement. A person punished for overestimates but rarely exposed for missed opportunities may bias an estimate downward. A reporting system can look appropriately safeguarded while serving another interest. Stinchcombe treats the causal explanation of such arrangements as a problem: identifying an apparent useful consequence does not prove that it caused the structure or that the structure actually performs as advertised. [UX-W003, ch. 1]

### Prepared routines economize on new decisions

Prepared routines economize on new decisions

The book distinguishes complexity inside a routine from discretionary decisions needed to choose or change it. A complicated sequence can be performed with little new decision-making if its relevant choices have been settled in advance. Stinchcombe uses the analogy of a computer program: once an appropriate routine is called, much of what follows is prescribed. The existence of many internal steps does not imply that a worker must invent each step anew. [UX-W003, ch. 2]

The selection of the routine can remain a substantial decision. Choosing a product mix, for example, can call several different production routines. The units then repeat the prescribed operations for that mix. Preparing, testing and improving those routines is different work again. The economy in recurrent choice

<!-- PDF page 250 -->

is therefore relative to a prepared set of options, dependable inputs and an appropriate selection process. [UX-W003, ch. 2]

The registrar example exposes the surrounding intelligence. A university's clerical routines can be highly standardized while professors decide course content, class schedules and grades, departments decide requirements, and students choose courses within the arrangement. The clerk's task can be simple because the system obtains complex decisions through other participants. Looking only at the clerical procedure would mistake a local reduction in discretion for a reduction of intelligence throughout the university. [UX-W003, ch. 2]

Craft skill includes a repertoire of routines and the discretion to choose among them. Professional principles can guide unfamiliar cases; experience can also allow someone to revise the repertoire itself. These are not interchangeable capacities. Stinchcombe uses occupational distinctions to ask who acquires, preserves and supplies the relevant knowledge, rather than assuming that a formal procedure carries all the competence needed to apply it. [UX-W003, ch. 2]

Fordist production, in his account, combines extensive advance programming with relatively few new decisions per unit produced. It nevertheless retains managerial choices, maintenance, toolmaking and engineering. Its favorable conditions include stable demand, a standardized product, relatively stable technology and standardized, available inputs in a suitable environment. If those conditions vary unpredictably, more discretion must be supplied locally or variability must be buffered elsewhere. [UX-W003, ch. 2, especially pp. 54–72]

That distinction changes the comparison between skilled and routinized work. The relevant question is not whether one worker uses more discretion in the abstract. It is how much preparation, selection, adjustment and repair are required to produce a specified quality under the given conditions. An apparent local saving can depend on training, machinery, management or another occupation's work. Stinchcombe also treats occupational jurisdictions and management ideology as influences on which arrangements are chosen. Existing division of labor is not assumed to be the uniquely efficient one. [UX-W003, ch. 2]

The book's displayed ratios of routinized decisions and skill help state its conceptual distinctions, but they do not provide an operationally validated universal scale of work. Decisions differ in significance, and design or debugging cannot simply be inferred from a count of repetitive actions. The impressionistic wage–age illustration and dated industrial figures remain the author's historical material. [UX-W003, ch. 2]

### Managers construct different information systems

Managers construct different information systems

Chapter 3 treats managers partly as builders and maintainers of information systems. Such systems are shaped by the decisions for which the information will be used. A cost-comparison account, a search for production improvements, a maintenance record and a commissioning procedure do not require the same categories, detail, timing or authority. Information flows laterally as well as upward through a hierarchy. [UX-W003, ch. 3]

The chapter identifies several dimensions of variation. Information can improve through experience, serve one locality or several users, require supplementary innovation, prioritize flexible categories or comparability, support audit, need reorganization from another activity, and require different approval procedures. The differences explain why a common store of data does not automatically become a useful system for every purpose. The material must be organized so that the relevant recipient can interpret and act on it. [UX-W003, ch. 3, pp. 76–99]

<!-- PDF page 251 -->

Design and construction documents supply a particularly concrete example. Near the end of a construction project, a builder making a change needs to know what work to perform. An operator or maintainer needs to know the final configuration: as-built drawings, technical data and parts lists. The project record and the operating record overlap, but they answer different questions. [UX-W003, ch. 3]

Stinchcombe says that much design information has to be extensively reorganized for operations. Spare-parts procurement may require supplementary information about vendors that the construction project  could obtain readily but does not itself need. The project can regard final documentation as marginal paperwork even though it is crucial to the organization inheriting the plant. The difficulty is partly responsibility and motivation, not merely storage capacity. [UX-W003, ch. 3]

Commissioning and steady operation also differ. Testing, approval and the authority to accept a plant occur under one set of conditions; ongoing operation and maintenance occur under another. A completed physical asset therefore does not deliver its own usable organizational knowledge. The source's Statoil-based discussion has an explicit empirical limit: the organization studied was not yet operating. Some  claims about its eventual information needs concern anticipated use rather than observed long-term performance. [UX-W003, ch. 3]

Preparation and handover connect physical design with continuing organizational knowledge. A designer may settle a physical relation in advance, while another group needs accurate records, intelligible categories and authority to maintain it. [UX-W003, ch. 3]

### Divisionalization combines local integration and corporate abstraction

Divisionalization combines local integration and corporate abstraction

Stinchcombe reconstructs Chandler's divisionalization argument in terms of information and decisions. A division can integrate detailed product and market decisions while the general office works with more abstract measures for allocating investment. This is not decentralization understood as simply giving every local unit more freedom. Some decisions become more tightly integrated within a division while others are summarized for a higher-level purpose. [UX-W003, ch. 4]

The time horizon matters. Product-market conditions can require detailed, relatively fast response. The returns to major investments develop over a longer period. Information appropriate to those slower decisions can be abstracted over time without requiring corporate executives to make every operating choice. The economy is selective: an abstraction has to retain what its recipient needs while allowing detailed expertise to remain where operating decisions are made. [UX-W003, ch. 4]

The DuPont, General Motors and Sears discussions concern different causal problems. DuPont supplies a relatively detailed account of diagnosing and changing organizational arrangements. GM raises the general office's investment-coordination role. Sears involves purchasing and information about the quantities wanted in different markets. Stinchcombe does not treat these as interchangeable examples of one beneficial decentralization slogan. [UX-W003, ch. 4]

He also asks how individuals, committees, concepts and authority actually produced the structural changes. A functional explanation has to connect useful consequences with a causal process. People may need a theory of what is going wrong before they can reorganize, and existing experience can make some proposals intelligible while others remain difficult. An organization chart appearing after the change does not itself explain the transition. [UX-W003, ch. 4]

The chapter acknowledges gaps, including what Chandler establishes about the general office's superiority in investment decisions. Its displayed relation between divisionalization and several graded conditions leaves the numerical function unspecified. It is a proposal about explanatory relationships rather than a ready quantitative prediction of the optimal corporate structure. [UX-W003, ch. 4]

<!-- PDF page 252 -->

### Invention becomes useful through an operating organization

Invention becomes useful through an operating organization

The innovation chapter distinguishes a technical invention from an operating concern capable of producing and supplying its benefits. Technical theory, investment, production, markets, the division of benefits and personnel all enter the problem. An attractive device or process still needs a social vehicle through which it can be made, financed, introduced and maintained. [UX-W003, ch. 5]

Learning curves in the chapter concern accumulated cost-reducing improvements to equipment, procedures and skill. An innovator can gain an advantage by developing those capabilities earlier, but followers' learning, input costs and other conditions can alter it. Converting an area under unit-cost curves indexed by time into money requires production-rate and pricing assumptions. [UX-W003, ch. 5]

Stinchcombe's replacement-board example shows the organizational work behind an apparently effortless improvement. A board can be designed to fit an existing computer and software arrangement so that users need not rewrite programs, change their own routines or learn a new system. From the user's perspective the innovation can be close to a zero-change event. The supplier's perspective is different. [UX-W003, ch. 5]

Engineers collect information about failures and limitations from maintenance and software work, design modifications and test that the interfaces remain compatible and that new defects have not been introduced. Investment and production decisions also remain. Stable interfaces are part of the supplier's market reasoning because forcing a client to reorganize can make switching suppliers attractive. The small burden visible to the client thus depends on a substantial supplier organization. [UX-W003, ch. 5]

The example preserves a specific distinction between reducing a user's need to adapt and eliminating adaptation work altogether. It also gives continuing service relations an informational role: maintenance brings knowledge of problems back to the producer and provides a route for improvements to reach users. [UX-W003, ch. 5]

Incentives and the distribution of gains affect whether an improvement is introduced. A technical reduction in cost is not sufficient if the parties needed to make it happen cannot obtain a worthwhile return or expect to lose valued rights. The chapter's criticism of technological utopianism concerns precisely the omission of the organization, training, investment and power surrounding a technology. [UX-W003, ch. 5]

The author does not infer that bureaucracy necessarily prevents innovation. An innovative division can require dependable routines as well as rapid adaptive information links. The issue is whether the structure can support the different kinds of work, not whether the organization has escaped every procedure. [UX-W003, ch. 5]

### A contract can constitute hierarchy across firm boundaries

A contract can constitute hierarchy across firm boundaries

Chapter 6 examines contracts as organizational arrangements. A legal firm boundary does not necessarily mark the end of hierarchical coordination. A contract can establish authority, incentives, procedures, dispute resolution and a method of pricing changes. These functions can support integrated work across legally separate organizations. [UX-W003, ch. 6]

Stinchcombe identifies five forms of hierarchical content. Command structures allocate authority. Incentives guide discretionary action. Operating procedures specify actions involving both contractor and client. Dispute-resolution arrangements reduce reliance on fresh market bargaining or court proceedings. Pricing provisions, including cost-related methods, govern variations in performance. Together these can create relationships resembling an internal hierarchy, despite separate ownership. [UX-W003, ch. 6, pp. 194–236]

<!-- PDF page 253 -->

The reasons include uncertainty over specifications, costs and measurable performance. A client may not yet know precisely what it wants because development is unfinished. Engineering errors and execution inefficiency may be difficult to distinguish in an overrun. A rigid original description can then be inadequate for the work that must actually be done. Adaptive authority and agreed procedures permit changes without reconstructing the relationship through a new market transaction each time. [UX-W003, ch. 6]

Such adaptation retains knowledge and bargaining. The client still needs enough understanding to specify aims, recognize problems, evaluate information and participate in changes. A supplier's discretion has to be related to authority, compensation and accountability. The chapter distinguishes constituting an organizational arrangement through a contract from making its continuing information operations work. Outsourcing does not remove those functions by changing the legal location of the people performing them. [UX-W003, ch. 6]

The book reuses and develops material from the author's related work. The relevant knowledge is the concrete organization of adaptive cooperation and the distinction between legal and functional boundaries. [UX-W003, ch. 6 and notes]

### Personnel information can economize on judgment and preserve privilege

Personnel information can economize on judgment and preserve privilege

The labor-market chapter asks how employers and others know about skill. Direct observation of future performance is difficult. Educational records, tenure, experience, peer judgments and other certificates can substitute for repeated complete assessment. Such devices are information arrangements: people rely on knowledge produced and maintained elsewhere. [UX-W003, ch. 7]

The arrangements have requirements that can conflict. Information should be relevant, competent, honest, auditable and comparable, yet the procedures that support one quality can obstruct another. A standardized certificate can support comparison while losing local detail. A judgment from someone who knows the work can carry expertise while creating opportunities for reciprocal favoritism or exclusion. [UX-W003, ch. 7]

Access to opportunities for producing a credible record is itself uneven. Occupational groups and institutions can control training, certification and recruitment, creating segmented labor markets and preserving advantages. An information system useful to those making personnel decisions can still reproduce unjust distributions of opportunity. Stinchcombe explicitly distinguishes functional explanation from moral justification and acknowledges that his explanation does not fully account for discriminatory allocation. [UX-W003, ch. 7]

The chapter’s national, gender and class generalizations are historical interpretations. Its wage illustration also has an arithmetic problem: a thirty-percent premium requires a reciprocal cost comparison to determine the corresponding labor hours, rather than a direct thirty-percent reduction. Production rates, other costs and causal estimates enter any wider monetary comparison. [UX-W003, ch. 7]

Chapter 8 gives cultural interpretation and political organization a larger role. Incentives and standardized work categories do not uniquely determine perceived interests, collective action or citizenship. People interpret fairness, authority and careers through histories and institutions. Stinchcombe's information is therefore not simply a quantity of signals: its meaning, purposes and use can be contested. [UX-W003, ch. 8]

These chapters qualify any inference that a structure's persistence proves a universally favorable economy. An arrangement can survive because it serves the interests of people with the power to

<!-- PDF page 254 -->

maintain it. The criterion of whose work is reduced and whose purposes are served remains within the author's explanation of the institution. [UX-W003, chs. 1, 7–8, 10]

### University space: local knowledge, reserves and credible promises

University space: local knowledge, reserves and credible promises

University administration supplies a case where managers cannot readily judge the detailed work being performed. Research space is specialized, demand changes with grants and projects, and people know more about their own future needs than central administrators do. A simple aggregate measure cannot capture every relevant difference between laboratories, offices and equipment. [UX-W003, ch. 9]

Individual researchers may retain space to insure against future expansion or uncertainty. A common reserve can reduce that incentive only if space is usable for different claims and people trust that giving it up now will not destroy their future access. Stinchcombe's discussion connects a larger liquid reserve with less need for private hoarding, conditional on a credible return guarantee and the physical suitability of the space. [UX-W003, ch. 9]

Physical flexibility matters alongside administrative promises. Movable partitions can help with some reallocation, while drains, water and exhaust requirements make laboratory space harder to treat as interchangeable. The arrangement thus includes a material problem and an authority problem. A central claim that all space is available does not make every room useful for every research activity. [UX-W003, ch. 9]

The proposed strategies are not reported as universally tested remedies. They show how the distribution of knowledge, uncertainty and responsibility can produce reserve holdings that look redundant from one viewpoint but protect important local activity from another. Changing the rules without sustaining trust or usable capacity may leave the underlying demand for insurance intact. [UX-W003, ch. 9]

### The connected argument and its own limits

The connected argument and its own limits

The conclusion joins these accounts through lasting task-related substructures, prepared routines, skill and the handling of useful news. Different parts of an organization can embody different rationalities because their tasks, uncertainties and response tempos differ. Abstraction can allow one part to rely on another, while expertise and correction maintain the adequacy of that reliance. The connections are Stinchcombe's own organizational explanation. [UX-W003, ch. 10]

He also names limits. The book explains structures more than particular individual errors, and its cultural treatment is incomplete. Functional accounts need causal pathways, and the historical evidence is uneven. A principle of decoupling or a category of uncertainty must be mapped to a specific situation rather than assumed to determine its structure on its own. [UX-W003, chs. 1, 4, 7–8, 10]

### Later formalization through du Gay and Lopdrup-Hjorth

Later formalization through du Gay and Lopdrup-Hjorth

Paul du Gay and Thomas Lopdrup-Hjorth's 2024 Organizing States provides a selected reconstruction of Stinchcombe's later work on formality. In their account, useful formalization requires abstraction, communication and correction. People can act through an established representation without independently checking every detail because others have checked, and continue to check, what the abstraction allows them to rely on. [SB-W001, “Formality and Formal Organization”]

This explains a particular economy of reliance. An abstraction must preserve something useful, be communicable to its users and remain open to correction when its relation to practice fails. A formal document by itself does not establish those conditions. The reconstruction therefore differs from treating formality as either inherently obstructive or automatically trustworthy. Its relevant mechanism includes the organization that maintains the abstraction. [SB-W001, selected section]

<!-- PDF page 255 -->

Du Gay and Lopdrup-Hjorth draw on Stinchcombe's When Formality Works: Authority and Abstraction in Law and Organizations (2001). [SB-W002, through SB-W001]

### Zhou and Zhao: historical and institutional organization

Zhou and Zhao: historical and institutional organization

Zhou Xueguang and Zhao Wei’s 2009 review of research on Chinese organizational phenomena discusses Stinchcombe’s 1965 argument about organizations and social structure. They emphasize the resources, legitimacy, behavioral patterns and opportunity structures supplied by an organization’s institutional environment. [SB-W003, pp. 1–6]

The authors also recover historical influences on organizational structures and the role of formal organizations in stratification. Formal organizations help shape access to education, employment and other positions, rather than merely responding to external social categories. Their discussion places information and organizational arrangements within legal, cultural and political conditions. [SB-W003, pp. 5–6]

Their introduction distinguishes studying organizations from explicitly using organizational analysis. Economic, political and organizational models can illuminate different aspects of a decision process, but one does not automatically replace the others. This is the authors' methodological argument in a Chinese research setting. [SB-W003, pp. 3–4]

### Expertise, routines and organizational relationships

Expertise, routines and organizational relationships

The selected book material explains more than the presence of information in organizations. It shows who supplies expert inputs to a routine, how documents must change between construction and operation, which details a corporate abstraction can omit, what supplier work makes an upgrade easy, and how contracts sustain adaptation across legal boundaries. The personnel and university accounts also show that incentives, privilege, material differences and credible commitments affect whether a seemingly economical arrangement works for particular participants. [UX-W003, chs. 2–9]

<!-- PDF page 256 -->

## S51 Organizational silence, dissent and learning

S51   Organizational silence, dissent and learning

An organization can possess information that never becomes available to the people deciding what to do. It can also receive a warning and interpret it through assumptions that make the warning seem unimportant. The historical accounts in this section examine the organization of voice, learning, commitment and the interpretation of danger. They explain how reporting channels, authority, shared expectations and ordinary work practices affect what can be questioned and corrected.

Stinchcombe's account in S13 already connects useful information with tasks, incentives and recipients' ability to act. Beer's treatment in S22 explains how ignorance can filter the world into an apparently manageable form, while operational examination supplements routine reporting. The sources developed here examine more closely why people withhold concerns, how disagreement becomes usable, and why some decisions resist revision. The relevant engineering interventions concern the conduct of inquiry and the institutional relations that support it.

### Hirschman: exit and voice are different responses to deterioration

Hirschman: exit and voice are different responses to deterioration

Albert Hirschman's 1970 book begins with organizations and firms that can deteriorate and potentially recover. Dissatisfied customers or members can leave, withdrawing purchases or participation. They can also attempt to change the objectionable condition. Hirschman calls the latter response voice. It ranges from a direct complaint to collective organization, appeals to higher authority and public protest. A person deciding whether to remain and speak faces a different problem from one deciding whether another supplier or organization offers a better alternative. Voice requires some prospect that effort can influence what happens. [OI-W007, opening; ch. 3]

The distinction gives deteriorating performance two possible routes back to management. A loss of customers or members can create pressure through reduced revenue or participation. Complaints and organized demands can convey more specific information about what is wrong and what might repair it. These routes need not reinforce each other. Easy departure can remove the people most willing to object, leaving managers with a quieter organization whose surviving members appear more satisfied. Whether exit supplies an effective corrective signal depends on how sensitive the organization is to the loss and whether those responsible can recognize and respond to it. [OI-W007, chs. 3–4]

Hirschman's discussion of Nigerian railways makes that dependency concrete. Dissatisfied shippers could turn to road transport. This alternative relieved their immediate difficulty, but it could also weaken the constituency pressing for railway improvement. Public financial backing could cushion the railway against the consequences of lost business. Competition would then provide an escape for dissatisfied users without necessarily producing the expected recovery inside the railway. The argument depends on both relations: access to a substitute and the organization's weak response to departure. [OI-W007, ch. 4]

Who leaves matters as well as how many leave. People particularly sensitive to quality may notice deterioration early and have strong reasons to complain. If they are also especially capable of finding an alternative, their departure can remove disproportionately valuable pressure for correction. The organization loses potential advocates for improvement along with their custom. Hirschman's analysis therefore asks about the composition of those who leave, the experience of those who remain and the relation between an exit signal and the specific knowledge that voice could have supplied. [OI-W007, chs. 3–4]

Voice itself has costs. A complaint can require time, coordination, information and confidence that somebody will respond. A person may wait for others to bear those costs. Repeated, ineffective protest can discourage further effort; excessive protest can also impede an organization's attempts to recover. Hirschman treats channels for complaints and the organization of collective action as capacities that can

<!-- PDF page 257 -->

develop. A judgment that voice is presently ineffective need not describe its permanent potential. Choosing departure can terminate the effort through which a more effective form of influence might have emerged. [OI-W007, ch. 3]

Loyalty changes the relation between these responses. Attachment can postpone exit long enough for someone to attempt repair, or to invent a way of influencing an organization that initially seems unresponsive. Yet an available exit can make voice more effective by supplying bargaining power. Hirschman distinguishes the willingness to speak from the ability to make speaking count. A credible possibility of leaving can strengthen a complaint even while an easy alternative reduces the incentive to make that complaint in the first place. [OI-W007, ch. 7, pp. 76–84]

Remaining is consequently ambiguous. A member may stay out of attachment, hope that others will intervene, lack an acceptable alternative, or fail to recognize deterioration. Management may also impose entry costs or penalties that obstruct both departure and opposition. Hirschman's selected discussion distinguishes such restraints from loyalty that sustains active efforts at repair. Continued membership can therefore conceal quite different responses to deterioration. [OI-W007, ch. 7, pp. 91–93]

### Argyris: questioning the assumptions that govern correction

Argyris: questioning the assumptions that govern correction

Chris Argyris's 1976 article distinguishes correcting action within accepted goals from questioning the goals, policies and assumptions that govern it. He calls these single-loop and double-loop learning. An organization can encourage improvements while excluding inquiry into its fundamental design. He also distinguishes what people say guides their conduct from the theory of action inferred from their observable behavior. A professed commitment to openness can coexist with unilateral control and avoidance of threatening questions. [OI-W003, pp. 365–368]

His proposed alternative combines advocacy with inquiry: people state their reasoning, make it open to challenge and share control with those relevant to the problem. Changing an organization chart or teaching the vocabulary does not, in his account, produce that behavior automatically. Existing practices can make candor risky and recreate the old pattern inside a nominally different structure. The article presents an explanatory and prescriptive argument drawing on earlier studies; its discussion acknowledges incomplete evidence and the difficulty of testing the transition. [OI-W003, pp. 369–373]

### Staw: responsibility for an earlier choice can affect the next allocation

Staw: responsibility for an earlier choice can affect the next allocation

Barry Staw's 1976 experiment examines a particular way that an unfavorable outcome can strengthen a commitment. An investor can respond to disappointment by changing an interpretation, but can also commit additional resources in an attempt to justify or rescue the earlier decision. Staw asks whether personal responsibility for the initial choice changes the response to subsequent performance information. The question concerns the interaction between responsibility and outcomes, rather than persistence considered in isolation. [OI-W005, pp. 27–30]

Participants took the role of a financial vice-president allocating research and development funds between two divisions of a hypothetical company. In the high-responsibility condition, they made an initial choice and explained it. In the low-responsibility condition, they inherited an allocation attributed to another officer. Favorable or unfavorable financial outcomes were then presented independently of that manipulation. Participants subsequently divided a new pool of hypothetical funds between the divisions. This design separated having made the prior choice from learning that its consequences were disappointing. [OI-W005, pp. 30–35]

The largest allocation to the previously selected division occurred when participants had personally chosen it and then received unfavorable results. The corresponding response to negative outcomes was

<!-- PDF page 258 -->

not significant among those who inherited the decision. Nor did responsibility significantly change allocation following favorable results. These conditional comparisons are central to the finding. The experiment supports a combined effect of responsibility and outcome valence, rather than a claim that any unfavorable news necessarily increases investment or that taking responsibility always impedes correction. [OI-W005, pp. 36–39]

The analysis included 239 undergraduate business students, after one participant was excluded because the initial choice could not be made. The experiment measured one subsequent allocation of hypothetical funds in a stylized financial task. [OI-W005, pp. 30–39]

Staw interprets the result through self-justification and discusses competing accounts of how people infer their own attitudes. He also distinguishes maintaining a coherent image of oneself from demonstrating to other people that an earlier costly decision was defensible. The latter could matter especially where status and evaluation depend on the appearance of competence. Those motives were not separately manipulated in this experiment. They are parts of the explanatory discussion that follows the observed interaction. [OI-W005, pp. 40–42]

### Morrison and Milliken: how silence becomes an organizational property

Morrison and Milliken: how silence becomes an organizational property

Elizabeth Wolfe Morrison and Frances J. Milliken's 2000 article asks how withholding concerns about organizational problems can become a collective practice. Their object is more than the reluctance of an isolated employee. People can come to share an expectation that speaking is dangerous or useless, even when they possess different information and have never explicitly agreed to remain silent. The article develops a conceptual explanation linking managerial beliefs, organizational arrangements and employees' interpretation of their experience. [OI-W001, pp. 706–710]

The proposed mechanism begins partly with managers' fear of negative feedback and their assumptions about employees. If managers regard employees as self-interested, believe that management knows best, and interpret agreement as a sign of organizational health, they have reasons to retain decisions centrally and restrict the channels through which objections reach them. Informal conduct matters alongside formal design. Dismissing an unwelcome suggestion, soliciting advice mainly from agreeable people, or reacting defensively to adverse news can teach employees what happens to those who speak. Middle managers may withhold subordinate concerns because they anticipate the reactions of people above them, even when they do not personally share the senior managers' assumptions. [OI-W001, pp. 708– 714]

Employees also learn from one another. They discuss encounters with managers, observe the treatment of colleagues and infer the local rules. Morrison and Milliken explain how these interactions can produce a shared climate of silence. An unfavorable career event following an objection may be interpreted as retaliation even when the two events were unrelated. This is an illustration of their proposed sensemaking process: beliefs about the danger of speaking can spread beyond the people who directly encountered a discouraging response. Silence itself supplies a further cue, since the absence of objections can make an unwritten prohibition seem established. [OI-W001, pp. 714–717]

The consequences in their model include impoverished information, fewer challenges to prevailing interpretations and weaker correction of errors. Management can mistake acquiescence for agreement. Employees who withdraw psychologically may then appear to confirm the managerial suspicion that workers lack commitment, reinforcing the conditions that discouraged voice. The authors nevertheless distinguish useful participation from unlimited input, which can overload and delay decisions. [OI-W001, pp. 719–721]

<!-- PDF page 259 -->

### Edmondson: interpersonal risk and the observable work of learning

Edmondson: interpersonal risk and the observable work of learning

Amy Edmondson's 1999 field study treats learning as observable activity within teams: asking for help, seeking feedback, discussing errors, sharing information and experimenting. These activities can reveal uncertainty or failure to colleagues and supervisors. Someone may recognize that an inquiry would help the task and still avoid it because of the expected personal consequences. The paper examines team psychological safety, a shared belief that interpersonal risk-taking is safe, as a condition associated with carrying out that work. [OI-W004, pp. 350–355]

Psychological safety in this account differs from confidence that the team has the ability to succeed. A team can think itself competent while making it difficult to admit a mistake. It also differs from cohesion or an atmosphere in which every view must be agreeable. The survey asks about the treatment of mistakes, the ability to bring up difficult issues, asking for help and the acceptance of differences. The construct concerns the expected interpersonal consequences of participating, while team efficacy concerns confidence in collective capability. [OI-W004, pp. 351–355, appendix]

The study covered 51 work teams in one office-furniture manufacturing company. Team-member surveys were complemented by interviews, observation and measures from people receiving the teams' work. Psychological safety was positively associated with learning behavior, including measures supplied by outside observers. The analysis also examined whether learning could help account for the relation between safety and performance. Because the principal measurements were cross-sectional, those relationships do not demonstrate that an intervention increasing safety would cause learning or performance to improve. [OI-W004, pp. 358–368, 378–379]

The qualitative cases show what learning activity could look like. Members of the Stain Team described responding to reports of defects by working on the defects instead of attacking the person who reported them. They also sometimes sought another person's opinion without first announcing which defect they suspected. This practice made an additional inspection less dependent on the team's initial interpretation. [OI-W004, pp. 371, 375–377]

Resources and leadership remain part of the account. Time, staffing and access to support affect the opportunity to learn, while coaching and reactions to problems affect what team members expect from speaking. Some teams worked around material constraints; teams with apparently similar formal support could nevertheless differ in their learning behavior. Edmondson investigates those relations together. Learning also consumes time, and its value depends partly on uncertainty and task demands. The detailed failure-analysis account by Edmondson and Cannon in S31 develops a separate contribution concerning the work after a failure has been recognized. [OI-W004, pp. 354, 376–379; AFC-W015]

### Vaughan: warning evidence is interpreted within a history of work

Vaughan: warning evidence is interpreted within a history of work

Diane Vaughan's 1997 article examines how earlier policy decisions and ordinary engineering work contributed to the Challenger launch decision. It condenses her larger historical reconstruction, drawing on archival material and interviews. Her argument challenges accounts that locate the explanation chiefly in the final teleconference, the moral character of particular managers or a simple opposition between engineers concerned with safety and managers concerned with schedules. She traces how production concerns, bureaucratic accountability and the inherited technical culture affected both groups. [OI-W017, pp. 80–82]

The history of the booster joints matters to that explanation. Damage to O-rings was initially an anomaly relative to design expectations. Engineers analyzed the damage and accepted explanations under which a second O-ring would preserve the required seal. Subsequent decisions could rely on that analysis and on the precedent of flights that returned successfully. Vaughan describes a gradual extension of acceptable

<!-- PDF page 260 -->

risk: individual decisions could appear reasonable within the established assessment process while cumulatively accepting conditions that had originally been anomalous. Her term normalization of deviance concerns this development of official risk judgments, including judgments made by working engineers. [OI-W017, p. 85]

She distinguishes patterns in the evidence that helped sustain those interpretations. A danger signal followed by successful flights could suggest that a repair had worked. An unclear or seemingly unlikely event could remain a weak signal. Repeated erosion could become routine when engineers believed its occurrence confirmed their understanding of the joint. The same recorded observation could therefore have a different significance to someone reconstructing the disaster than to someone assessing the next flight within the accumulated history. Vaughan's explanation concerns the interpretation and sequence of information, as well as whether information was transmitted. [OI-W017, pp. 86–87]

The eve-of-launch discussion introduced circumstances that did not fit the routine. Predicted temperatures were below those of earlier launches, the contractor's engineering presentation was being handled by teleconference, and its engineers recommended against launching. Preparing charts under time pressure divided the work among specialists. Some participants assembled the final recommendation without examining the other charts as a complete set. The group did not collectively review all those charts before transmitting them. These details connect organizational divisions of work and timing to the evidence available in the decision itself. [OI-W017, pp. 91–92]

Within Vaughan's reconstruction, the presentation contained signals that weakened the recommendation as others interpreted it. Charts reused from earlier launch recommendations looked familiar. Damage at a warm launch complicated a simple temperature argument, while some statements about redundancy appeared inconsistent with the proposed launch limit. A culture requiring quantitative support for engineering recommendations made the engineers' observational concerns difficult to defend in the expected form. Hierarchy and the separation of participants among locations also affected who spoke and what they knew about support for their position. The warning was voiced, but the way it was assembled, challenged and interpreted reduced its force. [OI-W017, pp. 92–94]

The article's practical discussion addresses policy, culture and signals. Vaughan argues that leaders need to examine how goals and resource decisions change the conditions of hazardous work, including consequences appearing after the original decision makers have moved on. She also asks how an organization can preserve coordination through rules while recognizing a situation for which familiar rules are inappropriate. Her warning about organizational change includes the loss of memory, disrupted working relations and new opportunities for error during a transition. [OI-W017, pp. 96–99]

The concrete problem of preserving the reasons behind a decision also appears in Leveson's safety account in S29 and in the treatment of records and traceability in S42. The sources here add detailed accounts of voice, interpretation and the personal and collective consequences of questioning a course of action. S52 turns to the related work of generating and testing alternatives, including situations in which people are willing to discuss a decision but have considered only a narrow range of possible responses.

S106   Difficult conversations under emotional and relational pressure

### Deciding who should have the conversation

Deciding who should have the conversation

The Acas guide treats preparation as a decision about who has the authority and information to address a problem. Its timekeeping scenario follows a sales manager who has kept a record of an employee’s late arrivals and long lunches. The manager begins by asking if anything is wrong. The employee says all is well. When the manager produces the record, the employee disputes its accuracy and asks why he is being singled out. As he leaves, he mentions that his wife has been unwell. A few days later he says he will meet again only with a union representative and is considering a grievance. [T08-W001]

Acas uses this instructional scenario to ask whether the manager had raised the issue earlier, told the employee about the monitoring or noticed a change in his behavior. The guide credits the opening question and the use of specific evidence. The scenario ends with the terms of a second meeting in dispute. [T08-W001]

Reasons for avoiding an exchange

King, Edlington and Williams interviewed 20 clinical supervisors in Australia about avoiding difficult conversations.
