## S48 Burden, autonomy, power and evaluation

S48   Burden, autonomy, power and evaluation

These sources examine effort, authority, care, autonomy and alienation, asking whose purposes and experiences enter judgments of an economical arrangement.

### Knowledge and power inside hierarchies

Knowledge and power inside hierarchies

Dosi, Marengo and Virgillito treat hierarchy as an arrangement of knowledge and power as well as a means of organizing production. In this historical and interpretive framework, authority can shape who knows what, whose decisions count, and which choices remain available to others. The organization of knowledge is therefore not necessarily independent of the organization of control. Making a worker’s local task simpler can coincide with relocating understanding and discretion into managerial routines. Productivity alone does not describe that redistribution. [W093, §§1–3]

Their comparison of Taylorism and Toyotism concerns different ways of using and organizing workers’ knowledge, rather than a simple contrast between an organization possessing knowledge and one lacking it. Participation in improvement and discretion over execution need to be read alongside the surrounding authority relations. The consequences of local simplification depend on who acquires the corresponding knowledge and power. [W093]

### Tainter: complexity as a costly problem-solving investment

Tainter: complexity as a costly problem-solving investment

Tainter’s selected introduction, definitions and discussion of problem-solving costs present social complexity as an investment made in response to problems. More elaborate organization can provide benefits, but it must also be supported. As solutions accumulate, the resources required to sustain institutions and specialized activities can become consequential to sustainability. In this argument a successful response to an immediate difficulty can create continuing obligations rather than simply remove a problem from the system. [UX-W006, printed pp. 91–94]

The relevant material is historical and organizational reasoning about returns and support requirements. Tainter expressly cautions about transferring ecological generalizations to societies. [UX-W006]

### Work and care are different evaluative concerns

Work and care are different evaluative concerns

Murphy and Parry examine household sustainability through work and care. Counting domestic activities as unpaid work can reveal effort hidden by monetary accounts, but the authors argue that this description can also lose personal and relational aspects of the activity. Their selected care discussion reconstructs scholarship in which maintaining people and their world is an ongoing relational activity. Who undertakes care, and whether adequate care occurs, are consequential questions in addition to the number of hours recorded. [GL-W006, care section]

Their integration discussion consequently does not equate a more equal division of household work with every possible improvement in care. Technology can alter expectations, standards and relations as well as the duration of a task. Its relevance is the more discriminating question: which work changes, whose work it becomes, and which quality or relation the proposed improvement is intended to preserve. Equal allocation and better care remain distinct normative goals. [GL-W006]

### Administrative burden: three kinds of cost

Administrative burden: three kinds of cost

Moynihan, Herd and Harvey distinguish learning, psychological and compliance costs in citizen–state interactions. Learning includes discovering that a programme exists, determining eligibility and

<!-- PDF page 328 -->

understanding its procedures. Compliance concerns the actions required to meet those procedures, such as supplying information or satisfying process requirements. Psychological costs concern experiences such as stress, stigma or loss of autonomy associated with the interaction. These categories distinguish burdens that an account of administrative processing time alone can miss. [GL-W018, introduction and table 1, printed pp. 46–47]

The allocation of these costs between citizen and state can be political. A procedure that is inexpensive for an agency may require the applicant to assemble information, interpret requirements or repeatedly establish eligibility. Conversely, reducing citizen effort can require the agency to perform additional work. The authors also recognize that procedures can protect legitimate public values. “Minimum burden” is therefore not automatically the institution’s sole objective. [GL-W018]

### What the administrative-burden review covers

What the administrative-burden review covers

Halling and Bækgaard’s selected systematic-review passages distinguish government actions, citizens’ experienced burdens and subsequent outcomes. These are links in an explanatory account, not interchangeable observations. A formal requirement can exist without affecting everyone in the same way; an experienced difficulty does not by itself identify which state action caused it; an outcome can have several causes. The review identifies a larger research agenda while flagging missing causal links and questions about legitimacy. [GL-W019]

Its corpus comprises 119 English-language studies from 2012 to February 2023 within the administrative-burden framework. The authors note the predominance of Western settings. [GL-W019]

### Relational autonomy: dependence does not settle the question

Relational autonomy: dependence does not settle the question

The selected Stanford Encyclopedia account distinguishes causal from constitutive relational theories of autonomy. On a causal account, relationships and social conditions can develop or undermine a person’s capacity for autonomy. Support from parents, teachers or friends can enable agency; oppressive socialization can impede it. On a constitutive account, certain interpersonal or social conditions belong to what autonomy itself consists in, rather than merely explaining how it arose. The distinction changes what would count as an adequate explanation of a person’s autonomy. [GL-W040]

The selected discussion of stronger substantive and social-relational views also considers severely constraining relationships in which routine aspects of a person’s life remain under another’s control. Subjective endorsement alone need not settle the autonomy question for those theories. Other positions resist making every preferred way of life subject to the same substantive test. The entry presents a controversy, not a single established metric. Dependence on a person, institution or technical aid cannot simply be read as absence of autonomy. The quality and structure of the relationship matter within the competing accounts. [GL-W040, selected lines 246–260]

### Alienation: technology and its social employment

Alienation: technology and its social employment

Leopold’s selected reconstruction separates objectification from alienation and distinguishes a criticism of technology’s social employment from a rejection of technology as such. Producing an object does not, merely because the product exists outside its maker, establish an objectionable separation. A theory of alienation must identify the relationship that has become problematic. Similarly, a machine’s technical capability does not determine the social relationship in which people use it. [GL-W049, objectification/fetishism discussion]

The entry’s selected later discussion raises problems of measurement and of connecting a diagnosis of alienation to a practicable account of unalienated production. This prevents a short circuit from “less

<!-- PDF page 329 -->

effort” or “more automation” to emancipation. Whether an arrangement improves control over activity, its products or its social meaning is a further question within the theory being discussed. [GL-W049, §§6.2 –6.3]

### Peripheral case: coordinated roles in a traditional account

Peripheral case: coordinated roles in a traditional account

China’s National Health Commission’s 2017 institutional description presents traditional Chinese medicine as treating a person’s condition holistically and tailoring formulations to that condition. Its selected account assigns differentiated roles within a formulation: a chief ingredient, an ancillary ingredient, an ingredient intended to reduce adverse effects, and one intended to coordinate the others. The source is relevant here as a public description of how a tradition conceptualizes an organized combination, rather than as evidence that every ingredient has the proposed effect. [GL-W061]

The NCCIH public evidence orientation distinguishes modalities and outcomes instead of validating traditional Chinese medicine as a unitary whole. It reports that some physical or psychological approaches may help particular outcomes, while results for herbal products vary; it also identifies contamination, substitution and other safety problems. The relevant lesson within this source is that an account of a coordinated formulation must remain distinguishable from evidence about specific interventions and harms. [GL-W062, selected effectiveness, safety and definition sections]

### Effort, care, autonomy and power

Effort, care, autonomy and power

These source accounts leave their evaluative objects distinct. Task effort, allocation of knowledge, political control, experienced burden, adequacy of care, autonomy and alienation cannot be substituted for one another merely by calling an arrangement efficient.

## S96 Negotiation: preparation, bargaining and agreements

S96   Negotiation: preparation, bargaining and agreements

Negotiation can change the proposal under discussion, the alternatives available outside it and the parties' understanding of what they want. Reaching an agreement also creates questions about representation, implementation and continuing relationships. The accounts developed here examine these activities through practitioner methods, training exercises, reviews and experiments. Institutional bargaining and brokers have their developed account in S15; deception during negotiation is discussed in S93.

### Preparation and the choice to negotiate

Preparation and the choice to negotiate

Алла  Стремовская's 2012 discussion makes strategy depend on the importance of substantive results and of the relationship with the other party. Avoidance, accommodation, competition and cooperation consequently have different purposes. Her account includes the possibility that someone already satisfied with their position has little to gain by entering a negotiation. A presidential candidate leading in the polls, for example, may decline an opponent's request for additional debates. Preparation includes identifying other parties' strategies and adjusting one's own conduct as the exchange develops. The article brings together earlier writers' approaches and examples. [NN-W007]

Aníbal Sierralta Ríos places commercial negotiation within institutions and their histories. People represent firms, states and other organizations whose policies, market positions and experience shape what their representatives can pursue. His account of negotiator education recalls the OEA–Brazil initiative CICOM and its contribution to training in Latin America. Preparation in this setting concerns the organization represented as well as the person speaking: institutional experience and commitments enter the encounter through the negotiator. His opening discussion gives these collective circumstances a place alongside the individual's conduct. [NN-W008]

### Fisher and Ury: interests, options, standards and alternatives

Fisher and Ury: interests, options, standards and alternatives

Roger Fisher and William Ury's Getting to Yes, first published in 1981, develops principled negotiation through four connected practices: separating interpersonal difficulties from the substantive problem, investigating interests behind positions, generating possible agreements and discussing standards for choosing among them. The parties can remain concerned about their relationship while examining a disputed question on its merits. Their method asks negotiators to discover what a demand is meant to accomplish, rather than treating the demand as the only possible expression of the interest. [NN-W001]

Their orange illustration makes the distinction concrete. Dividing the fruit appears to require a compromise until the parties discover that one wants the flesh to eat and the other wants the peel for baking. The uses differ, so an exchange can satisfy more of both parties' interests than equal division. Their interpretation of the Sinai settlement develops a larger example. They describe Egypt's concern with sovereignty and Israel's concern with security: returning territory while restricting military deployment addresses different interests within what initially appears to be an incompatible territorial demand. This is the authors' explanation of the settlement. [NN-W001]

Generating an option and judging it are distinct activities in their method. The discussion of objective criteria asks the parties to examine standards and the reasons for selecting them. In a disagreement about an insurance settlement, the relevant question can become the cost of replacing the destroyed car with a comparable one. In a disagreement about foundations, construction requirements provide a different kind of standard. The proposed change is in what the negotiators argue about: they can examine a basis for the decision instead of merely repeating how far they are willing to concede. Competing standards can themselves require discussion. [NN-W001]

<!-- PDF page 331 -->

The book's best alternative to a negotiated agreement, or BATNA, is developed through three operations. First, list possible actions if agreement fails. Second, improve promising possibilities into practical alternatives. Third, select the best available option. Thinking about a job in another city is a possibility; obtaining an offer there makes it an alternative against which a current offer can be assessed. The book similarly describes turning possible union action into operational decisions, such as obtaining authorization for a strike. Negotiating power in this account includes work performed outside the exchange. [NN-W001]

The resulting alternative supplies a basis for accepting or rejecting an offer. Fisher and Ury also ask negotiators to investigate the other party's alternatives, including whether that party overestimates them. If both sides have attractive alternatives, discovering that no agreement would improve their positions can itself bring the negotiation to a satisfactory close. Their treatment therefore joins the creation of possible agreements to the development of a feasible course of action without agreement. [NN-W001]

James White credits the book's search for mutual gains but argues that it neglects distributive bargaining, where an additional benefit to one party imposes a cost on the other. His labor-contract example distinguishes changing an insurance provider to obtain better services at lower cost from bargaining over wages that reduce the profits available to shareholders. Discovering a mutually beneficial adjustment does not, in his account, eliminate the subsequent dispute over distribution. [NN-W009, pp. 115–116]

White also questions the distinction between objective criteria and persuasive rationalizations. A seller may obtain different prices from buyers with different needs, while numerical tables for pain and suffering can give subjective judgments an appearance of objectivity. He regards standards as useful arguments, but disputes the suggestion that they generally remove the influence of bargaining power. His objection concerns the scope claimed for the method, alongside his appreciation of its practical techniques. [NN-W009, pp. 116–117]

### First offers and the unfolding exchange

First offers and the unfolding exchange

John Oesch and Adam Galinsky's review manuscript examines four connected questions: who opens, how extreme the opening is, how it affects the final agreement and how participants subsequently evaluate the outcome. An opening can convey information about a bargaining position, signal an intention or establish a reference point. Their discussion of resistance to anchoring concerns the recipient's attention. Considering the opponent's alternatives or reservation point, or concentrating on one's own target, can direct judgment away from the initial proposal. They also discuss the possibility that an implausibly extreme offer undermines agreement. [NN-W004]

Wolfram Lipp, Remigiusz Smolinski and Peter Kesting's review of 119 articles distinguishes a first settlement proposal from anchoring, the judgment process that it may activate. A proposal can contain qualitative conditions as well as a numerical amount. Their process model connects antecedents and offer characteristics to the counterpart's response and to subsequent interaction. What the recipient knows and does consequently belongs within the explanation of an opening's effect. Economic results and subjective evaluations occupy different places among the outcomes considered. The review develops comparisons and open research questions across this literature. [NN-W003]

张真 and 皇甫刚 organize influences on integrative negotiation into contextual and process factors. Their contextual category includes cultural values, social motives and emotions already present when formal negotiation begins. Process factors concern the frequency and sequence of strategies and their use at different stages of the exchange. This distinction separates initial circumstances from conduct that unfolds between the parties, allowing a question about a tactic's use to include when it occurs and what precedes or follows it. [NN-W011]

<!-- PDF page 332 -->

苏勇, 程骏骏 and 吴展's review of cooperative negotiation argues that much of the research has remained dominated by linear and static models. They propose developing dynamic and relational perspectives on the mechanisms of cooperation. Their criticism concerns the way a research setting represents negotiation over time and among people in relationships. Their proposed direction gives the evolving exchange a different emphasis from a comparison of isolated strategies or average outcomes. [NN-W010]

Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney and Maurice Schweitzer's review likewise emphasizes interactions, evolving conversations and real settings. Its relationship discussion treats relational outcomes as part of what negotiation produces. Its cultural discussion includes adaptation and flexible exchange of information alongside knowledge of the setting. The authors also examine how simplified role-play paradigms shape available evidence. These accounts distinguish a settlement's economic terms from whether agreement is reached and from what happens to the relationship between the participants. [NN-W005]

### Discovering trades and making an agreement operate

Discovering trades and making an agreement operate

The Organisation internationale du Travail's 2010 training manual makes differences in preference tangible through an exchange between Mariama and Abdoulaye. Mariama has a green sweet and two orange sweets, dislikes green and particularly wants yellow. Abdoulaye has a yellow sweet and two brown sweets, dislikes yellow and particularly wants green. Both also value variety. Exchanging the unwanted green and yellow sweets benefits both; exchanging an orange for a brown creates a further opportunity. The exercise asks participants to discover interests that a simple division of the stock would conceal. [NN-W002]

The manual carries the exchange into the work of establishing an agreement. Participants assemble acceptable options, prepare a draft and check whether the parties understand it in the same way. Responsibilities then require specification: who will do what, where, when and how. Evaluation, follow-up and procedures for difficulties make the agreement an operating arrangement. Partial, trial and time-limited agreements appear among the possibilities when a final settlement is difficult. Its labor-dispute  setting also includes consultation with constituencies and assistance from third parties. [NN-W002]

Maurice Schweitzer and colleagues' handbook chapter distinguishes opportunity negotiations from disputes arising after loss or conflict. Preparation includes recognizing the setting, identifying issues, gathering information and considering alternatives and the counterpart. Its account of logrolling develops exchanges across issues valued differently by the parties. Bringing a start date into a salary discussion, for example, introduces a further dimension on which preferences can differ. Its phases extend through closing and subsequent behavior, placing continuing relationships and implementation within the subject. [NN-W006]

The handbook also distinguishes teams negotiating against one another from negotiation among several parties. A team can bring several participants to the interpretation and exchange of information. Several parties introduce additional questions about coalitions and whose agreement is required. Economic gains and relational outcomes remain separate matters in the chapter's assessment of group negotiation. These distinctions connect preparation and exchange to the people entitled to participate and to the rules under which a decision can be made. [NN-W006]

### Decision rules and procedural fairness

Decision rules and procedural fairness

Bianca Beersma and Carsten De Dreu's experiments assign participants to represent a bakery, flower shop and grocer planning a joint market. They negotiate design, temperature and rental-cost allocation with private profit schedules. Their first experiment involves 90 students; the second involves 141. The instructions vary social motives, and the second experiment also varies the decision rule. Unanimity

<!-- PDF page 333 -->

requires all three parties to agree. Majority rule allows two to settle, making it possible to impose an agreement on the third participant. [NN-W025]

Under majority rule, prosocial groups report greater procedural fairness than egoistic groups; the corresponding difference does not appear under unanimity. Joint agreement points and participants' fairness ratings are distinct outcomes. The experimental construction makes the mechanism of exclusion concrete: the minority's consent has a different role under the two rules, while motive instructions change what the participants are encouraged to pursue. The available coalition is a feature of the task, distinct from what every group actually chooses to do. These experiments give a particular institutional form to the broader bargaining and veto questions developed in S15. [NN-W025]

## S97 Building, maintaining and renewing personal and professional networks

S97   Building, maintaining and renewing personal and professional networks

A relationship can provide companionship, belonging, advice or practical assistance. Its development involves encounters and communication over time, while changes of workplace, residence or activity can alter the opportunities for contact. The accounts here examine how people form relationships, sustain them and reconnect after an interval. Friendship and mutual support are purposes in their own right alongside professional access and advancement.

### Encounters and the development of a friendship

Encounters and the development of a friendship

Claire Bidart describes sociability through repeated encounters that acquire a shared history. As a relationship develops, its participants cease to be interchangeable: knowing this person involves a history that another person does not simply replace. Her discussion distinguishes a network centered on an individual from the network of a collective. Specifying which relations are included is part of describing the network. This account gives particular relationships and their development a place within a picture that might otherwise appear to consist of nodes and connections alone. [NN-W018]

Jeffrey Hall examines friendship formation among 355 recently relocated adults and begins a nine-week longitudinal study with 112 first-year students. Participants identify acquaintances, report time and activities together and describe their closeness. Shared work or study does not carry the same association with closeness as chosen social time: leisure and everyday interaction help distinguish developing friendship from merely being present in the same workplace or classroom. The studies examine both the amount of time together and what people do during it. [NN-W013]

In the relocated-adult study, the logistic models put the probability of the casual-friend to friend transition above one half at approximately 164 hours together, and the friend to good/best-friend transition above one half at approximately 219 hours. These retrospective modeled estimates concern different relationship categories among the sampled adults, distinct from the students' longitudinal observations. They describe observed relationships between time and closeness rather than durations that guarantee friendship. [NN-W013]

岡田涼's review brings friendship research together with achievement goals, social goals, social cognition and self-determination accounts. His proposed model distinguishes motivation, conduct toward a friend and the relationship that develops through their interaction. Environmental conditions, including parent– child relations and classroom climate, and individual characteristics influence motivation for friendship. Motivation in turn encourages actions such as initiating conversation, helping and disclosing personal thoughts. The model places these actions between motivation and the closeness, satisfaction, trust and affection characterizing a friendship. [NN-W016, pp. 578–580, Figure 1]

The resulting relationship feeds back into later motivation while also contributing to adjustment and

mental health. 岡田 distinguishes possessing social skills from being motivated to use them: someone may know how to help or disclose appropriately without taking the initiative to engage. His discussion therefore follows the emergence of interaction, not just the qualities of an already established friendship. The review proposes this explanatory framework using findings primarily about schoolchildren and university students; it identifies developmental differences and tests of motivational intervention as questions for further research. [NN-W016, pp. 580–582]

<!-- PDF page 335 -->

### Maintenance, motives and reciprocity

Maintenance, motives and reciprocity

Debra Oswald, Eddie Clark and Cheryl Kelly identify positivity, supportiveness, openness and interaction as dimensions of friendship maintenance. Across three studies they develop and confirm a measure and examine the interdependence of friends' behavior. Their findings connect both partners' reported conduct with dyad-level satisfaction and commitment. Maintenance in this account belongs within a reciprocal relationship: what one person does and what their friend does contribute to the relationship-level picture. The dimensions describe a family of maintenance behaviors rather than a count of how  many contacts a person possesses. [NN-W014]

本田周二 studies relatively less intimate friendships, asking how motivation relates to communication, responses to conflict, satisfaction and mental health. Participants nominate a less-close friend of the same sex and answer questions about that relationship. Of 247 surveyed students, 211 remain in the analysis after exclusions. The study distinguishes motives arising from enjoyment or personal importance from motives involving obligation, anxiety or internal pressure. It also records communication through different media and responses to actual interpersonal conflict. [NN-W015]

In 本田's analyses, introjected motivation is associated with avoidance and self-concession in conflict and with lower relationship satisfaction. More autonomous motivation has few associations with the measured communication behaviors. The finding gives a particular difficulty in maintenance an explanatory home: continuing a relationship can involve pressure to retain it, and that pressure relates to how disagreements are handled. These are associations in the students' reported relationships. The reasons for continuing contact and the frequency or form of communication remain distinct parts of the investigation. [NN-W015]

李松, 刘峻君, 鲍秀琴 and 陈旭 review interpersonal gratitude in relationship maintenance. They distinguish buffering a relationship against threats from strengthening it after the threat has subsided. Their account also includes maladaptive maintenance, in which preserving a relationship conflicts with a person's wishes or social norms. They propose self- and other-evaluation as explanatory links and call for investigation at the dyadic level. Gratitude thus enters their account in both repair and further development of a connection, with the value of preserving the connection itself remaining part of the question. [NN-W017]

### Professional contacts inside and outside an organization

Professional contacts inside and outside an organization

Hans-Georg Wolff and Klaus Moser's 2006 measurement work crosses two distinctions: contacts inside versus outside the organization, and building, maintaining versus using contacts. The resulting six subscales concern conduct, rather than network size alone. Three studies examine the proposed structure and validity. This formulation separates meeting a person from continuing the relationship and from seeking help through it, while keeping the organizational boundary explicit. Their later longitudinal investigation uses this measurement tradition to examine career outcomes. [NN-W019]

In the 2009 study, examples of the measured conduct include using company events to make contacts, catching up with colleagues in other departments about their work and seeking confidential business advice through those contacts. Building an internal relationship, maintaining it and making use of it consequently appear as different activities. External contacts receive the corresponding distinction. The three-wave analysis includes 235 participants using available repeated observations, a different number from the respondents present at the final wave. [NN-W020]

Networking is related to salary level and salary growth in this study. Career satisfaction is related to networking concurrently, with no corresponding satisfaction-growth effect. The different results matter

<!-- PDF page 336 -->

to the interpretation of professional success: income trajectories and satisfaction trajectories are separate outcomes. The study follows behavior and careers over time; its account does not reduce professional relationships to attendance at events or treat every favorable career measure as the same result. [NN-W020]

Tiziana Casciaro, Francesca Gino and Maryam Kouchaki distinguish deliberately instrumental professional networking from personal support and spontaneously formed relationships. Their experiments examine feelings of moral contamination, while a law-firm survey relates networking experiences to networking frequency and billable work. In that setting, relationships with clients and colleagues are consequential for work allocation. The study makes the experience of forming an instrumental tie part of the account of whether people engage in professional networking. [NN-W021]

The 2024 correction records an independent reanalysis of the available data for Studies 2–4; Study 1's original data were unavailable. In Study 3, eight participants began the survey twice but completed it only once, and the analyses used their complete entries. The correction also clarifies the office-location controls in models predicting billable hours; supplementary controls did not change the key findings. In Study 4, correcting a coding error involving two participants changes the interaction between networking content and power on cleansing-product preference to p = .072. [NN-W022]

### Reconnecting after losing touch

Reconnecting after losing touch

Daniel Levin, Jorge Walter and Keith Murnighan investigate the usefulness of dormant ties for work-project advice. They ask 224 Executive MBA participants to reconnect with two contacts after at least  three years without communication, one formerly strong and one formerly weak. Participants select people who might help with an important current project, locate them, reopen communication and seek their advice. Ultimately, 129 executives complete both surveys. The comparison concerns the usefulness and features of these exchanges relative to current ties. [NN-W012]

Reconnected strong ties combine novel knowledge with retained trust and shared perspective in the authors' findings; dormant weak ties are also useful. A past relationship can retain something relevant to a new exchange while the participants have acquired different knowledge during their separation. The authors also examine contact selection in a further sample by asking participants to rank possible contacts and try lower-ranked choices. Their account describes purposeful selection and project-related reconnection. Its demonstrated outcome is useful renewed exchange, rather than sustained restoration of a close friendship. [NN-W012]

### Mentorship and support communities

Mentorship and support communities

Lillian Eby and colleagues' meta-analysis combines 116 independent samples comparing mentored and non-mentored individuals across youth, academic and workplace settings. Their definition involves a more experienced person taking an interest in and encouraging someone less experienced or disadvantaged. The review considers behavioral, attitudinal, relational, motivational, health and career outcomes. Associations are generally favorable and small, with differences across settings and outcome categories. [NN-W023]

Mentorship includes attention and encouragement extended to another person rather than only access sought for oneself. Its developmental and supportive outcomes differ from the salary and networking-frequency measures in the professional-contact studies. Sponsorship through advocacy and allocation of  opportunities has its related account in S91, while S92 examines enrolling support for strategic work. [NN-W023]

<!-- PDF page 337 -->

Giovania Maesima, Lívia Gomes and Daniela Levandowski review 25 studies of internet use and interpersonal relationships. Their account describes online communication as part of existing relationships and as an entrance to new ones. Shared activity and support communities give the practices a concrete setting. Among the populations considered are parents of autistic children and people affected by cancer; exchanges can provide practical knowledge and a sense of belonging. These examples are the review's accounts of the studies it examines. [NN-W024]

The review challenges a simple division between online and offline relationships by examining particular media practices and communities. Communication can continue a connection across separation, support participation in a group or help a new relationship develop. The relevant conduct concerns what participants do together and what they exchange, as well as the medium available to them. Alongside Hall's relocation and university transitions, these accounts show relationships developing and continuing as the conditions for encounter change. Encounters and the pursuit of unexpected connections receive their complementary account in S83. [NN-W024]
