## S91 Acquiring, maintaining and contesting power

S91   Acquiring, maintaining and contesting power

Getting a proposal approved, controlling a resource and holding an office present different problems of influence. An office supplies certain rights; practical dependence can give someone influence well beyond those rights. Support may have to be assembled before a decision, renewed after it or protected against a rival. The accounts developed here examine how people acquire room to act, obtain cooperation, establish dependence and sustain positions of control.

### Political skill and willingness to act

Political skill and willingness to act

Liam Maher, Aqsa Ejaz, Chi Lan Nguyen and Gerald Ferris distinguish the ability to act politically from the willingness to do so. Their review describes political skill through four connected capacities: understanding other people and situations, influencing interpersonal encounters, building networks, and appearing sincere. Social astuteness helps someone recognize an opportunity; relationships make resources accessible; interpersonal influence concerns using the understanding effectively in an encounter. Apparent sincerity concerns how the conduct is received. The same overt attempt to please a superior may be accepted as appropriate or dismissed as transparent flattery. [PWR-W001, pp. 6–10]

The distinction matters for interpreting a repertoire of influence tactics. Knowing a tactic's name does not establish an ability to perform it successfully, and possessing that ability does not establish a willingness to incur the relational or reputational risks of using it. The review follows political skill into relationships, reputation and evaluations by others, including supervisors and colleagues. These outcomes explain much of its relevance to careers: an employee's work is performed and assessed among people whose cooperation, information and judgments affect what becomes possible. [PWR-W001, pp. 5–10]

### Dependence outside the hierarchy

Dependence outside the hierarchy

Michel Crozier's investigation of French factories gives practical dependence a concrete organizational form. Elaborate rules specify work, rights and relations between occupational groups. Seniority governs movement within a category, while recruitment from outside limits promotion between categories. Security and impersonal procedures reduce the personal discretion of supervisors. Yet machine breakdowns interrupt the otherwise regulated activity, and repairs depend on the maintenance workers. Production workers consequently experience dependence on people who are not their formal superiors. [PWR-W002]

Crozier asks why breakdowns become so consequential in these particular factories. When much of working life is specified beforehand, the events escaping the rules acquire exceptional importance. The maintenance workers control the response to one such uncertainty. Foremen object to the relationship but cannot resolve it through their own technical competence. Their position in the official hierarchy does not supply mastery of the practical problem on which production depends. [PWR-W002]

The maintenance group's position also has protection higher in the organization. An operations engineer possesses practical knowledge that formally superior engineers need, while his career prospects remain subordinate to theirs. Crozier interprets his support for the maintenance workers as protecting his own advantage. The resulting relationship runs across ranks: practical competence, dependence and backing reinforce a pattern that the official chart does not describe. Baldwin's strategic bottlenecks in S07 and Stinchcombe's occupational authority in S13 provide neighboring accounts of dependence and knowledge; Crozier develops the relations among the people occupying these particular positions. [PWR-W002]

<!-- PDF page 339 -->

Robert Greene's The 48 Laws of Power presents dependence as a deliberate objective. Its numbered prescriptions recommend keeping others in need of one's contribution and avoiding teaching them enough to dispense with one's services. Other prescriptions concern allowing a superior to feel secure, protecting reputation, controlling disclosure and taking credit for other people's work. These recommendations direct attention to different objects of political action: the distribution of capability, the attribution of achievement and others' beliefs about an actor. Greene treats preserving dependence and managing recognition as conduct to cultivate in the pursuit of power. [PWR-W004, laws 1, 3–7, 11]

### Assembling support before a decision

Assembling support before a decision

Jeffrey Pfeffer's Power Play begins with the difficulty of implementing an agenda among people who have competing purposes. Discretion over money, equipment, space or information can supply a means of recruiting support. Access to influential people can also be valuable. His account treats favors and resource distribution as ways of creating reciprocal support, alongside the substantive case for a proposed change. [PWR-W003]

Laura Esserman's efforts to change breast-cancer care illustrate several avenues of support operating over time. At the University of California, San Francisco, she sought more integrated care, easier enrollment in clinical trials and better collection of treatment information. When local changes met resistance, she continued building scientific and clinical visibility and relationships beyond the immediate organization. She also maintained relationships with patients and former patients, some of whom had substantial resources and connections. In Pfeffer's account, these activities kept adding advocates while parts of the program remained obstructed. [PWR-W003]

The account makes the construction of support part of implementing the clinical agenda. A relationship established outside the immediate dispute could become useful within it. Continuing on several fronts meant that resistance to one part did not stop every means of advancing. Pfeffer's reported case supplies this history of persistence and relationship building; the proposal itself was accompanied by efforts to acquire the practical capacity to carry it through. [PWR-W003]

大嶋玲未 and 廣川佳子 examine preparatory influence in new proposals within large Japanese firms. Their 2020 study draws on interviews with seven managers, analyzed using the KJ method. They identify

understanding the informal decision process, preparing the surrounding conditions and 根回し, or advance approaches to relevant participants. The managers needed to know who actually mattered, what concerns would arise and which parts of the approval process could be influenced through prior discussion. [PWR-W005, pp. 61–64]

The actions are specific. A manager might tell a key person about an impending proposal and ask which points mattered. Participants could develop a compromise before a formal confrontation, exchange concessions or speak beforehand to someone likely to obstruct the discussion. An intermediary could approach a person more effectively than the proposer could. Table 2 includes an account of asking a vice-president to supplement a presentation to the president where additional support was needed. The  sequence of approaches and the choice of messenger form part of the work. [PWR-W005, Table 2]

Formal procedures continue alongside these activities. The managers' preparation sought both timely approval and cooperation once an approved proposal had to be implemented. The authors describe functions of coordinating intentions, avoiding stalled decisions and making subsequent collaboration easier. Their evidence concerns proposal situations in hierarchical firms. They also observe that short, single interviews may make improper political conduct difficult to disclose. [PWR-W005, pp. 68–69]

<!-- PDF page 340 -->

### Opponents, superiors and subordinates

Opponents, superiors and subordinates

Pfeffer describes incorporating opponents into an institution as one way of changing a conflict. In his university example, a committee, modest resources and an official role gave critics a stake in the organization they had been challenging. Their attention came to include sustaining the committee itself. Another example concerns helping rivals obtain attractive positions elsewhere: Willie Brown supported assembly rivals' moves to other elected offices. A departure could remove local opposition while giving the departing person an opportunity worth accepting. These cases concern changes in participants' positions and interests, as well as arguments addressed to them. [PWR-W003]

Fong Keng-Highberger, Zhiyu Feng, Kai Chi Yam, Xiao-Ping Chen and Hu Li study a different configuration: a middle manager situated between a superior and subordinates. Their account distinguishes coercive power over subordinates from relational empowerment supplied by a senior manager. They propose that Machiavellian middle managers can cultivate close upward relationships while using abusive supervision downward. The two relations concern different dependencies and different sources of power. [PWR-W006, §§2–3]

The proposed coercive mechanism involves the expectation of punishment. A subordinate may comply to avoid abuse, making the withholding of an undesirable consequence valuable. Upward closeness supplies a different route, through the superior's relational support and empowerment. Perceived threats to the existing hierarchy enter the authors' explanation of why both strategies may intensify. In the laboratory manipulation, subordinates challenged the middle manager's usefulness and threatened to report the manager to the senior manager. [PWR-W006, §§3–4]

The research combines a laboratory study with 338 students in Singapore, a multiwave and multisource field study in China, and a two-wave study of 716 managers from the United States and United Kingdom. The results did not support every proposed relationship uniformly. The association between Machiavellianism and abusive supervision appeared in the laboratory and US/UK study but not in the China field study. The authors' general discussion preserves that inconsistency alongside the broader support for their model. Laboratory responses to a manipulated threat and reports of relationships at work are distinct parts of the evidence. [PWR-W006, §§4–7]

### Positions that control access

Positions that control access

Alexander Beresford's account of gatekeeper politics examines the African National Congress through party documents, interviews and observations around its 2012 centenary policy conference. Party or public positions can place their occupants in control of access to resources and opportunities. Granting or denying that access helps form relations of support and dependence. Rivals consequently compete over the positions through which distribution is controlled. [PWR-W010]

Beresford follows this relation into patronage networks, accumulation and factional struggles. Access is important to aspiring elites, but also to ordinary people seeking opportunities amid inequality, unemployment and poverty. The relationships are therefore sustained by several kinds of need. His account does not restrict patronage to kinship or inherited traditional authority: loyalties can run through modern party organization and become volatile as alliances and positions change. Holding the gate and fighting over who holds it are connected parts of the political process he describes. [PWR-W010]

This gives organizational reform a difficult setting. Integrity measures, political education and membership procedures address conduct within the party, while access to office and resources continues to support the relationships under examination. Beresford questions whether disciplinary measures alone can resolve that problem. He places gatekeeping within a broader political economy of patronage

<!-- PDF page 341 -->

and accumulation, explicitly resisting an interpretation of it as a uniquely African deviation. [PWR-W010, conclusion]

В. П. Пугачев's 2006 discussion of public human-resource management uses a narrower conception of micropolitics. He identifies sustained action to obtain, use and preserve power or resource-distribution positions for personal interests conflicting with official organizational purposes. Scarce resources, weak accountability, areas left to discretion and mismatches between individual and organizational interests help explain the opportunities for such action in his diagnosis. [PWR-W008]

Pugachev also recognizes defensive motives. Employees who experience injustice or neglect may seek protection for themselves and those close to them. His account follows increasing suspicion into additional preparation, safeguards and monitoring, with energy diverted into protecting positions and countering other people's moves. This adverse conception of micropolitics differs from the broader treatment of informal coordination in the proposal study. The difference concerns which activities the authors include in the category, as well as how they evaluate them. [PWR-W008]

Ezequiel Alpuche de la Cruz, José Luis Bernal López and Cesaire Chiatchoua examine organizational power through property rights, contracts and hierarchy. In their institutional account, ownership supports appropriation of the benefits attached to rights, while contracts organize exchanges and the allocation of resources among competing uses. Control is consequently embedded in legal and organizational forms as well as exercised through personal relationships. Their discussion connects these forms with bounded rationality, transaction costs and control of uncertainty. S15 develops the neighboring history of property and residual authority in greater detail. [PWR-W012]

### Historical networks and room to maneuver

Historical networks and room to maneuver

John Padgett and Christopher Ansell reconstruct the rise of the Medici through the marriage, economic and patronage networks of early fifteenth-century Florence. Cosimo's position linked relations that did not coincide neatly with a single unified faction. Their interpretation of robust action centers on multivocality: the same conduct could have coherent but different meanings for different participants. Ambiguity could preserve options when others sought to narrow them. [PWR-W011, pp. 1262–1264]

The historical development of the position is central to their explanation. They argue that Cosimo did not design the centralized party from the outset. Earlier oligarchic efforts to consolidate control helped produce the network configuration around the Medici. The political potential of that configuration became apparent through subsequent events. The authors therefore describe a process in which actors learned to use relationships formed partly through their opponents' actions. [PWR-W011, pp. 1286– 1287]

Cosimo's restrained public role and multiple identities also enter their account of control. Different participants could interpret his actions through their particular relations with him, while he maintained discretion and an appearance above the immediate conflict of interests. The authors' explanation combines the relational position with its historical formation and the style of action it made possible. It does not depend on Cosimo having specified the eventual outcome in advance. [PWR-W011, conclusion]

### Personality, conduct and responses within the organization

Personality, conduct and responses within the organization

Cameron Anderson, Daron Sharps, Christopher Soto and Oliver John investigate whether disagreeable people attain more power at work. Their preregistered longitudinal studies connect personality measured before entry to the labor market with power assessed about fourteen years later. In Study 1, the 457 participants reported workplace power, control over subordinates and organizational rank. Disagreeableness did not predict greater power overall. [PWR-W007]

<!-- PDF page 342 -->

The authors' examination of conduct helps interpret the result. Dominant-aggressive behavior was associated with greater power, while less communal and generous conduct was associated with less power. The opposing associations could offset one another at the level of personality. This concerns a different predictor and time horizon from a particular upward or downward influence tactic. The study examines attained workplace power rather than treating a single successful confrontation as the outcome. [PWR-W007]

Juliana Mansur and Filipe Sobral examine employees' experience of organizational politics in three private firms based in Rio de Janeiro. Their 2011 study analyzed 157 valid questionnaire responses. It related perceived politics to satisfaction, reported performance evaluations, neglect and intentions to leave. The authors found adverse relationships with satisfaction and performance and positive relationships with neglect and exit intentions. [PWR-W009, §§3–4]

Their discussion situates these findings in a setting associated with jeitinho, while the observations concern the particular firms and respondents studied. The measured outcomes show how employees experience and respond to a political workplace. The Japanese proposal study, by contrast, develops managers' accounts of using informal preparation to secure decisions and subsequent cooperation. Their objects of inquiry and outcomes differ: one follows employees' perceptions and work responses, the other the conduct of a proposal through an approval process. [PWR-W009, §5; PWR-W005]

<!-- PDF page 343 -->

## S92 Being strategic at work

S92   Being strategic at work

Being strategic at work can concern the course someone pursues, the understanding brought to a situation, the attention obtained for a problem or the opportunity to participate in deciding what happens. These questions arise in implementing an established direction as well as proposing a different one. The accounts below examine the work through which direction is formed, interpreted and pursued, and the organizational conditions under which a contribution becomes possible or recognized.

### Intention and a course of action

Intention and a course of action

Henry Mintzberg and James Waters distinguish intended strategies from patterns realized through action. Their 1985 account places deliberate and emergent strategies along a continuum. An umbrella strategy sets boundaries while allowing others to determine details. Leaders can specify the kinds of activity they want without possessing the information or control needed to settle every action. A process strategy instead influences who makes decisions and the organizational setting in which they work. [ST-W001, pp. 263–265]

Their National Film Board example concerns Norman McLaren's sustained production of experimental films. His individual course could appear emergent from the organization's perspective. The authors question whether he needed an advance intention to continue for decades: a sequence of worthwhile projects could develop into such a course. Their architectural-firm example similarly distinguishes the partners' broad preferences from the performing-arts commissions clients supplied. Both examples make the actor and level of intention consequential to the interpretation of a strategic pattern. [ST-W001, pp. 265–269]

### Carrying a direction through everyday work

Carrying a direction through everyday work

Linda Rouleau and Julia Balogun's 2008 working paper examines practical knowledge in middle managers' strategic sensemaking. At Radio-Canada, Mary entered a technical directorate without its established technical credentials. She acknowledged that she was there to organize the work, listened to technicians' difficulties and related the proposed changes to problems they experienced. The account gives conversation a specific setting: what could be said credibly depended on knowledge of the people and their work. [ST-W003, pp. 15–18]

Mary also prepared production-meeting reports and discussed them with colleagues and employees. These records helped consolidate compromises between program and technical production and could subsequently inform disputes. Visits to television sets supplied further opportunities to learn and establish relationships. Rouleau and Balogun describe enacting conversations and enrolling networks through semantic and sociocultural knowledge. Their vignette locates strategic implementation in continuing interpretation, documentation and relationships, alongside formal appointment and technical expertise. [ST-W003, pp. 15–18]

Christophe Torset's 2005 conceptual account questions a simple progression from reflection through decision to action. Ideas can remain active without producing a discrete decision; decisions about different questions can affect one another; action can contribute to subsequent understanding. His proposed conception of strategic reflection brings these activities into the same inquiry rather than treating thought as an isolated preliminary stage. [ST-W005, §1]

Torset also treats strategic reflection as an object and an instrument of research. Attention to how ideas arise and circulate can bring contributors into view who disappear when inquiry follows only formal decision makers. He includes analysis and planning practices within this account of meaning creation. His

<!-- PDF page 344 -->

argument changes what a researcher follows through an organization: the development of an idea and its practical influence may cross several decisions and levels. [ST-W005, §3]

### Obtaining attention for an issue

Obtaining attention for an issue

Jane Dutton, Susan Ashford, Regina O'Neill and Katherine Lawrence examine 82 issue-selling accounts from 42 individuals. Their concern is how people influence attention to developments with organizational significance. Presentation can make an issue intelligible through a business case; bundling connects it to valued goals or other concerns. One reported proposal for additional intensive-care space required work with physicians and data specialists on trends, demand and financial considerations. [ST-W002, pp. 716– 724]

Involvement and timing extend the process beyond presenting an argument. Earlier conversations can build support before an opportunity to act, while persistence can include setting an issue aside and returning later. The authors distinguish relational, normative and strategic contextual knowledge: knowing the people, acceptable ways of proceeding and organizational priorities affects the conduct of selling. Preparation also appears in unsuccessful accounts. These retrospective accounts describe how participants sought consideration for an issue and understood the outcome. S51 develops the conditions of voice, and S91 examines the construction of support and dependence. [ST-W002, pp. 724–731]

### Participation and access to direction

Participation and access to direction

Saku Mantere and Eero Vaara study strategy work in twelve organizations, drawing on interviews with 301 people across hierarchical levels and additional organizational material. Their six discourses concern how strategy is understood, who is entitled to define it and what others are expected to do. They associate mystification, disciplining and technologization with restricted participation, and self-actualization, dialogization and concretization with wider participation. These tendencies coexist in several of the organizations. [ST-W004, pp. 344–347, Tables 2–3]

Mystification gives strategy a special status accessible to a privileged few. Visions and missions arrive from senior management, while others are expected to accept their authority and implement them. In the telecommunications firm of their second vignette, access to strategy documents depended on rank. A manager described learning the organization's intended direction only after promotion. Another employee contrasted earlier experience of participating in planning with a new employer's small inner circle and annual presentation. The authors connect restricted information and unquestionable direction with the expectation that employees lack either the standing or the knowledge to contribute. [ST-W004, pp. 347–349]

Disciplining makes hierarchy and obedience central to strategy work. In a retail chain, military language cast managers as commanders and operating personnel as followers; sanctions for noncompliance formed part of that understanding. A governmental office used an educational version: managers appeared as teachers or parents, and attendance at strategy discussions was an obligation. Being present in a discussion could thus accompany a subordinate role rather than an opportunity to help determine direction. [ST-W004, pp. 349–350]

Technologization places a particular system in command of what can be discussed and measured. An insurance firm adopted a balanced scorecard throughout its strategy process. Senior managers welcomed its greater controllability, but some employees found organization-level specifications difficult to use in departmental work. A team leader could not find a measure that would make excessive workload visible. The authors describe tools becoming control devices: employees were responsible for supplying measures within the system while having little opportunity to question its starting points. [ST-W004, pp. 350–351]

<!-- PDF page 345 -->

The participation-promoting discourses give people different roles. Self-actualization concerns finding meaning and defining objectives through one's own involvement. In an expert governmental office, people interpreted shared goals in relation to their work, and an employee with an idea could seek an appointment with the chief executive. Dialogization instead emphasizes organized exchange between levels and groups. In a financial organization, management supplied broad plans, teams developed action plans and sent them upward, and targets were discussed before being finalized. Senior management retained its role in setting direction while others had a recognized part in developing it. [ST-W004, pp. 351–352]

Concretization makes strategy intelligible through the continuing specification of activities, rules and procedures. In a municipal health authority, practitioners helped craft guidelines for problems encountered in their own work. Specifications were developed at different levels rather than simply arriving from the center. The distinction from disciplining lies in the roles that the rules make possible: the people doing the work can help construct its practical direction. Mantere and Vaara also describe concretization as a demand voiced within organizations where strategy remained remote and obscure. Their analysis follows how these understandings legitimize or restrict participation through meetings, information access, systems and everyday interaction. [ST-W004, pp. 352–355]

### Roles connecting decisions and implementation

Roles connecting decisions and implementation

李炜文, 高岩 and 李晓彤's 2022 review examines 103 articles published between 1986 and 2020. It organizes middle managers' roles around knowledge management, relationship connections, participation, autonomous decisions and implementation. Knowledge and relationships supply routes through which managers influence decisions, while implementation entails interpreting aims and coordinating their realization. The review brings decision and execution into the same account of middle-management work. [ST-W006, research method and Table 2]

The review distinguishes benefits attributed to participation from a contrary explanation of managerial conduct. Studies it discusses associate middle managers' involvement with correcting senior decision makers' cognitive biases, improving decision quality, aligning objectives and enabling strategic change. It also reports Natarajan and colleagues' finding that managers may make unnecessary resource allocations to demonstrate their management ability and increase personal income. Such activity can reduce operating efficiency. The disagreement concerns what managers do with their position and the consequences of that conduct, rather than whether they take part in decisions at all. [ST-W006, decision participation]

Implementation requires work on both interpretation and activity. The reviewers describe managers developing shared understandings with peers and making strategic aims meaningful in particular settings. They also discuss dividing complex objectives into tasks that employees can understand and carry out. Their reconstruction of Beatty and Lee's study of computer-aided systems in companies in Britain and Canada emphasizes managers solving employees' difficulties through communication, encouragement and control of the implementation process. [ST-W006, strategic implementation]

Emotions enter this account through managers' own commitment and through their responses to other employees. The review describes resistance arising when middle managers question the legitimacy of a major change, alongside accounts of managers responding to employees' negative emotions during implementation. It identifies institutional differences, cultural settings and digital forms of work as questions for further investigation. S86 examines project governance, and S88 follows the continuing responsibilities of product development. [ST-W006, strategic implementation and discussion]

<!-- PDF page 346 -->

谷口正一郎's 2021 study reconstructs an employee innovation program at Company X, a food manufacturer, through interviews with eight people across functions and ranks. Introduced by a new president in 2011, the program asked employees to report initiatives outside their ordinary duties to directors. Selected initiatives could receive awards and become new businesses or formal company practices. Employees initially differed over what innovation meant for their work. Some associated it with patented products and could see little opportunity for someone in sales to contribute. The president's explanation of an award-winning example helped broaden their understanding of what could qualify. [ST-W008, pp. 26–28, 31–32]

Participation developed through changes to the program and its relationship to ordinary management. One interviewee recalled that it had not initially been required of everyone, but that roughly one initiative per person was encouraged from the second year. Participation became part of appraisal, and a manager reported that subordinates' failure to participate could affect the manager's own evaluation. Employees who preferred routine work consequently experienced an obligation to contribute. A dedicated budget made initiatives possible that otherwise lacked funding; an employee also described approved funding as a commitment to carry the work through. [ST-W008, pp. 32–33]

These arrangements changed supervisors' responsibilities. One interviewee described managers helping teams finish routine work earlier or reduce it so that employees could devote time to innovation. Other departments' assistance and senior managers' attention to individual initiatives made support visible. The program office coordinated the scheme, training and adjustments, while department heads retained appraisal authority. Its office therefore worked with personnel planners on the appraisal system rather than directly assigning employees' evaluations. [ST-W008, pp. 30–34, note 4]

The case also follows difficulty sustaining involvement. Employees could run out of ideas, struggle to combine initiatives with operating targets or feel that another department had better opportunities to win recognition. Adjustments emphasized the reasoning and experience behind an attempt: what need the employee had identified, what hypothesis had been tried and what happened. Reporting formats asked for that explanation, and interviewees described being encouraged to try even when an initiative failed. The author's process model connects these responses with renewed participation. [ST-W008, Table 5, Figure 2, pp. 34–35]

Developing an initiative brought employees into contact with the work of other departments: pricing required finance, volumes required product management and logistics, and an idea could require training staff in stores. Interviewees described improved internal communication, greater visibility for their abilities and links between recognition, promotion and transfers. Some also described reorganizing routine duties to create time for further initiatives. The account follows participation through changes in working relationships, career opportunities and the organization of everyday work. [ST-W008, pp. 35– 36]

### What judgments and measures observe

What judgments and measures observe

许志行 and 曹骞's 2019 review distinguishes attention to strategic activities from attention to kinds of thinking. Its landscape includes management-oriented accounts and game-theoretic reasoning. The reviewers show how conceptions of strategic thinking shape the instruments used to recognize it. An attribute scale begins with proposed characteristics, such as a systems perspective or attention to the future, and turns them into questionnaire items. Differences over the characteristics therefore become differences between the scales. [ST-W007, §§III–V]

The cognitive logic approach described in the review is also a questionnaire. It distinguishes ways of gathering information, through intuition or sensation, from ways of evaluating it, through logic or feeling.

<!-- PDF page 347 -->

Their combinations produce four proposed modes of thought; the instrument treats strategic thinking as their interaction. Written-text analysis takes another route, examining semantic features of an author's work to estimate tendencies such as risk-taking and foresight. Experimental approaches instead observe choices in structured tasks or games, including how participants recognize similarities and respond to risks and rewards. [ST-W007, §V]

The reviewers' objections are specific to these approaches. The proposed division into four cognitive modes remains disputed. Text analysis depends on the quantity and quality of available writing. Experiments can narrow strategic thinking to reasoning within a game. Widely used attribute scales inherit disagreements over what the capability consists of, making findings difficult to accumulate and compare. The reviewers also question scales developed without sufficiently rigorous item refinement and reliability and validity evaluation. Naming desirable characteristics does not by itself establish a sound measure. [ST-W007, §V]

Their criticism of attribute lists also concerns explanation. They criticize one comprehensive model for simply packaging characteristics collected from earlier authors. They also question whether existing attribute definitions distinguish strategic thinking sufficiently from other thought. The reviewers connect concept definition, attributes, instruments and research on effects: a change in what the concept means changes what subsequent measurements can tell us. Their treatment separates individual from organizational influences and asks how they interact over time. S71 discusses practice and skill development. [ST-W007, §V and prospects]

Stefan Kühl's 2017 interview with Martin Claßen supplies a different diagnostic perspective on managerial judgments. Kühl describes pressure on newly appointed managers to display change even where continuity may be appropriate. He distinguishes formal hierarchy from influence arising through expertise, customer access and informal communication. His argument directs attention to organizational expectations that make some conduct visible as an achievement. [ST-W009]

Kühl's account also places the possibility of retaining a course alongside the expectation of intervention. The workplace questions consequently concern what is being pursued, who can contribute to it and how that contribution is recognized. The historical accounts give these questions different practical settings: a sustained individual activity, the interpretation of an established direction, a concern seeking attention and an institution organizing participation.

<!-- PDF page 348 -->

## S115 Charisma, follower recognition and continuing authority

S115   Charisma, follower recognition and continuing authority

### Recognition and the work of a continuing staff

Recognition and the work of a continuing staff

In the posthumously published Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft, Max Weber examines what happens as a relationship sustained by recognition of an exceptional leader has to continue in ordinary conditions. The administrative staff acquires interests in recruitment, economic opportunities and the regular conduct of its work. People initially joined through devotion may later occupy positions with more stable claims to resources or authority. Weber describes ways in which those claims and procedures can change the relationship through which authority is recognized. [T17-W001]

François Chazel distinguishes two layers of Weber’s analysis. In his reading, the question of succession is also a question of the basis on which a successor can be recognized. An expectation that authority passes within a lineage differs from attaching it to an office with its own recognized conditions. Chazel connects these variants to different aspects of everyday continuation and objectivation in Weber’s writings. The distinctions are part of Chazel’s textual reconstruction. [T17-W002]

### Continuation and disputed succession

Continuation and disputed succession

Claudia Jetter compares Joseph Smith Jr. and Ralph Waldo Emerson through what each made of continuing revelation. In her account, Smith gave church-wide revelation a place in a hierarchy. Emerson treated access to revelation as a capacity individuals could exercise and rejected an exclusive institution as its center. Jetter uses the contrast to explain why their accounts of revelation supported different kinds of religious organization. [T17-W003]

Joseph F. Smith Jr.’s later polemic locates succession in the authority of the Twelve Apostles and their recognition by the church. He cites votes in August and October 1844 at which, in his account, the assembled members sustained the Twelve as the presiding quorum. He treats those votes as confirmation of the quorum’s right to preside and disputes the authority of those who later ordained Joseph Smith III. [T17-W005]

Community of Christ’s institutional history recounts the recognition of a different successor. It describes Joseph Smith III, the founder’s son, as coming to believe he had a divine calling, accepting leadership and being ordained president at Amboy, Illinois, on 6 April 1860. It also describes the Herald, first published in 1860, as a forum where leaders and members exchanged accounts of their missions and discussed the church’s affairs. The ordination and the periodical are two concrete acts in that institution’s account of its reorganization. [T17-W006]

### Behaviors that observers rate

Behaviors that observers rate

Antonakis, Fenley and Liechti examine whether speakers and managers can learn behaviors judged charismatic. One study randomly assigned 34 managers and reassessed them after three months. In a second, 41 MBA participants gave a speech and delivered it again six weeks after instruction, with ratings by independent assessors. The authors report increases in ratings of charisma and discuss how those ratings relate to judgments of who looks like a leader or emerges as one. The outcomes are behavior and leadership impressions under specified measures. Continuing authority, in Weber’s account, concerns the relationships and arrangements through which people keep recognizing a claim. [T17-W004]

<!-- PDF page 349 -->

## S93 Deception, cunning and misdirection

S93   Deception, cunning and misdirection

A concealed intention, a misleading statement and a sporting feint present different problems. Writers have asked how an opponent interprets appearances, how people sustain deceptive practices together, how an audience reconstructs what it has seen and which forms of confidence may legitimately be invoked. Their accounts include strategic prescriptions, exemplary narratives, organizational interpretations, experiments and legal distinctions.

### Assessment, appearances and military strength

Assessment, appearances and military strength

In 孫子兵法, assessment precedes the instructions to present misleading appearances. 始計 compares

rulers, commanders, conditions and discipline. 兵勢 develops the combinations of straightforward and

extraordinary operations; 虛實 connects concealment of one's disposition and inducement of the enemy with the concentration and dispersal of forces. An opponent obliged to prepare in many places must distribute defenses, while a commander who conceals the intended point of engagement can concentrate.

軍爭 adds the management of direct and roundabout routes. Preparation, display and deployment therefore work together in the text's strategic prescriptions. [DC-W01]

Lisa Raphals reconstructs a disagreement within early Chinese thought over deception and military strength. Her Sunzi combines direct and indirect operations; she objects to interpretations that make Chinese strategy uniformly indirect or equate its deliberate preparation with effortless action. Her

reading of 荀子 distinguishes morally constructive artifice from deception. In 議兵, Linwu praises positional advantage and dissimulation, whereas Xunzi makes popular attachment and orderly government the basis of military strength. He argues that deception cannot break the army of a humane ruler. Raphals also identifies substantial agreement on military preparations. The disagreement concerns the sources of strength, deception's acceptability and its efficacy, within a textual dialogue whose teaching rhetoric shapes the presentation. [DC-W02]

### Stratagem collections and princely dissimulation

Stratagem collections and princely dissimulation

Frontinus's Strategemata arranges examples for commanders seeking usable precedents. Its preface distinguishes the broad conduct of strategy from particular ingenious stratagems and organizes material around situations before battle, in battle and in siege warfare. Book I.1 tells how Ventidius used an intermediary known to pass information to the Parthians. He displayed fear of the route he wanted them to take and confidence about the route he feared. In Frontinus's telling, the enemy chose the slower crossing, allowing reinforcements to arrive. The intermediary's reporting makes the expression of preference consequential: the intended recipient hears it as intelligence about what Ventidius wants to avoid. Frontinus presents the sequence as an instructive example. [DC-W03]

Chapter XVIII of Machiavelli's Il Principe places dissimulation within the problem of preserving princely rule under changing circumstances. The fox recognizes traps and the lion frightens wolves; neither capacity substitutes for the other. Machiavelli argues that promises may cease to bind a ruler when the conditions that occasioned them disappear. He distinguishes possessing admired qualities from appearing to possess them and remaining able to act otherwise when necessity requires. Alexander VI illustrates the contrast: Machiavelli describes him as exceptionally forceful in his assurances and oaths, exceptionally unreliable in observing them, and nevertheless successful in deceiving people. The example supports his argument that an appearance of fidelity can coexist with conduct that violates it. He also

<!-- PDF page 350 -->

argues that people judge largely by what they see, while few can test the reality behind appearances. Public recognition and adaptability therefore enter his account of maintaining princely power. [DC-W04]

### Practical intelligence and political counsel

Practical intelligence and political counsel

Marcel Meulder's 1975 review presents Détienne and Vernant's account of mētis as practical, resourceful intelligence operating amid unstable circumstances. It enables people to overcome another's strength and find ways around natural obstacles. Its reach includes human crafts as well as deliberate deception. Navigation and chariot guidance connect skilled direction with the construction of ships and chariots; in Meulder's reconstruction, the pilot must know the available passages and anticipate chance and the opportune moment. The relevant intelligence deals with changing, multiple and ambiguous circumstances. Meulder places this practical intelligence against its devaluation in Plato and praises the book for challenging an excessively Platonic picture of Greek antiquity. His review thus gives cunning a place in human skill and practical judgment beyond the production of false beliefs. [DC-W05]

Olga Torres reads al-Harawi's manual as political and military counsel associated with Ayyubid state-building. Its chapter outline places officials, counsel and envoys alongside campaigns and sieges. Torres  describes advice to receive an enemy envoy warmly, seek counsel and encourage dissatisfaction with the envoy's own patron. She connects this with an attempted inducement of the Green Knight, who refused. The recommended approach and the reported response reveal different aspects of the account: a prescription for cultivating disaffection and a historical reconstruction in which the intended recipient resisted. Torres also discusses uncertainty over whether the manual's intended patron was Saladin or his son. [DC-W06]

Michel Pretalli's introduction to Ruse et magie de l'Antiquité à nos jours follows an earlier inquiry into military stratagems. He recalls that project's definition of military ruse through ingenious artifice, mistaken representations and surprise, then emphasizes its moral ambiguity. An ingenious escape from a desperate situation can appear honorable in one telling and dishonorable or diabolical in another. Moving into magic changes the setting and the meanings attached to secrecy and extraordinary effects. His historical project brings these practices into conversation while investigating the judgments made about them. [DC-W21]

### Strategic assessment and reflexive control

Strategic assessment and reflexive control

Richards Heuer applies cognitive psychology to intelligence assessment. Reinforcing an existing interpretation, he argues, is often easier than replacing it: discrepant information can be absorbed into a settled diagnosis, while organizational commitment to earlier reports makes revision harder. He also examines the planner's vulnerability. Familiarity with a planned message can make its meaning seem clearer than it will be to an opponent. Greater suspicion is not his sole answer to counterdeception. Salient stories may encourage analysts to overestimate deception's prevalence, and more collection or alertness may leave interpretation unchanged. He recommends cognitive aids and a counterdeception staff to give the analytic problem sustained attention. [DC-W07]

Georgy Smolyan explains reflexive control as influencing a decision by supplying the grounds on which another participant chooses. He opens with Lefebvre's illustration of Brer Rabbit pleading with Brer Fox to do anything except throw him into the thorn bush. The plea presents a destination as something Rabbit fears. In Smolyan's illustration, that apparent aversion supplies Fox with a reason to choose the very action Rabbit seeks. The influence works through the grounds of the opponent's choice rather than an overt command. Smolyan connects this with concealed direction that preserves a participant's conviction that the choice is free. His conceptual account concerns manipulation of the decision, including what the

<!-- PDF page 351 -->

target regards as desirable or threatening. Reflexive control in this account differs from the market reflexivity discussed in S59. [DC-W08]

João Ricardo da Cunha Croce Lopes's professional exposition distinguishes demonstrations of force, false information, effects on the decision process and effects on decision timing. Demonstrations include overt threats and readiness displays; false information includes concealed dispositions and apparent strengths. A timing intervention can seek to delay the opponent by directing attention elsewhere. The repertoire he reconstructs through military writers, including Ionov, therefore reaches beyond lying. Pressure and concealment enter alongside attempts to shape interpretation. These distinctions form part of Lopes's interpretation of reflexive control and its military uses. [DC-W09]

Hayden Peake's review describes Whaley's STRATAGEM as a way of reasoning about deception operations, supported by a collection of surprise cases. He distinguishes its discussion of history, theory, ethics and counterdeception from its summaries of 115 instances of wartime surprise, divided into strategic and tactical cases. Peake reports Whaley's objection to a signals-obscured-by-noise explanation of deception: the objection concerns its failure to predict deception, whereas Whaley proposes looking for clues that point to deception itself. Peake presents this as a way of thinking and studying operations, rather than a step-by-step recipe for assessing or conducting them, and notes Whaley's acknowledgment of chance. His appraisal also raises a problem within the case collection: he reports that one celebrated ruse attributed to Richard Meinertzhagen was fabricated, while accepting the principles it illustrates. Peake thereby distinguishes the standing of an illustrative story from that of the principles associated with it. [DC-W10]

### Lying within organizations

Lying within organizations

Sarah Jenkins and Rick Delbridge relate lying to organizational contexts and social relations. Coercion, compensation and condoning describe different pressures or permissions; cooperative, caring and conflictual relations help explain why employees comply, cope or challenge. Their reconstruction of Sallaz's CallCo study supplies a concrete sequence. Short call-handling targets, a concealed depot contact and promises of same-day redelivery helped staff end calls without resolving customers' problems. Their account distinguishes tolerated coping from an explicit order to lie. Targets, working relationships and the practical handling of calls enter the authors' relational explanation together. [DC-W11]

David Shulman separates notorious criminal fraud, familiar workplace deception and forms easily overlooked in nonprofits. Misleading donors, favoring clients and diverting budgets to preferred causes differ from the crimes that dominate public discussion. His exploratory explanation connects resource pressure, moral commitment, small size, autonomy and limited career paths with opportunities and inducements to mislead. A worker may defend an organization's mission while hiding how its work is carried out. His essay challenges the inference that benevolent purposes make deception unlikely, while warning that American sector divisions and scandal reporting do not establish worldwide rates. [DC-W12]

David Arellano Gault examines corruption as an organizational process. A small lie that passes unnoticed may require further lies to sustain it, while colleagues and authorities can draw others into maintaining the account. Rationalizing language can recast bribery as ordinary assistance to getting work done. Repeated action, shared justification and socialization support his explanation of persistence. His conceptual interpretation concerns how corruption becomes normalized, beyond the identification of an individual's moral defect. Deception enters this account through practices and justifications that participants sustain together. [DC-W13]

<!-- PDF page 352 -->

### Emotion and misleading truths in negotiation

Emotion and misleading truths in negotiation

Joseph Gaspar and Maurice Schweitzer explain deception decisions through present and anticipated emotion, as well as incentives and information asymmetry. Present feelings may arise from the negotiation itself or unrelated events. Their emotion-deception model proposes that these feelings affect both what negotiators think about and which opportunities they notice. Anticipated consequences, including guilt, can influence the decision before it is made. Their discussion of incidental anger proposes a path through reduced trust to defensive deception. Their review also questions the dominance of one-shot role-play studies: later discovery, retaliation and continuing relationships can change what an  account of negotiation must explain. [DC-W14]

Todd Rogers and colleagues distinguish paltering, the active use of true statements to create a false impression, from false assertions and silence. In Study 4B, buyers with private knowledge about rezoning negotiated with sellers online. Buyers instructed to palter could answer a question about intended use by invoking their history of residential development. The authors report more mistaken seller beliefs in that condition. Buyers obtained more surplus among completed deals; including impasses removed the profit difference. Sellers also judged discovered paltering more harshly than buyers judged themselves. The study connects an assigned response, the inference it encouraged and measured outcomes in an incentivized role-play negotiation. [DC-W15]

### Misdirection and sporting feints

Misdirection and sporting feints

Gustav Kuhn and colleagues distinguish misdirection affecting perception, memory and reasoning. Attention control is only part of their taxonomy. Separating a method from its apparent effect can make the earlier action difficult to reconstruct. Incidental actions, convincing apparent shuffles and retrospective descriptions can shape what an audience remembers. The spectator must nevertheless see enough of the effect to experience the impossibility; preventing observation altogether would defeat the performance. Their psychologically based taxonomy links craft practices and research through the relation between a concealed method, the visible event and its later reconstruction. [DC-W16]

Mustafa Alhaj Ahmad Alaboud and colleagues investigate whether a head fake's frequency changes its effect. Participants identify pass direction while a pictured player's gaze agrees or conflicts with it; blocks vary the proportion of deceptive trials. The experiments use static and apparent-motion displays. Conflicting gaze interferes with identifying the pass, and the effect is reduced when deceptive displays become frequent. Immediate trial history also enters the analysis, with differing strength across experiments. The measured result concerns identifying a displayed pass under these conditions. [DC-W17]

### Plausible requests and security procedures

Plausible requests and security procedures

Fatima Salahdine and Naima Kaabouch describe security attacks that combine a plausible social situation with a technical or physical action. In pretexting, an invented scenario gives a request for information a reason. In tailgating, a request to hold a door substitutes social cooperation for a credential check. Baiting supplies an apparently desirable object carrying the technical compromise. These sequences differ in what the participant is asked to accept and do. The survey also classifies attacks by contact and medium, organizing a security repertoire that crosses social, physical and technical activity. [DC-W18]

### Ruses and protected confidence

Ruses and protected confidence

Article 37 of Additional Protocol I distinguishes perfidy from permissible ruses of war. Its prohibition addresses killing, injuring or capturing an adversary through betrayal of confidence in protection under

<!-- PDF page 353 -->

the applicable law. Feigned surrender is one example. Paragraph 2 permits ruses that mislead or induce recklessness without breaching applicable rules or invoking legally protected confidence; camouflage, decoys, mock operations and misinformation are examples. The operative boundary concerns the confidence invited, the intention to betray it and the prohibited result. The legal classification gives a different question from whether the misleading conduct achieves its purpose. [DC-W19]

吉田靖之 examines how rules developed around visual identification bear on contemporary naval deception. His discussion distinguishes navigation lights, an apparent ship identity and a claim to protected legal status. Lights can indicate movement or vessel characteristics without necessarily asserting immunity from attack. His treatment of false flags distinguishes conduct before an attack from conduct during one and identifies specially protected categories that cannot simply be impersonated as an ordinary ruse. Signals and appearances acquire legal significance through the status they claim and the circumstances in which they are used. His analysis makes those distinctions within the naval rules and manuals he discusses. [DC-W20]

The accounts place judgment in different settings: preparing an enemy's interpretation, sustaining an organization's explanation, reconstructing an apparent impossibility and invoking a protected status. Their practical questions involve what others can observe, what they infer, how they respond and which expectations the participants are entitled to rely on.

<!-- PDF page 354 -->

### Part 6 Choice, commitment, and exchange

Part 6   Choice, commitment, and exchange

These accounts examine how people decide what to undertake under uncertainty, when they commit resources, and how they organize exchange and market relationships.

## S32 Antifragility and responses to variability

S32   Antifragility and responses to variability

### The response to variation is the object of inquiry

The response to variation is the object of inquiry

The sources considered here ask how variation in an input changes a specified outcome. Taleb and Douady formulate sensitivity to changes in distributions and nonlinear exposure. Axenie and colleagues organize technical and biological applications across several scales. De Florio proposes a scheme for choosing between provisioned resources and more elaborate adaptive behavior. Danchin, Binder and Noria investigate biological maintenance and molecular flexibility.

The relevant distinction is more exacting than survival after disturbance. A system can withstand a change without benefiting from greater variability. It can also improve a selected outcome while imposing losses elsewhere, or benefit over one range and fail beyond it. The sources' definitions and examples therefore require the reader to identify an input, an outcome, a range of variation and a boundary.

### Taleb and Douady: exposure beyond a threshold

Taleb and Douady: exposure beyond a threshold

In the 2012 preprint of Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility, Taleb and Douady begin with the sensitivity of an object or outcome to environmental variability. Their coffee-cup example separates small ordinary disturbances from events large enough to break the cup. The accumulated effect of many harmless movements need not resemble that of one sufficiently large movement. A bridge, building or balance sheet can likewise tolerate a range of stresses and then encounter a sharply adverse region. Their interest is the shape of the exposure, including the threshold, rather than merely the average magnitude of an input. [AFC-W001, 2012 preprint, pp. 1–4]

The paper distinguishes this exposure from a person's attitude toward a gamble. A cup need not possess a utility function for its breaking response to be nonlinear. Taleb and Douady criticize definitions of risk centered on subjective preferences and seek measures applicable to objects with distributions of outcomes. This is their position in a methodological debate; it does not make economic preferences irrelevant to the choice of an outcome or to the distribution of its consequences. Their mathematical development concerns the sensitivity of the selected exposure.

Their initial formal construction uses a reference level, conventionally denoted Ω, a lower stress threshold K, and a one-parameter family of probability densities. The scale parameter is related to a left semi-absolute deviation: the expected magnitude of departures on one side of the reference. A finite first semi-moment is required for that construction. It is not simply an assumption that every distribution has finite variance. They require the relation between the family parameter and this dispersion measure to be continuous and strictly increasing over the specified range, allowing the dispersion measure to parameterize the family. The tail sensitivity then concerns the change in the expected adverse exposure below K as this dispersion changes. [AFC-W001, pp. 5–8]

The restrictions matter. A result for movement within a specified family is not automatically a result for every possible replacement distribution. Nor does a semi-deviation identify every feature of a tail. For nonsmooth threshold effects, the authors also supply a finite-difference version rather than requiring the derivative to exist everywhere. Later two-sided definitions and regularity qualifications extend the treatment beyond the introductory left-tail picture. [AFC-W001, pp. 12–14]

### Nonlinear transformation and uncertainty about a model

Nonlinear transformation and uncertainty about a model

Taleb and Douady distinguish the distribution of an input from the transformation through which an object inherits exposure to that input. The same disturbance can have different consequences for

<!-- PDF page 356 -->

different arrangements. Their analysis connects nonlinear transformations with sensitivity to the tails and develops a heuristic for detecting an unfavorable response to additional dispersion. The aim is practical detection even when a confidently specified probability model is unavailable. The authors apply this reasoning to stress testing, forecasting and hidden exposure. [AFC-W001, pp. 2–4 and subsequent transfer-function development]

The account of model error follows the threshold example. If an arrangement is engineered to tolerate a specified range but fails outside it, uncertainty about the stressor distribution can increase the chance of reaching the failure region. Treating the estimated distribution as exact may conceal this sensitivity. Their argument asks what happens to exposure when uncertainty itself changes. It is consequently possible to be robust to familiar disturbances while remaining fragile to error in the assumed range or distribution.

For gambits engineering, the relevant information in this paper is the specified mapping from stress to outcome and the consequences of changing that mapping or its domain. A favorable response over a local range can turn adverse beyond it.

### Axenie and colleagues: three scales of response

Axenie and colleagues: three scales of response

The 2024 Perspective by Axenie and colleagues treats antifragility as benefit derived from variability in environmental perturbations. It asks how the response should be described in technical and natural systems and emphasizes the need to specify the scale. The article proposes three technical categories— intrinsic, inherited and induced—with ecological, evolutionary and interventional counterparts in its biological discussion. This is the authors' taxonomy. Its applications are reconstructed from cited work. [AFC-W008, pp. 1–2, figures 1–2]

Intrinsic antifragility concerns the response associated with the system's internal dynamics. The authors discuss the shape of the input–output relation and its second-order effects. Inherited antifragility brings in external signals that modulate those internal dynamics. Induced antifragility adds a closed loop: a controller or driving signal guides the system toward a desired region of operation. The categories therefore distinguish sources of response capacity. A favorable curve obtained under active control cannot be described as a property supplied solely by passive internal structure.

Time is also explicit in their account. Technical systems may be designed around known constraints and specifications; heterogeneous natural systems involve entities that differ in speed, strength, proximity and other characteristics. The relevant time scale can alter which response is being measured. The measured response depends on its metric, time scale and environment. [AFC-W008, pp. 2–3]

### Curvature, payoff direction and the meaning of improvement

Curvature, payoff direction and the meaning of improvement

Axenie and colleagues use Jensen's inequality to explain why a nonlinear response to variable inputs can differ from the response to the mean input. For an integrable convex response, the expected response is at least the response evaluated at the expected input. Strict improvement requires appropriate strictness and nondegeneracy conditions; the article's displayed strict signs should not be read as excluding equality cases. The direction reverses for a concave response. [AFC-W008, p. 3, equations 1–2]

The meaning of the response remains essential. Increasing the expectation of a benefit differs from increasing the expectation of a cost. A convex damage function makes variability more harmful, even though the same inequality applies. Likewise a desired effect on one population can be an adverse outcome for another. The article's treatment examples illustrate the dependence on a response curve and dose distribution. [AFC-W008, pp. 3–5, figure 4]

In the evolutionary discussion, the authors distinguish the fate of individuals from changes in a heterogeneous population. Some individuals can die while the surviving population becomes better fitted

<!-- PDF page 357 -->

to fluctuating conditions. That boundary prevents a population-level claim from being reported as an individual benefit. [AFC-W008, pp. 3–4]

### Induced response retains a controller

Induced response retains a controller

In the technical discussion of induced antifragility, Axenie and colleagues describe combinations of time-scale separation, redundant overcompensation and variable-structure control. A controller chooses  signals intended to move the dynamics into an advantageous operational region. The robot illustration measures such matters as tracking and the speed of reaching desired dynamics under uncertainty. The favorable behavior belongs to a specified closed-loop system, including the control law. [AFC-W008, pp. 4 –5, figure 5]

The traffic applications are described in terms of response to disruptions, including their amplitude and timing, and comparisons with particular baseline controllers. Machine-learning approaches are also reported. The intervention changes how the system responds, and the claimed benefit is assessed against an operational objective and alternatives.

### De Florio: fidelity and the cost of adaptation

De Florio: fidelity and the cost of adaptation

De Florio's preliminary 2014 paper begins from fidelity: correspondence between figures of interest in two communicating domains. A physical quantity and its computer representation provide one example. Real time and a system's representation of time provide another. The relevant engineering problem is not only whether the device continues running, but whether its representations and behavior remain sufficiently faithful for the application. The paper develops an algebraic treatment of the correspondence and a behavioral treatment of the changing relation between system and environment. [AFC-W009, arXiv version, pp. 1–5]

One design approach anticipates conditions and provisions resources through worst-case analysis, redundancy or diversity. De Florio calls attention to its simplicity and low nonfunctional overhead. Unfavorable events can be masked within the provisioned range without extensive runtime reconfiguration. The corresponding assumption is that the system and its intended environment are sufficiently known and stable. Reserved resources are part of this arrangement, even when the runtime behavior is simple.

The behavioral approach allows more elaborate awareness, planning and adaptation as conditions drift. Such capabilities can be necessary in open cyber-physical settings, but they introduce overhead and can complicate the very timing analyses on which guarantees depend. De Florio therefore does not equate more adaptation with a costless improvement. He explicitly frames a tradeoff between the advantages and costs of the approaches. [AFC-W009, pp. 4–5]

His proposed scheme monitors fidelity and environmental conditions, maintains a comparatively simple model while conditions remain safe, and invokes more complex reactive or proactive models when identity is at risk. Actions can include self-reconfiguration or entering and leaving relationships with neighboring systems. The listed relationships include improving one's own position at a neighbor's expense and mutual assistance.

The final learning step measures attempted solutions, ranks them against past solutions, retains conclusions and updates models. That stored experience is the basis for the conjecture that repeated challenges might improve future response. Monitoring, comparison, memory, model revision and implementation remain active functions. The title's expression, Antifragility = Elasticity + Resilience + Machine Learning, is a conceptual proposal, not a measured additive identity. The paper presents a

<!-- PDF page 358 -->

preliminary scheme and conjecture without a simulation result demonstrating effectiveness. [AFC-W009, pp. 5–7]

### Danchin, Binder and Noria: maintaining a cell rather than merely reproducing it

Danchin, Binder and Noria: maintaining a cell rather than merely reproducing it

Danchin, Binder and Noria approach antifragility through tinkering, molecular flexibility and the persistence of living systems. Their account distinguishes stationary life from reproduction. Their thought experiment asks what functions would be needed to construct a long-lived organism. A cell that is not multiplying still needs a maintained envelope, metabolism, energy supply, import and export, sensing and the replacement of components. Dormancy and continued low-level metabolism are distinct possibilities. [AFC-W013, introduction and §§2.1–2.3]

The paper describes salvage and turnover as ways of reducing dependence on fresh environmental supply. It also distinguishes functions whose redundancy or low demand permits gradual deterioration from those required at the front line of maintenance. Molecular chaperones are important in its account because temperature changes and ageing can both disrupt folding. Repair and refolding cost energy; when they fail, degradation and replacement must occur. The authors discuss degradation machinery that consumes energy even when the underlying chemical breakdown is energetically favorable. Selection and orderly processing, rather than the mere release of energy, are part of the biological work being described.

The relevant observation about long proteins is deliberately puzzling. Their production can be vulnerable to transcription or translation errors, yet the authors identify large proteins in important maintenance and information-processing machinery. They discuss flexible regions and report experiments from other sources as evidence relevant to possible functional advantages. A molecule can have a vulnerability in its production and a different advantage in its operation.

### Flexibility, ageing and the boundary of biological benefit

Flexibility, ageing and the boundary of biological benefit

In their discussion of flexible molecules, Danchin and colleagues consider how modifications need not always be damage. Some modifications participate in regulation or protection, and time-dependent structural changes may alter interactions with control mediators. A protein's changing state can, in their proposed account, help time a later response. Cooperation among imperfect molecular clocks is another possibility they discuss. The question is whether some molecules can acquire useful functional properties after synthesis, including under challenging conditions. [AFC-W013, §§3–4]

The authors present aspects of the antifragile interpretation of protein ageing as proposals and questions for investigation. Their account contains reported biological examples, explanatory conjectures and an agenda for further study. Expansion or adaptation of a lineage can involve turnover, destruction and replacement of organisms or components. [AFC-W013, §5]

Flexibility has a material carrier; retained information requires continued physical processes; and maintenance distinguishes functions by their timing, replaceability and importance.

### Related book and risk-analysis critique

Related book and risk-analysis critique

Taleb also develops antifragility in Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder. [AFC-W002, publication description]

In his abstract, Terje Aven argues that antifragility contributes to risk analysis by emphasizing how risk and performance develop over time. Some exposure to variation, uncertainty and error can support improvement at later stages, making the time horizon part of the appraisal of risk. He relates this argument to established risk-management ideas. [AFC-W006, abstract]

<!-- PDF page 359 -->

### Reading across these accounts

Reading across these accounts

Taleb and Douady analyze sensitivity to variability; Axenie and colleagues distinguish sources and scales of response; De Florio considers provision, monitoring and learning; Danchin and colleagues examine maintenance and flexible molecular processes.

<!-- PDF page 360 -->

## S34 Optionality, flexibility and commitment

S34   Optionality, flexibility and commitment

### Arrangements that preserve a later choice

Arrangements that preserve a later choice

The real-options passages and the scholarly reconstruction of Katsenelinboigen concern decisions whose consequences cannot all be specified in advance. An intermediate arrangement can preserve a future action, improve a position or avoid premature commitment.

### Smit and Trigeorgis: cash flows, flexibility and strategic interaction

Smit and Trigeorgis: cash flows, flexibility and strategic interaction

The opening of Strategic Investment: Real Options and Games links corporate finance and strategic planning. Smit and Trigeorgis distinguish appraisal of projected cash flows from the additional value that managerial flexibility and strategic interaction can bring to growth opportunities. Their framework treats those opportunities as a package of real options actively managed by a firm, with competitors and new technologies capable of changing their value. It is therefore an account of contingent choices in a competitive setting, not simply a favorable valuation of uncertainty. [AFC-W017, chapter 1, selected opening, printed pp. 3–7]

Their diagram relates project appraisal, planning of growth opportunities and competitive strategy to an expanded valuation. Discounted cash-flow analysis contributes one part; real-option reasoning considers adaptive capability; game-theoretic industrial organization addresses the interaction with competitors. The point of linking the approaches is that a firm's action need not leave the strategic environment unchanged. Waiting, expanding or committing can affect, and be affected by, other actors.

The selected deferral passage uses partly irreversible capacity investment to explain why timing can matter. A plant that becomes unattractive after prices fall may not be saleable at its original cost. Exercising the investment opportunity destroys the possibility of waiting for further information before making that expenditure. In such a setting, a project just at a conventional zero-net-present-value cutoff need not be worth undertaking immediately: the authors describe a premium associated with giving up the option to defer. [AFC-W017, flexibility/deferral passage]

Their analogy to a call option separates the opportunity from its exercise. Holding the right to acquire an asset at a specified cost differs from already owning the asset. The passage also states a qualification: postponement to expiration in the analogy assumes no opportunity costs of waiting or dividend-like benefits of holding the asset. Those foregone benefits are not erased by calling waiting flexible. Similarly, the book's opening places competitors' moves in the problem.

An irreversible commitment changes the future choice set. Its value depends on cash flows, the exercise cost, information revealed over time and the opportunities lost by delay. The object is the firm's strategic investment valuation under specified circumstances.

### Katsenelinboigen through a scholarly reconstruction

Katsenelinboigen through a scholarly reconstruction

The selected portions of the Filosofia encyclopedia entry reconstruct Katsenelinboigen's theory of predispositioning. The account distinguishes material, positional and relational parameters. Material resources form part of an arrangement; position concerns relations such as proximity or centrality; relational parameters in its biological and social examples include relations among entities. A predisposition is an intermediate arrangement whose connections are partly formed, rather than a complete program linking an initial state to a determined outcome. [WME-W016, selected definition and parameter sections]

<!-- PDF page 361 -->

Chess is the principal explanatory model in the account. A forced combination can be evaluated through a specified sequence toward an outcome, while positional play must assess a state without such a complete chain. Material can be sacrificed to improve a position whose later use remains uncertain. The relevant question is not only how many pieces remain, but what their arrangement allows.

The entry also distinguishes valuations tied to a particular initial position, goal, program and rules from more general valuations based primarily on the rules. Even the latter are not literally conditionless; the reconstruction explains their partial or qualified unconditionality. A broadly useful piece value and its value in a particular position answer different questions. The theory's strategic valuation is meant to support action when the eventual sequence cannot yet be specified. [WME-W016, selected valuation and style sections]

The account describes programming, predispositioning and randomness as different methods of relating stages of development. Programming supplies complete, consistent links; predispositioning prepares partly connected possibilities. The evaluation of an intermediate position is itself the difficult work. The entry's discussion of the calculus of predisposition emphasizes decomposing material and positional parameters and assigning weights; it also retains the role of experience and subjectivity when unique situations lack repeatable frequency data. [WME-W016, selected calculus and subjectivity sections]

A positional sacrifice is a judgment under uncertainty: it prepares possibilities whose eventual use cannot yet be specified. The resulting position can fail to produce the anticipated advantage.

### Valuing a future choice and preparing a position

Valuing a future choice and preparing a position
