Smit and Trigeorgis supply an attributed argument about valuation, irreversibility, timing and strategic interaction. The Katsenelinboigen reconstruction supplies an account of preparing and evaluating an intermediate position without a complete program. These accounts can help a reader locate questions about retained choice without turning real options and predisposition into synonyms.

<!-- PDF page 362 -->

## S89 Constructing portfolios through relationships among investments

S89   Constructing portfolios through relationships among investments

A portfolio is more than a list of investments. Holdings can move together, duplicate an exposure or supply cash at times when liabilities must be met. The following constructions make relationships among investments part of the decision: covariance in portfolio selection, factor exposure in risk allocation and timing in asset–liability immunization.

### Expected returns and joint variability

Expected returns and joint variability

Markowitz's 1952 account begins by separating maximizing expected return from choosing a combination of investments. Expected return alone can favor concentration in the holding with the greatest expected return. Diversification requires another consideration. His mean–variance approach represents the portfolio through both its expected return and the variability produced by the holdings together. [MG-W014]

If x_i is the share assigned to asset i and μ_i its expected return, portfolio expected return is the sum of x_i μ_i. Portfolio variance contains terms x_i x_j σ_ij, where σ_ij is the covariance of returns on assets i and j. The cross terms express how holdings vary together. Adding names therefore does not automatically make risk disappear: correlated movements remain in the combination even when the number of holdings grows. [MG-W014]

With nonnegative weights summing to one and specified probability beliefs, feasible combinations occupy an attainable region of expected return and variance. An efficient combination has no attainable competitor offering a higher expected return without greater variance, or lower variance without less expected return. The construction separates identifying these combinations from the investor's choice among them. It also separates the calculation from obtaining credible expectations and covariances, which the paper leaves as further work. [MG-W014]

### When another asset repeats the same exposure

When another asset repeats the same exposure

Roncalli and Weisang's 2012 working paper examines the distinction between risk contributions attached to named assets and contributions attached to underlying factors. Their motivating example starts with four assets and introduces a fifth that duplicates one of them. The economic exposure available has not become more diverse merely because the same investment appears under another label. Yet allocating equal risk contributions across the asset list can change the resulting allocation. [MG-W020]

The example tests what the allocation rule treats as its units. Dividing risk equally among five asset labels is a different instruction from dividing it among four underlying exposures. The authors turn toward factor risk contributions to address this dependence on the nominated universe. Their motivating argument gives a reason to inspect exposure beneath asset counts; the particular factors and their representation remain part of specifying the allocation problem. [MG-W020]

### Matching assets to liabilities

Matching assets to liabilities

Redington's 1952 treatment of life-office valuation asks how assets relate to the payments the institution must make. Immunization concerns the effect of a general interest-rate change on that relationship. The starting calculation values asset proceeds and liability outgo consistently. Equal present values establish a balance at the chosen rate; matching first-order sensitivity makes a small change in that rate have no first-order effect on their difference. [MG-W015]

The second-order condition then matters. Positive second-order behavior of the asset-minus-liability value supplies local protection around the valuation rate. The timing of interest receipts enters the

<!-- PDF page 363 -->

calculation alongside repayment of principal, so matching asset maturity dates alone does not reproduce the construction. Redington distinguishes the term of an investment from the mean discounted time of all the proceeds it supplies. [MG-W015]

His numerical illustration considers a unit liability payable in ten years at a valuation rate of 2.5%. A single coupon-bearing security can need a maturity of 11.485 years to give the asset proceeds the appropriate mean term. Earlier interest receipts shorten that mean relative to the final maturity. The example shows why a longer-maturing security can perform a matching role that its maturity date, viewed alone, would conceal. [MG-W015]

This is a local construction for a small uniform rate change under the stated valuation setting. Exact matching of cash flows is a different construction. The relationship also changes as time passes, rates change or new business enters, requiring reconsideration of the asset arrangement. Redington's objective is meeting obligations; Markowitz's efficient combinations use expected return and variance. Their different criteria explain why a portfolio can be well constructed for one purpose without settling another. [MG-W015]

<!-- PDF page 364 -->

## S90 Position sizing, rebalancing and investment rules over time

S90   Position sizing, rebalancing and investment rules over time

Investment rules act repeatedly. A fraction of current capital determines a changing monetary stake; market movements alter portfolio weights; a trigger determines when those weights are restored. The accounts here develop these temporal arrangements and then consider uncertainty about the return distribution used to choose an allocation.

### Sizing for repeated participation

Sizing for repeated participation

Kelly's 1956 paper attaches a value to information through a betting construction. A noisy channel supplies information about outcomes, giving the bettor an advantage without certainty. Betting all capital can maximize expected wealth in the simple favorable game, yet a single loss eliminates the capital required to continue. Repeated participation changes the significance of a favorable expected payoff. [MG-W016]

In his even-money example, q is the probability of winning and p the probability of losing. Betting a fraction ℓ of current capital multiplies wealth by 1 + ℓ after a win and 1 − ℓ after a loss. Over many independent repetitions, the logarithmic growth rate is q log(1 + ℓ) + p log(1 − ℓ). Maximizing this expression gives ℓ = q − p. Both the multiplication and the objective matter: expected wealth and long-run logarithmic growth need not favor the same fraction. [MG-W016]

The monetary stake adapts even when the chosen fraction stays constant. It rises after gains and falls after losses because it is applied to current wealth. Kelly connects the resulting maximum growth to information rate in his specified channel model. The known probabilities, odds and nonterminating comparison define the result; the investor's valuation of a finite-horizon outcome is another question, which Kelly explicitly recognizes. [MG-W016]

### Maintaining weights rather than holding quantities fixed

Maintaining weights rather than holding quantities fixed

Willenbrock distinguishes a constant-weight portfolio, restored through rebalancing, from a buy-and-hold portfolio whose weights drift. After relative gains, an asset occupies more of the portfolio; after relative losses, less. Restoring weights sells some of the relative gainers and buys some of the relative losers. Maintaining the allocation is an ongoing rule of action, rather than a property secured by the initial purchase. [MG-W017]

His diversification-return analysis distinguishes arithmetic returns from compounded, or geometric, returns. It compares portfolio geometric return with the weighted geometric returns of the component investments. The difference uses that specified baseline. In his 2000–2009 illustration, a portfolio initially split equally between the S&P 500 total-return index and a long-Treasury total-return index is rebalanced annually. Its geometric return is 4.44%, against a 3.32% weighted component baseline, a difference of 1.12 percentage points. [MG-W017]

Willenbrock argues that rebalancing is operative in this increment and examines why attributing the entire effect to a reduction in variance is misleading. Buy-and-hold also has a changing composition: its successful holdings become more influential without corrective trades. The decomposition and the historical example explain these different mechanisms; the stated difference is not a comparison establishing that rebalancing always beats buy-and-hold. [MG-W017]

<!-- PDF page 365 -->

### Deciding when to rebalance

Deciding when to rebalance

陆靖昶 and 朱坤 distinguish calendar rules from tolerance-band rules. A calendar rule checks an elapsed period; a band rule checks how far actual weights have moved from targets. The observation controlling action differs. A portfolio can reach a calendar date with little drift, or cross a band long before that date. Defining target weights is therefore only one part of specifying the allocation process. [MG-W018]

Their practitioner account relates rebalancing to maintaining intended exposure and discusses frequency, turnover and market movement. Repeated restoration during a trend and restoration amid reversals need not produce the same comparison. The method consists of observing actual weights, testing the chosen trigger, trading when called for and continuing to monitor drift. More frequent trading is not itself a definition of better maintenance. [MG-W018]

### Allocating when the distribution is uncertain

Allocating when the distribution is uncertain

Li's 2023 Wasserstein-Kelly formulation addresses uncertainty in the distribution used for growth optimization. Historical observations supply an empirical distribution, but treating that distribution as exact can make a chosen allocation sensitive to sampling and misspecification. The formulation constructs a neighborhood of distributions around the empirical one and chooses an allocation against the worst expected log growth within that neighborhood. [MG-W019]

This changes the optimization problem rather than merely replacing one return forecast with another. The size and form of the permitted departures, together with restrictions on possible returns, determine which adverse distributions enter the comparison. Support assumptions matter because historical observations alone may not include outcomes that the investment can experience. The selected formulation explains how distributional uncertainty enters the decision alongside the growth objective. [MG-W019]

The temporal rules developed here specify different objects: a fraction of current wealth, a target allocation and trading trigger, or a set of distributions over which an allocation is evaluated. Each account makes its object and objective explicit. Financial allocation complements the histories of retained choice and investment timing in S34 and S61, where the decisions concern options and commitments of a different kind.

<!-- PDF page 366 -->

## S61 Late-mover advantage and strategic waiting

S61   Late-mover advantage and strategic waiting

Entering later can mean arriving after someone else has paid to discover what works. A follower may encounter a proven technology, informed customers, trained workers and an established market. Delaying an investment can also leave a choice open until better information arrives. These possibilities raise different questions about what becomes available with time, who produces the knowledge and whether the opportunity remains open to the actor who waits.

The investment and organizational literatures examine these questions through accounts of pioneering and imitation, irreversible commitments, observable investment decisions and shared experimentation. The treatment of optionality and flexibility elsewhere concerns the choices an actor preserves; the accounts here develop the timing of investment and the relationships between pioneers and followers. Absorptive capacity provides a related explanation of how firms acquire and use external knowledge. [AFC-W017; AB-W001]

### What followers can obtain from pioneers

What followers can obtain from pioneers

Marvin Lieberman and David Montgomery’s 1988 First-mover advantages organizes the benefits of entering early around technological leadership, control of scarce assets and buyer switching costs. Its account of first-mover disadvantages explains why pioneering can also create opportunities for followers. A pioneer may pay for research, the discovery of a viable market and the education of buyers, while later entrants use knowledge and demand that those expenditures helped create. The follower does not necessarily reproduce the pioneer’s sequence of unsuccessful trials. [SW-W001]

The authors separate several channels through which this happens. Technical knowledge can spread through published information, imitation and the movement of personnel. Infrastructure and buyer education can serve more than the firm that financed them. A pioneer’s marketing may establish that a category of product is useful, making the task of a subsequent seller easier. How much the pioneer retains depends on the ability to appropriate these gains. Patents, secrecy, cumulative learning and specialized complementary assets can give an early entrant advantages that a follower cannot simply purchase. [SW-W001]

Waiting can also resolve uncertainty about the product and the market. An early entrant must choose a design before knowing which characteristics customers will value or which technical approach will prevail. A follower can observe that experience and concentrate on a more clearly defined target. The opportunity is particularly visible when an industry moves from competing designs toward a dominant design. Early entry may help a firm shape that outcome; later entry may let it avoid commitments to designs that disappear. In Lieberman and Montgomery’s analysis, those are different possible consequences of the same period of uncertainty. [SW-W001]

Technological change and incumbent inertia provide two further routes. A new technology may make an established firm’s knowledge and equipment less valuable while allowing an entrant to start with the newer approach. An incumbent may rationally continue harvesting an existing investment or hesitate to displace its own profitable products. Organizational routines can also make a new opportunity difficult to perceive or pursue. These explanations differ from a follower merely copying a finished invention: they concern the relationship between past success and the firm’s ability to change direction. [SW-W001]

Complementary assets can decide which firm captures an innovation’s returns. Lieberman and Montgomery discuss EMI’s computed-tomography scanner and Pilkington’s float-glass process as contrasting illustrations of the ability to retain the benefits of pioneering. Manufacturing, marketing, distribution and the organization of licensing can matter alongside the invention itself. Their question is consequently more precise than whether being first is good. It concerns which advantage an early

<!-- PDF page 367 -->

position creates, how durable it is and whether a later entrant possesses assets that make the innovation easier to exploit. [SW-W001]

### Entry order and the resources of the entrant

Entry order and the resources of the entrant

In their 1998 retrospective, Lieberman and Montgomery give greater emphasis to the two-way relationship between entry timing and resources. Entering early can build customer recognition, experience and privileged access to resources. But a firm’s resources also influence when it can enter and whether it is better suited to pioneering or following. An organization with strong manufacturing and distribution may be able to exploit an opportunity that another firm first developed. A firm without the knowledge needed to enter early may arrive late without having chosen delay as a strategy. [SW-W002]

This distinction changes how evidence about entry order is interpreted. Successful early entrants may have possessed advantages before entering, rather than receiving all of them from being first. Conversely, comparing surviving pioneers with surviving followers can hide pioneers that failed. The retrospective discusses research distinguishing inventors, product pioneers and market pioneers, and shows why the category being defined matters. The first supplier of a technology need not be the first firm to develop the market in which a later product succeeds. [SW-W002]

The authors also locate some resources outside the entrant’s own organization. Customers’ beliefs, habits and switching costs can preserve an early firm’s position, while standards and network effects can make a market more difficult to enter after it has developed. Their resource-based interpretation therefore includes both what a follower can acquire from earlier activity and what that earlier activity may make harder to obtain. [SW-W002]

### A profitable investment that is worth postponing

A profitable investment that is worth postponing

Robert Pindyck’s 1991 Irreversibility, Uncertainty, and Investment explains why an investment with positive net present value can nevertheless be worth postponing. His opening factory example makes one widget a year forever at no operating cost. Construction costs $800. The widget sells for $100 initially; a year later its price will either rise to $150 or fall to $50, with equal probabilities, and then stay there. At a 10 percent discount rate, immediate construction has a net present value of $300. Waiting a year and building only after the favorable price change is worth about $386. [SW-W004]

The comparison includes the production forgone while waiting. The gain comes from retaining the ability to reject the unfavorable investment. Immediate construction exchanges that choice for an operating factory. Pindyck treats the opportunity given up as part of the cost of committing now. In this example, the difference of about $86 is the value of waiting after allowing for delayed production and discounting. A positive conventional net present value does not by itself establish that immediate construction is the best available action. [SW-W004]

Irreversibility gives the later choice its force. The investor cannot undo construction and recover the full outlay when the price falls. The opportunity to invest must also remain available next year. If construction could be reversed without loss, or if the opportunity would disappear unless taken immediately, the alternatives would change. Pindyck’s example makes the information arrive through the passage of time. His separate account of research and demonstration projects, discussed in Learning before commitment, concerns information that early expenditure itself produces. [SW-W004]

### Learning from another investor’s action

Learning from another investor’s action

Christophe Chamley and Douglas Gale’s 1994 model investigates delay when investment decisions reveal information. Each agent knows whether it has an investment opportunity, while the distribution of

<!-- PDF page 368 -->

opportunities contains information about the state of the economy and hence the attractiveness of investment. An agent observes how many others invest and can use that evidence when deciding whether to exercise its own opportunity. Waiting can improve its information without requiring it to undertake the first investment. [SW-W005]

The informational relationship is isolated from ordinary product-market competition. Another agent’s investment does not directly reduce the investor’s payoff by taking a customer or increasing supply. Its action matters because it is informative. That separation makes it possible to examine a pure informational externality: an investment can provide useful evidence to other decision makers, while the investor does not capture all the value of that evidence. [SW-W005]

The timing of information is endogenous. There is no independent announcement that automatically supplies everything the agents want to learn. Information appears through actions, so an agent’s wish to observe others affects the very process from which it hopes to learn. The model produces costly delay and the possibility that investment collapses. An absence of investment can itself discourage further investment, rather than providing a neutral pause in an otherwise unchanged sequence. [SW-W005]

Chamley and Gale also examine the interval between opportunities to revise decisions. Faster reaction does not automatically improve the collective result: their analysis shows how a rapid succession of responses can bring investment to an early halt. It explains a mechanism by which individually useful waiting can reduce the supply of informative actions. [SW-W005]

### Experimentation as a shared source of knowledge

Experimentation as a shared source of knowledge

Patrick Bolton and Christopher Harris’s 1999 Strategic Experimentation studies actors who can actively generate information while also learning from one another. Each chooses how much effort to allocate between a safe activity with a known return and a risky activity whose underlying quality is uncertain. The risky activity can be good or bad. Its noisy results gradually reveal which state holds. The players observe one another’s actions and outcomes, so an experiment undertaken by one player informs the others. [SW-W006]

The players share a changing belief about the risky activity. When they are sufficiently optimistic, they devote their effort to it; when sufficiently pessimistic, they abandon it in favor of the safe return. Between those regions, the symmetric equilibrium divides effort between the two activities. Compared with a team that jointly values all the experimental information, independent players have an incentive to rely on the experiments of others. Each receives only part of the total benefit created by its own information-producing effort. [SW-W006]

Bolton and Harris identify an encouragement effect alongside free-riding. A player’s experiment may produce favorable evidence that induces others to experiment in the future. Their subsequent observations then benefit the original experimenter. An action can therefore be attractive partly because it changes the future willingness of other players to supply information. This feedback can sustain experimentation that would be missed by considering only the immediate return and the information generated by one isolated experiment. [SW-W006]

The balance is more complicated than a fixed amount of experimentation divided among more beneficiaries. The equilibrium allocation changes as beliefs change; an additional player changes both the opportunity to free-ride and the prospect of receiving future observations. Bolton and Harris show that individual equilibrium payoffs rise with the number of players, while aggregate experimentation need not vary monotonically. Even an arbitrarily large group does not in general attain the payoff available with full information. These results preserve both the gains from shared experience and the incentives governing its production. [SW-W006]

<!-- PDF page 369 -->

### When competition accelerates commitment

When competition accelerates commitment

Shinsuke Kamoto’s 2006 study of market entry under uncertainty examines the competing pressure to enter before a rival. Two firms face irreversible investment and uncertain demand. The first entrant initially serves the market alone. After the second enters, the first retains an advantage through its ability to choose output first. The model makes the attraction of a first position part of the timing problem rather than assuming that each firm can preserve its investment opportunity independently of its competitor. [SW-W007]

The option to wait, familiar from a single-investor calculation, now interacts with preemption. Waiting for a more favorable demand level can expose a firm to being overtaken. The first-mover advantage can bring entry forward relative to the timing that would be chosen without that race. Kamoto’s analysis also considers demand jumps and the risk that demand falls soon after an irreversible outlay. A firm can win the early position while still undertaking the investment at a moment that exposes it to an unfavorable subsequent state. [SW-W007]

This model gives the timing question a different structure from Chamley and Gale’s informational externality. There, other investments are informative without directly changing the agent’s payoff through competition. Here, who enters first changes the competitive relationship itself. The choice preserved by waiting depends on whether the actor will still be able to obtain the position it wants. [SW-W007; SW-W005]

### How latecomers acquire the knowledge to compete

How latecomers acquire the knowledge to compete

Momoko Kawakami’s 2018 study follows MediaTek and MStar into systems-on-chip for LCD televisions. The transition from analog cathode-ray-tube sets to digital LCD televisions shifted many integration tasks into semiconductor components. A chip supplier could supply a larger part of a television’s functioning system, rather than one narrowly separated part. Kawakami examines how these later entrants acquired both component knowledge and knowledge of the finished television, allowing them to supply what she calls problem-solving core components. [SW-W008]

Her interview-based account identifies five routes for acquiring component knowledge. The firms transferred technologies and integration experience from their existing businesses, bought intellectual property from specialist suppliers, learned through commercial integration with established chip vendors, obtained technical information through television manufacturers and worked directly with manufacturers on tasks such as picture adjustment. Some transfers were paid and formal; others passed through working relationships and informal circulation of technical material. The possibility of learning from earlier suppliers was realized through identifiable channels. [SW-W008]

The existing businesses supplied different starting points. MediaTek brought knowledge from optical-disc-drive chips, while MStar drew on LCD-monitor chips. Suppliers of complementary components  sometimes shared integration knowledge to secure a place for their own products in a recommended design. Over time, the Taiwanese firms could replace some of those components with their own developments. Such exchanges connected a supplier’s immediate interest in selling its product with the recipient’s accumulation of technical competence. [SW-W008]

Product-level knowledge developed through helping customers solve problems. Newer television manufacturers faced shortages of chips, limited technical support, differing regional specifications and the need to combine panels and software rapidly. MediaTek and MStar offered extensive support and reference designs, including engineers working near or within important customers’ development activities. Solving a customer’s problem exposed the supplier to requirements and adjustment knowledge

<!-- PDF page 370 -->

that it could use in later designs. Better support helped it obtain further customers, whose problems opened further learning opportunities. [SW-W008]

Kawakami’s history explains more than access to an already developed technology. It describes the accumulation of an ability to integrate components and satisfy product requirements. The later entrants’ opportunities included purchasable knowledge and transfers from established firms, but their advance also drew on prior experience and continuing engineering with customers. [SW-W008]

### Testing latecomer advantage at the regional level

Testing latecomer advantage at the regional level

Dou Lichen and Li Guoping’s 2004 analysis of technological innovation and diffusion examines latecomer advantage across 29 regions of China during 1991–2002. Their question is whether a region’s distance from the technological frontier supplies an opportunity for faster productivity growth. The empirical analysis uses labor productivity to represent technological levels, patents to represent innovation, investment per worker to represent absorptive conditions and foreign direct investment as a route for external technological diffusion. [SW-W009]

The authors investigate a nonlinear relationship between technological distance and the benefit obtainable from diffusion. A gap creates room for catching up, while the ability to receive and use incoming knowledge affects whether that room becomes productive growth. Their regional comparisons find stronger evidence of effective diffusion among more developed regions; the corresponding relationships are weaker or statistically unconvincing for less developed groups. Being further behind is therefore a different property from possessing an effective route for using knowledge developed elsewhere. [SW-W009]

This is an observational regional study, with proxy measures for innovation and absorption. It adds an empirical account of the conditions under which a latecomer position can become useful. The fuller organizational treatment of recognizing, assimilating and applying external knowledge appears in Absorbing new resources and capabilities. [SW-W009; AB-W001]

<!-- PDF page 371 -->

## S62 Learning before commitment

S62   Learning before commitment

An organization can begin learning before it decides exactly what to build or whether to undertake a large investment. It can test a technical principle, investigate customers, develop several compatible designs or build the ability to use a technology whose final form is still changing. These activities alter what a later decision can be based on. Their histories concern the organization of investigation as well as the timing of commitment.

The accounts below develop sequential investment, discovery-driven planning, set-based engineering and software-investment management. Information acquisition, experiments and dual control treats actions that serve both operational and informational purposes. Generating alternatives and organizing exploration examines the production and evaluation of alternatives. Here the emphasis is on what is learned before a particular choice is closed, how the knowledge is retained and how subsequent decisions use it.

### Information produced by early expenditure

Information produced by early expenditure

In his 1991 discussion of irreversible investment, Robert Pindyck distinguishes waiting for information from spending to obtain it. His exposition of Kevin Roberts and Martin Weitzman’s work on research, development and exploration considers projects that reveal more about their value as successive stages are undertaken. The investor can stop after an unfavorable discovery instead of completing the entire sequence. An initial expenditure can therefore be worthwhile even when a calculation that assumes unconditional completion gives the project a negative net present value. [SW-W004]

The informative activity changes the alternatives available at the next decision. A drug-development program, an aircraft prototype or a demonstration plant can disclose something that the mere passage of time would not reveal. In the sequential-learning formulation Pindyck discusses, the project’s underlying value is fixed but unknown. Learning requires investment. Deferring every stage also defers the acquisition of the information that could justify, redirect or end the project. [SW-W004]

Pindyck also describes a market study costing $50 in a version of his widget example in which the factory opportunity is available only in the current year and costs $1,200. The study reveals whether the future selling price will be high or low, allowing the investor to condition construction on the result. Its value lies in changing the construction decision. This gives the early expenditure a different purpose from buying a smaller amount of production capacity: it purchases a better-informed choice about the larger outlay. [SW-W004]

### Planning around assumptions that can be tested

Planning around assumptions that can be tested

Rita Gunther McGrath and Ian MacMillan’s 1995 Discovery-Driven Planning addresses ventures whose plans contain many assumptions that cannot yet be treated as facts. Their method connects four working documents: a reverse income statement, a specification of the operations needed to deliver the business, a list of important assumptions and a milestone plan. Together these identify what would have to be true for the venture to justify its investment and when those propositions can be tested. [LC-W002]

The reverse income statement starts with the profit needed to make the venture worthwhile and works backward to required revenue and allowable cost. The operations specification then asks what activities, capacity and resources would be needed to produce that result. Putting those two descriptions beside one another exposes assumptions about prices, market size, production, distribution and the time needed to reach scale. The assumption list makes the uncertain parts explicit so that a detailed forecast does not quietly turn them into established knowledge. [LC-W002]

<!-- PDF page 372 -->

The milestone plan orders expenditures around opportunities to learn. A milestone is useful when reaching it tests an assumption that matters to continuation. McGrath and MacMillan use Kao’s entry into floppy disks as a retrospective worked illustration, assembled from public information. They show how prototype production, technical testing with prospective buyers, subcontracted production and sales, a pilot plant and full-scale production could form a sequence. Each stage addresses a different question about performance, demand or the production economics required by the intended business. [LC-W002]

The worked plan does not require all of these questions to be settled before any activity begins. It gives each uncertain proposition a place in the sequence before the commitments that depend on it. Evidence from a technical test can alter an operations estimate; a sales result can change the volume assumed in the reverse income statement. The documents are meant to be revised together, so that a newly learned fact changes the plan rather than remaining an isolated observation. [LC-W002]

McGrath and MacMillan assign responsibility for maintaining the assumptions and updating the linked documents. This makes the procedure more than a list of risks written at the start. A changing account of what is known governs the next commitment. [LC-W002]

### Keeping compatible designs open

Keeping compatible designs open

Allen Ward, Jeffrey Liker, John Cristiano and Durward Sobek’s 1995 account of Toyota describes an engineering process in which a broader early exploration can support a faster later convergence. A point-based process selects a particular design and then revises it as problems appear. Because subsystem  decisions interact, revising one part can invalidate another team’s work. The alternative they call set-based concurrent engineering maintains sets of possibilities, communicates the ranges other teams can  work within and narrows those ranges as knowledge improves. [LC-W003]

The authors compare coordination to finding a meeting time. Asking each person for a single preferred time can lead to repeated proposals and rejections. Asking for each person’s available times reveals an intersection that can satisfy everyone. In engineering, the corresponding sets describe acceptable dimensions, performance, manufacturing conditions and other requirements. The task is to find combinations that remain compatible across the system while investigating the choices that have not yet been settled. [LC-W003]

Their account links five activities: describing possibilities at both system and subsystem levels; investigating several possibilities in parallel; narrowing them as knowledge accumulates; deriving feasible specifications from that knowledge; and preserving the commitments once the selected set has been settled. Parallel work is supported by information about allowable variation. A team does not need to know one final design to establish that an entire family of proposed shapes would be difficult to manufacture. [LC-W003]

The Nippondenso example concerns advanced component development that begins before a particular Toyota vehicle program. Engineers explore ideas and partial prototypes, combine promising features and progressively reduce the candidates. The reported sequence reaches three designs and five prototypes in its fourth year and a chosen design in the fifth year of an eight-year cycle. Compatible component families and interchangeable parts allow the development to serve several vehicles and customers. The early work creates knowledge that a later vehicle program can draw on. [LC-W003]

Toyota’s lessons-learned books give that knowledge a form that can outlast the project. They describe manufacturing limits and relationships between design choices and outcomes, rather than merely recording the sequence of changes that produced the last vehicle. A body designer can use them to recognize troublesome shapes before asking manufacturing engineers to evaluate a completed design. What is retained is a map of workable possibilities, available for a future design that may occupy a different part of that map. [LC-W003]

<!-- PDF page 373 -->

Ward and colleagues also explain how progressively narrower communications can make independent work more reliable. A later message refines an earlier range instead of replacing one promised point with an incompatible point. Suppliers know how much variation remains and can judge how far to advance their own work. The authors develop these ideas from observed practices and present the relationship to Toyota’s development performance as a hypothesis. [LC-W003]

### Moving investigation ahead of design completion

Moving investigation ahead of design completion

Jeffrey Liker and James Morgan’s 2006 account of lean product development explains the timing of Toyota’s early investigation in greater detail. In the body-development comparison they describe, engineering at other manufacturers often begins in earnest after the stylists’ clay model is frozen. At Toyota, substantial investigation of the product and its manufacturing process begins during an earlier study period. Cross-functional teams produce study drawings and examine alternative solutions while the shape and detailed design still have room to change. [LC-W006]

The intended result is system compatibility before individual designs are completed. Structural and manufacturing questions can influence the developing product while alternatives remain available, instead of arriving as demands to revise finished work. The authors connect this front-loading to a more stable execution phase. Their account places delayed selection within an active engineering process: investigation starts earlier even though some final decisions are taken later. [LC-W006]

### A cheap test before expensive redesign

A cheap test before expensive redesign

Brian Kennedy, Durward Sobek and Michael Kennedy’s study, first published online in 2013, distinguishes purposeful experimental iterations from rework caused by premature decisions. In their Teledyne TapTone case, engineers used carpenter’s clamps costing $14 on an existing machine to vary rigidity and investigate its effect. A few hours of testing helped establish a relationship between structural stiffness and performance before detailed redesign. The resulting knowledge supported a smaller, less rigid and less costly design than an untested assumption would have suggested. [LC-W011]

The case also describes customer input on cleanable rounded stainless-steel legs and metric components before drawings and tooling fixed the design. The authors advocate expressing ranges and tradeoffs that teams can use to coordinate decisions. The clamp experiment is a concrete instance of learning a design relationship with inexpensive equipment; it did not require first producing a complete candidate machine. [LC-W011]

### Representing preferences and feasible ranges

Representing preferences and feasible ranges

Haruo Ishikawa and Naoko Sasaki’s 2018 treatment gives set-based design a computational form for simultaneous structural and control design. They represent both required performance and design variables as ranges with preferences within those ranges. A preference value indicates which portions are more desirable, from acceptable boundary regions to the most desired region. The method propagates the design-variable ranges into predicted performance ranges and compares them with the requirements. [LC-W007]

When a predicted range includes unacceptable performance, the method narrows the design-variable ranges. It evaluates candidate subranges using both desirability and robustness, then seeks common ranges that satisfy the multiple performance requirements together. In this formulation, choosing acceptable ranges and expressing preferences are distinct operations. Designers can retain a region of acceptable choices while still indicating that some parts of it are more attractive. [LC-W007]

<!-- PDF page 374 -->

The worked example is the controlled rotation of a stepped rectangular arm containing holes. Its six design variables include structural dimensions, the number of holes and three controller gains. Four performance requirements concern rise time, overshoot, settling time and mass. The authors compare two preference patterns over the same initial variable ranges: an equal preference throughout each range, and a triangular pattern favoring the midpoint. [LC-W007]

The different preferences produce different retained ranges while meeting the specified performance targets in the example. The initial arm-width range of 0.12–0.18 metres narrows to 0.135–0.150 metres in the first case and 0.150–0.165 metres in the second. The selected ranges of controller gains also differ. Thus the result includes a family of structural and control choices shaped by both the performance limits and the designer’s stated preferences, rather than a single supposedly inevitable optimum. [LC-W007]

### Investing in a technological position

Investing in a technological position

Rita Gunther McGrath’s 1997 paper distinguishes expenditure to establish a technological position from the later decision to commercialize it. An early research investment can build knowledge and a right or practical ability to pursue a business if conditions become favorable. Commercialization is a further exercise of that opportunity. The organization may instead license the result, redirect it or stop. The initial investment and the final business are therefore different decisions with different information available at their respective times. [LC-W004]

McGrath separates uncertainty that the investor’s work can reduce from uncertainty that evolves outside the project. A technical question about whether a design can function may require experiments. An input price or a regulatory decision may become clearer through other events. Some external conditions may also be influenced by strategic action. These distinctions affect whether an organization gains more by waiting, investigating or taking action that changes the conditions under which it might later commercialize. [LC-W004]

Her pollution-control illustration separates the smaller investment needed to establish a technological position from the much larger outlay required for commercialization. The attraction of the later business depends partly on regulation. Initial work can create a position from which the firm can respond if the market develops, without paying the entire commercialization cost at once. Sequential milestones allow the project to absorb information and change direction as this process unfolds. [LC-W004]

The paper develops a real-options logic for these decisions rather than treating the research investment as a miniature version of the eventual business. The relevant opportunity can be created or improved by the investor’s own activity. Its value depends on what that activity makes possible and on the decisions that remain available afterward. [LC-W004]

### Connecting tests to decisions that can still change

Connecting tests to decisions that can still change

Ian MacMillan, Alexander van Putten, Rita McGrath and James Thompson’s 2006 account of real-options discipline connects discovery-driven planning to the management of uncertain technology investments. Their argument requires actual freedom to make a later decision. Dividing an already unavoidable expenditure into accounting stages does not create the same opportunity as funding an investigation whose result can lead to continuation, alteration or abandonment. [LC-W005]

The procedure uses the proposed business, its operating requirements and its assumptions to identify what must be learned before further resources are committed. Its BioBarrier illustration concerns a proposed hospital hand-washing product. Assumptions about the market, production capacity and selling costs influence whether the business could meet its financial requirements. Simulation is used to examine

<!-- PDF page 375 -->

uncertain outcomes and identify assumptions that deserve attention; milestone tests then address the assumptions that materially affect the next decision. [LC-W005]

The illustrative business makes the connection between analysis and action inspectable. A simulation does not itself improve the product or reveal customer behavior. It helps identify which unknowns matter to the choice of another expenditure. The managerial procedure then links an investigation to the decision it can inform. This extends the earlier discovery-driven account by making the freedom to stop or change the investment part of its real-options interpretation. [LC-W005]

### Exploration before a customer has specified the product

Exploration before a customer has specified the product

Sylvain Lenfle and Christophe Midler’s 2002 study at Usinor concerns an upstream supplier developing an innovative offer before a customer has defined a particular product. Their hydroforming case involves shaping metal tubes through pressure and deformation, with possible uses across several markets. The project must discover both what the process can accomplish and which applications are worth pursuing. A conventional development plan with one agreed object and a delivery date does not yet describe the work. [LC-W009]

The authors organize the effort as a portfolio of studies and experiments. Research on forming possibilities, process capability and crash behavior can interact with particular customer applications. Bringing these investigations into a common project makes their combined significance visible and can justify shared experimental equipment. A customer study can redirect technical research, while technical knowledge can reveal an application that was not apparent at the start. [LC-W009]

They distinguish two kinds of achievement within this exploration. A study may produce a sale with little new technical knowledge, or it may fail to produce immediate revenue while supplying knowledge important to several later applications. Their proposed evaluation therefore follows both commercial results and the growth of knowledge across the portfolio. An unsuccessful application can still establish a useful boundary of the process; a successful part can serve as evidence about a broader field of possible uses. [LC-W009]

Tests play a central coordinating role because no finished product yet provides an agreed schedule. Experiments, simulations and presentations to customers challenge the project’s starting assumptions and can redirect the exploration. The research program is a provisional organization of what to investigate. It changes as the team learns, rather than requiring a complete specification of the discovery before work begins. [LC-W009]

Lenfle and Midler also describe a masked urgency in this upstream work. A new material or process must be validated in time to enter a customer’s own design sequence. A vehicle may seem six or seven years from the market, while the practical choice to include or exclude the innovation comes within two or three years. Learning has to begin early enough to reach that choice. The late market launch does not mean that the opportunity to influence the design remains open until then. [LC-W009]

### Making flexibility exercisable in software investment

Making flexibility exercisable in software investment

Philip Weihs’s 2008 Steuerung von Flexibilität develops a framework for managing software investments with real options. Its selected project-management and case-study chapters follow investment beyond the initial appraisal. The framework separates initialization from use, includes a continuing search for new options and assigns roles to the investment decision maker, an adviser on real options and the project manager. The decision maker owns the relevant choices and commissions the work; the project manager implements the projects through which the investment is realized. [LC-W010]

<!-- PDF page 376 -->

The distinction matters when the investment is larger than any single delivery project. A first project may establish a platform or capability from which later projects can be undertaken. Those later choices require identification and management during use, not merely a statement of their possible value at the original approval. Weihs permits ranges or qualitative assessments when a numerical option value cannot be established, with further valuation as the parameters become clearer. [LC-W010]

One retrospective case concerns a configuration-management application intended to organize software, plans and documentation, support version control and enable reuse. The project began in 2004, stopped late that year, resumed with changed requirements in 2005 and was then put into service. Weihs’s analysis found that the needs actually extended across configuration management, project management and customer relationship management. Treating all of them as additions to one project had obscured what the first investment should contain. [LC-W010]

The thesis proposes two alternative interpretations of that history. One would define the larger investment in business-process support, implement a clearly bounded initial application and retain the others as possible subsequent expansions. The other would explicitly recognize a right to interrupt or abandon the narrower project as its requirements became clearer. These are retrospective redesigns of the investment decision; the case does not measure savings from a framework implemented at its start. [LC-W010]

The comparison across the thesis’s cases connects options to practical authority. A project consciously organized in small increments offered more scope for adjustment than projects with fixed long-term plans. Decisions requiring approval through several levels, including a senior body meeting only twice a year, could not be exercised promptly when conditions changed. The ability to choose later consequently depended on who could decide and when, as well as on the technical form of the software. [LC-W010]

### A contemporary model of enterprise AI pilots

A contemporary model of enterprise AI pilots

Gaurav Tewari’s 2026 preprint Pilot Early, Commit Late formulates an enterprise AI adoption problem with three choices: deploy immediately, wait or conduct a pilot before deciding whether to deploy. The two-date model separates the external technological frontier from the organization’s ability to use it. Deployment produces current operating value and learning by doing. A pilot costs money and produces no full operating return in the first period, but increases capability available for the later decision. Waiting preserves the later choice without creating that internal capability in the model. [LC-W008]

The installed system can capture a specified fraction of subsequent technological improvement. That fraction represents the economic effects of modularity, portability and the ability to upgrade without another sunk implementation cost. Immediate deployment can therefore remain attractive when it captures future progress well, produces substantial current returns or teaches the organization a great deal through production use. The model makes these advantages comparable with the flexibility of choosing a later technology. [LC-W008]

Piloting is preferable to pure waiting when its cost is no greater than the expected increase it creates in the value of the later deployment choice. The increase can come from making adoption profitable in more future states or making profitable adoption more valuable. In this formulation a demonstration with little transferable organizational learning contributes little to that option, however polished the demonstration may be. [LC-W008]

The analysis also derives conditions under which faster expected technological progress makes immediate deployment less attractive relative to waiting or piloting. A low ability to capture future improvements favors that result; strong production learning or a large present operating benefit favors earlier deployment. These are comparisons within a theoretical model that omits strategic competition and financing constraints. [LC-W008]

<!-- PDF page 377 -->

## S87 Discovering valuable problems and choosing what to build

S87   Discovering valuable problems and choosing what to build

Choosing what to build involves representations of needs, technical possibilities and a firm's offering mix. A customer can report a present difficulty without imagining a new product, while a technically attractive concept can fit poorly with other products. The accounts here develop ways of representing product decisions and finding users whose experience contains information about emerging needs.

### Representing the product decision

Representing the product decision

Krishnan and Ulrich organize product-development literature around decisions. Their 2001 review compares the concerns of marketing, organizational research, engineering design and operations management. A product can appear as a bundle of attributes, an organizational undertaking, an interacting assembly or a flow of development activities. These representations make different relationships and measures prominent. Stating the decision helps identify which representation supplies useful information. [MG-W008]

The review distinguishes decisions within a development project from decisions that establish its setting. Concept development, architecture, variants, shared components, prototyping and launch occur within a context of product strategy, project selection and development organization. Choices about an individual component can therefore depend on a product-line decision that the local design problem takes as given. Optimizing one project does not settle which projects should exist. [MG-W008]

Their launch-sequencing discussion illustrates the connection. An earlier introduction can earn profit sooner, yet a new offering can displace sales of another product. Likewise, offering variants and sharing components can change both market coverage and development work. Their review locates these relationships across research traditions, rather than reducing product-development performance to minimum lead time. Its decision map helps a reader distinguish the object being chosen, the objective used to compare alternatives and the related decisions outside the immediate project. [MG-W008]

### Finding needs ahead of the market

Finding needs ahead of the market

Von Hippel's lead users have two characteristics: they encounter needs ahead of a significant market trend and expect substantial benefit from solving those needs. Those conditions make them informative in different ways. Being ahead provides experience with a problem others may face later; expecting a large benefit supplies a reason to search for or construct a solution. An early purchaser is not necessarily a lead user, since buying a new offering does not itself establish either condition. [MG-W007]

The inquiry begins with a consequential trend and seeks users who are already confronting its demands. It then examines their needs, adaptations and solutions, before assessing which findings transfer to the intended market. Von Hippel argues that typical users can be constrained by their experience of familiar products and attributes. Lead-user inquiry instead finds people for whom an emerging problem is already practical experience. [MG-W007]

The search can extend beyond the producer's existing customers and industry. Users facing demanding conditions elsewhere may already have addressed a related need: the paper discusses such connections as lightweight materials in aerospace and automotive uses, and controls for commercial buildings and homes. Transfer is a further question, however. A demanding user's solution provides something to inspect and evaluate, rather than a substitute for understanding the target users. [MG-W007]

The IBM component-insertion machine illustrates a user-developed solution moving into supply. In von Hippel's account, the user developed the design and supplied drawings with an order to a manufacturer. Permission to sell the machine more widely followed. The sequence matters: an experienced user's work

<!-- PDF page 378 -->

supplied a concrete design before the supplier treated it as a general commercial offering. Information about need and information about a possible solution had been produced together in use. [MG-W007]

Lead-user inquiry therefore includes both discovery and evaluation. Finding an inventive user can reveal a possibility; assessing its applicability determines whether that possibility belongs in a proposed product. Product-line decisions remain another level of choice. Krishnan and Ulrich's review concerns how those decisions relate, while von Hippel supplies a particular route for obtaining information about needs and solutions. The histories of inventive and associative methods elsewhere develop further ways of generating concepts.

<!-- PDF page 379 -->

## S88 Organizing product development and evolution

S88   Organizing product development and evolution

Product management continues through development, introduction, use, revision and withdrawal. Its work includes deciding what information is needed before a commitment, which aspects of a design can remain changeable, and how an existing offering fits a changing portfolio. The following accounts examine processes and continuing responsibilities across that span.

### Stages of work and gates of commitment

Stages of work and gates of commitment

Smolnik and Bergmann's 2020 review traces the evolution of the Stage-Gate process. Stages gather and analyze information; gates decide whether further resources should be committed. Discovery and screening lead through scoping and a business case toward development, validation and launch, with post-launch review. The distinction between work and authorization explains how a process can organize inquiry while reserving a decision about proceeding. [MG-W009]

The review also describes adaptations involving iteration and agile work. Iterating within a stage and deciding whether to continue the larger undertaking need not be the same event. That distinction allows repeated development cycles to coexist with broader investment decisions. The authors discuss the evidence available for hybrids, including its limitations for some physical-product applications. Their historical review presents a changing family of processes rather than a single unaltered sequence. [MG-W009]

### Making changes less expensive

Making changes less expensive

Thomke and Reinertsen define development flexibility through the economic cost of modifying a product under development. Its value depends on what may change and when. Improving a forecast can reduce surprises; changing a process or technology can make a later revision cheaper. Their account considers both routes and explains why a design strategy should reflect the cost of changing its underlying technology. [MG-W010]

Progressive freezing makes commitments piece by piece. A requirement or design feature can be approved when sufficient information is available, while other features remain open. Qualifying a backup material early similarly prepares an alternative before it becomes urgently needed. These arrangements require identifying which changes have consequential downstream effects and which permissions can be granted independently. [MG-W010]

The Boeing 777 illustration makes authorization granular. A part drawing could have six or more release levels, permitting such different downstream activities as purchasing material, designing tools or machining them. Releasing a drawing was therefore a statement about what someone could safely begin, rather than a declaration that every detail was final. The authors contrast this with one release that freezes the entire part at its procurement lead time. [MG-W010]

Their tooling-shop discussion also changes the criterion used to manage a supporting activity. Minimizing the unit cost of a tool can delay an iteration whose timing matters to the larger program. Delivery timing brings that relationship into the measure. Their survey of 391 integrated-circuit projects compares development using technologies with different change costs; respondents were not randomly assigned to those technologies. The comparison supports their investigation of flexibility and development strategy within that observed setting. [MG-W010]

<!-- PDF page 380 -->

### Actual processes and long-lived platforms

Actual processes and long-lived platforms

Jetter, Albar and Sperry compare prescribed processes with development practice through literature and high-technology cases. Their measurement-tool company maintains a platform over years while adapting interchangeable heads or modules. Several projects can therefore contribute to the evolution of an offering whose life exceeds that of any one project. Platform continuity and project closure are different time horizons. [MG-W011]

The case research describes departures from standard processes, including agile software development and decisions concentrated in the owner of a small firm. Its second phase includes twelve project cases and interviews concerning project management offices. These qualitative accounts show why a standard process may be modified and how monitoring is carried out. They also distinguish disciplined management of projects from choosing a successful product mix: following a process supplies information about execution without by itself determining whether the right offerings were selected. [MG-W011]

### Strategy throughout the product's life

Strategy throughout the product's life

Bauch's 2020 process navigator distinguishes product, product-portfolio and enterprise strategy. A product moves through definition, development, launch, growth and improvement toward withdrawal, while its business plan and strategy continue alongside that work. The roadmap communicates a time dimension across functions. It connects intended changes with the continuing offering rather than serving only as a schedule for an initial release. [MG-W012]

The portfolio perspective compares the current and intended offering mix. Introducing one product and phasing out another must be coordinated with product-level plans and enterprise direction. Bauch also identifies supporting work, such as troubleshooting and assisting sales, that competes for attention with strategic work. His practitioner framework makes these continuing processes visible as product-management responsibilities. [MG-W012]

Springer and Miler investigate software product-management challenges through a literature review, ten interviews and an 89-person survey. Reported difficulties include establishing customer value, changing priorities, technical debt, organizational silos and balancing reactive with proactive work. Their categories distinguish core product decisions from participation in related work and orchestration across functions. The product manager's responsibility can consequently extend across activities over which that person has no direct command. [MG-W013]

The study reports perceived frequency and severity. These reports describe difficulties experienced in practice, including continuing maintenance and withdrawal as well as development. Together with the lifecycle frameworks, they give substance to product management after delivery: the offering, its dependencies and the organization supporting it continue to change. S62 develops learning before commitment, and S80 examines the connection between sales work and customer value. [MG-W013]

## S100 Founding and developing technology ventures

S100   Founding and developing technology ventures

### Who founded the firm and when

Who founded the firm and when

Arnold Cooper’s 1971 account gives a semiconductor company that nearly failed with its first founders. A later group brought management and capital and got the enterprise operating. The episode makes the founding date a question about what event counts: organizing the original company or assembling the group that made it viable. In another firm, an early founder took up product development before a later founder took responsibility for management and marketing. The histories of the team and the legal organization can therefore begin at different dates. [T02-W001]

Cooper also describes the previous employer as an incubator in a specific sense. Prospective founders encounter one another through their work and learn what their future colleagues can do before forming a venture. In S83 the Nairobi incubator is a program that deliberately connects entrepreneurs with contacts. Cooper’s example concerns an employing organization that can become a source of founding teams. [T02-W001]

### The changing work of a founder

The changing work of a founder

榊原清則 and colleagues asked founders of Japanese technology ventures which duties they performed as the business developed. The report describes a pattern of founders covering many functions at the beginning and gradually concentrating on line functions. The same broad shift appears among firms aiming for an initial public offering, although the report finds a stronger tendency for the chief executive to combine several functions in that group. The study compares reported allocations of duties across stages and groups of respondents. [T02-W002]

Sarasvathy distinguishes deciding on an objective and finding means to reach it from starting with means already at hand and considering which ends those means make possible. A conventional marketing sequence begins with a market and a selected target. Her example of a business developing through contingent problem solving illustrates the second direction of choice. It explains a proposed logic of founding and the place of opportunity in it. [T02-W003]

### Which ventures enter a survival estimate

Which ventures enter a survival estimate

Arcuri, Russo and Gandolfi matched the Italian register of innovative start-ups with financial records. Their analysis covers 9,171 firms from 2013 to 2021 and excludes firms founded after 2020 and known exits such as mergers or acquisitions. They measure survival from foundation and identify failure from the cessation of annual reporting, with non-failing firms observed through the study cutoff. The three registration criteria they examine concern research spending, staff qualifications and ownership of industrial property. Firms could satisfy more than one. [T02-W004]

Table 4 puts estimated five-year survival for the whole sample just under 90 percent. The curves in Fig. 2 compare firms that met each criterion with the other registered ventures in the sample. Those meeting the research-spending criterion had lower estimated survival in that comparison. The curves went the other way for staff qualifications and for ownership of industrial property. The authors then used a model that included firm characteristics and regional, sector and year differences. In their further models accounting for selection into the criteria, the results for staff qualifications and industrial property stayed positive, while the association for research spending was less clear once the other criteria were included. These are comparisons within the register of innovative ventures. [T02-W004]

<!-- PDF page 382 -->

The Kauffman Firm Survey uses a different frame. Its baseline report records 4,928 completed surveys and a weighted response rate of 43 percent, with an oversample of high-technology firms. A firm founded in 2004 that closed before the sampling frame was constructed could be absent even though the survey describes a cohort of new firms. The report identifies this interval explicitly. Each survey therefore offers evidence about a defined population of entrants and survivors, while the founding episodes in Cooper describe events before such a count is possible. [T02-W005]
