## S76 Classical selling models and accounts of buying

S76   Classical selling models and accounts of buying

### Attention, interest, desire, action and satisfaction

Attention, interest, desire, action and satisfaction

AIDAS describes five successive objects of attention in a selling encounter: attention, interest, desire, action and satisfaction. In Pramod Kumar Nayak’s teaching account, the seller first establishes rapport and a receptive audience, then develops the relevance of the offering. A presentation can attract attention without producing interest, and interest can remain weaker than a desire to obtain the benefit. Objections and the buyer’s concerns enter the work of developing that desire. The seller must then recognize an appropriate point to seek a purchase, rather than assuming that wanting something automatically produces action. [SL-W003]

The Sales and Distribution Management course illustrates the sequence through insurance and family security. The concern for a family’s future gives a proposed policy its relevance; the presentation connects the policy to that concern, addresses questions and seeks the purchase. Satisfaction extends the account beyond closing. Delivery, reassurance and subsequent service bear on whether the experience fulfils what the buyer expected. AIDAS consequently gives follow-through a place within the selling sequence rather than treating the order as its sole endpoint. [SL-W004]

### What the early formulations meant by a completed sale

What the early formulations meant by a completed sale

Akinori Iwamoto’s historical investigation questions the familiar attribution of AIDA to E. St. Elmo Lewis in 1898. He compares dated formulations and their later retelling, including Strong’s accounts, rather than treating repetition of an attribution as evidence for it. His reconstruction distinguishes Dukesmith’s connected selling argument in 1903–1904, Sheldon’s discussion of conviction, resolve and action, and Brown’s 1904 ordering of the familiar four terms. Differences among these formulations matter because they concern what completes a sale. [SL-W005] Iwamoto argues that Sheldon can be regarded as the originator and that Sheldon and Dukesmith contributed decisively to formulation; this is the historical conclusion advanced by his reconstruction. [SL-W005]

Conviction that an offering is suitable, a resolve to buy and an actual purchase are different accomplishments. An account that ends with conviction may leave the transition to action unexplained; adding another mental state does not by itself identify the practical step that completes the transaction. Iwamoto uses the early texts to examine this distinction as part of the history of the formula. His argument contests an inherited origin narrative while preserving the differences among the formulations that narrative had grouped together. [SL-W005]

One of the Sheldon discussions reproduced by Iwamoto concerns the retail customer who arrives knowing what is wanted. Attention, interest, desire and resolve may already have developed before the encounter. The seller can then assist completion instead of recreating each state through a fresh presentation. This example qualifies a mechanical use of the familiar sequence: where the encounter begins depends on what the customer has already done. [SL-W005]

### The right set of circumstances

The right set of circumstances

The Right Set of Circumstances account directs attention to a seller’s use of the situation. Suitable circumstances, stimuli and appeals are expected to secure attention and interest and produce the desired response. Nayak presents it as a seller-oriented situation–response formulation. The practical object is the selling setting and the action taken within it, rather than only the sequence of mental states named by AIDAS. [SL-W003]

<!-- PDF page 384 -->

The university-course exposition similarly makes the seller’s creation or use of circumstances central. Choosing an appeal, arranging the occasion and presenting it to a particular prospect belong to the proposed influence process. The formulation is a teaching account of what the seller should attend to; it does not provide a calibrated prediction of how a given buyer will respond. [SL-W004]

### Need, product, source and satisfaction in the Buying-Formula

Need, product, source and satisfaction in the Buying-Formula

The Buying-Formula treats a purchase as a set of connections on the buyer’s side. A need or problem is connected to a product or service, then to a particular trade name or source, purchase and satisfaction. Recognizing a kind of solution differs from accepting a particular supplier. A buyer may want the product category while remaining unconvinced that this source will supply it satisfactorily. Nayak’s teaching diagram makes both connections explicit. [SL-W003]

At the product/service connection and again at the trade-name connection, the account places adequacy alongside a pleasant anticipation of satisfaction. The proposed purchase must answer the problem, and thinking about it must carry an agreeable expectation. The seller’s problem-solving work therefore concerns more than making the brand familiar: it may concern whether the product will do the job, whether the supplier can be relied upon, or what experience the buyer anticipates. Satisfaction after purchase feeds the continuing relationship and later buying. The corresponding university-course exposition develops these links as a guide to understanding buying. [SL-W003; SL-W004]

### Drive, cues and reinforcement in the Behavioral Equation

Drive, cues and reinforcement in the Behavioral Equation

Nayak’s Behavioral Equation connects a buying response with learning. Its printed expression is B = P × D × K × V: B is the buyer’s response, P predisposition or habit, D drive or motivation, K incentive potential, and V the intensity of cues. Incentive potential concerns the product’s value or potential satisfaction. A familiar response can thus be supported by habit while still depending on motivation and the attractiveness of the anticipated result. [SL-W003]

The account distinguishes cues that trigger a decision from cues that influence a choice without initiating one. Product colour, weight and price can provide product cues; advertising and conversation can provide informational cues. The categories concern what a cue does in the decision: a price can also trigger action. A rewarding result reinforces the response and can strengthen the predisposition to respond when a cue appears again. [SL-W003]

Multiplication makes a strong claim inside the formulation: if drive is zero, the proposed response is zero even when habit is strong. The slides use that implication to explain why predisposition alone is insufficient. They supply meanings and a learning account rather than fitted coefficients or a probability scale for estimating purchases. [SL-W003]

### Confidence, evidence and participation in the customer’s work

Confidence, evidence and participation in the customer’s work

The chapter of 销售管理实务, edited by 安贺新, compares several ways of organizing a selling argument. GME concerns the seller’s own confidence in the goods, the enterprise and personal capability. FABE separates features, advantages, benefits and evidence, making support for a benefit claim a distinct part of the presentation. The six steps printed under DIPDA move through definition, identification, proof, acceptance, desire and action. The related discussion connects discovering a need, showing the offering’s relevance, demonstrating it and obtaining acceptance. [SL-W006]

The chapter also distinguishes attending to customer needs in order to sell a fixed product from participating more broadly in the customer’s work. Its consultative comparison gives the seller roles as team member, adviser and partner. Two-way information, knowledge of the customer’s business,

<!-- PDF page 385 -->

participation in decisions and subsequent service become part of the relationship. These distinctions appear in the third edition of a work first published in 2009. [SL-W006]

The Changan illustration brings a service adviser and technician into continued contact with the customer. They visit, inspect the vehicle and answer questions; the chapter reports renewed intentions following that contact. The pairing joins technical examination to the service relationship, extending the encounter beyond an initial product argument. [SL-W006]

<!-- PDF page 386 -->

## S77 Questions, diagnosis and commitments in selling

S77   Questions, diagnosis and commitments in selling

### SPIN questions and the development of an explicit need

SPIN questions and the development of an explicit need

SPIN places questions inside an encounter that includes preliminary contact, investigation, demonstration of capability and obtaining commitment. In Huthwaite’s exposition, situation questions establish relevant background; problem questions elicit difficulties and dissatisfaction; implication questions explore their consequences; and need-payoff questions invite the buyer to articulate the value of a resolution. The next question responds to what has been learned, rather than merely moving to the next letter. [SL-W008]

A difficulty can constitute an implied need without yet becoming a buyer’s explicit desire for a solution. Implication questions develop why the difficulty matters, while need-payoff questions help the buyer express what improvement would be worth. Capability can then be demonstrated in relation to that expressed value. Huthwaite treats the questioning pattern as a logical framework rather than a fixed interview script. Relevant preparation also reduces the need to ask buyers for background that a seller could already know. [SL-W008]

Chaker and colleagues’ reconstruction of Neil Rackham’s 1988 SPIN Selling preserves a distinction about the scale of the sale. In a smaller sale, responding to an implied need may be sufficient; a larger commitment may require developing the seriousness of the problem and the value of acting before presenting a solution. This is the Rackham account reported in the review, alongside Huthwaite’s current exposition of the method. [SL-W001; SL-W008]

### An advance, a continuation and the work of implementation

An advance, a continuation and the work of implementation

The Urgo account first distinguishes a feature, an advantage and a benefit. A feature names a technical or functional capability; an advantage describes its generic usefulness; a benefit connects that capability to the particular customer’s expressed problem and valued result. Its illustrative wound-care conversation links recovery time with care costs, staff pressure and the customer’s operating targets. The seller’s earlier questions establish why these consequences matter to that customer, so the eventual benefit statement answers a developed need rather than reciting product properties. [SL-W009]

Huthwaite’s Urgo Medical account distinguishes a concrete advance from a pleasant continuation. An advance commits resources to an agreed action that moves an opportunity forward. Access to a board presentation, a trial with an agreed reporting date, and an order differ from an invitation to send another proposal or meet for lunch. In the report’s coding, orders and advances count as successful call outcomes; continuations and no sale do not. An advance can therefore be successful under this scheme without being a completed sale. [SL-W009]

The implementation joined training to coaching and common records. Sellers and managers needed a shared way to recognize what had happened during a call; recorded outcomes then supplied material for coaching and subsequent calls. Tablets, marketing involvement and management support belonged to the same arrangement. The report describes 104 calls by sixteen sellers, with a nested set of 48 recently coached calls. Its comparison concerns this implementation package and selected calls, rather than an isolated experiment on the four SPIN question types. [SL-W009]

### Sandler: agreements, pain, investment and the decision process

Sandler: agreements, pain, investment and the decision process

David Mattson’s Sandler account connects rapport and equal business stature with an up-front agreement, exploration of pain, investment, decision arrangements, matched fulfilment and post-sale confirmation. Up-front agreements establish the purpose, conduct and possible outcomes of the present

<!-- PDF page 387 -->

conversation. They can be renewed as an opportunity develops. Investment includes time and other resources as well as money; decision arrangements concern who will decide, how and when. [SL-W010]

Mattson’s budget example concerns a seller who knows that money should be discussed but regards asking about it as rude. The seller postpones the issue until after presenting and receives an indefinite response. His distinction among attitude, behaviour and technique explains why knowing the appropriate question does not ensure that it will be asked. Beliefs about the conversation affect enacted behaviour, and a learned technique can remain unused. [SL-W010]

The presentation follows qualification and is matched to what has been established. Post-sale work confirms the decision and next steps, including the possibility of buyer remorse. Chaker and colleagues’ reconstruction of Sandler’s earlier rules similarly places qualification, pain, money and decision authority before matching the offering. The review’s account and Mattson’s exposition together show both the qualification logic and the work around its use. [SL-W001; SL-W010]

### Consultation and the creation or revision of a buying vision

Consultation and the creation or revision of a buying vision

Ben Taylor distinguishes working with a buyer whose challenge remains unclear from responding to a request already framed around a solution. Consultation in the first situation develops understanding of the problem before an offering can be matched to it. The historical title Consultative Selling, by Mack Hanan, James J. Cribbin and Herman C. Heiser, dates from 1970 [SL-W029]; the later accounts discussed here give the operative comparisons between consultation and other selling approaches. [SL-W021]

In Chaker and colleagues’ reconstruction of Michael Bosworth’s Solution Selling, the seller locates the buyer within a buying process. Latent or acknowledged pain without a vision calls for creating a vision; an existing vision calls for reconsidering or re-engineering it. The resulting vision is commercially directed toward the seller’s product or service. The account therefore joins inquiry into the buyer’s difficulties with an attempt to shape how an eventual solution is understood. [SL-W001]

### Pain chains, sponsorship and coordinated evaluation

Pain chains, sponsorship and coordinated evaluation

The current Solution Selling exposition connects preparation with a pain chain: how a business problem affects different people. Preparation identifies relevant participants and makes an opening inquiry more useful. Subsequent work includes vision creation or revision, sponsorship and access to power, collaboration planning, evaluation criteria, proof of value and negotiation. A user’s recognized problem does not by itself supply the authority or arrangements needed to proceed. [SL-W021; SL-W027]

The collaboration plan coordinates actions and evaluation so that proof can be judged against criteria the participants have accepted. Sponsorship connects a conversation with the people able to authorize a commitment. Evaluation and negotiation then concern a proposal whose intended value and assessment have already been discussed. Cooper and Winters’ separate account of sales and project coordination develops how such conversations can span people and meetings within the work of defining a deliverable solution. [SL-W027; SL-W022]

### From control to consensus: related qualification formulations

From control to consensus: related qualification formulations

The Eades account reconstructed by Chaker and colleagues treats Solution Selling as a philosophy, map, methodology and management system aligned with buying. Situational fluency joins knowledge of the buyer’s job and problems to knowledge of the seller’s relevant capabilities. Preparation is consequently part of the capacity to ask useful questions and interpret an answer. Its Pain × Power × Vision × Value × Control = Sale formulation expresses qualification conditions; it is not an estimated probability equation.

<!-- PDF page 388 -->

Control in that account concerns facilitating a process within which buyers direct their choices. [SL-W001]

Richardson’s current PPVVC account instead names Pain, Power, Vision, Value and Consensus. It asks whether the issue is acknowledged, authority is engaged, a desired outcome is articulated, value is measurable and the buying group agrees. A compelling problem and offering can coexist with missing authority or agreement. Those missing conditions focus subsequent conversations and coaching. Consensus in this current account should therefore be understood in its own terms alongside the earlier Control formulation. [SL-W027]

<!-- PDF page 389 -->

## S78 Teaching, reframing and buyer indecision

S78   Teaching, reframing and buyer indecision

### The sequence of commercial teaching

The sequence of commercial teaching

The current Challenger exposition organizes commercial teaching into six connected steps. The warmer demonstrates informed understanding of the customer’s setting. The reframe then makes an unfamiliar problem or opportunity visible. Rational drowning supplies a quantified account of the consequences of continuing as before; emotional impact makes those consequences recognizable in a situation the customer can imagine inhabiting. The seller is developing a reason to reconsider the existing course before asking the buyer to consider a product. [SL-W020]

The fifth step, a new way, establishes the value of a different approach. Only the sixth, your solution, introduces the supplier’s differentiated offering as a way to realize it. Moving directly from a problem to the product would omit the intervening argument. Challenger describes an adaptable choreography, supported by teaching, tailoring and taking control, rather than a script to recite regardless of the buyer’s answers. [SL-W020]

### Producing an insight and tailoring it across a buying group

Producing an insight and tailoring it across a buying group

Commercial teaching relies on an organizational supply of insight as well as a seller’s conduct. Challenger’s exposition connects knowledge of the customer’s business with message development, marketing, coaching and adaptation across a buying group. Tailoring concerns different stakeholders’ drivers, even when the underlying commercial insight is shared. The seller need not invent a new economic argument in each meeting. Taking control includes discussing money and commitments, while constructive tension asks the buyer to reconsider a familiar course. Stakeholder tailoring connects that challenge to what matters to each participant. [SL-W020]

The provider’s Metrie illustration concerns molding and the basis on which builders and distributors consider an offering. Prepared messages shift attention from purchase price toward what the offer contributes to their work. Implementation joins this changed conversation to organizational support. The case reports use of the approach, while the seller-profile research reconstructed by Chaker and colleagues concerns a different object: manager assessments across 44 attributes and their association with performance. Observing a profile associated with high performers differs from testing the effect of training sellers to enact it. [SL-W020; SL-W001]

### Trust-based selling and the dispute about relationships

Trust-based selling and the dispute about relationships

Avila and Inks organize trust-based selling as initiating, developing and enhancing a relationship. Initiation includes qualification and relevant information; development concerns value and commitment; enhancement includes reliable delivery and further opportunities. Competence and dependable performance belong to trust alongside interpersonal conduct. [SL-W024]

Their distinctions among need-satisfaction, problem-solving and consultation also preserve different tasks. A seller may match an expressed need, compare alternative solutions, or work on the buyer’s strategic goals. Relationship selling in this account is consequently more substantial than personal amiability. Their criticism of Challenger credits its value focus and marketing coordination while questioning whether inexperienced sellers are equipped to teach or challenge before understanding the buyer’s situation. The dispute concerns the preparation and knowledge that make an encounter credible. [SL-W024]

<!-- PDF page 390 -->

### JOLT and the fear of making the wrong decision

JOLT and the fear of making the wrong decision

Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna’s JOLT exposition distinguishes reluctance to change from fear of choosing badly. Strengthening the case against the status quo need not settle anxiety about making the wrong decision. In their account, another urgent argument or another menu of options can deepen indecision instead of resolving it. [SL-W025]

Judging indecision means investigating uncertainty about the choice and its outcome. Offering a recommendation supplies a reasoned path through tradeoffs. Limiting exploration directs further investigation toward information that can actually improve the decision. Taking risk off the table supplies an appropriate safety net, such as a trial, opt-out or smaller initial deployment. The authors connect these actions to realistic expectations about implementation, so that reassurance does not depend on an implausibly optimistic promise. [SL-W025]

A recommendation carries some of the responsibility for choosing; a smaller deployment makes the first commitment less final. These illustrations explain how the authors intend to address hesitation after a conceptual case for buying already exists. The four activities concern the buyer’s ability to move forward, rather than simply adding more reasons why the offering is attractive. [SL-W025]

## S79 Adapting sales encounters and assessing their results

S79   Adapting sales encounters and assessing their results

### Prepared responses and room to adapt

Prepared responses and room to adapt

Frédéric Buchet begins with a technical engineer entering sales who asks for effective techniques, buyer types and convincing tricks. Buchet separates tricks, reported best practices and organized methods. A reusable reply can keep a novice from being disconcerted, but a recognizable stock answer can also invite distrust. Transferring a star seller’s practice requires attention to whether the example is representative, whether conduct was actually observed, and whether it can be organized into something teachable. [SL-W023]

CNZ organizes objection handling through investigating the objection, reformulating it constructively and then giving a targeted argument. The first two actions change what the answer should address. PLAISIR places contact, expression of needs, clarification, an argued offering, use of opportunities, purchase and reassurance within a longer encounter. A method provides a common vocabulary for instruction and coaching, while leaving a practical question about how much discretion its implementation permits. [SL-W023]

Jolson’s prepared/adaptive continuum, reconstructed in Chaker and colleagues’ review, makes room between a memorized presentation and unrestricted improvisation. A seller can prepare usable modules and combine them for the encounter. Structure supplies a repertoire; adaptation concerns selecting and connecting it in response to the situation. measures complicate an unconditional claim that adaptation improves results. Its integrative framework is the authors’ proposed organization of that literature. [SL-W001]

### A verbal prompt at the point of ordering

A verbal prompt at the point of ordering

A field experiment at two Austrian fast-food branches examined a much smaller intervention: a suggestion when a customer had ordered a main dish but no side. Successive groups of ten transactions rotated among no prompt, a potato-salad suggestion, a fries suggestion and a salad-or-fries choice. The intervention was therefore a particular utterance at a particular point in ordering, rather  than a general instruction to be more persuasive. [SL-W026]

Across 2,160 transactions, side-dish purchases were approximately 61 percent under the control condition and 78 percent across the pooled prompting conditions. The forced-choice version did not significantly outperform the simpler suggestions. An added verbal device could thus fail to improve on a useful prompt. The measured result was purchase of a side dish; the authors’ discussion of fit with the main dish and unfamiliarity concerns interpretation of those choices. [SL-W026]

## S80 Organizing sales work and creating customer value

S80   Organizing sales work and creating customer value

### From seven selling steps to continuing organizational functions

From seven selling steps to continuing organizational functions

Moncrief and Marshall contrast the traditional seven selling steps with a changed organization of sales work. Prospecting, preapproach, approach, presentation, handling objections, closing and follow-up organize a familiar sequence. Their evolving functions include customer retention and relinquishment, knowledge and database management, relationship development, marketing the product, problem solving, adding value and relationship maintenance. These functions need not occur once each in a fixed order. [SL-W002]

Their argument follows changes in who performs an activity and what supports it. Prospecting can be supplied by another unit; preparation can use shared account records rather than an individual’s index cards; a team can work with several members of a buying centre. Problem solving and continuing service can span meetings and participants. The resulting account concerns an ongoing customer relationship and division of work, rather than simply renaming stages in a single conversation. [SL-W002]

### Situational, functional and process accounts of sales management

Situational, functional and process accounts of sales management

Руденко distinguishes situational, functional and process approaches to sales management. A situational approach attends to the particular conditions under which selling takes place. A functional approach makes responsibilities and management activities visible. A process approach follows connected work across those functions. Each directs attention toward a different object of management, from an encountered condition to an assigned responsibility or a sequence that crosses departmental boundaries. [SL-W016]

In the functional account, planning, organization, motivation and control organize management responsibilities. The process account instead follows market information through connected transformations and supporting activities toward results and satisfied needs. A situational response may solve an immediate issue without specifying that continuing whole. Rudenko’s comparison consequently concerns how a sales operation is managed, with conversation techniques located within a larger set of linked activities. [SL-W016]

Understanding a customer’s business and shaping a valuable offer

Terho, Haas, Eggert and Ulaga conceptualize value-based selling through understanding the customer’s business model, crafting a value proposition and communicating customer value. Understanding includes earning logic and operating facts, not just requested specifications. Crafting uses that knowledge to shape an offering; communication makes the proposed difference credible through calculations, comparisons, references or tests. Their qualitative investigation draws on eleven purposefully selected experienced firms, senior informants and 176 transcript pages. [SL-W019]

The truck illustration begins with a request for twenty vehicles. Investigation of materials, distances, time and maintenance requirements supports a proposal for eighteen. The seller changes the proposed fleet by understanding the work it must perform, rather than merely reducing the price of the requested twenty. The dairy illustration follows washing frequency and the use of water, energy, chemicals and time. Information about the process and relevant plant experience supports an estimate of a saving opportunity. Tests or a savings-sharing arrangement can connect that estimate to a commercial proposal.

The scope of becoming a solution provider

Evers and colleagues’ solution-provider report joins the scope of an offering to its realization, selling and management. ## S102 Marketing and the organization of market relationships

S102   Marketing and the organization of market relationships

### What the seller takes to be the market

What the seller takes to be the market

Wendell Smith’s 1956 article distinguishes product differentiation and market segmentation as alternative approaches to marketing. Differentiation seeks preference for a particular offering. Segmentation begins from differences in demand and asks which offerings or efforts fit the resulting groups. The distinction directs attention to a decision made before a selling encounter: whether to shape preference around an offering or to organize the offering and effort around differences already apparent in the market. [T04-W001]

小原博’s 2010 essay follows changes in Japanese accounts of sales management, marketing management

and market management. In his discussion of 光澤’s two books, the earlier work moves from the formation of marketing management through management of processes and strategy. The later work sets

aside space for what lies beyond marketing management. 小原’s account locates continuity in the turn

toward 市場管理, or market management. [T04-W002]

### Exchange as a continuing relationship

Exchange as a continuing relationship

Christian Grönroos argues that the conventional marketing mix leaves much of service and industrial exchange unexplained. His relationship account draws attention to continuing interaction and to contributions made by participants beyond the immediate buyer and seller. [T04-W003]

Robert Salle and Jean-Paul Valla’s Lyon Acier case in Håkansson’s 1982 volume shows what particular terms and adaptations can mean. Lyon Acier obtained refractory bricks from three suppliers within a larger pool and kept a reserve stock. Field, the British supplier, adjusted the alumina content to fit local working practices. When one of its early oven vaults failed after about 60 percent of its normal service life, Field sent a technical engineer and sales director and replaced the vault at its expense. It accepted Lyon Acier’s usual payment terms. The buyer reported preferring Field when prices were equal. The authors also describe the bearing of the exchange rate on Field’s position. [T04-W005]

In the same study, Lyon Acier accounted for little of a German supplier’s sales of oil coke. The supplier provided a standard product and required shorter payment terms. The French company’s large size provided little advantage in that exchange. Salle and Valla use the comparison to explain the different prospects for negotiation and adaptation across the buyer’s purchases. The report gives the buyer’s interview perspective and the authors’ interpretation of the terms and practices they found. [T04-W005]

### Organized action has purposes as well as demands

Organized action has purposes as well as demands

These sources examine how people act with environments, learned skills, conventions, other people and material things. Their purposes include artistic performance, education, cultural participation, religious practice and therapy. The value of these activities is not exhausted by minimizing effort.

### Kirsh and Maglio: an action can change what is easy to know

Kirsh and Maglio: an action can change what is easy to know

Kirsh and Maglio distinguish pragmatic actions, which advance a physical task, from epistemic actions, whose principal function is to improve cognition. Their Tetris account considers translations and rotations that can look unnecessary when judged only as moves toward a final board position. An action can instead expose information that is difficult to compute mentally, reduce a memory demand or make an error less likely. The extra movement can be part of a better problem-solving process. [W041, selected manuscript pp. 2–5 and 40–43]

The definition separates the apparent physical distance to a goal from the informational work needed to act. An external intermediate state can make a distinction visible. A reminder or partially organized work area can similarly change the memory or search task. Its informative contribution is that an account of action can miss its purpose if it considers only direct physical progress.

Maglio and Kirsh’s 1996 Epistemic Action Increases With Skill reports a relation between skill and actions such as backtracking, qualifying the supposition that expertise always eliminates such movements. [GL-W027, abstract and introductory and result passages]

Todd and Gigerenzer describe a shortcut for predicting the winner of a Wimbledon match. If you recognize only one of the two players, predict that player will win. They explain why recognition can be informative even for tennis novices. In a setting where successful players are more often discussed, knowing a name provides a clue about performance. [W040, pp. 167–168]

The other authors discussed here draw on Gibson's The Theory of Affordances. [W042, through the accounts below]

### Ecological interfaces: display functional relations rather than isolated readings

Ecological interfaces: display functional relations rather than isolated readings

Vicente and Rasmussen tested two displays for a simulation of a system of tanks, pipes and heaters. Both showed physical settings and target values. One also showed higher-level information about how the system was functioning. After viewing each sequence for 25 to 30 seconds, participants recalled values and diagnosed the system state. Diagnosis was more accurate with the display that included functional information, chiefly among participants with theoretical expertise. The authors report better recall of functional variables with the richer display on trials showing normal operation or a fault. More accurate recall of those variables was associated with more accurate diagnosis. [TA-W026, §VII]

Shi and Zhang's 2004 review explains an abstraction hierarchy and the distinction among skill-, rule- and knowledge-based behavior. A work domain must be represented in its complexity, while its information must also be communicated to an operator. Means–ends links can show how a lower-level variable relates to a higher-level purpose, rather than merely arranging readings by part–whole location. [TA-W027, printed pp. 65–67]

Shi and Zhang also review studies of fault detection and navigation. They report advantages for displays that include functional information in demanding tasks, with normal-operation completion times sometimes similar across displays. [TA-W027]

Its assertions about fixed cognitive styles are not adopted as settled current psychology. ### Sweller: solving a problem and acquiring a schema can compete

Sweller: solving a problem and acquiring a schema can compete

The analysis in Sweller's 1988 article distinguishes successful immediate problem solving from learning a reusable schema. His explanation concerns means–ends search: repeatedly comparing a current state with a goal and seeking moves that reduce the difference can consume processing capacity without directing attention to the relations needed for later generalization. Effort spent reaching an answer is not automatically effort spent learning how to solve a class of problems. [TA-W035, printed pp. 257–259, 273 –274 and 284]

The paper discusses domain-specific knowledge rather than a general superiority in memory or search. Reported expert–novice contrasts concern meaningful configurations, not simply random items. Its computational model and educational examples support a proposal for changing instructional tasks, including worked examples or less specific goals under appropriate conditions.

Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler and Sweller's review of the expertise-reversal effect adds a material qualification. Guidance that helps a novice can become redundant or interfere once a learner has acquired the relevant schemas. Instructional support has to be assessed in relation to existing knowledge, rather than assigned one permanent benefit. [TA-W036, printed pp. 23 and 29]

### Wood, Bruner and Ross: a tutor carries part of the task

Wood, Bruner and Ross: a tutor carries part of the task

The selected discussion of tutoring specifies six functions: recruitment, reduction of degrees of freedom, direction maintenance, marking critical features, frustration control and demonstration. The tutor can temporarily handle parts of a task that the learner cannot yet manage, leaving a component within reach. That arrangement explains the scaffold metaphor more precisely than simply saying assistance makes learning easier. [GL-W016, printed pp. 97–99]

Direction maintenance is not the same as repeated instruction. A learner can remain attached to a simpler success and need support to attempt the next step. Marking a critical feature also requires interpreting the discrepancy between the learner's production and what would satisfy the task. Demonstration is more than doing the task alongside the learner; it supplies a modeled solution relevant to the learner's attempt.

The source is a small tutoring study with proposed instructional functions. The tutor's knowledge, attention and judgment remain active. A reduced task for the learner is a distribution of work in this account, not evidence that the rest of the task has ceased to exist. [GL-W016]

Billett's abstract frames workplace learning through both workplace affordances and individual engagement. Opportunities offered by a workplace do not compel a person to learn, and participation can depend on how access and activities are distributed. [GL-W052]

### Ferrer i Cancho and Solé: a model with competing effort proxies

Ferrer i Cancho and Solé: a model with competing effort proxies

The language article models a binary association matrix linking signals and referents. It assigns a speaker-side effort proxy using signal entropy and a hearer-side proxy using uncertainty about the referent  conditional on a signal. Its stated objective combines the two with a weight. A single signal can be economical under one proxy while leaving the hearer unable to distinguish referents; a large differentiating vocabulary places a different demand on the speaker. [WME-W010, equation 9 and model definition]

The authors optimize the associations and report a transition between regimes, with a Zipf-like frequency pattern near a transition in their model. The proposition is not merely that language is short. It concerns a balance between the modeled demands of producing signals and distinguishing what they refer to, with assumptions including uniformly treated referents and the permitted association structure.

The effort variables are proxies, not direct measurements of all human effort or physical energy. The paper's governing objective in equation 9 specifies the tradeoff used in its model. [WME-W010]

Kirby, Tamariz, Cornish and Smith examine cultural transmission and communication using models and artificial-language experiments. Lucas's field guide reconstructs behavior-settings theory and provides an operative method. A room or physical milieu alone is insufficient. Maller and Hyysalo: practices are performed, reproduced and contested

Maller's selected practice-theory discussion relates materials, competences and meanings. A practice as an entity is distinguishable from its particular performances. The breakfast example places an apparently simple activity within interwoven practices and material arrangements. Public cultural guidance: knowledge has custodians and conditions of use

The Assembly of Alaska Native Educators' Guidelines for Respecting Cultural Knowledge addresses researchers, language specialists and community organizations in its own setting. The document is not represented as the view of every Indigenous people.

Armstrong and colleagues’ ethnoecological discussion concerning Gitxsan and nłeʔkepmx territories makes a related but distinct argument. It locates stewardship in laws, institutions, beliefs and relational views of land. Its account explicitly resists treating reciprocity merely as a useful management tool: reciprocity can be a moral or legal obligation within the described relationships. Reducing the account to a technique for lowering management effort would change its stated purpose. The authors also criticize extractive use of knowledge. [GL-W004, selected discussion]

<!-- PDF page 404 -->

### Xunzi through Wang: ritual and custom are not the same category

Xunzi through Wang: ritual and custom are not the same category

Wang Weiwei's scholarly abstract discusses the roles of ritual propriety and custom in Xunzi's thought. The relevant contrast concerns different ways that human conduct is shaped through learned forms and habitual social practice. [GL-W008]

礼义 and 习俗 have distinct normative and cultural roles in the interpretation.

### Ritual and ascetic practice can involve deliberately sustained effort

Ritual and ascetic practice can involve deliberately sustained effort

The Stockholm University field orientation presents asceticism and ritual self-practices as subjects of religious-studies inquiry. The relevant account concerns practices through which people cultivate or transform themselves in relation to religious aims. Reducing effort need not be their purpose; disciplined effort can be constitutive of the activity. [GL-W037]

The abstract and ritual-components discussion in Boyer and Liénard's article explicitly resist treating ritual as one scientific mechanism. Their proposed components occur in different combinations. The coalitional discussion concerns signals of affiliation, commitment and cohesion; costly initiation or training can be meaningful as a signal because commitment is difficult to establish in advance. It is an account of a proposed mechanism within some practices. [GL-W042]

An action that appears repetitive or costly under an external task criterion can have a different meaning within the practice.

### Assistance includes services and participation around an object

Assistance includes services and participation around an object

The WHO framework describes assistive technology as more than a product. Its five-part approach brings people together with products, provision, personnel and policy. A device's usefulness depends on selection, fitting, learning, maintenance, access and the wider service environment. A product can enable participation while still requiring continuing support. [GL-W041, 2024 framework and GATE five-P account]

Its relevance lies in the explicit support work that an apparently simple aid can depend on.

### Personal constructs: interpreting a situation is itself an organized activity

Personal constructs: interpreting a situation is itself an organized activity

Gaines's introduction presents Personal Construct Psychology through systems of constructs by which people anticipate and interpret events. It identifies research and elicitation resources, including repertory grids. [WME-W017]

The George Kelly Society FAQ supplies a field-native description, including the distinction from claims that a person simply creates reality. Its account of repertory-grid elicitation retains the respondent's distinctions and the interviewer's influence. A structured grid can make an interpretive system discussable, but eliciting it requires skill and can introduce bias. [WME-W018]

Repertory-grid elicitation makes assumptions explicit in a representation that can be discussed and examined.

### Kriz: influencing conditions differs from prescribing a result

Kriz: influencing conditions differs from prescribing a result

The selected translated chapter by Kriz proposes a person-centered systems account in which patterns arise through interaction. The environment supplies conditions but does not uniquely prescribe the resulting pattern. His family example asks how patterns once appropriate to one stage can become rigid when circumstances change. The therapist's role, in the argument, is to influence conditions under which

<!-- PDF page 405 -->

change becomes possible rather than dictate a new interaction in every detail. [WME-W022, translated chapter, pattern formation and family interaction]

### IFS: protective parts and internal relationships

IFS: protective parts and internal relationships

The IFS Institute outline describes parts, a leading Self, protective patterns and contextual constraints. It proposes that parts can take on different roles and that extreme beliefs or emotions can be described as burdens. The stated goal involves changing relations within the model rather than simply suppressing a troublesome part. These are the model's own terms and assumptions. Its therapeutic use of burden is not the monograph's accounting of material or informational demands. [WME-W023, selected public outline]

The outline also lists external unsupportive conditions and practitioner mistakes, including proceeding before a system is ready or mistaking a part's activity for the Self. Its account consequently retains interpretation, timing and the practitioner within the process. This is the institute's public model description.

### Bowen: apparent stability can leave a problem unresolved

Bowen: apparent stability can leave a problem unresolved

The Bowen Center's public theory presentation describes a triangle as a three-person emotional relationship in which tension can shift among relationships. It explicitly says that distributing tension can stabilize a system without resolving the underlying issue. The outsider position and changes in alliance can matter to the people involved even if the overall pattern continues. [SG-W028, Introduction to the Eight Concepts; Triangles]

Its emotional-cutoff account similarly distinguishes apparent improvement through reduced contact from resolution. The public presentation proposes that unresolved patterns can recur in later relationships. These are Bowen-theory descriptions, not universal facts established by the institutional page.

The useful relevant distinction is persistence of a pattern versus benefit to each participant or resolution of its causes. [SG-W028]

### Haken: order parameters summarize and influence collective patterns

Haken: order parameters summarize and influence collective patterns

Haken's 2017 conceptual article presents synergetics through control parameters, instability, collective order parameters and circular causality. The parts exchange matter, energy or information. Under appropriate conditions, a small number of collective variables can describe a pattern and constrain how the parts move. [RGC-W038, article]

The examples include coordinated movements, common rhythms and pattern recognition. A low-dimensional description is not automatically a low-energy implementation. It is a claim about relevant  collective variables within a model or observed organization. Applying it elsewhere requires identifying those variables, checking disturbance responses and the relation between slow collective change and faster component dynamics.

The pattern-completion example makes retained preparation particularly visible. Stored or learned prototypes and network dynamics allow an incomplete input to develop toward a complete pattern. Storage, learning, sensing, transmission and physical implementation remain. Haken's use of a landscape to discuss intention is an interpretation, not a direct physical energy measurement. [RGC-W038, PDF pp. 7 –10]

His discussion of embodied aesthetics goes on to proposed relations among perception, action, beauty and therapeutic conditions. Group consciousness and mind–body identifications are philosophical or speculative extensions, not experimentally proved consequences of the network. His conclusion explicitly

warns that the apparent generality of order parameters can be seductive and requires care. [RGC-W038, PDF pp. 9–12]

Environments, skills and shared practices

## S71 Designing practice and developing skill

S71   Designing practice and developing skill

### Practice tasks and performance tasks

Practice tasks and performance tasks

Seventeen advanced pianists were given the same three measures of Shostakovich to learn. They chose how to practise and returned about a day later to perform the passage. Robert Duke, Amy Simmons and Carla Davis Cash examined the recorded practice sessions alongside independent rankings of those later performances. Their 2009 study made the organization of practice visible: people could spend their time on the same notes while doing substantially different work. [LP-W006]

The three highest-ranked pianists dealt with errors in a distinctive way. They identified the precise place and source of a mistake, worked on its repair and changed tempo systematically. Slowing down meant slowing enough to play the passage correctly; speeding up followed what the player could already control. A successful correction was then repeated until it remained secure in subsequent attempts. Diagnosis, a changed attempt and stabilization formed a connected sequence. [LP-W006]

These sessions also included musical inflection early in learning. The players were preparing an expressive performance, not postponing interpretation until after mechanical accuracy. Silent examination of the score, singing, annotations and changes in playing could participate in that preparation. The later rankings included musical quality as well as correct pitches and rhythms. That matters when interpreting what the best practice sessions accomplished. [LP-W006]

Total practice time and the number of attempts did not significantly predict the retention rankings in this sample. The top performers had not simply learned the excerpt more quickly. Their handling of errors distinguished them, particularly the combination of precise diagnosis, controlled tempo changes and repetition that secured a repair. The researchers observed these strategies in the pianists’ chosen practice; they did not assign a strategy to each pianist experimentally. [LP-W006]

K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer’s 1993 account of deliberate practice distinguishes improvement-directed training from work and play. Occupational performance must deliver a result with the capabilities already available. Play may be organized around enjoyment. Deliberate practice instead constructs an activity to improve a particular aspect of performance. A practice task can therefore differ markedly from the activity for which someone is preparing. [LP-W001]

Their baseball example concerns opportunities that ordinary performance supplies only sparsely. A game gives a batter particular pitches at particular moments, amid other demands. Training can concentrate attempts on the kind of pitch or response that needs improvement. Selecting, repeating and adjusting those attempts changes what the player gets to learn from. The quantity of relevant opportunities is organized deliberately rather than left to the frequency with which the situation occurs in competition. [LP-W001]

In the authors’ account, a teacher or coach identifies a suitable task and helps the learner understand what to attempt. The learner then has opportunities to repeat it, obtain informative feedback and revise the attempt. As capability changes, the task can change too. Solitary practice by an advanced music student can belong to this relationship: what looks like independent repetition may carry forward tasks designed through individualized teaching. The existing tutoring account in S41 explains other ways support can organize what a learner is able to attempt. [LP-W001]

The 1993 paper connects this training account with expert development, including studies of musicians and their accumulated practice. It emphasizes sustained concentration and efforts directed at improvement, rather than treating enjoyable absorption as the defining condition of practice. Its definition of the activity, its studies of attained performance and its larger explanation of expertise

<!-- PDF page 408 -->

became objects of later debate. Those questions return below, after several accounts of how practice itself can be arranged. [LP-W001]

### Building an action in stages

Building an action in stages

Pyotr Galperin’s 1959 account asks how a mental action can be formed through instruction. He distinguishes the form in which an action is carried out from its degree of generalization, abbreviation and mastery. An action performed with objects can become more economical while still depending on those objects. Removing a visible step is therefore a different change from developing an action that can be performed mentally. [LP-W009]

The orienting basis specifies what the learner attends to in deciding how to act and whether the action is correct. Galperin distinguishes orientation built around a model, orientation supplied by complete instructions for particular tasks, and orientation that teaches a method of analysing a class of tasks. The third approach changes what instruction supplies: the learner is helped to establish relevant conditions in a new case, rather than receiving only another ready-made procedure. [LP-W009]

His account follows an action through material or materialized execution, overt speech, speech addressed to oneself and increasingly internal execution. Speech can make operations explicit after the learner ceases to rely directly on the objects. Subsequent abbreviation changes how the action proceeds without requiring every earlier operation to be expressed each time. The instructional sequence concerns the form and organization of activity as well as its speed. [LP-W009]

The counting example shows why withdrawing a support and teaching an unsupported action are different instructional events. A child counts two groups of objects and is then asked to determine their combined number when the objects are covered or no longer visible. Initially, the child may try to reproduce the objects in imagination and count those images. Galperin’s discussion treats acting without the objects as something that may need to be taught, rather than a result guaranteed by successful visible counting. His larger project concerns how an action is formed and transformed through these changing supports. [LP-W009]

### Practising parts and returning to the whole

Practising parts and returning to the whole

Judith Jiménez-Díaz and María Morera-Castro’s 2018 review distinguishes several choices involved in designing motor practice: physical or mental execution, the composition of the skill, variability, distribution of attempts and their ordering. These choices concern different properties of a session. Imagining a movement changes the form of execution; separating its components changes what is practised together; changing the order of tasks changes what must be selected or reconstructed between attempts. [LP-W015]

Their account of part practice separates fragmentation, progressive segmentation and simplification. In a swimming example, the learner works on kicking, arm movements and breathing separately, then performs them together. Progressive segmentation joins successively learned units: learn one group of dance steps, learn a second, combine them, then incorporate a third. Fragmentation separates coordinated components; segmentation rebuilds a sequence through successive combinations. Both accounts include returning to the activity whose performance is intended. [LP-W015]

Simplification can preserve the overall action while easing one of its demands. Hitting a stationary ball on a tee changes the difficulty of batting without requiring the learner to practise only an isolated body movement. Mental rehearsal provides another choice: imagining the execution of a skill without carrying out its full movement. The review discusses physiological and cognitive explanations for such rehearsal and organizes decisions about practice around the learner and task. Its distinctions describe alternatives

<!-- PDF page 409 -->

that can be combined within an instructional design, rather than one standard way to break every skill into pieces. [LP-W015]

### Building a route through a performance

Building a route through a performance

Roger Chaffin and Gabriela Imreh’s 1997 study follows Imreh’s learning and relearning of the Presto from Bach’s Italian Concerto. Recordings, verbal reports and analysis of practice starts and stops make the development of one concert pianist’s memory unusually visible. The account asks how a performer can use conceptual knowledge of a piece while also relying on highly developed motor memory. [LP-W007]

The piece’s formal structure organized practice. Boundaries between musical segments supplied places to begin and end attempts, and local difficulties received concentrated attention within that larger structure. Learning the notes was joined to identifying where the performer was in the piece and how one passage related to another. A repeated theme could require a different continuation at a different point in the performance; remembering the motor sequence alone did not describe the whole problem. [LP-W007]

The pianist identified conceptual, technical and expressive features that could function as performance cues. A fingering decision, a dynamic change or a musical interpretation could become a point of deliberate attention. Later work increased the speed with which the conceptual organization could bring the relevant feature to mind during playing. The resulting route through the music supported expression and control as well as the recall of a sequence. [LP-W007]

The study also examined memory after a long interruption, including written reconstruction and recall at the piano. Formal organization remained relevant to what could be recovered. Chaffin and Imreh describe a representation that helps elicit motor performance, keep track of location and retrieve important features when they are needed. Their case complements the rehearsal and transmission accounts in S66 by showing in detail how one performer develops access to a demanding performance. [LP-W007]

### Who chooses when feedback arrives

Who chooses when feedback arrives

Suzete Chiviacowsky and Gabriele Wulf’s 2002 experiment gives control over feedback a precise form. Thirty adults learned a four-key timing task. Some could ask for information about a completed attempt. Each participant in a comparison group received feedback on the same numbered attempts as a corresponding participant who chose it. The paired schedule held the occurrence of feedback and no-feedback trials together while changing who controlled those occurrences. [LP-W034]

The self-controlled group performed better on a delayed transfer test involving a changed version of the timing task. The participants tended to request feedback after attempts they thought had gone well. Questionnaire responses and comparisons of errors on feedback and no-feedback trials supported that pattern. Requests were serving partly to confirm a successful attempt, rather than simply to obtain correction after an obvious failure. [LP-W034]

This made the relation between an attempt and the subsequent information important. A schedule could be identical in numbered trials yet fit one learner’s experience differently from another’s. Chiviacowsky and Wulf proposed that self-controlled requests were more closely aligned with the learner’s needs. Their reported advantage concerned delayed transfer; the experiment’s value also lies in showing how the selection of feedback can be studied separately from simply supplying more of it. [LP-W034]

Chiviacowsky, Camila Neves, Liliane Locatelli and Cibelly Oliveira’s 2005 study examined forty children, approximately ten years old, using a timed four-key sequence and self-controlled or paired externally scheduled feedback. Its results separated relative timing, the proportions within the sequence, from absolute timing, its overall duration. On the relative-timing retention measure, the externally scheduled

<!-- PDF page 410 -->

group performed better. The absolute-timing comparison did not show the same significant difference. [LP-W013]

The authors considered children’s ability to recognize good and bad attempts when discussing why feedback control might work differently in this setting. Selecting when to ask for information itself requires a judgment about the attempt. Their developmental interpretation concerns that judgment and the demands of the task. It is a separate account from the adult study, with its own population, assessment and finding. [LP-W013]

### Grouping attempts and feedback

Grouping attempts and feedback

Satoshi Shibuya and Masanobu Ito’s 1999 experiment combined two scheduling choices. Participants practised timing tasks in blocked or random order and received feedback summarizing one, three or five attempts. Blocking repeated the same task together; random practice switched among tasks. Changing the summary size altered how many attempts preceded a presentation of their results. The experiment could therefore examine whether the effect of one choice depended on the other. [LP-W014]

For relative timing in the retention test, the random-practice group with three-attempt summaries performed best. Among the blocked groups, five-attempt summaries produced the best relative-timing accuracy. Relative timing and overall duration were assessed separately. The pattern concerned the combination of practice order and feedback summary, rather than establishing one summary size as preferable independently of the practice arrangement. [LP-W014]

The authors interpreted these findings through the information-processing demands created by switching tasks and retaining information about recent attempts. A longer summary changed the demands under which the learner interpreted feedback; switching among tasks changed them again. Their discussion asks how these arrangements interact in forming the timing structure of an action. [LP-W014]

Ivan Wallan Tertuliano, Orlando Pereira de Souza Júnior, Antônio Sabino da Silva Filho and Umberto Cesar Corrêa’s 2008 volleyball study used a larger motor activity. In 144 children, it combined four practice arrangements with feedback on every attempt or on approximately a third of attempts. The feedback concerned movement quality, and the study distinguished the score achieved by the serve from the pattern of movement used to achieve it. A later adaptation phase changed the task after the stabilization phase. [LP-W012]

The authors did not establish learning in the experiment and consequently did not infer a successful combination of schedules from the group comparisons. Their design nevertheless states the practical question concretely: organize where serves are directed, choose when to provide information about movement, then examine both the result and the developing movement pattern when conditions change. The intended skill, the information supplied and the measures used to assess adaptation were separate parts of that question. [LP-W012]

### Relating practice to expertise

Relating practice to expertise

Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald’s 2014 meta-analysis related accumulated practice to attained performance across music, games, sport, education and professional activity. It combined studies of structured activity intended to improve performance. The reported overall correlation was .35, with substantial differences across domains and ways of measuring practice and performance. The review treated practice as important while arguing that it left considerable variation among people unexplained. [LP-W002]

<!-- PDF page 411 -->

Those comparisons concern differences between people: whether participants reporting more practice tend to attain higher performance. They do not assign a percentage of one person’s skill to a cause. The review’s domain and measurement analyses also show why a single correlation conceals consequential choices about the activity counted and the result being explained. Retrospective reports, recorded practice and different performance assessments contribute different kinds of information to the pooled comparison. [LP-W002]

The authors’ broad structured-practice category became central to disagreement about what their estimates could test. A measure of accumulated activity can include practice that meets some descriptions of deliberate practice while failing stricter requirements advanced by its proponents. The dispute therefore concerns the identity of the activity as well as the size of its association with performance. [LP-W002]

Friedrich Platz, Reinhard Kopiez, Andreas Lehmann and Anna Wolf’s 2014 music meta-analysis organized its pool around accumulated task-relevant practice and objectively assessed musical achievement. Its final pool contained thirteen studies and 788 participants. It reported a correlation of .61, with a confidence interval from .54 to .67. The authors argued for comparisons in which the predictors and performance outcomes were sufficiently alike to support aggregation. [LP-W008]

Their category of task-relevant practice included deliberate practice but was not identical to the strict teacher-guided category subsequently defended by Ericsson. The music analysis supplies a developed example of how defining the domain, predictor and outcome changes a research question. Its larger association and the broader review’s smaller one describe differently assembled evidence, with the authors’ own reasons for their choices. [LP-W008]

Ericsson and Kyle Harwell’s 2019 criticism returns to what counts as expertise and what counts as deliberate practice. They distinguish reproducibly superior performance on representative tasks from some educational or professional proxies. They also require evidence that the measured activity fits the original account of improvement-directed, individualized training. Their argument challenges the inclusion of studies whose performance measures or practice categories do not meet those criteria. [LP-W003]

Their more restrictive reanalysis reports different practice-performance associations, including an adjustment for measurement error. They regard these changes as evidence that broader pools can underestimate the relationship they intend to study. They also recommend examining concentration, analysis and problem solving during practice. In their account, duration alone cannot represent the quality of a training activity whose very definition includes how it is organized. [LP-W003]

This position joins an empirical question to a methodological one. Which activity has been measured, and is the performance assessment appropriate to the domain’s expertise? Ericsson and Harwell argue that answers are required before a correlation can bear on their theory. Their proposed criteria specify the body of evidence to which they believe the theory applies. [LP-W003]

Macnamara and Hambrick’s 2020 commentary disputes how the terms have been used across publications. They compare earlier descriptions with later distinctions between purposeful and deliberate practice, and object to relabelling activities previously discussed under the latter heading. Their examples include the treatment of solitary practice and research on word-game performance. The criticism concerns whether changes in terminology alter what evidence is accepted as a test of a theory. [LP-W004]

For these authors, cumulative research depends on definitions that permit a finding to count against an explanation as well as for it. If an activity can be accepted under one description and excluded under another, the relation between prediction and evidence becomes unstable. Their commentary develops that objection rather than introducing another training intervention. It argues for practice as an

<!-- PDF page 412 -->

important contributor to expertise whose explanatory reach can be investigated alongside other factors. [LP-W004]

Ericsson’s 2020 reply defends continuity in the original definition. He specifies a task that the learner understands, opportunities for independent attempts, actionable feedback, repetition and individualized guidance from a teacher or coach. He calls activity satisfying the first four requirements purposeful practice; deliberate practice also includes the fifth. On this interpretation, broadly structured self-study is not automatically evidence about the narrower training category. [LP-W005]

The reply also explains why solitary activity and teacher-guided training need not be opposites. An advanced student can work alone on exercises established through individual instruction. What matters to Ericsson is the relation of those exercises to the student’s present performance and subsequent guidance. His answer defends a narrower training category, while Macnamara and Hambrick question whether its usage has remained stable across the research being debated. [LP-W005]

### What is carried into the next task

What is carried into the next task

Geneviève Oléron’s 1955 review begins with an operational definition of transfer. Compare learning task B after learning task A with learning B without that preceding experience. An improvement, an impairment or no measured difference supplies the corresponding positive, negative or null transfer result. The comparison asks about the effect of prior activity on a later one, rather than inferring transfer simply because the activities look alike. [LP-W011]

Oléron also emphasizes that an organized activity can combine movement, perception, memory and intellectual operations. Describing two tasks by one conspicuous surface feature may therefore miss what the learner is carrying between them. The analogy experiments developed in S64 give another concrete setting in which recognizing and using a relevant relation matters. The retention, transfer and scheduling accounts in S72 follow how different practice conditions affect what becomes available after the immediate attempt has ended. [LP-W011]

<!-- PDF page 413 -->

## S72 Challenge, difficulty and accelerated learning

S72   Challenge, difficulty and accelerated learning

### Learning that outlasts a good performance

Learning that outlasts a good performance

Training can make someone perform well while the training conditions remain in place. Richard Schmidt and Robert Bjork’s 1992 account asks what that performance reveals about the capability that will remain when those conditions change. They compare findings from motor and verbal learning and argue that practice should be judged in relation to the later performance for which it prepares a person. A successful attempt during instruction and a successful attempt after a delay answer different questions. [LP-W030]

Their comparison includes arrangements that make acquisition look less successful while improving later performance. Varying or switching tasks, reducing some forms of assistance and distributing activity can change what the learner must do during practice. The authors interpret such findings through the processes required by the eventual task. Their training argument begins with that criterion performance and asks whether practice exercises the processes it will require. [LP-W030]

This is an ambitious historical integration across experimental traditions. Schmidt and Bjork seek common principles in results that had often been considered within separate research paradigms. Their proposed account changes the role of the practice session: its immediate score becomes one observation among others, while retention and transfer become central tests of its value as training. [LP-W030]

Nicholas Soderstrom and Robert Bjork’s 2015 review develops the distinction between performance and learning through a larger literature. They use learning to concern relatively durable changes that support later retention and transfer, while performance is the behavior observed under present conditions. A temporary aid can improve current execution without producing the same improvement when removed. Conversely, a condition that initially disrupts fluent execution can prepare better later performance. [LP-W019]

The distinction also affects learners’ decisions. A fluent response can seem to show that material is mastered; a difficult attempt can seem to show that a method is failing. The review examines cases in which these judgments follow immediate performance more closely than later results. Its verbal- and motor-learning accounts explain why judging a learning procedure requires specifying what should become possible afterward and how that capability will be assessed. The schema-acquisition and guidance studies in S41 develop related instructional questions through their own accounts. [LP-W019]

### Effort and the learning edge

Effort and the learning edge

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi and Judith LeFevre’s 1989 study examined the quality of experience in work and leisure. Seventy-eight workers supplied repeated reports during a week, allowing experiences to be related to perceived challenge, perceived skill and the activity being undertaken. Their analysis distinguished situations with high challenge and high skill from those with little of either. Absorption and engagement were examined in relation to what a person was doing and felt capable of doing. [LP-W031]

Work and leisure did not simply divide experience into burdensome and rewarding states. The authors found patterns in which work supplied challenges and opportunities for skill that could be associated with a richer experience, even while participants might prefer to be doing something else. Their subject was the organization and felt quality of experience. That provides the setting for later arguments about flow without making experience-sampling reports measurements of how quickly a skill was acquired. [LP-W031]

Phillip Armour’s 2006 essay The Learning Edge brings competence and task difficulty into a practical argument about software work. His diagrams place routine activity toward boredom, demands far beyond

<!-- PDF page 414 -->

capability toward anxiety, and a zone of competence between them. The learning edge lies near the boundary of what the person can presently do. As competence grows, an unchanged task can move from challenge into routine; the edge moves with the learner. [LP-W018]

Armour argues that organizations should help people reach and remain near this moving edge. He makes a stronger claim about accelerated learning at its outer boundary: stress can be pushed far enough to force development, provided it does not cause the learner to shut down. Marine recruit training and Outward Bound supply his illustrations of people placed in demanding situations. The essay treats discomfort as potentially productive and challenges managers to attend to learning rather than viewing software work only as the delivery of already mastered activity. [LP-W018]

His account is a practitioner’s argument, supported by these illustrations and a proposed relation among challenge, competence and experience. Its useful practical question is how an organization supplies tasks beyond comfortable repetition while keeping a person able to engage with them. The instructional role of support is developed in S41; the interpersonal risks of exposing uncertainty are examined in S51. [LP-W018]

Elizabeth Ligon Bjork and Robert Bjork’s 2011 account of desirable difficulties concerns demands that can improve later learning even when they impede immediate performance. Their distinction between retrieval strength and storage strength separates current accessibility from the more enduring entrenchment of learning. Material can be easy to bring to mind now because it has just been seen, while that accessibility gives an unreliable impression of what will be available after an interval. [LP-W028]

Generating an answer, attempting recall, spacing encounters and switching among examples change the activity that must be performed. The authors explain their desirability through what those activities can contribute to learning, rather than through unpleasantness itself. Their chapter also addresses judgments made during study: familiar material can invite confidence without requiring the learner to reproduce or use it. The experiments below give particular procedures and outcomes behind several of these recommendations. [LP-W028]

### Matching challenge to the learner

Matching challenge to the learner

Mark Guadagnoli and Timothy Lee’s 2004 challenge-point framework distinguishes nominal task difficulty from functional difficulty. Nominal difficulty concerns the task’s demands. Functional difficulty also depends on the person attempting it and the conditions under which it is attempted. The same task can thus supply a different challenge at different stages of a learner’s development. [LP-W021]

Their golf example makes the distinction tangible. A pitch shot over water can be a substantial problem for a beginner and a familiar task for a skilled golfer. Keeping the physical shot unchanged does not keep the functional difficulty unchanged. Feedback and practice conditions further alter what information is available and what the performer must process. The account concerns a relation among task, skill and the organization of practice. [LP-W021]

The proposed framework distinguishes potential information from information the learner can interpret and use. Increasing difficulty can supply more opportunity to learn, until processing demands exceed what that learner can manage. Their diagrams consequently distinguish the functional difficulty associated with the best current practice performance from the difficulty associated with the greatest potential learning benefit. A session chosen solely to produce the cleanest immediate performance can occupy a different point on those proposed relations. [LP-W021]

As skill increases, the framework predicts that suitable functional difficulty should increase too. The golfer can attempt a more demanding task or practise under conditions that require more selection and interpretation. Guadagnoli and Lee use this argument to interpret findings about task order and feedback,

<!-- PDF page 415 -->

including why their effects can depend on task complexity. Their challenge point is a theoretical account of interpretable information and learning, rather than a scale for measuring emotional distress. [LP-W021]

### Learning by trying to remember

Learning by trying to remember

A memory test can change the memory it examines. In Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke’s 2006 experiments, students learned prose passages and then either studied them again or tried to recall them.
