The recall attempts supplied no corrective feedback. A later test compared what remained available after different delays. Replacing another encounter with the text by an attempt to produce it changed the subsequent course of remembering. [LP-W022]

In their first experiment, additional study produced better recall five minutes later: 81 percent of the scored idea units, compared with 75 percent after an initial recall test. Two days later the order reversed. Students who had previously attempted recall remembered 68 percent, compared with 54 percent after additional study. After a week, the corresponding figures were 56 and 42 percent. The apparent winner depended on when the outcome was measured. [LP-W022]

The second experiment arranged four learning periods in three ways: four periods of study; three periods of study followed by one recall test; or one period of study followed by three tests. Students wrote what they could remember rather than reproducing exact wording or a required order. Repeated testing provided further attempts to retrieve the passage without showing it again. It therefore changed both what students did and how often they encountered the original text. [LP-W022]

Again, repeated study led on the five-minute test, whereas repeated testing led after a week. The students who studied throughout read their passage approximately fourteen times, compared with about three and a half readings in the repeated-test condition. Nevertheless, after a week the repeated-test group recalled 61 percent of the idea units and the repeated-study group 40 percent. More exposure to the passage had produced stronger immediate performance but less durable recall in this comparison. [LP-W022]

Students’ expectations pointed in the other direction. Those who repeatedly studied were more confident that they would remember the material a week later. Repeated access to a readable passage could feel reassuring while a closed-text attempt exposed what was difficult to produce. The experiment thus joined a learning procedure to a problem of judgment: the experience that makes study feel successful need not identify the procedure that leaves more available later. [LP-W022]

Wang Zhixun and Zhang Jinkun’s 2017 review compares explanations of retrieval-practice effects. Additional exposure, effort during retrieval, elaboration and changes in episodic context make different claims about why attempting recall can benefit subsequent remembering. Their discussion moves from descriptions of an observed effect to processes that might produce it. In particular, a difficult attempt and a successful learning outcome do not by themselves identify the mechanism connecting them. [LP-W017]

The episodic-context account they discuss links an event with the context encoded when it was encountered. A later retrieval attempt uses present cues to reconstruct the earlier context. Successful retrieval then updates the representation so that elements of the old and new contexts can participate in subsequent remembering. On this account, repeated retrieval changes the cues and search conditions through which the material can later be found. [LP-W017]

Their review also examines how a retrieval cue can become more diagnostic: it can direct a search toward a target while excluding competing items. It compares this kind of account with explanations emphasizing semantic elaboration or the effort involved in retrieval. Wang and Zhang develop the integration of

<!-- PDF page 416 -->

encoding and retrieval as an explanatory direction. The review’s contribution is this comparison of proposed processes, beyond merely repeating the recommendation to test oneself. [LP-W017]

### Returning after an interval

Returning after an interval

In the selected experiments from Hermann Ebbinghaus’s 1885 work on memory, learning continued through returns to material on successive days. He learned series of syllables to the point of a first successful reproduction, waited twenty-four hours and relearned them to that criterion. The number of repetitions required on later days made the persistence of previous work observable even when the material could no longer simply be reproduced at once. [LP-W027]

The chapter considers series of different lengths and stanzas from Don Juan. These materials posed different learning demands, but the repeated procedure made later savings comparable with earlier effort for the material being learned. Each new occasion began with whatever remained from the previous occasions and continued until the specified reproduction criterion was reached. Learning was being examined as a history of returns, not only as the progress made within one sitting. [LP-W027]

The number of repetitions needed fell over successive days. Ebbinghaus examined the relation between repetitions performed and later savings, while keeping the outcome criterion stable. His self-experimental procedure made the effort of relearning a measure of persistence. It could reveal retained effects of earlier work that a simple present-versus-absent memory judgment would miss. [LP-W027]

He also distinguished the observed series from an estimate of the isolated contribution of a particular day’s repetitions. To calculate that contribution, one would need to know how much relearning would have been required had those repetitions not occurred. Subtracting consecutive daily totals would not supply that missing comparison. Ebbinghaus set aside uncertain assumptions about it and reported the relations actually observed. [LP-W027]

Nicholas Cepeda, Edward Vul, Doug Rohrer, John Wixted and Harold Pashler’s 2008 study varied two intervals separately: the gap between learning occasions and the later delay before the final test. Its 1,354 participants contributed to twenty-six combinations of study gap and test delay, using learned facts. A spacing schedule was therefore evaluated against a specified future occasion for remembering. [LP-W023]

The procedure can be followed on two clocks. Learn the facts, wait the selected gap and study them again; then wait the separately selected retention interval before testing what can be recalled. Altering the first interval changes when relearning occurs. Altering the second changes how long that learning must remain useful. The design examines their relationship rather than treating all delayed tests as equivalent. [LP-W023]

The best-performing gap changed with the intended retention interval. Cepeda and colleagues described the resulting surface as a temporal ridgeline: effective spacing depended on the horizon over which memory was being assessed. Their empirical account provides a way to investigate a scheduling decision that a simple instruction to spread practice out leaves unspecified. [LP-W023]

### Relearning to a criterion

Relearning to a criterion

Katherine Rawson and John Dunlosky’s 2012 review asks when practice testing can support learning that is both durable and efficient. Its question includes the time or effort needed to obtain a later result. Correct recall during an initial session is one possible stopping criterion, but it leaves open what should happen at later encounters with the same material. The authors examine a schedule that combines initial retrieval with returns to successful recall on subsequent occasions. [LP-W029]

<!-- PDF page 417 -->

This changes the unit in which practice is planned. Instead of deciding only how many additional repetitions to perform before ending the first session, the learner plans several sessions in which the material must again be produced correctly. The review’s accounts connect initial learning, later relearning and the final retention measure. Durability and efficiency are evaluated together, so a schedule can be considered in relation to both what is remembered and what it took to establish that memory. [LP-W029]

Julian Roelle and Tobias Richter’s 2025 review develops successive relearning as the combination of retrieval practice with distributed returns to a mastery criterion. Their example begins with an explanation of a biological mechanism learned until it can be given correctly. The learner then practises the explanation again after two, nine and sixteen days, each time relearning until correct. The return is an attempt to reconstruct the explanation, followed by whatever additional learning is needed to meet the criterion. [LP-W016]

A mathematical procedure can be organized similarly. Having applied it successfully in the first learning phase, the learner returns on several later occasions and continues until successful application is again possible. These examples distinguish a return to a criterion from a return for a fixed number of minutes. The later session responds to what the learner can then produce. [LP-W016]

Roelle and Richter also distinguish learning to recognize similarities within a category from learning to discriminate between categories. Blocking can keep related examples together; interleaving can put contrasting examples close enough to compare. Their review uses these distinctions to explain why retrieval, spacing, successive relearning and interleaving are separate design choices, even when more than one occurs within a learning programme. [LP-W016]

### Mixing what must be distinguished

Mixing what must be distinguished

Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork’s 2008 experiments asked participants to learn painters’ styles from examples. In blocked study, examples by the same artist appeared together. In interleaved study, paintings by different artists were mixed. A later test used previously unseen paintings and asked who had painted them. Success required using what had been learned about a style to classify a new instance. [LP-W024]

Interleaving improved classification in the reported comparisons. Yet participants tended to judge blocked study more effective. Seeing several works by one artist in succession could make the style seem easier to grasp while that sequence was present. The later task required distinguishing among possible artists, which made comparisons across styles important. The authors discussed improved discrimination as an explanation for the interleaving benefit. [LP-W024]

The manipulation also clarifies a difference between interleaving and temporal spacing. Alternating artists increases the interval between examples by one artist, but it fills that interval with potentially informative examples from others. Kornell and Bjork explicitly distinguish their arrangement from simply waiting before showing another example of the same category. Both the time between related examples and the material placed between them belong to the procedure. [LP-W024]

Stanisław Czyż, Aleksandra Wójcik and Petra Solarská’s 2024 review concerns contextual interference and motor transfer. It included forty-two studies, with thirty-four entering its quantitative analysis of delayed transfer. The review separated that outcome from immediate transfer and examined blocked and random practice in relation to performance on a changed task after an interval. Its average result favored random practice, with differences across settings and age groups. [LP-W032]

The review gives a broader empirical setting for motor scheduling experiments such as those in S71. It keeps transfer delay, the transfer task and the practice setting within the comparison, rather than pooling every later score as the same kind of result. Laboratory and applied conditions can organize substantially

<!-- PDF page 418 -->

different learning situations. The authors’ synthesis makes those distinctions part of interpreting the estimated effect. [LP-W032]

### Problem solving and productive failure

Problem solving and productive failure

Manu Kapur’s 2008 study placed 309 eleventh-grade students in three-person groups working on Newtonian-kinematics problems in a computer-supported collaborative setting. The students had already completed the relevant curricular unit. Groups were assigned more or less structured problems. Car-accident scenarios supplied situations requiring the students to interpret events, propose approaches and  assess their attempts. The manipulation concerned problem structuredness after that prior instruction. [LP-W025]

The ill-structured groups struggled during their collaborative work, but the article reported better later individual near and far transfer. Their discussions provided occasions to generate and examine approaches without following the same well-specified path through the problem. Kapur investigated whether the apparently unsuccessful group activity could prepare resources for a later individual task. Initial solution quality and subsequent learning were deliberately examined at different points. [LP-W025]

The term productive failure gives that difference a practical force. A group’s difficulty in reaching a satisfactory answer need not exhaust what its members have gained from trying. In this study, that argument is tied to the structure of the problems, the prior curriculum and the later tests. It concerns students working on physical problems; S31 develops separate histories of how organizations identify and learn from failures. [LP-W025]

Tanmay Sinha and Kapur’s 2021 meta-analysis examines another explicit comparison: problem solving followed by instruction, against instruction followed by problem solving. The review included fifty-three studies and 166 comparisons. Its overall result favored problem solving first, and it examined how closely interventions followed productive-failure design principles. The sequence includes subsequent instruction as part of the learning arrangement. [LP-W026]

In this research family, learners’ generated approaches can supply material on which instruction builds. Comparing an incomplete or unsuccessful attempt with a developed solution can make relevant features and distinctions available for discussion. The instructional phase is consequently more than a reward supplied after struggle: its connection to the preceding attempts is part of the proposed design. Sinha and Kapur examine implementation along with conceptual knowledge and transfer outcomes. [LP-W026]

Sinha and Kapur also report comparisons favoring instruction first, particularly among younger learners in second through fifth grades and in work on domain-general skills. Their analysis considers grade level, intervention duration and the experimental or quasi-experimental design alongside fidelity to productive-failure principles. It develops the question of when a sequence works, including how instruction makes  use of the attempts that precede it. [LP-W026]

### Learning techniques in classrooms

Learning techniques in classrooms

John Dunlosky, Katherine Rawson, Elizabeth Marsh, Mitchell Nathan and Daniel Willingham’s 2013 review evaluates ten learning techniques through several dimensions: learning materials, conditions of learning, learner characteristics and the tasks used to assess the result. A technique’s utility is considered in relation to the breadth of evidence and the situations in which it can be used. This supplies an evaluation framework as well as findings about particular techniques. [LP-W020]

Practice testing and distributed practice receive high utility assessments in that review. Testing includes low-stakes attempts to retrieve information, including self-testing; it need not mean another

<!-- PDF page 419 -->

consequential examination. Distributed practice concerns how learning opportunities are placed over time. The review’s practical question is how these activities can be incorporated into studying and teaching, with evidence about retention beyond the initial encounter. [LP-W020]

Its interleaving discussion also concerns selecting what to do. A blocked run of one kind of problem can repeatedly cue the same procedure. A mixed set may require identifying the kind of problem before choosing a method. Thus changing the order can change the operation practised, even when the set contains the same problems. The review develops this explanation alongside the state of the evidence, while S70 examines the distinct content and outcomes of training in creative methods. [LP-W020]

Sterre Ruitenburg, Mieke Goos, Guus Lambert, Paul Kirschner, Halszka Jarodzka and Gino Camp’s 2026 classroom meta-analysis examines retrieval practice, distributed practice and interleaving in school settings. It includes fifty-three studies, 233 effect sizes and 7,303 participants. The reported average effects favor the techniques in the selected comparisons. Its analysis also retains information about the alternative activity against which a technique was compared. [LP-W033]

For spacing, a comparison with massed practice differs from a comparison with practice that is already distributed to some degree. The ratio of study interval to retention interval and the form of the later test further distinguish the reported outcomes. For interleaving, the analysis examines whether feedback is immediate, delayed or absent. These are concrete differences in classroom arrangements, rather than interchangeable instances of a technique’s name. [LP-W033]

The classroom review brings the scheduling questions back to activities conducted within teaching. A pupil can be asked to retrieve, to return after an interval or to choose among different problems, while the teacher also determines feedback and assessment. Its findings develop the study of these arrangements in their actual instructional settings. They extend a history in which what is practised, when it is practised and what later performance should show remain central questions. [LP-W033]

<!-- PDF page 420 -->

## S101 Fear, avoidance and learning to approach

S101   Fear, avoidance and learning to approach

### What an avoidance procedure observes

What an avoidance procedure observes

Krypotos and colleagues distinguish arrangements in which a designated response prevents an aversive event from arrangements in which withholding a response prevents it. The act can precede an event or terminate one already under way, depending on the experimental contingency. Unsignaled avoidance schedules give researchers a way to ask whether a warning cue is necessary for the behavior under study. The procedure specifies the available action, the timing of the aversive event and how the two depend on one another. [T03-W001]

Hofmann and Hay’s account asks what function avoidance serves in its setting. Avoiding an actual threat can protect the person. In other circumstances, a protective action can keep the person from finding out that the feared outcome would have failed to occur even without it. Their discussion brings both functions into clinical assessment. The costs of silence discussed in S51 arise in organizational settings where an adverse response can be a real possibility. [T03-W002]

### What is learned during approach

What is learned during approach

Craske and colleagues organize exposure around a prediction about a feared event. Their treatment illustrations describe eliciting the prediction, arranging the exposure, observing what occurs and revisiting the expectation. Reduction in distress within the exercise and a change in expectation are different observations. Their account gives varied contexts and retrieval cues a role because the person may need to draw on the learning in circumstances different from those of the treatment. The cases illustrate the procedure and its rationale. [T03-W003]

Shiban, Pauli and Mühlberger compared exposure in one virtual context with exposure in several contexts in a study of spider phobia. The subsequent renewal test asked whether the feared response returned in another context. The authors reported less renewal with the multiple-context arrangement under their test conditions. This result concerns transfer between specified experimental settings. Practical functioning in everyday settings requires its own observations. [T03-W005]

Magdalena Sich’s 2024 dissertation asked 62 patients receiving inpatient or day treatment to rate how willing they would be to undertake exposure in virtual reality or in person. They viewed example videos of the two formats and rated them before and after an experience with the virtual medium. They rated their willingness to undertake virtual exposure higher at both points. In the separate forced choice between formats, 40 initially preferred virtual reality and 38 did afterward. Eleven switched to in-person exposure and nine switched the other way. The study measured willingness and preference for the format. [T03-W004]

<!-- PDF page 421 -->

## S73 Brief therapy: goals, exceptions and practical change

S73   Brief therapy: goals, exceptions and practical change

### When attempted solutions sustain a problem

When attempted solutions sustain a problem

In the Palo Alto model of brief therapy, an effort to remove a difficulty can become part of what keeps it going. Michael Rohrbaugh and Varda Shoham's 2001 account calls attention to the interaction between a complaint and the attempted solutions surrounding it. A partner presses for discussion because the other withdraws; the other withdraws further under pressure; the first responds by pressing harder. The complaint need not be imaginary, and neither participant need intend the result. The repeated response to it supplies a pattern that the therapist can try to interrupt. [TD-W001]

The therapist first asks what actually happens, what the participants have tried, and what follows those attempts. A complaint such as poor communication becomes a sequence of observable actions. The intervention is then fitted to that sequence: reducing pursuit, changing the circumstances of a conversation, or asking someone to observe a pattern instead of immediately trying to correct it. The next encounter examines whether the response changed. The point of reconstructing the sequence is to locate an intervention, rather than to require a complete explanation of the person's history before anything useful can be attempted. [TD-W001]

Rohrbaugh and Shoham describe other ironic processes, including reassurance that invites further requests for reassurance and efforts to force sleep that increase wakefulness. Their account distinguishes a complaint's origins from the transactions maintaining it. It also makes the therapist's manner of proposing a change consequential. An instruction that encounters opposition may need to acknowledge the client's position or take an indirect form. The same complaint label can conceal different interaction patterns, so the proposed interruption depends on the attempted solution and the response it evokes. [TD-W001]

Brevity in this tradition did not mean that an arbitrary smaller allowance was always better. The review reports a small experiment comparing limits of five and ten sessions, with thirteen and fourteen cases respectively. Although the clinic's treatment averaged about six sessions, the five-session condition fared worse. An average describes what happened across cases; a cap changes the conditions under which each case can proceed. The authors' discussion of this experiment is particularly useful for understanding why a brief approach can seek economy without treating the shortest permitted treatment as its objective. [TD-W001]

### Developing solutions from exceptions

Developing solutions from exceptions

Steve de Shazer and his colleagues' 1986 paper described a further change of emphasis at the Brief Family Therapy Center. Instead of organizing every intervention around the attempted solution that maintained a complaint, they increasingly developed solutions from clients' goals and from exceptions to the complaint. Their distinction between an explanatory match and a practical fit was deliberate. A useful intervention might fit what the client needed to accomplish without reproducing a detailed model of the problem. The therapist therefore sought descriptions of what would be different, what was already happening on better occasions, and what the client could recognize as progress. [TD-W002]

One family was asked to observe, between visits, what each person did that the others wanted to continue. This assignment changed what the family was looking for. At the next meeting, particular acts worth preserving could be described and discussed, rather than only another inventory of failures. The therapists then asked how the family had helped those events occur and how they might encourage more of them. In the authors' account, the family invented its eventual solution between the first and second sessions; the later work helped it sustain and extend the useful changes. Observation was connected to

<!-- PDF page 422 -->

action through the selection of concrete events and the participants' account of their own contribution. [TD-W002]

Another task introduced a contrast into parents' efforts to get homework done. Coin-toss days determined when they would refrain from mentioning it, giving them occasions to notice what happened without their usual prompting. If the child did the homework on those days, the next conversation could examine a successful difference already present in the family's experience. The instruction was more specific than a general demand to be positive: alter a recurring response, observe the result, and use the result to decide what to continue. [TD-W002]

The first-session format connected the complaint, exceptions, goals and possible solutions. Concrete questions established who did what, when the difficulty occurred, and how anyone would know that it had improved. After a consultation break, the team delivered a message combining acknowledgments of the client's resources with a task or clue directed toward useful change. Even an initially vague complaint could lead to an observable goal. Asking what a close friend would notice when the person felt more certain of who they were made a broad aspiration answerable in terms of everyday conduct. [TD-W002]

At a subsequent session, the therapists elicited what was better, distinguished new changes from previously overlooked exceptions, and asked how the client had brought them about. A useful difference became material for the next action. When nothing had improved, the search shifted toward what was preventing deterioration or what small difference might still be amplified. When things were worse, the authors described questions about the course of that worsening and signs of an approaching improvement. These were the center's reported conversational practices, rather than results establishing the effectiveness of each question separately. [TD-W002]

Continuation also depended on the developing case. The center usually placed the second session a week after the first, then lengthened intervals when the client reported improvement: two weeks, followed by three weeks to a month. When the team thought the change might be sufficient, it asked the client whether another meeting was needed and when. The center reported about 1,600 cases from 1978 to 1983, averaging six sessions. Follow-up was based on self-report, and only twenty-eight of fifty-six clients in a separate first-task project were reached. Those service observations accompanied the description of an evolving practice; they were not a randomized demonstration that six sessions constituted a minimum effective dose. [TD-W002]

### How the conversation is built

How the conversation is built

The Solution Focused Brief Therapy Association's 2025 treatment manual develops the conversation itself as a sequence of listening, selecting and building. The therapist listens for the client's descriptions, selects an expression that can be developed toward the preferred future, and asks a question that builds on it. The client's words provide more than rapport. They supply the distinctions through which a change will be recognized and make the next question responsive to this person's situation. A preferred future becomes increasingly specific as the therapist asks who would notice, what they would see, and what would happen next. [TD-W003]

In the manual's mother–daughter example, a successful conversation about a science project supplies a concrete instance of better communication. The useful detail is that the mother listened without simultaneously doing something else. Following that detail reveals an interaction the participants can recognize and potentially repeat. The therapist can ask how it happened, what the daughter noticed, and what the mother did that made a difference. The exception thus supplies actions and circumstances for a goal that would otherwise remain an abstract wish to communicate better. [TD-W003]

Scaling questions develop another kind of specificity. A rating locates the client's current position relative to a desired state, after which the therapist asks what makes that position possible and what a small

<!-- PDF page 423 -->

further improvement would look like. The work lies in the descriptions attached to the numbers. Asking why the current rating is not lower can elicit resources already in use; asking what the next increment would reveal can identify an attainable difference. The scale is a conversational device for constructing and noticing change, rather than a substitute for every outcome measure. [TD-W003]

The manual's EARS sequence links eliciting a useful change, amplifying its details, reinforcing the client's contribution, and starting the process again. If the person reports no progress, coping questions can explore how they have managed to continue under difficult conditions. A report of worsening calls first for acknowledgment, followed by questions fitted to what has happened. The decision about another meeting remains joint. This later manual gives a developed account of the approach in 2025, including how its procedures adapt during an encounter, without imposing a fixed session count. [TD-W003]

### What outcome comparisons measure

What outcome comparisons measure

Wallace Gingerich and Lance Peterson's 2013 systematic qualitative review included forty-three controlled outcome studies. Thirty-two reported statistically significant favorable outcomes, ten reported favorable trends, and one reported no improvement. Their inclusion procedure accepted studies using at least one of ten identified solution-focused techniques. The resulting body of evidence therefore encompassed varied interventions, settings and comparators. A comparison with no treatment or usual services answered a different question from a comparison with another active psychotherapy. [TD-W004]

Only three studies in that review directly compared treatment duration. One comparison involved experienced therapists and trainees, making experience relevant to the interpretation of the difference. The review's broad conclusion that the approach was promising and often brief did not arise from forty-three independent dose comparisons. Nor does a nonsignificant difference between therapies establish  equivalence in the statistical sense. Reading the review by comparator and outcome makes it possible to distinguish evidence of beneficial change from evidence about the contacts required to obtain it. [TD-W004]

### Contacts, elapsed time and lasting improvement

Contacts, elapsed time and lasting improvement

The Helsinki Psychotherapy Study gives these distinctions concrete form. Paul Knekt and colleagues randomized 326 patients with mood or anxiety disorders among solution-focused therapy, short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy and long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy. The first report appeared in 2007, with the journal issue following in 2008. The solution-focused arm allowed up to twelve sessions over eight months; the short psychodynamic treatment provided twenty weekly sessions over about five to six months; the long treatment met two or three times weekly for approximately three years. These were three different treatment schedules, rather than equal-duration packages with interchangeable labels. [TD-W005]

Among those who started the assigned therapies, mean assigned contacts were 9.8, 18.5 and 232 respectively. Their mean elapsed treatment periods were 7.5, 5.7 and 31.3 months. The solution-focused treatment used fewer contacts than the short psychodynamic treatment while extending over a longer calendar interval. When auxiliary psychotherapy was included, mean total contacts rose to 29.9, 46.9 and 235. Counting only scheduled visits would have missed some of the treatment received during follow-up. [TD-W005]

The short treatments produced improvement earlier, while the long psychodynamic treatment achieved greater symptom improvement by the three-year assessment. No statistically significant difference was found between the two short therapies. The history is consequently intelligible at several scales: the pace of early relief, the number of meetings, the period over which they occurred, additional care, and

<!-- PDF page 424 -->

symptoms years later. Choosing a single one of these quantities as the meaning of “faster” would discard a substantial part of what this study measured. [TD-W005]

### A brief intervention in primary care

A brief intervention in primary care

Cooper and colleagues' 2024 primary-care trial tested three weekly solution-focused sessions lasting twenty to thirty minutes, alongside usual care. The comparison group received usual care and problem-focused assessment contacts matched in frequency and duration. The intervention was consequently  tested against more than an absence of professional attention. It was not a comparison with cognitive behavioral therapy. The brief schedule gave the researchers a defined intervention to examine, with goals and exceptions developed into actions and progress reviewed across the three weeks. [TD-W006]

Eighty people were randomized. The body of the report gives sixty-nine baseline participants and sixty-eight completing the intervention period. Mean depression scores on the PHQ-9 fell from 18.17 to 9.71 in  the solution-focused group, compared with 17.76 to 18.94 in the comparison group; anxiety and well-being measures also favored the intervention. The assessment horizon was three weeks. The trial  supports improvement under this short primary-care arrangement, while its design does not identify the fewest sessions that would have worked or establish how long the improvement persisted. [TD-W006]

### Constructing alternatives to harmful coping

Constructing alternatives to harmful coping

邹晓伟 and colleagues' 2021 analysis of solution-focused work with nonsuicidal self-injury begins with the function of a person's coping behavior. An attempt to regulate distress may pursue a comprehensible aim through a harmful means. The proposed therapeutic work recognizes the aim, explores occasions when the person coped differently, and develops safer actions that can serve a similar purpose. Preferred-future and scaling questions make the alternative specific: what would be happening at a slightly better  point, and what has already helped the person reach the present one? [TD-W007]

The authors connect conversation with practical aids such as a written repertoire of coping actions, reminders and crisis cards, together with rehearsal of alternatives. The repertoire must be available when the situation arises, rather than remaining an insight confined to the interview. This is a conceptual clinical account drawing on a limited research base, including some combined interventions. Its contribution here is the connected proposal: identify what the action is doing for the person, find an existing exception, construct an accessible substitute, and prepare to use it. [TD-W007]

### From a teacher's case knowledge to a workable response

From a teacher's case knowledge to a workable response

黒沢幸子 and colleagues' 2015 eleven-step consultation model applies solution-focused work to teachers seeking help with cases. The consultant first establishes the setting and history, then explores resources in the case, exceptions, earlier helpful and unhelpful actions, and the teacher's own capacities. The resource steps allow flexibility in order. The conversation then revisits the teacher's need, specifies a small positive goal, considers helpful actions, offers affirmative feedback, and brings in the consultant's professional proposal. The teacher's knowledge of the classroom and the consultant's expertise are both used. [TD-W008]

Closure includes an explicit test of the proposed response: does the teacher judge it feasible and useful? If either answer is unfavorable, the proposal needs alteration. This prevents the consultation from ending merely because the expert has supplied an intelligible recommendation. What the teacher can carry out in the actual setting becomes part of the construction of that recommendation. The eleven steps thus connect description, resource discovery, a revised goal and a workable next action. [TD-W008]

<!-- PDF page 425 -->

Twenty-seven teachers brought two cases each to the study, with the order of solution-focused and problem-exploration consultations randomized. Fifty-one consultations were usable for analysis, twenty-six solution-focused and twenty-five problem-exploration, all conducted by one consultant. Immediate  ratings favored the solution-focused format on such dimensions as usefulness, reduced difficulty and action planning. These were evaluations of the consultation and the teacher's readiness to act, rather than measurements of children's subsequent recovery. [TD-W008]

### The shape of the evidence

The shape of the evidence

Michele Orr, Sharlette Ryder and Julie Considine's 2026 scoping review of adult community mental-health services illustrates why the shape of a literature matters alongside its size. Twenty included papers did not represent twenty independent trials: fourteen arose from the Helsinki study. The review maps a range of applications and reports uneven specification of the intervention across studies. It directs attention to which populations and comparisons have actually been examined. Treatment benefit, efficient use of contacts, and a procedure that reliably chooses among modalities for a particular person remain distinct empirical questions. The earlier accounts of feedback and practice in S71 and S72 provide neighboring histories of change through activity and review; the therapeutic studies above retain their own interventions and outcomes. [TD-W009]

<!-- PDF page 426 -->

## S56 Shared language and collaborative memory

S56   Shared language and collaborative memory

A short expression can depend on a history of joint work. The following accounts examine how people establish a reference together, learn what another person knows, reuse local descriptions and remember an exchange. Their experiments also expose occasions when agreement, familiar wording and successful action come apart.

S41 treats language, learnability and shared repertoires; S42 develops context, interpretation and records. The sources here follow the interaction through which particular partners make an expression usable, and the consequences when participation, membership or memory changes.

### Clark and Wilkes-Gibbs: a reference is completed together

Clark and Wilkes-Gibbs: a reference is completed together

Herbert Clark and Deanna Wilkes-Gibbs's 1986 account treats referring as an activity that the speaker and listener complete together. A speaker presents a description or invites the other person to supply one. The listener can accept it, reject it or hold judgment while seeking more information. A problem can lead either person to repair the wording, add information or offer a different way of seeing the object. The resulting description is considered again. Their model follows this cycle through to mutual acceptance, including cases where an apparent acceptance is followed by another check. [CG-W025, pp. 7–9, 16–25, table 3]

The distinction among ways of changing a description matters. Adding that a person is standing up can supplement an earlier description of someone holding a book. Replacing an awkward description of an upside-down hat with a person pointing left proposes another perspective. In the recorded exchange, the original speaker subsequently uses the listener's replacement. The listener's contribution changes what both can say next. An acknowledgment can also accept the description so far while postponing a final decision about which object it identifies. [CG-W025, pp. 21–25]

Their experiment used eight pairs of students, with a screen preventing each person from seeing the other's twelve unfamiliar tangram figures. One person's ordering supplied the target; the other rearranged the cards through conversation. The same figures appeared in different orders across six trials. The experimenter identified mismatches after each trial, and the overall error rate was two percent. Transcripts recorded hesitations, interruptions, acknowledgments and repairs alongside the descriptions themselves. These features made it possible to examine how an exchange reached completion. [CG-W025, pp. 10–11, fig. 1]

The director's average word count per figure fell from about forty-one on the first trial to eight on the sixth. Speaking turns fell from 3.7 to about one. Requests for expansion and confirmation became less frequent, as did the speaker's repairs and follow-up checks. The authors explain the change through previously accepted perspectives: an elaborate description of a person skating can later support a compact reference to the ice skater. Their proposed economy concerns the work of both participants through the whole exchange. A brief initial formulation that requires extensive repair can demand more joint work than a somewhat longer one that is readily understood. [CG-W025, pp. 12–17, 21–28, figs. 2–3]

In their discussion, acceptance is judged against the purpose of the conversation. Directions intended to help someone reach a house require a different level of understanding from mentioning an address at a party. They also describe pressures that can make acceptance misleading: a listener may avoid requesting clarification to spare embarrassment, avoid offending the speaker or keep the exchange moving. The authors distinguish the participants' acceptance of an utterance from perfect comprehension, and allow an earlier acceptance to be reopened when a problem becomes apparent. [CG-W025, pp. 26, 33–35]

<!-- PDF page 427 -->

### Wegner: remembering an item and remembering where to find it

Wegner: remembering an item and remembering where to find it

Daniel Wegner's 1987 chapter develops a transactive memory system from individual memories and the communication connecting them. His distinction among an item, its label and its location explains how people can retrieve information they have not retained personally. Someone may remember the label of a needed document and who has it. Another person can therefore serve as a location for knowledge. The resulting system includes differences in what its members know, together with knowledge of those differences. [CG-W028, pp. 186–191]

Retrieval can require a transaction that changes the initial cue. Wegner describes a requester asking a colleague for information; the colleague cannot immediately supply it but remembers having given it to the requester on a previous occasion. That reminder lets the requester locate the document. The information is recovered through their combined exchange. At encoding, participants can likewise negotiate what an item should be called, who should retain it and where it will be available. These arrangements distribute responsibility as well as content. [CG-W028, pp. 190–192]

Wegner reports a study involving twenty dating couples who attempted to remember sixty-four items from different knowledge domains. Participants judged their own and their partners' relative expertise. One partner studied an item set for a minute before passing it to the other for thirty seconds, making the difference in exposure apparent to both. Recall varied with personal expertise and this circumstantial responsibility. When a person had the longer exposure, recall also depended on whether that person believed the partner possessed relevant expertise. Wegner interprets this as an individual's memory responding to what the other member of the pair is expected to remember. An inaccurate understanding of the partner's expertise can leave both relying on storage that has not occurred. [CG-W028, pp. 192– 194, table 9.1]

Labels can also change the information being retained. In Wegner's illustrative account, calling an ambiguous sighting a UFO supplies an organizing interpretation for later discussion. Recollection can come to reflect that discussion rather than the original observations. Retrieval can drift from its initial question, while bringing together separately held details can produce an interpretation that neither person initially possessed. These possibilities are part of his account of how the transactions transform information. [CG-W028, pp. 195–197]

The arrangement can be lost. When a group dissolves, a remembered location may point to a person who is no longer available. Private expressions can remain intelligible to former participants but convey little to someone outside the relationship. Wegner describes this as a loss of access and organization even when individuals retain portions of the information. [CG-W028, pp. 198–199]

### Schober and Clark: hearing an agreement and participating in it

Schober and Clark: hearing an agreement and participating in it

Michael Schober and Herbert Clark's 1989 study examined the difference between participating in such an agreement and hearing it develop. Ten pairs arranged twelve of sixteen unfamiliar figures across six trials. Forty other students later attempted the same arrangement while listening to recordings. Some heard the conversation from its beginning; others entered at the third trial. Half of each group could pause the recording. Listeners present from the beginning placed 88 percent of figures correctly, compared with 68 percent for those entering later. The original conversational partners nevertheless achieved 99 percent accuracy. Hearing every word had not supplied the same opportunity to establish what an expression meant. Pausing produced no statistically significant accuracy advantage. [CG-W009, pp. 214–220, figs. 1–3]

A second experiment addressed the possibility that recordings themselves caused the disadvantage. An overhearer now listened in the room, separated by barriers and presented as a coder so that the speakers

<!-- PDF page 428 -->

would not address that person. The principal analysis used ten triples after four exclusions, including two groups whose original matchers continued making unusual numbers of errors. Matchers achieved 98 percent accuracy and overhearers 85 percent. Including those two error-prone groups reduced matcher accuracy to 95 percent but preserved the difference. [CG-W009, pp. 222–223, fig. 4]

The difference was not simply a slower average response by overhearers. Their placements were spread much more widely around the points when the partners agreed to proceed. When overhearers placed a figure after that point, errors were more frequent. The authors' explanation concerns participation in grounding: a listener can request another description or propose a different perspective until understanding is adequate for the task. An overhearer must work with the perspective and stopping point chosen by the other two. Their experiment distinguishes access to the conversation from influence over how its references become established. [CG-W009, pp. 224–230, figs. 5–7]

### Brennan and Clark: provisional agreements with particular partners

Brennan and Clark: provisional agreements with particular partners

Susan Brennan and Herbert Clark's 1996 experiments examine what people establish when they agree on a way of referring to something. Their conceptual pact is a temporary agreement about how to conceptualize a referent. One person can propose a description, the other can question it or offer a substitute, and both can subsequently use the expression they settle on. In one recorded exchange, a listener did not recognize a proposed shoe name and initially wondered whether it named a dog. An explanation established an acceptable shoe description. In another, the listener supplied the fish identification that both subsequently used. [CG-W007, pp. 1484, 1487]

The first experiment separated this history from the information needed to distinguish an object at the present moment. Forty-eight students, working in pairs, arranged picture cards without seeing their partners' cards. An initial set contained only one shoe; another introduced competing shoes, requiring a more specific description. When the original set returned, the specific expression could remain useful as an established precedent even though a simpler term would now distinguish the target. Directors retained the same content words on that return 69 percent of the time after four trials with competitors, compared with 35 percent after one. The number of previous uses mattered, beyond simply repeating the most recent formulation. [CG-W007, pp. 1484–1487, table 2]

The pact could also change. In the second experiment, partners alternated the speaking and matching roles, and either could use an established description. Expressions became simpler, and markers of uncertainty became less frequent as an agreement developed. A third experiment introduced a different listener after four matching trials. Across fifty participants in ten continuing-partner groups and ten partner-switch groups, directors retained the previous description on the first subsequent trial 48 percent of the time with their existing partner, compared with 18 percent with a new partner. Some initially offered an elaborated version of the old description; over further trials they accommodated to the new listener. The authors describe agreements that participants can revise, rather than names fixed once and retained indefinitely. [CG-W007, pp. 1488–1492, table 5]

Their appendix preserves an informative exception. Two partners repeatedly used different terms for the same dog when their roles changed. The authors describe them as understanding each other's terms while maintaining different perspectives. Agreement sufficient to perform the task could therefore coexist with a failure to converge on one expression. [CG-W007, pp. 1492–1493, appendix]

### Mitsuda and colleagues: compare the layouts people believe they share

Mitsuda and colleagues: compare the layouts people believe they share

Koh Mitsuda, Ryuichiro Higashinaka, Yuhei Oga and Tetsuya Kinebuchi's 2021 study records a shared task as the participants negotiate and act. Each person sees a private screen containing the same collection of shapes, initially arranged differently. The pair chooses what to make through text chat and

<!-- PDF page 429 -->

moves shapes toward a common layout. The shapes can be moved but cannot be rotated, resized or deleted. The task therefore lets the researchers compare the conversation with the participants' changing arrangements, including occasions when verbal agreement and the resulting objects diverge. [CG-W026, pp. 1697–1698, fig. 1]

One pair discusses making a face, then agrees on Pinocchio. When a participant discovers that a triangle cannot be rotated, they decide to make the face tilted instead. They continue discussing the positions of its parts and eventually express satisfaction. Their final layouts nevertheless differ. A name for the intended whole and repeated assent have supported the interaction while leaving a consequential difference unresolved. [CG-W026, pp. 1698–1699, table 2, fig. 2]

The report describes a corpus of 984 dialogues involving 287 participants. To examine final outcomes, the authors developed seven layout categories and had a separate annotator classify two hundred sessions. Exact matches accounted for nineteen percent. Another six percent matched after allowing a translation of the whole layout, which the task instructions had not required participants to eliminate. Twenty-eight percent were wholly mismatched. Other outcomes included swapped shapes, a reflected arrangement and a difference in the overall scale. These categories give the researchers a way to describe what the apparent agreement had preserved and what it had left unsettled. [CG-W026, pp. 1698–1699, tables 1, 3]

They also introduce a distance based on the relationships between pairs of shapes in the two layouts. Following its changes over the conversation distinguishes arrangements that converge early, those that converge later and those that fail to converge. Inspection of unsuccessful exchanges reveals different interpretations of an oblique orientation and failures to check locations. In this preliminary analysis, common ground is made observable through the specified layout task and its operations. The researchers can compare what participants say with what they actually construct. [CG-W026, p. 1700, fig. 3]

### Naming a whole and describing its parts

Naming a whole and describing its parts

The human-dialogue analysis reported by 齋藤結, 光田航, 東中竜一郎 and 南泰浩 in 2023 examines how names enter the construction of a shared layout. Their annotation distinguishes a name for one shape, a name for several shapes forming the intended goal, and names for other groups of shapes. A separate classification describes what kind of thing the name invokes, including ordinary names already associated with the displayed shapes or building icons. This separates naming the intended whole from identifying a component. [CG-W027, pp. 1985–1986, §§2–3]

Their example begins with a proposal to arrange two circles like the wheels of a car. The other participant recognizes a truck. The conversation can then describe a quadrilateral as its passenger compartment, another part as its front and a particular orientation for those parts. The shared proposed object supplies relationships that the participants can use in subsequent instructions. Naming here participates in choosing and describing what to build. [CG-W027, p. 1985, fig. 1]

In the comparison of recorded dialogues, the first name for the overall goal appeared at a mean of 5.7 turns in successful dialogues and 8.1 turns in unsuccessful ones. The authors associate this earlier agreement with subsequent discussion of constituent parts. Their closer classification also preserves different routes. Many dialogues succeeded without naming an overall goal, using familiar names for the shapes instead. Conversely, repeated proposals for a goal in the middle of a dialogue could accompany participants talking past one another or losing track of which idea was under discussion. A goal agreed near the end could leave insufficient time for the remaining construction. The recorded examples and timing comparisons make the progression of the dialogue consequential alongside the availability of names. [CG-W027, pp. 1986–1987, §§5.1–5.2, figs. 4–5]

<!-- PDF page 430 -->

### Nault and colleagues: remembered words, remembered meaning and familiarity

Nault and colleagues: remembered words, remembered meaning and familiarity

Daniel Nault, Rohit Voleti, Matthew Nicastro and Kevin Munhall's 2023 experiments extend the referential task to delayed memory for what was said. Participants discussed images while arranging them to match a partner's screen. In a later individual test, they saw the same images and were asked to recall the most efficient descriptions used in the conversation. The images served as cues, and participants had not been told during the original interaction that their memory would later be tested. The study compares retained wording with an estimate of retained meaning. [CG-W011, Experiment 1, Procedure and Dependent Measures]

The first experiment analyzed twenty-four participants in twelve acquainted pairs; twenty-three completed the later recall task. They matched photographs of ordinary objects across two rounds, with three trials in each round and a change of roles between rounds. Delayed recall occurred seven to fourteen days later. A second experiment analyzed forty-eight participants, half in friendship pairs and half paired with a stranger, using unfamiliar faces whose visual similarity could be more systematically controlled. Recall in that experiment was supervised individually over a video call. Both experiments also included immediate recognition of previously seen images, a separate task on which performance was near ceiling. [CG-W011, Experiments 1–2, Methods and Recognition Memory]

The local common-ground measure was the director's normalized reduction in words between the first and third descriptions of an image. For later wording, the researchers measured word overlap with the final description, allowing specified spelling and word-root variants. For meaning, they used sentence-model estimates of semantic similarity between that final description and the typed recollection. These  measures let them ask whether the efficiency developed during the interaction predicted two different aspects of later recall. [CG-W011, Experiment 1, Dependent Measures]

In both experiments, greater local shortening predicted more overlap with the original words at follow-up. It did not significantly predict the estimated semantic similarity. The authors also found that shorter  final descriptions were easier to recall. They explicitly identify the need to separate that explanation from a contribution of common-ground formation itself. Their account therefore preserves an association with remembered wording while leaving the proposed relationship with richer remembered meaning unresolved. [CG-W011, Experiments 1–2, Recall Memory; Experiment 1, n. 1]

An additional control addressed a basic difficulty with image-cued recall. A picture can elicit similar words from people who never discussed it together. Twelve additional participants in each experiment described the images without the preceding conversation. The recalled descriptions from conversational participants overlapped their own original interaction more strongly than these independently generated descriptions did. The authors used that comparison as evidence for conversation-specific recollection, while recognizing that some raw overlap came from the images themselves. [CG-W011, Experiments 1–2, Control Experiment]

Friendship supplied a different pattern from local shortening. Friends described the faces with fewer words overall, but their descriptions did not shorten at a significantly different rate from those of strangers. They also showed no significant recall advantage in the principal mixed-model analyses. Secondary analyses that considered average description lengths favored strangers. The authors distinguish efficiency associated with prior familiarity from the change achieved during the task. They also argue that constrained picture descriptions may give a poor view of the richer semantic memories formed in ordinary conversation. Their results leave room for that further investigation while retaining the observed difference between concise communication and later recall. [CG-W011, Experiment 2, Description Lengths and Recall Memory; General Discussion]
