## S60 External memory and continuity of work

S60   External memory and continuity of work

How can someone continue an enquiry, a design or a collective undertaking after an interruption, or after the people who began it have left? A finished document may preserve the answer while losing the route to it. Meeting minutes may preserve the conversation while scattering one decision across many files. A conclusion may remain in a collection after the reasons for accepting it have changed. Historical approaches to external memory addressed these problems by changing what was recorded and how a later participant could work with it.

Records and archival context are treated in S42; collaborative remembering and knowing who knows what are treated in S56. The accounts here develop external working structures, recorded deliberation, the retrieval of project experience and the maintenance of a changing position. Their concrete objects range from a trail through documents to a design-review history and a program's reasons for believing a proposition.

### Bush and the preservation of an enquiry

Bush and the preservation of an enquiry

Vannevar Bush's As We May Think (1945) proposed the memex, a personal apparatus holding books, records and communications on microfilm. A user could bring material onto viewing screens, add notes and retrieve an item by its code. Bush's distinctive operation was associative indexing: connecting items so that calling up one could lead directly to another. Ordinary classification placed an item under a heading; a trail recorded a particular route through material that might belong to many different classifications. The same item could participate in several trails. [CM-W001, §§6–8]

The construction of a trail was itself intellectual work. Bush described a reader investigating bows and arrows, moving from an encyclopedia to historical accounts and material about the properties of wood and other materials. The example illustrated an enquiry, rather than a search for one already formulated answer. The reader selected passages, linked them, added comments and inserted an analysis of his own. A trail could branch into a subsidiary line of investigation and then return to the main route. Its organization recorded connections that the reader had found useful, including connections that no cataloguer would have anticipated.

Bush made continuation tangible by returning to this reader years later. A conversation revived the old interest. Instead of reconstructing the investigation from memory, the reader called up the trail and followed its steps. He could reproduce the trail and give it to his friend, who could insert it into another memex and connect it to further material. What travelled was consequently more than a list of references: it included the sequence of consultation and the reader's annotations. Another person could examine the path, depart from it or extend it.

The memex was a proposal, and Bush described its mechanisms through projected uses. Within that proposal, however, the preservation of unfinished intellectual work was quite explicit. He envisaged the inheritance of the scaffolding of an enquiry as well as its completed products. A private working path could become a usable contribution to someone else's work without first being rewritten as a conventional publication.

### Engelbart and a working structure that can be revisited

Engelbart and a working structure that can be revisited

Douglas C. Engelbart's Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework (1962) considered the person together with language, artifacts, methods and training. His concern was the organization of the activities through which someone understood a problem and developed a solution. External symbols belonged inside that activity: rearranging them could change what the participant could see, compare and

<!-- PDF page 432 -->

attempt next. A finished report was one possible product of a more extensive working structure. [CM-W002, Introduction; II.A; III.A–B]

Engelbart's own experiment with cards gave this distinction practical detail. He placed relatively small units of thought on separate cards, including source references and page numbers where appropriate, and used descriptors to help sort them. While preparing a memorandum he distinguished material concerning its specifications, its organization and its content. Within these groups he kept considerations, tentative possibilities and currently accepted product statements. A reader of the eventual memorandum would see the resulting exposition; the writer's working collection also contained the questions, alternatives and reasons through which that exposition had been developed.

One difficulty appeared when a product statement changed. A new consideration might suggest a revision, but the author might no longer remember why the earlier wording had been adopted. Being able to recover the other considerations linked to that statement would help him assess the revision. Engelbart also wanted to try several organizations of the same statements without making several copies of every card. Recorded associative trails could preserve these trial organizations so that an earlier structure could be reconstructed when needed. His card experiment exposed both the usefulness of these relations and the difficulty of managing them with the equipment available to him.

The report's computer-supported demonstration developed these possibilities through the imaginary worker Joe. Statements could be linked into an argument rather than confined to one linear sequence. A participant could inspect supporting reasoning, follow implications or change the view of a structure without rewriting all its contents. When an investigation had to be put aside, its assumptions, objectives, attempts and intermediate results could be left in an organized form. Later information or a new technique could then provide an occasion to revisit it. The retained structure gave the returning worker a place from which to proceed.

Engelbart extended this demonstration to collaboration. Several participants could examine a common working structure, explore alternatives and attach objections where they applied. Their separate contributions could enter the shared reasoning at the relevant statement, rather than waiting for a final report to circulate. These were capabilities illustrated in his proposed augmentation environment. The account made the coordination of tools and working methods central: storing symbols was useful because participants could manipulate their relationships while reasoning, revising and communicating.

### Doyle and conclusions whose support changes

Doyle and conclusions whose support changes

Jon Doyle's A Truth Maintenance System (1979) addressed continuity inside a reasoning program. A program could derive conclusions from assumptions and then encounter information requiring an assumption to change. Simply adding the new information left an important question unanswered: which earlier conclusions should still govern the program's reasoning? Doyle recorded reasons for potential beliefs and used their dependencies to maintain the current set. [CM-W003, §§1–2.1, 3.2, 4]

The system represented a potential belief by a node. A node could have several justifications. In a support-list justification, one list contained nodes that had to be currently believed and another contained nodes that had to be outside the current set of beliefs. This second list allowed a default to depend on the absence of a defeating belief. A node was in when it had an acceptable supporting justification and out when it did not. Doyle explicitly distinguished these statuses from true and false: they described the program's present support for a belief.

His scheduling example showed the operation. A program tentatively placed a meeting on Wednesday because it had no reason to reject that day. A rule connected Wednesday with a meeting time of 1 p.m. New scheduling information then supplied a reason against Wednesday. The system could trace the dependencies: the Wednesday assumption lost its support, and the conclusion about 1 p.m. lost the

<!-- PDF page 433 -->

support it had obtained from that assumption. The statements and their justifications remained represented, while their current status changed. A later change in the defeating reason could permit an assumption to become current again.

The maintenance procedure examined the changed node and its repercussions, seeking well-founded support rather than allowing beliefs to sustain one another through a circular argument. The problem-solving program supplied the statements, inference steps and declarations of contradiction; the  maintenance system operated on the recorded justification relationships. A node could stay in if another valid justification survived the loss of one route of support. Thus a change did not require indiscriminately discarding everything recorded after an earlier choice.

Doyle also described dependency-directed backtracking. When a contradiction was marked, the procedure traced its supporting argument to the assumptions involved. It recorded the incompatible combination as a nogood and revised an assumption with a reason tied to that incompatibility. In a second meeting example, a proposed time and room conflicted with an existing booking. Trying another room preserved the time preference until another contradiction required the time itself to change. The retained nogood helped the program avoid simply returning to the rejected combination. The example explained a revision mechanism; the implementation's arbitrary selection of an assumption to reject did not establish a generally good policy for choosing among revisions.

### Conklin and Begeman on recording deliberation

Conklin and Begeman on recording deliberation

Jeff Conklin and Michael L. Begeman's gIBIS system (1988) organized design discussion around issues, positions and arguments. An issue posed a question; a position proposed a response; arguments supported or objected to a position. Other links connected related questions and proposals. The arrangement preserved rejected possibilities and the reasons discussed around them, alongside proposals that participants continued to support. It offered a later reader an entry into the deliberation behind a design. [CM-W004, §§2–3, 5.1–5.7]

The interface combined a graph browser, a structured index and a window displaying the selected item's contents. Selecting an issue allowed the user to create a responding position with the appropriate link already established. Selecting a position made supporting or objecting arguments available as subsequent operations. These typed operations gave a contribution a place in the discussion as it was written. Nodes also carried attributes such as author and subject. Queries could retrieve, for example, nodes by a particular author, after a date and containing specified text, while showing the matches in the graph and index.

For a reader entering an unfamiliar network, gIBIS distinguished a node's primary connection from additional links. Hiding the additional links produced a simpler hierarchy. A NEXT operation followed the corresponding sequence in the structured index, while the graph showed where the current item belonged. Further passes could expose the cross-connections. Aggregation could also combine an issue, its positions and arguments into a larger unit. These facilities addressed a specific reading problem: a network could retain many relations while still providing a manageable first route through them.

The authors reported use by 32 people creating 33 issue groups; by February 1988 the collection contained 2,091 nodes. Some groups were largely individual workspaces, while others supported structured communication. Users reported that the framework helped them notice incomplete reasoning and make assumptions explicit. The authors also observed cases in which readers understood individual nodes but could not follow the larger line of thought. Their discussion connected this fragmentation to hurried, minimal entries and to the loss of the unfolding context supplied by continuous prose. Preserving discrete contributions and preserving an intelligible argument were distinguishable accomplishments within the same working system.

<!-- PDF page 434 -->

Issue resolution required its own representation. An issue-position-argument network could expose the alternatives without indicating which position a group had adopted. A recently added facility marked an aggregated discussion as resolved and recorded which position had been selected. Conklin and Begeman further noted that a resolution might need an explanation beyond a flag: it could combine earlier options or abandon an assumption they had shared. This observation concerned the meaning of a decision record. The selected position, its rationale and the discussion preceding it were related records with different jobs.

### Ackerman and a memory that grows through questions

Ackerman and a memory that grows through questions

Mark S. Ackerman's Answer Garden field study (1994) examined a different route into organizational memory. A user first navigated a diagnostic question tree to seek a stored answer. When the database could not answer the question, the system could forward it to a suitable human expert. The reply returned to the user, and an expert could add a commonly needed answer to the database. Repeated enquiries could therefore leave a record available to later users, while the system continued to provide access to people. [CM-W005]

The field-study version anonymized questions to reduce the social cost of exposing a gap in one's knowledge. Its initial database contained 98 nodes covering roughly 225 questions and answers about the X Window System. The study involved software engineers in a research group and a university extension setting over three months. Of 59 potential users, 35 used the system, accounting for 194 sessions. A little over half the sessions resulted in mail being sent. The stored collection and the expert route were both active parts of the service.

Ackerman combined usage records with interviews about particular incidents. Users valued finding an answer promptly and finding out promptly whether the database contained one. They also came to treat access to the human network as a natural part of the system. Experts answered questions and the database grew. An unanswered question was consequently useful input into the development of the memory: it could reveal an omission and bring an expert's response into a reusable form.

The study also explained why the form of that response mattered. Some experts saw their answers as a public representation of their professional competence and wrote formal, general explanations. Some users wanted a shorter answer suited to their immediate level of understanding. An answer could be technically sound yet poorly matched to the particular enquiry. Users' reluctance to bother experts also persisted in some interactions. Ackerman distinguished possible concerns about professional authority and about calling on volunteer labour, rather than assuming that anonymity had removed every social feature of asking for help.

Answer Garden's achieved combination was specific: it connected a searchable body of answers with an expertise network and allowed new questions to enlarge the recorded material. The three-month field study observed this combination in use.

### Matta and colleagues on project experience and design reasons

Matta and colleagues on project experience and design reasons

Nada Matta, Myriam Ribière and Olivier Corby's Définition d'un modèle de mémoire de projet (1999) proposed a model for making design-project experience accessible to future designers. It organized the memory into project characteristics and problem resolution. The first part described the setting in which work had occurred: requirements and constraints, methods, tasks, participants and roles, and results such as prototypes, software, tests and technical documents. A later designer could examine these characteristics when deciding whether earlier experience was relevant. [CM-W006, pp. 13–27]

<!-- PDF page 435 -->

The problem-resolution part retained the choices made during design. For a problem it recorded participants, methods, candidate solutions, rejected solutions and the arguments for rejecting them, as well as the selected solution and the arguments attached to it. The distinction between results and their rationale was operational. Finding an earlier product could suggest a solution; finding why one candidate had been rejected could explain why an apparently attractive alternative had not been pursued. The model linked such descriptions to project resources in their existing forms.

The authors described two access scenarios. A designer could start with the task currently being performed, retrieve comparable earlier projects and inspect their context, organization and results. Alternatively, the designer could start with a type of problem and retrieve earlier instances, then examine the methods and options considered in those instances. The two routes supplied different ways into the same project experience. Neither required a future user to know in advance the filename or chronological location of the relevant record.

The report presented an initial validation with industrial collaborators and access scenarios for the model; implementation support using intranet techniques and XML was planned. Its developed contribution was the organization of project experience around the later designer's activity and immediate need. The project description supplied context for judging relevance, while the problem account made the reasoning around alternatives accessible with the result.

### Kudo on retrieving a decision across successive reviews

Kudo on retrieving a decision across successive reviews

In his 2011 dissertation on knowledge use in information-system development and operation, Yutaka Kudo developed an account of a design-review management system built around meeting minutes. A single meeting could address many design items, while one item could recur in several meetings. Keeping one file per meeting preserved the meetings but dispersed the history of a design item. The system retained the familiar minute-taking practice while adding a way to retrieve that history directly. [CM-W007, Chapter 2]

The record format supplied the connection. Discussion headings corresponded to items in the review plan; each item paired a conclusion with its reason; reviewed design documents could be attached. The database separated project, meeting, discussion-item, attendee and related-document records. Heading numbers and heading text were stored separately so that the same design topic could be matched across minutes. The resulting relationships supported both an overview of review coverage and a detailed enquiry into a particular decision.

The cross-meeting search extracted the relevant conclusions and reasons and displayed them in date order, together with the meeting titles and participants. A link opened the full source minutes when the reader needed the surrounding discussion. Kudo's example followed changes to a client's computer specification. The display brought successive specifications together with the reasons for them, including a change in what processing the client needed to perform. The reader could see the development of the decision without opening each meeting file merely to locate its relevant paragraph.

The coverage view counted reviews of each design item and participation by responsible people or knowledgeable participants. It also provided a separate manager-approval field. A project manager could mark an item as sufficiently reviewed, with the system recording the approver and time. The display therefore distinguished the existence of recorded discussions from a manager's judgment that the review was complete. Kudo reported a practice of bringing the retrieved history into the next meeting so that participants could begin with the earlier conclusions and reasons in view.

The system entered service in August 1999. Kudo reported that by June 2011 it held 100,724 minutes for 2,469 projects across six divisions. These counts documented sustained operational use. His evaluation also compared the work of locating a topic's history in a project with 350 minute records. The manual

<!-- PDF page 436 -->

estimate was 130 seconds, based on opening 13 matching files at ten seconds each; the system's retrieval and ordered display took under four seconds. The comparison excluded reading and understanding the discussion. It measured the assembly of the relevant history for inspection, a distinct operation the system made much quicker.

In this account, the review heading carried a design concern across meetings, while conclusions, reasons and source links made its development inspectable. Participants could consult the assembled sequence instead of depending on their own recollection. The record remained connected to the meetings and people from which it came, and the team could resume its discussion with that history already assembled.

## S105 Forgetting, discarding and revising retained knowledge

S105   Forgetting, discarding and revising retained knowledge

### Recall after an instruction to forget

Recall after an instruction to forget

Robert Bjork’s 1972 chapter distinguishes instructions given during a sequence, after a set, or item by item. In the latter arrangement the cue can coincide with presentation or follow it. He separates two questions about the effect of such a cue. One concerns how much of the material designated for remembering is subsequently recalled. The other concerns how much of the material designated for forgetting remains accessible on recall or recognition tests. An instruction can reduce interference with what is to be remembered while leaving some of the other material accessible. [T07-W001]

Kluge and Gronau examine retrieval cues in organizations. Their proposal concerns an old routine that still comes to mind because familiar tools, records or circumstances cue it. Changing those cues while introducing conditions for the new routine is a way to change which practice is prompted in everyday work. [T07-W002]

### Written procedures and work that people continue to do

Written procedures and work that people continue to do

Martin de Holan and Phillips studied seven Cuban hotels through visits, documents and 78 interviews. Five hotels were associated with alliances and two were comparison properties. The authors distinguish failure to retain a new practice, decay of an established practice, and deliberately abandoning an adopted arrangement. Their Withwind account describes manuals and training specifying new procedures while managers repeatedly intervened to keep everyday practice aligned with them. The manager’s example of kitchen staff substituting ingredients illustrates how an old way of working could remain available. [T07-W003]

At Caribbean Hotel, management adopted another hotel’s structure and introduced corresponding operating and communication procedures. The manager reported that procedures went unused unless checked by the same level that had imposed them. Meetings were taking time without solving the problems. The organization changed its structure and routines. The authors discuss this as abandonment of an innovation. Their separate comparison of food and beverage costs per guest in three hotels concerns deterioration of an established practice. They relate it to turnover and dependence on supervision. Those hotels were the subset that could supply complete cost records. [T07-W003]

### Withdrawing support

Withdrawing support

The truth-maintenance system described in S60 concerns another kind of retention. Doyle’s 1979 memo explains how the current support for a proposition can change while the stored statement and its reasons remain available. The system can withdraw a conclusion without losing the record needed to reconsider it. The object being revised is the current set of supported conclusions. [CM-W003]

<!-- PDF page 438 -->

### Part 8 Inquiry, invention, and collective action

Part 8   Inquiry, invention, and collective action

These accounts examine how people frame problems, develop possibilities, create and perform work, and coordinate through shared practices or traces of earlier action.

## S44 Problem structuring, design and systems methods

S44   Problem structuring, design and systems methods

### Framing problems and organizing inquiry

Framing problems and organizing inquiry

The sources here propose ways to frame problems, make models, organize discussion, design arrangements and examine consequences. Some sources contain their own extensive methodological syntheses.

### Checkland: use declared activity models to question a situation

Checkland: use declared activity models to question a situation

Checkland's plenary summary describes the development of Soft Systems Methodology through action research in management situations. Its contrast is with a systems-engineering approach that takes objectives as given and systematically compares means. In the situations he describes, people act purposefully but do not necessarily share one objective or interpretation. SSM becomes a learning system rather than a procedure for optimizing an already agreed task. [SG-W001, sections I–VII]

Its purposeful-activity models are built according to declared worldviews. Several models can structure debate about a messy situation, helping people find accommodations that permit action. A model is therefore not simply asserted to be the uniquely true system hidden in the world. Connecting an activity model to information support asks what people would need to know to carry out that activity.

Checkland's 1999 retrospective summarizes his methodological development. [SG-W001]

### Ulrich: the boundary determines which facts and values count

Ulrich: the boundary determines which facts and values count

Ulrich's mini-primer defines boundary critique as examining the judgments that make some observations and values relevant while excluding or subordinating others. Its twelve-question framework, also developed in the Ulrich–Reynolds chapter, distinguishes sources of motivation, control, knowledge and legitimacy. It asks about an actual arrangement and what ought to be the case, including the difference between people involved in a decision and people affected by it. [SG-W002]

The contribution is not a command to include everything. It is a way to make the selection discussable and expose a claim that disguises its boundary as necessary or neutral. Relevant expertise does not remove normative choices, while a person affected by a choice can question those choices without possessing all of an expert's knowledge. The primer presents this as useful in cooperative inquiry and in critical challenges where agreement is absent.

The source explicitly does not offer a self-contained method that settles every issue. [SG-W002]

### Vickers: appreciation includes standards of fact and value

Vickers: appreciation includes standards of fact and value

Hudson's notes reconstruct Checkland's account of Vickers's appreciative systems. In this account, people respond to events and ideas through standards of fact and value, selecting what seems relevant and judging what relationships to maintain or change. Action can modify the situation, while experience can modify the standards through which later situations are interpreted. A situation is not first perceived without any selection and only afterward assigned a value. [SG-W010, text]

Hudson draws on Checkland's notes on Vickers, adding his own explanation.

The separate 1978 interview transcript supplies Vickers's own short discussion of people as agents and observers. It situates systems inquiry in the relationships people participate in, rather than only a detached description. [SG-W012]

<!-- PDF page 440 -->

### Shchedrovitsky: distinguish thinking, communication and practical action

Shchedrovitsky: distinguish thinking, communication and practical action

The chapter by Georgy Petrovich Shchedrovitsky presents a thought-activity schema with three relatively autonomous belts. Practical collective thought-action concerns what people do together; thought-communication is the polyphonic exchange through which positions and meanings are articulated;  schematic thinking works with organized representations. Understanding and reflection connect the belts. They are not three interchangeable names for the same process. [WME-W019, chapter and schemes]

The account of the 1980 game involving Meerovich makes this distinction concrete. A participant could share communication and collective action with other architects while insisting that his individual thinking differed. Separate boards made that difference visible. A common conversation is not evidence that all participants possess the same conceptual content. The scheme preserves individual and group representations rather than imposing identity by drawing one group box.

A schematic sign can retain a long chain of intellectual operations, but it still needs interpretation. The chapter describes reconstructing meaning, making it explicit through material boards or paper and learning the conventions through which a scheme can be used. Concision at the level of a diagram does not eliminate the history or competence needed to understand it.

The middle communication belt can accommodate conflict, questioning and multiple positions in a way different from formally checking a symbolic derivation. The author's concern is the work of problematization and coordination among heterogeneous practices. He also warns about isolating a belt: formal thought can become detached symbols, communication empty talk, and action mere repetition. These are his methodological evaluations. [WME-W019]

The organizational-activity game supplies a proposed operating process. Facilitated encounters expose incompatible practices, create opportunities for reflection, develop new schemes and lead toward programmes that participants enact and revise. It retains organizers, participant effort, conflict over days, shared material representations, learned norms, goal setting, testing and later institutionalization.

The chapter's conclusion also limits what its schema represents. It is an ideal theoretical basis for deriving models, rather than a model of one concrete real system. Its synthesis of thinking, communication and action is the author's philosophical and methodological proposal. The article was first published in the 1986 yearbook issued in 1987 and reprinted in Избранные трудыin 1995. [WME-W019]

Pyotr Shchedrovitsky's later thought-activity-ontology account develops a distinct formulation from Georgy Shchedrovitsky's original essay. [SG-W024]

### Midgley and Lindhult: systemic innovation includes inquiry into purpose

Midgley and Lindhult: systemic innovation includes inquiry into purpose

Midgley and Lindhult's article distinguishes several uses of systemic innovation: complementary technologies, enabling governance, sustainability transitions, collaborative value networks and systemic thinking-and-action practice. The authors favor the last as a way to engage with the others. This is their conceptual synthesis. [WME-W020, article, sections 1–8]

Their account relates boundaries, purposes and values in both directions. Values affect whom and what a study considers; established boundaries can also constrain which values count as legitimate. A system can be used as a tool for thinking without denying that the world has material consequences beyond the model. The authors' assumptions about interconnectedness, partial knowledge and action's consequences are philosophical starting points, not proved equations that determine every ethical judgment.

<!-- PDF page 441 -->

The critique applies to expertise and participation alike. Expert modeling can impose a client's purposes without examining affected interests. Participation can preserve bias, coercion, deception or groupthink. Dialogue is therefore not a sufficient condition of good outcomes. The article examines conflict, stereotypes, marginalization and the possibility that a ritual of participation conceals exclusion. [WME-W020]

The figures help articulate these relations: differing concerns, overlapping boundaries, conflict shaped by stereotypes and nested boundaries that marginalize people or issues. They are conceptual diagrams, not calibrated causal models. Broadening a boundary can also exceed available resources or collide with wider institutions.

Their examples include reframing in a water company, an imposed supplier-margin reduction followed by failure, and the marginalization of an innovation unit. These are author-reported vignettes. They illustrate why an apparently local improvement can fail within wider relations.

The article changes methodological questions across values, resource and risk distribution, delivery, scaling and governance, with a return to purpose when needed. It does not provide a universal algorithm for selecting the correct method. Internal expertise can sometimes replace an outside facilitator, while facilitation and knowledge work remain. The authors explicitly acknowledge no guarantee of success, call for evaluation and retain adaptation to context. [WME-W020]

### Ackoff: idealized design, realization and decision rules

Ackoff: idealized design, realization and decision rules

Ackoff's guide distinguishes removing disliked deficiencies from designing a desired future. Its idealized design is not a claim to create a perfect organization unconstrained by reality. The guide separates idealization from means, resources, implementation and controls, and asks how a design can learn and improve. Eliminating an unwanted condition need not produce the desired one. [SG-W040, guide]

The organizational questions make retained responsibilities visible: which services to provide internally or acquire, how to assure quality, how to change facilities and staffing, and how to respond when the situation changes. A stated ideal is therefore an input to further work rather than a complete plan of construction.

Its final decision procedure is especially important. Practical agreement can permit action without agreement on every principle. If participants cannot agree on alternatives, the guide first proposes a test they agree to accept. If a test cannot be agreed or completed in time, the responsible manager declares a position. Agreement among the other participants can override that position; if they fail to agree, the manager's position enters the design. Authority remains in the procedure. [SG-W040, final decision pages]

The guide also seeks comments from stakeholders not involved in preparation and asks for explanations when suggestions are not incorporated. These are prescriptive procedures.

### Inquiring organizations: different ways of warranting a claim

Inquiring organizations: different ways of warranting a claim

Courtney, Croasdell and Paradice reconstruct Churchman's five inquirers and apply them to learning organizations. The Leibnizian account relies on derivation from axioms; the Lockean emphasizes observation and agreement; the Kantian combines models with data; the Hegelian develops knowledge through opposed interpretations; the Singerian treats measures and the inquiry arrangement as revisable. The different guarantors are the point of the comparison, rather than five names for a universally reliable search. [SG-W039, selected main review and table]

<!-- PDF page 442 -->

In the Singerian discussion, persistent disagreement can motivate sweeping in new variables or revising measures. That expands the inquiry rather than forcing agreement under a fixed representation. Yet the authors explicitly warn that a community's knowledge generation can drift toward its own illusion without monitoring. Their IT-support discussion retains debate, justification and checks on inquiry.

Courtney and colleagues reconstruct and apply Churchman's inquiring-systems account. [SG-W039]

### Gigamapping, SODA and Interactive Management

Gigamapping, SODA and Interactive Management

Sevaldson's Gigamapping account proposes rich, large mappings to explore complex relations across disciplinary boundaries. Creating the map is a way to investigate and communicate. [SG-W016, selected account]

Ackermann and Eden's selected SODA opening uses cognitive mapping to represent participants' construals and means–ends relationships. The central example helps organize an issue through connected concepts. A link records an understood relation in the inquiry; it is not thereby a demonstrated causal law. Map construction, merging, facilitation and political feasibility remain part of the method. [SG-W051]

The Warfield archive's Interactive Management exhibit is more concrete about the support arrangement. Sessions can require several days from selected participants, trained facilitators, a room with extensive display space and computational support. Structured questions and consensus methods organize contributions. The sponsoring organization helps identify the participants, so a room designed to hear every voice does not itself determine whose voice was invited. [SG-W060, main exhibit]

The Warfield archive reconstructs a structured group-inquiry process. Facilitators help participants develop and organize their judgments into a problem representation.

### Meadows: leverage depends on the structure and purpose

Meadows: leverage depends on the structure and purpose

Meadows's essay distinguishes parameters from stocks, flows, delays, feedback, information, rules, self-organization, goals and paradigms. The stock–flow explanation makes a useful initial point: a stock  changes through rates of inflow and outflow, and an intervention's timing can matter as much as an isolated numerical setting. The essay's ranking is a heuristic account of leverage, not a universal theorem. [W107, selected printed pp. 1–6 and 12–18]

Information-flow changes can expose consequences that actors previously did not see, while rules govern incentives and permitted action. The examples are reported anecdotes or interpretations. Changing a parameter is not always weak: the essay itself contains qualifications to that kind of ranking.

The selected goal and paradigm passages concern changing what a system is organized to do and the beliefs through which it is interpreted. Such a change may be consequential, but it changes the comparison. A new purpose cannot be counted as supplying the same outcome with fewer resources unless that equivalence is separately established. [W107]

The selected introduction and table of Crielaard and colleagues' 2026 review of twenty-nine studies discuss systems archetypes in public-health applications. Recurring feedback patterns can help formulate a hypothesis about a problem, but a causal-loop diagram does not itself validate an intervention. [W106]

### Schwarz: a three-plane metamodel and six cycles

Schwarz: a three-plane metamodel and six cycles

Schwarz's 2005 formulation proposes a metamodel with physical, information and existential planes, associated with objects, relations and wholes. It distinguishes cycles supplying persistence—material circulation, homeostasis and self-reference—from morphogenesis, autopoiesis and autogenesis as change

<!-- PDF page 443 -->

processes. The metamodel organizes his proposed interpretation of viable systems and informs his intervention discussion. [SG-W003, central diagram and dynamics, PDF pp. 5–9]

Schwarz offers an authorial synthesis with ontological commitments. Its necessity across physical, biological, social and cognitive systems is asserted rather than established through comparative tests. [SG-W003]

### Suh: functional independence and probability of success

Suh: functional independence and probability of success

Suh's chapter introduces functional requirements, design parameters and process variables in distinct domains. Its independence axiom concerns satisfying the selected functional requirements without undesired coupling. Some designs can preserve independence directly, while others require a sequence that avoids interactions. The account concerns the relation among stated requirements and the parameters used to realize them. [SG-W052, chapter discussion of domains and design axioms]

The information axiom evaluates success using a probability-based information content. That quantity is not automatically knowledge possessed by an actor, sensing demand or total lifecycle cost. Functional independence is also different from statistical independence: multiplying probabilities requires assumptions about their joint relation.

Suh’s chapter introduces the axiomatic-design approach associated with his 1990 The Principles of Design. [W037, through SG-W052]

### Altshuller and Shapiro, and a later QFD–function-analysis–TRIZ proposal

Altshuller and Shapiro, and a later QFD–function-analysis–TRIZ proposal

The selected 1956 article organizes inventive work through analytic and operative stages, examining a technical difficulty and seeking changes or transfers that can overcome it. Its examples and stated limits provide an account of organizing search rather than treating invention as an unexplained inspiration. Later formulas of TRIZ ideality are not retroactively attributed to this early article. [W022, analytic and operative stages]

León-Rovira and Aguayo's later proposed integration assigns different tasks to QFD, function analysis and TRIZ. QFD helps identify what customers want and how existing functions relate to those wants; the authors explicitly say it is not a problem-solving tool. Mapping the relationships is nontrivial and requires experienced designers. The proposal therefore retains expertise inside a structured method. [SG-W057, integration of QFD, function analysis and TRIZ]

Their account reports problems when a team tries to define new functional parameters before establishing the existing relationships. The ideality expression combining benefits, costs and harms is a heuristic, not a universal commensurate measure. A ratio cannot establish comparable quantities or remove a conflicting requirement simply by being written down. The source's tool boundaries and reported inappropriate use matter as much as its promised integration.

### Theory of Constraints: a bottleneck can move

Theory of Constraints: a bottleneck can move

The practitioner account presents five focusing steps: identify a constraint, exploit it, subordinate other activity, elevate it and repeat when the constraint changes. The method asks why improving a nonbinding part may fail to improve overall throughput, and why relieving one constraint can make another important. Buffers and the distinction between investment and operating expense are part of the account. [SG-W019, five focusing steps and accounting distinctions]

<!-- PDF page 444 -->

Single-constraint rules have difficulties in product-mix problems with multiple constraints; ratio heuristics can then give misleading priorities. [SG-W019, practitioner account and abstract-level counterpoint]

### Robust Decision Making: inspect vulnerabilities across possible futures

Robust Decision Making: inspect vulnerabilities across possible futures

RAND's account describes an iterative process of decision framing, evaluating strategies across futures, vulnerability analysis, tradeoff analysis and developing new futures or strategies. It seeks strategies that perform acceptably across a range rather than relying on one predicted future. A vulnerability summary can help stakeholders understand where a strategy fails. [SG-W031, main body and FAQ]

The futures are simulations, not automatically probabilities. Model construction, computation, storage, training and stakeholder judgments remain.

The EPTA method orientation addresses technology assessment through examination of consequences and options in relation to public decision making. The Collingridge dilemma concerns limited early knowledge versus costly later change. Constructive assessment is a response to that difficulty, not a guarantee that anticipatory knowledge can be made complete. [SG-W030]

### Dori, DSRP, grey prediction and Extenics: representations with stated limits

Dori, DSRP, grey prediction and Extenics: representations with stated limits

Dori's selected Object-Process Methodology opening relates structure and behavior in a common representation. Its bread-baking example connects objects, states and transforming processes rather than leaving a static parts list separate from action. Representational coherence can help an inquiry, but does not ensure that the model corresponds to the world. [SG-W058]

Cabrera and Cabrera's selected DSRP primer organizes questions through distinctions, systems, relationships and perspectives. These operations supply a vocabulary for making a model explicit and examining its implications. The primer advances universal claims and strong comparisons with other approaches. Its proposed ratio between model and reality does not specify operational resource quantities. [SG-W041]

Yang and colleagues' selected grey-prediction account uses satellite observations of vegetation recovery after a landslide. Classification and observation feed a particular modeling method with its own assumptions. [SG-W048]

Cai, Yang and He's publisher abstract describes Extenics as formalizing and transforming descriptions of contradictions or incompatible requirements. The application discussion develops this orientation. Changing a goal or constraint is different from satisfying the original task. [SG-W050, abstract and application discussion]

### Brand: different rates of change can retain different functions

Brand: different rates of change can retain different functions

Brand's selected pace-layering essay proposes that faster-changing layers explore or respond while slower layers preserve continuity and impose constraints. Their interaction, rather than uniform speed, is the explanatory idea. The forest and social-layer examples are conceptual illustrations, not proof that every durable system has one fixed hierarchy. [SG-W059, pace-layering discussion]

Slow structures can also obstruct needed change, and fast or slow does not constitute a moral ranking. The proposal supplies a way to ask about timing and retained memory.

<!-- PDF page 445 -->

### Purposes, expertise and the organization of inquiry

Purposes, expertise and the organization of inquiry

The sources explain substantial operations: making a boundary explicit, separating kinds of activity, modeling a requirement, inviting criticism, guiding a search or comparing a strategy across futures. They also retain the people and institutions that choose purposes, supply expertise, facilitate disagreement, build representations and test consequences.

<!-- PDF page 446 -->

## S63 Systematic accounts of methods for generating ideas

S63   Systematic accounts of methods for generating ideas

Accounts of creativity methods organize different kinds of knowledge. Some compare named techniques, some examine their instructions and some relate procedures to stages of innovation or conditions of use. A method may specify both an operation on ideas and an arrangement of participants, time and materials. The accounts below make those parts available for study and show several ways authors have classified them.

### Kirjavainen and Hölttä-Otto and the parts of a method

Kirjavainen and Hölttä-Otto and the parts of a method

Senni Kirjavainen and Katja Hölttä-Otto analyse the instructions of eighty-eight documented idea-generation methods. They identify twenty-five mechanisms used as coding categories and distinguish  implementation mechanisms from idea-promoting mechanisms. The first group concerns how an activity is organized; the second concerns sources of ideas and operations during generation. Several mechanisms can occur in one method, and the same mechanism can recur under different method names. [CRE-W001, §§3.3–4.2, tables 1–3]

Their examples begin with actual instructions. Asking participants to draw possible solutions specifies a visual modality. Providing a card with an action prompt can supply stimulation and invite modification of an existing idea. Asking for many possibilities specifies a quantity aim. These are separable features even when one exercise includes all of them. A method's name does not by itself reveal the combination. [CRE-W001, table 1]

The idea-promoting categories include analogy, association, building on other people's contributions, incubation and stimulation. They also include operations such as combining, modifying, framing, classifying, evaluating and selecting ideas. Analogy and association have different definitions in the coding: one concerns a pertinent relationship between domains, while the other can follow a word, image or idea without requiring that relationship. Suspending judgment appears as one component within this larger account. [CRE-W001, table 3]

The implementation categories distinguish individual and team participation, given or open duration, written and spoken expression, physical activity, visualization and thought. Facilitation and special tools are also recorded. A method designed for a team can contain individual phases. The arrangement of participation is therefore more specific than simply calling an exercise collective. [CRE-W001, table 2]

The authors refine their categories through coding and comparison. A second coder examines fifteen percent of the instructions, disagreements lead to revised guidance and the definitions are used in the remaining analysis. Their framework gives a way to inspect and compare the operations present in documented methods. It also makes the organization of a session visible as part of what a method specifies. [CRE-W001, §§3.3–4.2]

### Geschka and Zirm and connected procedural families

Geschka and Zirm and connected procedural families

Horst Geschka and Andrea Zirm distinguish free association, structured association, configuration, confrontation and imagination. Their descriptions connect these families to ways of carrying out an exercise. In free association, an initial contribution becomes a source for another. Structured association introduces successive directions of thought. Configuration organizes combinations of features. Confrontation introduces material from outside the immediate problem, while imagination uses internally developed images and perspectives. [CRE-W002, §§4.1–4.5]

Their rotating-sheet procedure replaces a single stream of speech with parallel writing. A sheet has three columns, and each participant enters an idea in each column. After roughly five minutes, the sheet passes

<!-- PDF page 447 -->

to another participant, who develops ideas beneath the earlier entries. The page supplies both material to respond to and a position for recording a continuation. A contribution can be developed without first winning an opportunity to speak. [CRE-W002, §4.1]

In a circulating-card variant, participants put one idea on each card and pass cards in a common direction. During this phase they do not speak. Cards received from a neighbor can stimulate new ideas. The later phases group contributions by possible solution direction, remove duplicates, clarify understanding and make an initial selection through adhesive dots. The exercise includes both the circulation that generates material and a way to organize what has accumulated. [CRE-W002, §4.1, fig. 4-2]

Confrontation techniques use a different sequence. First the problem is clarified and participants briefly express the familiar solutions that occur to them. Only then is unrelated material introduced. A stimulus word is examined for its properties, structure and function; those features can be carried back to the problem. The intended departure is supported by an actual intervening object of attention. [CRE-W002, §4.4]

Visual confrontation can proceed through images, and one described variant combines them with written circulation. Participants inspect picture cards and record ideas before circulating their contributions. Other imagination exercises ask the participant to identify with a problem or picture it in another way. These procedures specify a route between an initial task, a change in attention and a return to possible solutions. [CRE-W002, §§4.4–4.5]

The chapter's families consequently contain different operations and different session arrangements. A confrontation technique may use a technical principle as stimulus; a written technique may circulate a visual or verbal contribution. The descriptions show how procedures can be combined while preserving the particular role of each step. S52 develops experimental accounts of group interaction and production blocking, and S68 develops other material and collaborative methods.

### Takahashi and four purposes of creative techniques

Takahashi and four purposes of creative techniques

Makoto Takahashi's classification, presented by the Japan Creativity Society, distinguishes divergent, convergent, integrative and attitude methods. Divergent methods produce facts or ideas. Convergent methods bring that material together. Integrative methods are characterized by repeated movement between divergence and convergence. The classification therefore gives organizing material a place inside creative activity. [CRE-W004]

The fourth category concerns the creator's attitude. Such a method is intended to cultivate a disposition rather than directly solve the current problem. Its immediate purpose differs from that of a technique for producing a particular collection of alternatives. Readiness to participate and operations on a present problem can be addressed through different activities. [CRE-W004]

The distinction also changes how a procedure can be understood over time. An integrative method includes recurring transitions, while an attitude method can concern capacities brought to later work. Takahashi's short account provides a classification by those purposes. The particular methods described elsewhere give concrete forms to generating, organizing and developing material. [CRE-W004]

### Yao and Chu and methods across an innovation process

Yao and Chu and methods across an innovation process

Yao Wei and Chu Zhaowei review systematic innovation methods as a subject wider than TRIZ. They distinguish methods drawing on human inventive experience from those abstracted from natural phenomena. They also follow the use of methods across identifying an opportunity, formulating a problem, developing a response and putting it into use. Their account treats a method's place in the process as part of its practical significance. [CRE-W003, §§1–2]

<!-- PDF page 448 -->

The integration examples assign different jobs to different methods. Quality function deployment can help articulate requirements; TRIZ can address a technical contradiction; other analyses can examine implementation or failure. Joining methods in this way concerns the output of one activity becoming useful to the next. The important question is what contribution each method makes within the connected process. [CRE-W003, discussion of integrated application]

Computer assistance enters that account through knowledge and retrieval. Case-based assistance can draw on earlier experience within a domain, while inventive principles seek connections across domains. The authors' proposed AI engineer is a prospective development of such assistance. Their review also separates learning about a method from using it effectively in an enterprise. Training, application and practical outcome are examined as different parts of its development and assessment. [CRE-W003, §§3–4]

### Aznar and what an exercise is intended to accomplish

Aznar and what an exercise is intended to accomplish

Guy Aznar distinguishes imaginative expression, artistic creation, the production of ideas and innovation. His account of imaginative expression includes collective drawing, storytelling and imagined journeys within a permissive group. The immediate point is participation and the development of expression. A drawing need not become an exhibited artwork for the activity to serve that purpose. [CRE-W005, pp. 26– 28]

Producing ideas for a stated problem has another direction in his account. An idea must become both new and fitted to a situation. The work includes departures from an existing organization and a return toward a possible response. Aznar describes this process through tension and transformation, rather than identify it solely with a relaxed expressive state. [CRE-W005, pp. 28–30]

The distinction helps make the task of a session explicit. An expressive exercise and an inventive working session can share operations while pursuing different accomplishments. Aznar presents artistic creation as responding chiefly to an internal demand and idea production as responding to an external problem. His characterization is one historical account of those purposes. S66 develops collaborative artistic practices in which teachers, performers and shared material have substantial roles. [CRE-W005, pp. 27– 30]

### Leopoldino and colleagues and a comparative inventory

Leopoldino and colleagues and a comparative inventory

Kleidson Daniel Medeiros Leopoldino and colleagues map fifty-six publications and report 120 creativity techniques. Their detailed comparison treats nine frequently cited techniques. It distinguishes individual and collective application, the type of thinking, session time, operating criteria, material resources and the approach assigned to each technique. The table makes several different aspects of a technique available for comparison. [CRE-W006, §§3–4, tables 1–2]

Their operating criteria are exploration, combination, transformation and validation. The resulting descriptions compare such matters as whether the session is time-bounded, whether materials are needed and whether work is organized around several kinds of operation. These dimensions concern how techniques are described in the selected literature. The frequency with which a technique is cited is another part of the review, separate from the comparative description. [CRE-W006, §4]

The article gives a route into a wider literature and an inspectable comparison of its selected techniques. The reported inventory and the detailed table have different scopes: naming 120 techniques does not supply 120 complete procedures. Its useful contribution includes showing which features a comparative account can make explicit, alongside the instruction-level decomposition developed by Kirjavainen and Hölttä-Otto. [CRE-W006, §§4–5]

<!-- PDF page 449 -->

### Acar and colleagues and different kinds of constraint

Acar and colleagues and different kinds of constraint

Oguz Acar, Murat Tarakci and Daan van Knippenberg review empirical research on constraints in creativity and innovation. Their taxonomy distinguishes input, process and output constraints. Restricted time or materials limit inputs; a prescribed procedure governs the process; a specification defines what an outcome must contain or achieve. These restrictions act on different parts of the work. [CRE-W045, taxonomy of constraints]

The authors also distinguish motivational, cognitive and social routes through which constraints may affect activity. A restriction can alter willingness to experiment, the information attended to or relationships among participants. Classifying a constraint and explaining its effect are therefore different steps in their review. A time limit and a rule for exchanging ideas can both constrain a session while changing different conditions of action. [CRE-W045, underlying mechanisms]

The evidence discussed includes arguments that resources enable experimentation and findings in which pressure or restriction redirects effort. The framework relates these apparently different results to the object of a restriction and to proposed mediating processes. It also attends to the situation in which the restriction operates, rather than assign every constraint the same effect. [CRE-W045, input constraints]

These systematic accounts provide several ways to examine a method: its instructions, procedural family, immediate purpose, place in innovation and conditions of use. The developed practices in S64–S70 give those distinctions substantial cases. The classifications remain useful as guides to what a particular account explains.

<!-- PDF page 450 -->

## S81 Systematic invention through contradictions and available resources

S81   Systematic invention through contradictions and available resources

### From an inventive situation to a conflict model

From an inventive situation to a conflict model

Altshuller’s ARIZ-85-V begins by changing the description of a difficulty. An inventive situation can contain many inconveniences and possible ambitions. The mini-problem asks for a useful effect to be obtained, or a harmful effect removed, while retaining or simplifying the existing system. This formulation directs attention away from immediately adding a device and toward what, precisely, the system must do differently. The mature 1985 procedure develops the earlier inventive-problem tradition discussed in S44. [NC-W001]

The next task is to identify a conflicting pair and state two opposed conditions of an element. Improving one desired result under one condition can worsen another. The system’s principal function determines which condition to retain as the starting point. Intensifying that condition makes the conflict more explicit. The X-element names the change required to resolve it; the name does not commit the solver to another component. A change in a substance’s state can fulfil the requirement. [NC-W001]

In the radio-telescope example, conducting rods provide lightning protection but disturb reception. Reducing their presence helps reception while weakening protection. Because reception is the principal function, the worked analysis retains the condition that avoids interference and intensifies it to the absence of the conductor. The question becomes how protection can be obtained where the interfering rod is no longer present. [NC-W001]

This is a provisional model to be checked against the original situation. The procedure repeatedly returns the solver to the initial requirements rather than treating the first formulation as final. Choosing a conflict and intensifying it supplies a more precise problem; it has not yet supplied a physical means of solving it. [NC-W001]

### The place and time of the contradiction

The place and time of the contradiction

The operating zone locates the conflict, and operating time distinguishes when the opposed requirements must hold. In the telescope analysis, the zone is the air column where a lightning conductor would have been. Air is already present and becomes a candidate resource. The ideal-result direction asks for protection without the obstruction that had accompanied it. Altshuller uses ideality to direct the search toward the required effect with less added complication. [NC-W001]

The opposed requirements can now be stated at a different scale. The column should conduct when a lightning discharge develops and remain nonconducting during ordinary reception. These conditions need not apply at the same time. At the particle level, free charges are wanted during discharge and neutral molecules otherwise. The reformulation separates a general demand for a transparent protector into a particular place, occasion and material behaviour. [NC-W001]

A resource inventory considers substances and fields in and around the system, including their states and possible changes. The fact that air has been identified does not yet explain how it will acquire the required charges. The next part of the worked analysis must make the behaviour physically attainable. Altshuller’s ideal-result formulation is a direction of inquiry, not a claim that an ideal answer is always obtainable; the program also permits outside substances or fields when existing resources are insufficient. [NC-W001]

<!-- PDF page 451 -->

### Turning a physical requirement into a design

Turning a physical requirement into a design

The little-people representation develops the particle requirement by asking what must differ between the selected air column and the surrounding air. In technical terms, the selected gas must ionize more readily. Combining air with emptiness suggests reduced pressure. That change makes a resource already implicated in the problem behave differently under the developing field. [NC-W001]

The technical scheme then places gas in a sealed dielectric tube with pressure selected for discharge as the lightning field develops. Altshuller cites author’s certificate 177497 in connection with this answer. The ending of the example is therefore more specific than a proposal to use an ionized column: it includes the pressure change and the construction that maintains it. The source presents a worked design and cited invention. [NC-W001]

Later stages distinguish a physical answer from its technical realization. A composite problem may need to be divided, the selected conflict reconsidered, or the system placed within a larger one. Checks ask what contradiction has actually been removed, how the result can be controlled, and whether it works over repeated cycles. An unsatisfactory answer sends the solver back to the initial mini-problem. Other uses and an examination of the route to the answer follow. [NC-W001]

The thermal-protective suit is a separate example of moving to a supersystem. Liquid oxygen removes heat while evaporating and warming; it subsequently supplies respiration. Cooling and breathing become connected functions within a larger arrangement. This example changes the boundary of the technical problem, whereas the telescope example develops the material behaviour required within a selected zone. [NC-W001]

Standards, physical effects and other inventive principles form part of the program’s wider repertoire. The worked analysis shows why choosing among tools is embedded in reformulation, development and checking. A diagram of successive stages would miss the returns and changes of direction that the instructions make conditional on the emerging answer. [NC-W001]

### Making a new dependency visible

Making a new dependency visible

Goldenberg and Mazursky’s Creativity in Product Innovation organizes invention through representations of products and their relations. Their attribute-dependency procedure distinguishes components from variables. Connecting a chair leg to a backrest concerns components; making the length of one vary with the length of the other concerns a dependency between attributes. The latter representation can expose a relation that a component list alone would not show. [NC-W002]

Their forecasting matrix places manufacturer-controlled internal variables in columns, with internal and external variables in rows. Existing dependencies are marked. Selected empty cells then become possible changes: what would follow if these variables were made dependent? The direction of a proposed dependency matters because it specifies what is to change with what. [NC-W002]

A candidate relation is developed into a feasible construction and examined for a useful consequence, market benefit or new segment. The representation supplies possibilities that still require technical and commercial interpretation. It is a way of generating a different product concept, rather than simply ranking completed concepts already supplied by an inventor. [NC-W002]

Their ice-coated antenna-pole example has a different conflict from Altshuller’s lightning problem. A transportable pole is light enough to carry but insufficiently strong under ice loading. Installed freezing conditions allow strength to depend on a resource that is absent during transport: a roughened pole collects an ice coating while the antenna acquires its load. The source of the difficulty becomes part of the

<!-- PDF page 452 -->

proposed support. Lightness in transport and strength in service are separated by circumstances and time. [NC-W002]

### Reassigning a function to what is already there

Reassigning a function to what is already there

Replacement temporarily removes a component from a product or process representation while retaining its function. The unassigned function prompts a search among components already available. Goldenberg and Mazursky illustrate the procedure with rejected butter patties that had been melted slowly in a steam-jacketed vat. Steam provides heat indirectly through the vessel. [NC-W002]

Removing the steam component leaves heating as a function that must still be supplied. The search is constrained by what else is present and by the properties needed for the task. Hot milk already used upstream can carry the function: it contacts and melts the butter directly. The resulting mixture can return to the production process. [NC-W002]

The intermediate steps explain the change. The inventors do not merely substitute the word milk for steam; they change the heat-transfer relation and the role of an existing process material. The butter and vessel remain intelligible parts of the revised arrangement, while a separate steam system is removed. [NC-W002]

The authors report faster melting and reduced time and energy costs. The case’s contribution is the connected reassignment from a removed component to an available one, followed through to the changed process. [NC-W002]

### Six informational stages in USIT

Six informational stages in USIT

中川徹’s six-box USIT account distinguishes information produced during problem solving from a flowchart of named techniques. Its boxes contain a user’s concrete problem, an appropriately defined problem, understanding of the present and ideal systems, ideas for a new system, a solution concept, and the user’s concrete solution. The difference between an idea fragment and a technically coherent concept is explicit. [NC-W003]

Analysis develops objects, attributes and functions alongside relations in space and time. The present system is examined in relation to desired behaviour and properties. Operators then help generate nuclei of change. Technical knowledge is needed to combine those fragments into a concept that can answer the problem, rather than leaving the process at a collection of suggestions. [NC-W003]

Problem definition and concept construction form interfaces between practical work and the thinking process. Nakagawa identifies the conceptual solution as USIT’s output; concrete realization belongs to the user’s practical activity. He credits Sickafus’s earlier development and explains his own reorganization of TRIZ operators. His argument for a route that does not depend on first finding an external analogy concerns analysis of one’s own problem and construction from its results. [NC-W003]

### What application and training studies report

What application and training studies report

Goldenberg and Mazursky’s Study 3 compared methods with 120 participants divided among six method-by-product groups, using baby ointment or mattresses. Template instruction lasted about four hours,  compared with about two hours for lateral thinking or random stimulation. A thirty-minute task produced 277 ideas, which three senior marketers rated blind for originality and investment value. Template ideas received higher ratings, including comparisons of selected leading ideas. Training time was therefore one difference in this design alongside the methods. [NC-W002]

<!-- PDF page 453 -->

Study 4 changed that comparison. Eighteen template trainees, nineteen HIT trainees and eighteen untrained participants generated drinking-glass ideas. Both trained groups received four hours of instruction. A different panel of three marketers rated the 82 ideas, again favouring the template condition. The two studies concern originality and value judgments of generated ideas, with the second addressing the earlier training-time difference. [NC-W002]

Birdi’s review chapter treats creativity training as a family of interventions whose tasks, delivery and setting matter. Systematic cognitive instruction, realistic practice, and support for evaluation as well as generation recur in his account. In his later description of the TRIZ workplace evaluation he coauthored, trainees showed stronger subsequent idea generation, while support for implementation change was more limited and included self-reported impact. The chapter distinguishes developing ideas from securing their use in an organization. [NC-W004]

Dumas, Schmidt and Alexander’s study of 44 engineering graduate students separates fluency from originality before and after TRIZ instruction. The reported post-instruction pattern contains fewer ideas but greater originality. Relational reasoning is the strongest reported predictor of originality, with antinomous reasoning implicated in the TRIZ-supported work. Their distinction among similarity, anomaly, incompatibility and opposition gives several kinds of relation a place in understanding the task. [NC-W005]

Spreafico and Russo classify more than two hundred published industrial applications by purpose, design activity, tools, combinations and output maturity. Contradictions and inventive principles predominate among reported tools, with QFD, FMEA and patent tools among their partners. The survey describes how tools are selected and combined in published engineering cases rather than treating TRIZ as a single intervention used identically everywhere. [NC-W006]

Their output distinctions range from a physical-effect hint to a concept with behaviour and structure, a detailed design and a market-ready product. Fewer than a quarter of the surveyed cases are classified as market-ready. The classification identifies what the reported application produced: a promising principle and a finished product are different endpoints, both of which may be useful in an engineering history. [NC-W006]

姚威、储昭卫 and 胡顺顺 examine 148 usable project reports from 216 collected in a supported innovation-method program. Two experienced researchers code tool uses and concepts, while expert ratings provide separate benefit measures. Productivity, quality and reliability are prominent aims in these reports of engineering problems. The method makes actual uses and the form of the resulting proposals available for comparison. [NC-W007]

Generating a concept and adopting it as a solution are counted separately. Contradiction and principle use is common, with a lower concepts-per-adopted-measure ratio than some other tools in the reports. This describes the relation between concepts and adopted measures in the selected field material. Alongside the published-case survey and the training studies, it gives a distinct view of how a proposed method enters engineering work. [NC-W007]

<!-- PDF page 454 -->

## S64 Invention and scientific discovery

S64   Invention and scientific discovery

An inventive task can begin with a difficulty in an existing design, an unexplained result or a representation that makes some possibilities hard to see. The accounts in this section follow transformations of a technical problem, the recognition of a mathematical relationship, the use of analogy and the construction of new terms in a computational search. They make the work between encountering a problem and obtaining a candidate solution available for close examination.

### Bush and transformations of the technical problem

Bush and transformations of the technical problem

G. Ya. Bush's Methods of Technical Creativity, published in 1972, classifies inventive methods along several dimensions. A method can be general or specialized, simple or complex, and directed toward a particular stage of creative work. His stages include preparation, forming a conception, searching for a solution and realizing it. The classification gives problem formulation and implementation a place alongside generating ideas. Bush describes heuristic methods as recommendations or incomplete procedures whose use requires judgment. [CRE-W007, §3.1]

Inversion is one of his developed families. It includes changing an object's orientation, reversing an action, substituting a physical state, changing the course of a process in time, or turning an unwanted influence toward a useful purpose. The operation begins by identifying something in the situation that has been taken for granted. A specific reversal can then be considered. The question is not simply whether an object can be turned upside down, but which relation, property or sequence might usefully be changed. [CRE-W007, §3.3]

Bush's turbine-shaft example gives this change of direction a concrete form. He recounts the difficulty of obtaining stable operation at high rotational speed by shortening, thickening or strengthening a shaft. In his account of de Laval's experiment, a deliberately flexible shaft supplies an alternative to pursuing greater rigidity. The example belongs to Bush's explanation of antithesis: examine a response opposed to the one that has organized the unsuccessful attempts. The technical function provides the reason to reconsider the conventional remedy. [CRE-W007, §3.3]

His complex methods distinguish several kinds of combination. Established elements can be combined with new ones, new elements with one another, or established elements in a new relationship. Integration can bring functions together within an object. Agglutination attaches something to a principal object, potentially without redesigning the connected parts and potentially only for a time. Bush's computing example joins peripheral devices to a principal machine as their functions are required. The combination changes what the larger arrangement can do. [CRE-W007, §3.4]

An intermediate element can also make a combination possible and then be removed. Bush describes an assembly method in which a film helps position components for a printed-circuit board. After the connections have been made, the intermediate film is removed. The temporary support participates in making the final object without remaining one of its permanent parts. This example explains why an inventive method may concern the sequence of construction as much as the finished geometry. [CRE-W007, §3.4]

Bush's account supplies several different questions to put to a technical difficulty. What has been held fixed? Which property could be reversed? What functions could be joined? Could an intermediate object or operation make a desired connection possible? His examples give those questions specific operations and technical settings. S44 develops the earlier account of inventive creativity by Altshuller and Shapiro; Bush's selected method families provide a further substantial treatment of technical invention.

<!-- PDF page 455 -->

### Poincaré on recognizing a fruitful combination

Poincaré on recognizing a fruitful combination

Henri Poincaré's 1908 chapter on mathematical invention begins with a problem of selection. New combinations of familiar mathematical objects are easy to describe in the abstract; most would have little interest.
