Invention, in his account, includes discerning the rare connections that reveal an unsuspected relationship between facts previously treated as separate. A connection across distant areas can be fruitful, but mere distance does not make it so. [CRE-W008, Livre I, §III]

He illustrates the work through the history of his first memoir on Fuchsian functions. For about a fortnight he made sustained attempts without obtaining the result he sought. One night, after taking black coffee contrary to his habit, he experienced a crowd of ideas while unable to sleep. He describes two ideas forming a stable combination. The next morning brought work that could be written out. The episode appears within a longer sequence of deliberate attempts and subsequent mathematical development. [CRE-W008, Livre I, §III]

A later episode occurs during a geological excursion. Boarding an omnibus, Poincaré suddenly recognizes a relationship between transformations used in defining Fuchsian functions and those of non-Euclidean geometry. He does not verify it on the spot. He continues the conversation and later checks the result at leisure. Other episodes include unsuccessful work, a stay by the sea and an interruption for military service. The chapter gives mathematical invention a temporal texture: directed effort, interruption, recognition and renewed deliberate work. [CRE-W008, Livre I, §III]

Selection raises a further question for him. The inventor cannot inspect every possible combination one after another. Poincaré proposes that mathematical sensibility admits some combinations into attention because of their promise of order, elegance or useful relation. His aesthetic explanation concerns the recognition of fruitful structure. It does not equate mathematical invention with generating arbitrary novelties and later checking all of them. [CRE-W008, Livre I, §III]

He also distinguishes the felt certainty of an arrival from a completed demonstration. Sudden ideas can be mistaken. Conscious work is required to formulate and verify them, as well as to prepare the problem that precedes them. The chapter joins a first-person history to a proposed explanation of why some combinations attract attention. Its description of interrupted work gives a historical setting for the later experimental accounts of incubation in S67. [CRE-W008, Livre I, §III]

### Gick and Holyoak and the analogy that must be noticed

Gick and Holyoak and the analogy that must be noticed

Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak's 1980 experiments use two stories with different objects but a corresponding problem structure. A general wants to capture a fortress. Roads leading toward it are mined: small groups can pass safely, while a large force would trigger destruction. The army is divided, approaches along different roads and converges at the fortress. The separate passages preserve the surroundings while concentrating the force where it is needed. [CRE-W009, pp. 308–312]

The medical problem concerns a tumour that cannot safely be treated by sending a destructive intensity of radiation through healthy tissue along a single path. Several low-intensity rays can approach from different directions and combine at the target. Mapping the general's solution requires relating troops to rays, separate roads to different paths and convergent attack to combined treatment. The analogy concerns organized relations among the elements. [CRE-W009, pp. 308–312]

The fourth experiment separates knowing the source story from using it. Twenty-seven participants learn the critical story among other stories. Twelve receive a hint that a previous story may help solve the radiation problem. Eleven of those twelve produce the complete dispersion solution. Among the fifteen without the hint, three produce complete or partial dispersion solutions, and the authors examine whether those participants actually noticed the analogy. [CRE-W009, pp. 340–343]

<!-- PDF page 456 -->

The source can therefore be available in memory while its relevance goes unrecognized. Gick and Holyoak's procedure brings retrieval and mapping into the problem-solving account. A participant must find a useful earlier situation, identify the relations that matter and use them to construct a response in the target setting. Learning an instructive example and recognizing when to apply it are distinguishable accomplishments. [CRE-W009, pp. 340–343]

### Dunbar and Blanchette and analogies used at work

Dunbar and Blanchette and analogies used at work

Kevin Dunbar and Isabelle Blanchette study analogy during scientists' laboratory meetings. Their initial analysis covers sixteen meetings in four laboratories and finds more than ninety-nine analogies. Most comparisons stay within biology or immunology. A useful analogy need not cross into a remote intellectual area: a familiar experiment can supply the comparison needed to understand why another experiment behaved unexpectedly. [CRE-W010, discussion of analogy in laboratory meetings]

A near comparison can isolate a consequential difference. Two experiments may share a gene, proteins and temperature while differing in incubation time. Drawing attention to that difference can help scientists repair an experimental problem. The authors therefore give superficial similarity a useful role when the immediate goal is troubleshooting. The relation between the comparison and the goal matters more than a general preference for distant analogies. [CRE-W010]

When the goal changes to formulating a hypothesis, the comparisons also change. Scientists draw on underlying structural relationships, including similarities between genetic sequences, to suggest a possible common function. The paper reports that structural analogies were a minority of the analogies observed, but more than eighty percent of those structural analogies were used to formulate hypotheses. What scientists compare is responsive to what they are trying to accomplish. [CRE-W010]

The authors connect these observations to laboratory tasks in which participants generate analogies rather than merely remember or choose a supplied one. Constructing a comparison, recognizing a reminder and using a comparison in a discussion are different activities. Their combined observational and experimental approach makes that distinction visible. It gives analogy a place within continuing research, where an anomaly, a colleague's suggestion and the design of another experiment can redirect the conversation. [CRE-W010]

### Klahr and Simon and connected spaces of discovery

Klahr and Simon and connected spaces of discovery

David Klahr and Herbert Simon's 2001 review examines historical studies, laboratory tasks, naturalistic observations and computational models of discovery. Their account describes a researcher searching among hypotheses, experiments, representations and instruments. Work in one space changes what is worth trying in another. The initial problem is not always a fully specified question waiting for a single correct answer. [CRE-W011, pp. 75–78]

In the device-learning studies they discuss, participants investigate an unfamiliar control on a simulated rocket ship. They must propose an account of what the control does and choose manipulations that reveal its function. Some give greater emphasis to developing explanations; others concentrate on experiments. The task makes the coordination of the two searches observable. An intervention is informative in relation to a question, and its outcome can create a new question. [CRE-W011, discussion of dual search]

The review also gives surprise an active place. A result that contradicts expectations can become the beginning of an inquiry into a phenomenon. The Curies' encounter with unexpectedly strong radioactivity in pitchblende is one of its historical examples. Their attempt to obtain a substance helps reveal a problem about what else is present. The review follows this reversal between hypotheses motivating experiments and phenomena motivating hypotheses. [CRE-W011, discussion of surprise]

<!-- PDF page 457 -->

Representations and instruments can join the search as well. A different way to describe a problem can make a new analogy or experiment possible. The review's contribution is an account of discovery in which generating, testing and reformulating are connected activities. It complements the treatment of experiments and dual control in S33 by explaining how the possible objects of investigation themselves change. [CRE-W011, discussion of multiple search spaces]

### BACON.5 and a discovered relation used as new data

BACON.5 and a discovered relation used as new data

Pat Langley, Gary Bradshaw and Herbert Simon's 1981 BACON.5 paper describes a program that seeks regularities in numerical and nominal data. Its user specifies independent terms, values to consider and dependent variables. The program applies heuristics for constancy, trends and combinations of terms. Its ideal-gas example shows how these operations build on one another. [CRE-W012, pp. 121–122]

The program first holds temperature and amount of gas fixed while pressure varies. Volume decreases as pressure increases, suggesting that the product of pressure and volume should be examined. That product is found to be constant for the setting. Changing temperature produces different constant products. Relating those products to temperature suggests a ratio. Changing the amount of gas leads to a further relation, ultimately expressing the ideal-gas law through a constant value of pV/(nT). [CRE-W012, p. 121]

Each step supplies a term that can be used at the next level. The product pV is a hypothesis about the lower-level observations and becomes data for investigating its relationship to temperature. The program reapplies similar heuristics to the resulting descriptions. A useful representation is produced during the search instead of being supplied only as the final name for what was found. [CRE-W012, pp. 121–122]

The discovered pattern also changes data collection. Once the program expects a lower-level relation, later settings need not repeat the entire earlier variation. A selected observation can be used to estimate the relevant constant. The paper contrasts this procedure with a complete factorial search. Representation and control of investigation work together: finding a relation can reduce the observations required to investigate a higher-level relation. [CRE-W012, pp. 121–122]

The authors present BACON.5 as a computational way to perform part of discovery, including demonstrations on known physical laws. Their aim is to exhibit productive heuristics, not to reconstruct every action taken by the historical discoverers. The worked example makes the program's inputs, transformations and use of intermediate results explicit. [CRE-W012, Introduction]

### Bonnardel and Lubart and constraints that make an analogy useful

Bonnardel and Lubart and constraints that make an analogy useful

Nathalie Bonnardel and Todd Lubart describe creative design through an interaction between analogy and constraint management. Analogy can expand the field of ideas. Constraints help direct attention, evaluate a candidate and progressively determine what a satisfactory solution requires. Some constraints are prescribed; others are inferred from the consequences of those already accepted. A requirement for a lightweight but resistant aerospace component raises further questions about material and manufacture. [CRE-W013, §2.4]

Their field observations give this account a physical example. Designers need a reflector larger than those they normally make, but it must fit beneath a rocket fairing during transport. An umbrella suggests a structure that can be compact for launch and deployed later. Another designer draws on the movement of curtains in the office to propose a different solution. Ordinary objects become sources of invention when a designer recognizes a relation to a specific difficulty. [CRE-W013, §3.1]

The transport constraint makes deployability relevant. The analogy then supplies something concrete to examine and develop. In the authors' model, analogy, association and management of constraints continue to interact as representations and evaluations change. Their account gives a developed

<!-- PDF page 458 -->

alternative to treating creative work as an unrestricted generation phase followed by an entirely separate judgment phase. [CRE-W013, §2.4]

Across these histories, the work can concern what is varied, what is compared, what becomes a new term and what counts as a promising relation. The technical transformations, mathematical memoir, experiments and observational cases give those questions different forms. Their detailed operations can be studied alongside the accounts of form in S08 and problem structuring in S44.

<!-- PDF page 459 -->

## S82 Association, bisociation and the construction of new ideas

S82   Association, bisociation and the construction of new ideas

### Accounts and measurement of creative connection

Accounts and measurement of creative connection

### Two frames for one situation

Two frames for one situation

Koestler’s The Act of Creation distinguishes association within an accustomed frame from apprehending a situation through two self-consistent but habitually incompatible frames. A matrix is a pattern of possible activities; its code supplies governing rules; strategy is the particular course taken within those rules. His chess comparison separates the rules that define a game from the many ways a player may proceed. Bisociation brings frames into an intersection that ordinary conduct within either frame would not supply. [NC-W008]

The distinction gives surprise a structure. In the opening jokes, a situation that appears intelligible under one social code is reinterpreted through another. A reply can be reasonable within one frame while overturning the expectation established by the other. The connection is more specific than the occurrence of two thoughts: a situation is made to belong to two organized patterns of meaning or action. [NC-W008]

Koestler deliberately extends this account across humour, scientific discovery and artistic creation. The domains differ in what happens when frames meet, but his theoretical ambition is to describe creative activity through their encounters. Matrix, code and strategy preserve room for established organization as well as a course that departs from habitual expectations. Learning a domain’s code and discovering an unexpected intersection are consequently distinguishable activities within his account. [NC-W008]

His printing-press discussion connects practices of making impressions with the use of a press. The example makes a relationship between established activities, rather than a wholly unprecedented component, central to the proposed creative episode. Koestler presents a historical reconstruction of this connection. It explains his argument without requiring his account of Gutenberg’s private reflections to be taken as an independently authenticated discovery record. [NC-W008]

The opening of his discussion of false inspirations also separates the experience of an idea arriving from a connection that survives development. An apparent intersection can be suggestive before its implications have been worked through. Elaboration therefore belongs within the theory’s own account of creation. The sudden interpretation is part of a longer activity in which its usefulness, coherence or expressive possibilities become clearer. [NC-W008]

### A concert contract seen through two financial problems

A concert contract seen through two financial problems

Chabrillat, Lecoutre and Lièvre follow a managerial innovation at the concert venue they call Le Cabestan. A changed grant rule replaces a fixed subsidy with an amount calculated as a percentage of actual expenditure. At the same time, reopening the venue requires renewed relations with private concert coproducers. The manager initially faces these as separate financial and commercial problems. [NC-W019]

Revised coproduction agreements allow the venue to pay some production expenses directly while maintaining the agreed financial result and profit sharing with a partner. This reassignment can support concessions and negotiations needed to rebuild the commercial relationship. Expenses are not simply renamed; who pays and records them changes under the contract. [NC-W019]

A tense conversation with the financial manager connects that arrangement to the grant problem. Expenditure now borne by the venue affects the base used to calculate its public subsidy. A practice developed in the private coproduction relationship thus becomes consequential under the public-

<!-- PDF page 460 -->

financing rule. The connected operation depends on both the contractual allocation and the particular subsidy basis. [NC-W019]

The authors trace partner responses, contract versions and stabilization of the practice. Their concurrent observation and consulting involvement from February 2014 to March 2015 supplied meetings, interviews and documents as the activity developed. They interpret the case through matrices of public financing and private coproduction, with stages of an unresolved problem, a creative clash and validation in practice. Expertise in both domains and the longer work of stabilization are part of that interpretation. [NC-W019]

### Associative routes and practical requirements

Associative routes and practical requirements

Mednick describes creative thinking as combining associative elements in ways that meet specified requirements or prove useful. Remoteness contributes to his account of creative quality, but an unusual conjunction is not useful solely because it is remote. Serendipitous contiguity, similarity and mediation provide different routes by which elements can be brought together. His account of steep and flat associative hierarchies concerns how readily common and more remote responses become available. Requisite knowledge remains important to what can be connected. [NC-W010]

The refrigerator example keeps practical requirements beside the association. Preventing frost is different from reacting after it has accumulated, but a proposal never to open the door defeats the refrigerator’s purpose. A counter responding to door openings suggests a different way of controlling defrosting. The useful connection concerns an event associated with frost accumulation and an operation that can be controlled, while retaining the appliance’s ordinary use. [NC-W010]

The Remote Associates Test turns mediation into a research task. A participant finds an associate connecting three cues; in Mednick’s example, rat, blue and cottage can each be joined with cheese. A candidate that fits one cue must be tested against the others. The task gives associative theory an operational instrument, with a specific kind of successful answer. [NC-W010]

### What an association test measures

What an association test measures

Wu, Huang, Chen and Chen’s systematic review retained 172 studies from 256 screened records covering 2000–2019. The review shows RAT tasks being used for different research purposes and with differing relations among cues. Producing candidate associates can involve divergent search; finding one that satisfies all cues involves convergence. Vocabulary, retrieval and overcoming a prominent wrong answer can also influence the result. A test score therefore needs to be interpreted through the task and version that produced it. [NC-W011]

王硕阳、林崇德 and 孙汉银 distinguish what is connected from the efficiency with which a connection is retrieved. Language-based co-occurrence differs from relations built through experience, function or shared features. Their account develops partly independent associative abilities and different roles in problems that do or do not require restructuring. A person’s facility with conventional verbal relations need not capture every way that relations can support a new problem representation. [NC-W012]

西田勇樹、服部雅史 and 織田涼 compare a compound-word RAT with insight problems, alternative uses, vocabulary and cognitive reflection. Their version requires a character that makes compounds with each cue. After vocabulary was controlled, their first experiment did not find the expected association with the combined insight or creativity tasks. The result concerns those tasks and the contribution vocabulary makes to answering them. [NC-W013]

<!-- PDF page 461 -->

Their second experiment retained 68 of 91 recruited participants and found a relation to making fewer typical cognitive-reflection errors. The relation with the correct-answer score did not persist in the same way after vocabulary control. The authors resist a binary verdict that RAT either is or is not insight: insight tasks themselves need not correlate closely. Their discussion gives inhibiting a salient but wrong response a visible role alongside vocabulary and associative search. [NC-W013]

### Constructing and interpreting ideas

Constructing and interpreting ideas

### Making the familiar strange and returning to the problem

Making the familiar strange and returning to the problem

Gordon’s Synectics seeks to make deliberate work possible around activities often described only as intuition. Making the strange familiar is the analytic effort to understand a problem. Making the familiar strange changes its habitual representation, allowing a group to approach it through a different experience or image. The departure is followed by a return to the technical problem; an excursion that never returns would leave the original task unanswered. [NC-W009]

Personal analogy asks participants to identify with an element or process. Direct analogy draws on another phenomenon. Symbolic analogy compresses a problem into an evocative expression or image, while fantasy analogy imagines a desired fulfilment. Gordon treats these mechanisms as ways to encourage useful psychological states, not simply four labels for any unusual comparison. The mechanism chosen affects how the group leaves its accustomed account of the problem. [NC-W009]

Appendix II joins the initial problem, analytic understanding, excursions through the mechanisms, integration with the problem, a new viewpoint and a solution or research target. Some targets require a model that tests a principle; others require work on materials. The return to a technical viewpoint can change or reverse part of the image that prompted it. What is retained is a relation useful to construction, rather than a demand that a product imitate every feature of the analogy. [NC-W009]

### From an imagined stitch to a space-suit closure

From an imagined stitch to a space-suit closure

The space-suit session concerns an opening that must close strongly and reliably. Familiar fasteners give the group an established set of possibilities but do not settle the task. Insect and stitching imagery opens a different way of thinking about joining the sides. The group’s responses move between imagined conduct and the load the closure must bear. [NC-W009]

The discussion develops steel stitching into overlapping springs embedded in the rubber lips of the opening. A wire passed through the springs can pull the sides together. This proposal gives the image an arrangement of materials and connections: the opposed lips carry the springs, the springs overlap, and the wire supplies the joining action. [NC-W009]

The load requirement brings the excursion back to the suit. The mechanism must answer the difficulty that made an alternative to ordinary fastening worth seeking. Gordon’s account ends with a proposed construction, so the significant result is the route from an unfamiliar image to a technically describable closure. The session’s ingenuity lies in the successive interpretations and their return to the original requirement. [NC-W009]

### A roof that changes its exposed colour

A roof that changes its exposed colour

A second session asks for a roof that is light in hot weather and dark in cold weather. Changes in animal appearance supply possible analogies, but the time scale matters. A seasonal coat does not give the rapid response wanted for the roof. Chromatophores suggest coloured elements whose exposure can change instead. [NC-W009]

<!-- PDF page 462 -->

The technical viewpoint transforms that suggestion. White elements embedded in a black roof would expand into view when heated, changing what the surface exposes. The construction does not copy the animal unchanged; it selects a relation between temperature, element behaviour and visible colour, and reverses part of the analogy for the building’s purpose. [NC-W009]

Gordon presents a research target for materials and construction. The group has obtained something more definite than an animal metaphor: a proposed response and arrangement whose realization can be investigated. His account thus connects imaginative departure with a specification for further technical work. [NC-W009]

### A form before its purpose

A form before its purpose

Finke’s constrained imagery task asks participants to combine three selected object parts into a form before deciding what useful object it will become. Size, material and some relations can change while specified geometric constraints are retained. The result is a preinventive structure, open to interpretation rather than a drawing of a finished purpose already chosen. [NC-W015]

Supplying an interpretation category after form generation changes what the participant is doing. A structure first assembled without that category can subsequently be explored for functions that were not its initial rationale. Broad functional categories also leave different interpretive possibilities from narrow object categories. Finke reports especially creative inventions under conditions that delayed the category, judged through originality and practicality ratings. [NC-W015]

The operation is construction followed by a search for meaning under constraints. A part can acquire a role not apparent when it was selected, and its relation to another part can suggest a function for the whole. Interpretation then supports refinement, expansion or the generation of a different structure. Delaying a category in this task preserves a particular set of possibilities; it does not imply that every purpose should be postponed in every design problem. [NC-W015]

Geneplore makes the return paths explicit. Generation produces a preinventive structure; exploration interprets it under product constraints, and the interpretation can lead back to further generation. Constraints act on both activities. The process distinguishes a suggestive form from a developed invention while giving the former an active role in producing the latter. [NC-W015]

### Comparing taught methods

Comparing taught methods

Azadyekta compared brainstorming, forced association and synectics with a control condition in 160 elementary pupils. Eight weeks of training were assessed with pre- and post-training Torrance pictorial tests. All three trained groups improved on the reported measure relative to the control pattern, while the overall differences among the trained methods were not statistically significant. This is a comparison of taught activities and task scores in those conditions. It supplies a different kind of evidence from Gordon’s accounts of technical sessions and preserves the distinction between improving on a measure and establishing a general ranking among invention methods. [NC-W018]

### Exploring a space and changing what it permits

Exploring a space and changing what it permits

Boden’s 1997 account distinguishes what is new to an individual from what is new in recorded history. A person can produce an idea without copying it even when someone else has already produced it. That distinction separates a psychological question about the individual’s creative activity from a historical question about priority. [NC-W014]

The paper organizes its discussion under combinational creativity and exploratory-transformational creativity. Exploration works within a conceptual space of permitted structures and operations.

<!-- PDF page 463 -->

Transformation changes that space so that something previously excluded becomes possible. The distinction concerns the representation that defines what can be generated, rather than only whether the resulting item looks unfamiliar. [NC-W014]

Computer examples make the representation consequential. Permitted structures, generative operations and changes to them affect a program’s productions; Copycat illustrates flexible representations. Evaluation remains a separate issue involving values and historical or cultural context. Boden’s account therefore connects producing possibilities to the conditions under which they can count as valuable, without treating a generator’s output count as an adequate assessment of creativity. [NC-W014]

### A combinatorial account of discovery

A combinatorial account of discovery

Simonton proposes a combinatorial account of scientific discovery and invention that includes activities Boden distinguishes as exploration and transformation. His formalization concerns an individual scientist’s subjective episode. It defines p as the initial probability or response strength of an idea, u as its final utility and v as prior knowledge of that utility, each ranging from zero to one. The proposed creativity measure is c = (1 − p)u(1 − v). [NC-W016]

The expression assigns its maximum to a useful idea that initially had low probability and whose usefulness was little known beforehand. An unlikely candidate is insufficient if it proves useless; a useful result whose utility was already known has a different status in the model. The extreme combinations distinguish such situations as expertise, blind problem solving, lucky guesses and perseveration. They expose the difference between producing a candidate and knowing that it will work. [NC-W016]

The formalization is Simonton’s proposed way of characterizing creative episodes, with its variables and interpretation kept together. His discussion of optimization and no-free-lunch reasoning depends on the averaging assumptions of that argument. His broader account and Boden’s conceptual-space account remain distinct theoretical positions. [NC-W016]

### Running an imagined combination

Running an imagined combination

Fauconnier and Turner describe mental spaces as partial representations constructed for local understanding. Counterparts can be mapped between input spaces, a generic space captures shared structure, and a blend selectively projects elements from the inputs. Composition forms relations, completion recruits background frames, and elaboration runs the imagined situation. Emergent structure in the blend can then inform the understanding of an input. [NC-W017]

Their monk walks up a path on one day and down on another, with arbitrary changes in pace and stops. The question is whether a location is occupied at the same time of day on both journeys. Imagine the journeys occurring simultaneously, with two monks moving in opposite directions on the same path. They must meet. Mapping the meeting back to the separate days supplies the shared time and location. [NC-W017]

The inference depends on selective combination: the path and time of day are shared in the imagined scene, while the two journeys remain represented by distinct travellers. Running that scene makes a relation apparent that was harder to see in the separate accounts. The model explains the representational work of the inference rather than merely naming combination as its cause. [NC-W017]

<!-- PDF page 464 -->

### Literature-based discovery and computational bridges

Literature-based discovery and computational bridges

### Finding a hypothesis between disconnected literatures

Finding a hypothesis between disconnected literatures

Swanson and Smalheiser ask what may follow from complementary literatures that do not cite one another. One literature connects A with B; another connects B with C. Reading them together can suggest an A–C hypothesis that neither states. The absence of citation concerns the public literature and does not establish that no person has privately made the connection. Nor do the two links alone prove the proposed hypothesis. [NC-W020]

ARROWSMITH begins with provisional A and C literatures, collects MEDLINE title files, filters shared-word candidates and displays titles and citations for guided reading. The expert interprets whether a  common term marks a substantive connection. The representation and filtering make a large set of possible links examinable; interpretation identifies which might be scientifically complementary. [NC-W020]

The authors recount the fish-oil and Raynaud connection through literatures involving blood viscosity and report later corroboration by others. Their retrospective account preserves the difference between proposing a relation from public knowledge and testing it subsequently. A separate migraine/magnesium history supplies a benchmark for later computational work on recovering bridge terms. [NC-W020]

### Representing and ranking bridges

Representing and ranking bridges

Kötter and Berthold’s information networks represent heterogeneous concepts, relations and pieces of evidence. A network can accommodate incompletely typed information, with weights expressing confidence in evidence. The representation provides relations that can be explored across domains without requiring every link to be treated as a causal assertion. [NC-W021]

Their bisociative patterns are distinct. A bridging concept links dense groups; a bridging graph connects domains through several elements or returns through another domain; structurally similar disconnected subgraphs supply a comparison without an existing connecting edge. The last pattern is especially different from finding a shared word: the relation lies in how structures correspond. [NC-W021]

Juršič and colleagues begin with two known literatures, represent documents as term vectors and identify outliers classified toward the other domain. These documents may contain ideas atypical of their labelled field and closer to the other. Frequency, similarity and outlier-related heuristics then rank candidate terms. Selected relations can be turned into a weighted network with pruning options. [NC-W022]

Their retrospective migraine/magnesium experiment uses 8,058 pre-1988 titles and 43 historical bridging terms. All tested rankings already put terms shared by both domains ahead of other terms, which gives the baseline a substantial advantage. Improvements in ranking concern recovery of known bridges, not a percentage of correct new hypotheses. The constructed network supports examination of possible relations after that retrieval step. [NC-W022]

### Topics as sources of design inspiration

Topics as sources of design inspiration

Ahmed and Fuge use topics, represented by collections of words, rather than isolated bridging words. Their data contain 3,918 OpenIDEO ideas across fourteen challenges. Topic proportions represent each idea; a classifier identifies ideas that resemble another challenge more than their assigned one; topics prominent in these outliers receive higher bisociation scores. Topic co-occurrence and proportion relations supply network edges. Both the classifier and the bridging stage affect what the resulting network proposes. [NC-W023]

<!-- PDF page 465 -->

The approach seeks inspirational frames across several domains without requiring a designer to nominate only two literatures in advance. In the city-vibrancy example, a gardening and urban-farming topic prompts an idea for a community garden on vacant land, growing and selling produce. A paired response to a common topic centres on city, government and economic activity. The example shows a change in the proposed idea, not construction of a garden by the network. [NC-W023]

One experiment compares perceived promise of topics. Another asks workers to generate paired ideas from bridging and common topics, with other workers judging the results in two challenges. Novelty generally benefits, while quality findings are mixed and depend on the challenge and prompt. The authors thus connect a computational representation, a source of inspiration and an observed judgment of resulting ideas, with each stage retaining its own outcome. [NC-W023]

<!-- PDF page 466 -->

## S65 Literary and visual creation through constraint transformation and estrangement

S65   Literary and visual creation through constraint transformation and estrangement

A word, a sentence, an image or a way of attending can become material for deliberate transformation. The practices examined here include changing perception, suspending familiar control during writing, substituting words through a rule, following associations and assembling images taken from different settings. Their artistic purposes give the operations a particular direction. What is being generated may be a text, an image, a new relation to familiar material or a starting point for further work.

### Rimbaud and the cultivation of perception

Rimbaud and the cultivation of perception

Arthur Rimbaud's letter to Paul Demeny, written on 15 May 1871, places the transformation of the poet within the work of poetry. He calls for knowing and cultivating the self and for a sustained, reasoned disordering of the senses. The ambition is to reach what has not yet been apprehended and find a language capable of expressing it. The letter addresses a way of becoming a poet as well as the making of individual poems. [CRE-W014]

The programme joins experience to form. If perception reaches something unfamiliar, inherited ways of writing may fail to express it. Rimbaud's demand for new forms follows from that ambition. The poet is not simply asked to vary the surface of conventional verse while leaving the conditions of perception untouched. The creator's habits of sensing, interpreting and speaking become part of what is to be changed. [CRE-W014]

The letter also imagines a future of poetic work beyond its present participants and conventions, including women's future place as poets. Its rhetoric is expansive and extreme, and its practical object is an artistic life and language. The text's historical force lies partly in making those capacities a matter of deliberate cultivation. Written in 1871, the letter first appeared complete in print in 1912. [CRE-W014]

### Breton and the procedure of automatic writing

Breton and the procedure of automatic writing

André Breton's 1924 Manifesto of Surrealism includes explicit instructions for automatic writing. The writer first obtains materials and chooses a setting favorable to concentration. Breton asks for a receptive state, a departure from judgments about one's own or other people's talent, and rapid writing without a preconceived subject. The pace is intended to keep the writer from holding back and rereading what has just been written. [CRE-W015, “Composition surréaliste écrite”]

The sequence changes when ordinary control begins to return. If the writing falls silent or its continuation becomes too clear, Breton recommends breaking the line of development. After a word whose origin seems suspect, the writer can impose a fixed letter as the beginning of the next word. The arbitrary letter interferes with the expected continuation. A procedure intended to allow a flow therefore includes an intervention for restarting it. [CRE-W015, “Composition surréaliste écrite”]

Breton's account is concerned with the relationship between conscious supervision and expression. Preparing the place and materials, writing quickly, suspending rereading and disrupting an overly controlled continuation belong to one exercise. Removing immediate judgment does not mean that no conditions have been established. The conditions are directed toward changing what can emerge before the familiar act of approval or correction takes over. [CRE-W015]

The manifesto gives this practice its surrealist purpose and explanation. Breton treats the activity as a means of encountering thought and expression that ordinary literary monitoring can inhibit. The instructions make that claim available through an actual way of working. They also show how a writer can detect a change in the exercise and alter the procedure in response. [CRE-W015]

<!-- PDF page 467 -->

### Lescure and a rule that produces an unexpected text

Lescure and a rule that produces an unexpected text

Jean Lescure presented the S+7 procedure at an Oulipo meeting on 13 February 1961. It begins with an existing text and a chosen dictionary. Each noun is replaced by the seventh noun following it in that dictionary. The source supplies much of the grammatical frame, while the dictionary supplies the replacement vocabulary. The writer does not choose each new noun because it seems the best expression of an intended message. [CRE-W016]

The Oulipo account demonstrates the operation through a transformation of Baudelaire's L'Étranger into L'Étreinte. The question-and-answer pattern remains recognizable, but the successive nouns disturb what a reader expects the exchange to concern. The result invites another reading of an inherited form. Both the starting text and the dictionary matter: changing either changes what the counting rule encounters. [CRE-W016, example]

Once those inputs and the rule are fixed, the substitutions are determined. Their effect can be surprising without arising from a random draw. Creative decisions have partly moved to the choice of material and operation. The produced wording then becomes something to read, interpret and potentially develop. Cage's chance-selection procedures in S66 place the source of variation differently. [CRE-W016]

The extensions show the procedure itself becoming material for invention. Raymond Queneau applies related substitutions to adjectives, verbs and other grammatical categories. Another rule admits a replacement only if metrical or rhyme requirements are met. A simple instruction can thus be combined with further constraints that govern which candidate is accepted. [CRE-W016, Extensions]

Other variants alter the displacement number, change the kind of dictionary or construct reciprocal texts. In Jacques Jouet's example, one part is the S−7 of the other, while the other is its S+7. The two parts share a syntactic organization but exchange related vocabulary through the rule. The account develops a family of operations with specified inputs and relations, rather than an instruction to be novel in general. [CRE-W016, Extensions]

### Rodari and the word that sets other things moving

Rodari and the word that sets other things moving

Gianni Rodari opens Grammar of Fantasy, published in 1973, with the image of a stone entering a pond. It produces movements at several depths, disturbing things that had seemed separate. He uses the image to describe what can happen when a word enters the mind. Sounds, meanings, memories, images and earlier experiences become active together. The mind also intervenes, connecting, accepting and rejecting what arises. [CRE-W017, chapters 1–2]

His example begins with sasso, a stone. One path follows initial sounds; another follows rhyme; another follows meanings associated with stone and other materials. These are different ways to continue from the same word. Personal memory supplies another path. Rodari recalls a place, a friend, conversations and musical instruments. A word's usefulness as a starting point can therefore depend on the person who encounters it and the experiences available to that person. [CRE-W017, chapter 2]

A later association joins a brick to a song. Rodari develops the conjunction into a musical house whose parts can be sounded, then into a musical village. The image is not complete when the first unexpected pair appears. It can be expanded by asking what follows from the relation and letting remembered music, social experience and further images change the development. Rodari's account follows that movement closely enough to show a story becoming possible. [CRE-W017, chapter 2]

He then changes the form of the starting material. The letters S A S S O are written vertically, each supplying the initial of another word. One result suggests seven geese on a swing. A further attempt produces seven hundred lawyers playing seven hundred ocarinas. The second attempt develops material

<!-- PDF page 468 -->

already active in the exercise: seven becomes seven hundred, and geese helps prompt ocarinas. The formal positions remain the same while the material continues to accumulate associations. [CRE-W017, chapter 2]

The chapter supplies a repeatable operation without expecting the first output to be valuable. An initial word can be followed through sound and memory, split into letters, rebuilt as a sentence and developed into an image or story. Rodari distinguishes the educational purpose of such activity from using an imaginative task solely to rank children. His exercise is intended to make the capacities available to the participants themselves. [CRE-W017, chapter 2]

### Álvarez Rodríguez and the writing workshop

Álvarez Rodríguez and the writing workshop

Maritza Isabel Álvarez Rodríguez describes adapting Rodari's techniques for a university course in children's literature. Students are asked to produce texts through the techniques, rather than encounter them only as a theoretical topic. The workshop supplies prompts, a coordinator and other participants. The resulting activity joins the beginning of a text to reading, discussion and further work on what has been written. [CRE-W018]

Her account stresses an experimental relationship to language. Students attend to sound, images, oral expression and alternative ways of reading everyday experience. The prompt initiates activity, but revision and rewriting also belong to the workshop. The coordinator helps participants sustain writing and makes it possible to discuss the material they produce. [CRE-W018, characteristics of creative writing and workshop adaptation]

The article reports the course experience and argues that the arrangement helped students approach writing with less fear and develop expression. Its practical contribution includes this passage from a named technique to a teaching situation. Reading, speaking, generating and revising are organized around the production of texts for children. S70 develops other accounts of how creative methods are taught and assessed. [CRE-W018, conclusions and recommendations]

### Pérez Jiménez and the operations of image making

Pérez Jiménez and the operations of image making

Mauricio Pérez Jiménez distinguishes the material equipment of image production from the rules, decisions and intentions through which it is used. A camera or digital tool supplies possibilities, but a procedure determines what is done with them. Acquiring a technique also changes ways of seeing: isolating a detail, framing a subject, attending to a relation or imagining a transformation. [CRE-W019, pp. 72–75]

His discussion develops operations such as changing apparent size, combining events separated in time or space, reversing movement and altering its speed. A small detail can be emphasized until it stands for a larger event. Something motionless can be given movement, or an action can be slowed enough to invite a different perception of it. The artistic choice concerns both what is represented and how the technical operation transforms it. [CRE-W019, pp. 72–75]

The distinction between equipment and operation also makes room for purposes and attitudes. Identical equipment can support different work because the maker selects, combines and interprets differently. Pérez Jiménez explains the image as the result of a sequence involving an idea, material means and a developing representation. His account gives technically mediated creation an operative vocabulary rather than treating a new device as a creative method by itself. [CRE-W019, pp. 72–75]

<!-- PDF page 469 -->

### Adamowicz and the selection and assembly of images

Adamowicz and the selection and assembly of images

Elza Adamowicz's Surrealist Collage in Text and Image begins with the 1921 Paris exhibition of Max Ernst's work. Her historical account identifies materials taken from encyclopaedic plates, anatomical treatises, engineering diagrams, commercial catalogues and advertisements. Printed elements and photographs are cut and joined in new combinations. Words and inscriptions can participate in the work as well. [CRE-W046, pp. 1–3]

These operations move material out of the contexts in which it ordinarily has a recognizable use. A technical illustration can acquire a poetic role through its placement beside another image. Selection, combination and accompanying language alter what the familiar element can suggest. The material remains recognizable enough for its new relationship to have force. [CRE-W046, pp. 2–4]

Adamowicz examines the interpretations offered by Breton and Louis Aragon. Breton emphasizes the encounter of disparate realities and the disorientation it can produce. Aragon gives a different emphasis to the diversion of an image into a new role and to the relationship between literal and figurative meanings. Their interpretations are part of the history of what artists understood collage to make possible. [CRE-W046, pp. 3–5]

She also places collage beside automatism. Deliberate cutting and assembly and the flowing production of automatic writing become two significant modes in the development of surrealist practice. Their relationship does not erase the difference between their operations. Adamowicz gives both material process and intellectual interpretation enough detail to explain why joining fragments can concern a transformation of meaning, not merely an altered surface. [CRE-W046, pp. 4–5]

The sources in this section work on perception, words, images and the conditions of expression. Their procedures can be followed through particular changes to material and activity. The related performing practices in S66 extend the account to bodies, partners, scores and rehearsals.

<!-- PDF page 470 -->

## S66 Generating performance in music theater and choreography

S66   Generating performance in music theater and choreography

A performer may need a way to begin, a partner to respond to, a rule that redirects attention, or material that can be varied in rehearsal. The practices described here organize those conditions in different ways. Theater games make a shared problem available for action and observation. Choreographic work develops movement through images, imitation, discussion and recording. Chance composition specifies operations through which material becomes a score. Each account explains a practice in which generating something and learning how to work with it are closely connected.

### Spolin and the shared acting problem

Spolin and the shared acting problem

Viola Spolin's Improvisation for the Theater, first published in 1963, organizes learning around games that give actors a concrete problem. Its Point of Concentration is the focus that keeps participants working together. At an early stage it might concern a cup, a rope or a door. Later problems can involve more complex events. Spolin compares the focus to a ball in a game: participants attend to something they can act upon together, rather than continually assess themselves as performers. [CRE-W020, pp. 21–25]

The simplicity of the immediate task is deliberate. Acting involves many simultaneous relationships between body, voice, setting, partners and audience. Spolin divides this complexity into problems that can be experienced. A player can concentrate on the object or action while developing other capacities through participation. The teacher understands how the exercise fits within the larger work, but need not give the player a lecture on every capacity it is intended to develop. The focus supplies enough direction to act and enough openness to respond to what happens. [CRE-W020, pp. 21–25]

Mirror Exercise #1 shows how that arrangement works. Two players face each other. One initiates an ordinary activity such as washing or dressing; the other reflects the movements and expressions as a mirror. They later exchange roles. The task requires attention from head to foot. Spolin asks the observer to notice whether the reflecting player stays with the partner or anticipates a familiar sequence. Knowing what usually happens when someone applies makeup can become an obstacle if it replaces observation of what this person is doing now. [CRE-W020, pp. 60–61]

The initiating player has a different opportunity. Actions can vary in rhythm and inventiveness and can challenge the partner's attention. Spolin also suggests performing the exercise without telling the audience who initiates. Concealing that distinction intensifies the pair's concentration on one another. A small change to the conditions of presentation therefore alters how the exercise is played. Its parts include an activity, differentiated roles, a shared focus and an audience with something specific to observe. [CRE-W020, pp. 60–61]

Side coaching helps sustain the task while the action continues. Spolin recommends short, direct interventions that return attention to the problem: share the stage picture, make contact with an object, continue working. The teacher is responding to what is happening, rather than stopping the experience to deliver an explanation after every difficulty. The intervention must also preserve the nature of the game. A stream of commands directed toward the teacher's approval would replace the shared problem with a different one: satisfying the teacher. [CRE-W020, pp. 28–29]

Evaluation completes the arrangement. Players and observers ask what was actually communicated and whether the concentration was sustained. Spolin recommends questions about the acting problem rather than personal verdicts about a good or bad actor. The teacher joins this inquiry instead of supplying the entire judgment. The audience consequently has an active responsibility: watch closely enough to help the players understand what occurred. Acting, observing, coaching and evaluation become related ways of working on the same problem. [CRE-W020, pp. 25–29]

<!-- PDF page 471 -->

The discipline of the exercise is compatible with spontaneity in Spolin's account. A player does not have to invent every condition of an encounter before entering it. The task supplies a point of engagement, and its demands change as the other player acts. Her handbook develops this relationship through instructions, coaching suggestions and observations attached to particular exercises. The practical knowledge includes how to keep an exercise alive, not merely its opening rule. [CRE-W020, pp. 21–29, 60–61]

### Itani on similar exercises and different explanations

Itani on similar exercises and different explanations

Nobuhiko Itani's historical comparison of Spolin and Konstantin Stanislavski examines what can differ when an exercise looks similar. Both ask actors to work with objects that are not physically present. A performer must give an action enough detail for an absent object to become part of theatrical experience. Itani relates Spolin's space-object exercises to Stanislavski's work on action without objects, then examines the purposes attached to them. [CRE-W023, §§2.4–2.5]

In Itani's interpretation, Spolin emphasizes contact and present physical activity, while Stanislavski gives belief in the truth of the action a different explanatory role. The similarity of an instruction therefore does not settle its place within a teaching practice. Itani also discusses Spolin's resistance to deliberately recalling past emotions. Her body memory describes experience becoming available through present action, rather than a requirement to retrieve and display an earlier feeling. [CRE-W023, §§2.4–2.5]

This comparison gives a history to the relationship among exercise, attention and explanation. The physical action of handling an absent object can be taught within different accounts of what the actor is learning. Itani's analysis preserves both the overlap and the disagreement, including the distinction between avoiding forced emotional recall and excluding past experience altogether. [CRE-W023, §§2.4– 2.5]

### Waterhouse on making and learning Duo

Waterhouse on making and learning Duo

Elizabeth Waterhouse's Processing Choreography follows William Forsythe's Duo through archival rehearsal videos, interviews and her experience as a dancer. Her account moves between the creation of the piece and the practices through which dancers continued to perform and transmit it. The chronology of the 1996 creation begins with Forsythe developing movement while Jill Johnson and Regina van Berkel observe, imitate and repeat it. Recording is already part of the encounter: he checks that the camera is running as the material takes shape. [CRE-W021, chapter 10, pp. 221–224]

Imagery helps make a movement available to the dancers. A gesture can be described through a steering wheel, a suitcase or another familiar action. The image does not simply name an appearance to reproduce. It gives a direction for making and attending to movement. Waterhouse describes a moment in which Forsythe's steering-wheel image becomes a view over trees for van Berkel, while Johnson imagines something else. Their exchange can proceed with several images in play. What matters in the rehearsal is how those images help the dancers produce and recognize the movement. [CRE-W021, pp. 231–234]

The movement called showerhead receives particularly close attention. Dancers imagine the fingers moving around a circular shower dial. The action begins with an image that seems local to the hand, but its development involves shoulders, torso and both sides of the body. Waterhouse explains the twists and counter-twists through épaulement, the coordinated orientation of the upper body in ballet. The body is not held rigid while a hand draws a circle. The image invites movement that passes through a trained, responsive body. [CRE-W021, pp. 138–146]

Her discussion of Improvisation Technologies gives other examples of this relationship between an image and an operation. A dancer can imagine a line between the fingertips, extend or match lines with the arms, or write in space with different body parts. In the instructional videos, white lines make some of

<!-- PDF page 472 -->

that imagined geometry visible. The operations begin from knowledge familiar to ballet dancers, including points, lines, circles and planes, then use it to explore unfamiliar movement. Going backward or downward can enlarge a range that habitual movement would leave unused. [CRE-W021, pp. 143–146]

Waterhouse describes these procedures as ways to develop perception and movement rather than routines to reproduce verbatim. Her account of residual response gives the rest of the body an active place in what follows an initiated action. A movement can be deliberately begun and then developed through its physical consequences. Learning involves becoming sensitive to those consequences and coordinating them, as well as acquiring a recognizable shape. [CRE-W021, pp. 143–146]

The office rehearsals show another part of the creative work. Johnson and van Berkel study the recorded material together without Forsythe present. They alternate between watching the small viewing device and getting up to move. They ask where an action begins, which parts of the body participate and what paths they take. The video permits a developing movement to become something that can be inspected repeatedly. Their discussion, bodily attempts and occasional use of a mirror develop its details. [CRE-W021, pp. 234–235]

They also name phrases and make decisions within material that contains variants. Waterhouse recounts how seven phrases from the initial rehearsal became nine sequences as the dancers worked through the movement. Names help the dancers refer to parts and retain them. Forsythe's recorded comments sometimes indicate a preferred version, while other details become settled through the dancers' joint interpretation. Making a piece includes this passage from an improvised event to material that others can remember and perform. [CRE-W021, pp. 233–235]

The wider creation practice permits changes of position, reversals, restrictions and exceptions. Waterhouse's dancers describe an exploratory situation in which neither the final piece nor the precise path toward it is fully known in advance. Their existing skills and shared practices make it possible to continue under those conditions. The detailed Duo history gives this openness a concrete setting: people work with particular movements, images, recordings and one another over time. [CRE-W021, §4.5, pp. 115–117]

### Cage and the composition of chance

Cage and the composition of chance

In Silence, John Cage describes the procedures used to compose Music of Changes and Imaginary Landscape No. 4. The procedure begins with prepared possibilities. Charts provide elements for sounds, durations, dynamics, tempi and the number of events occurring together. Coin operations derived from the I Ching select among them. Three coins tossed six times yield a hexagram that can be related to one of sixty-four positions. The selection is put to work through the contents and organization of the charts. [CRE-W022, pp. 57–59]

The charts have different behaviors. Some are fixed; others change after an element has been used, allowing a new element to take its place. In the sound charts, silence is represented alongside sounds. A decision about how many events can occur together interacts with the durations and sounds selected for those events. The musical result arises through these connected selections. Chance enters a prepared compositional system whose different components have specific jobs. [CRE-W022, pp. 57–59]

The radio piece changes the relationship between selection and sounding material. Numbers on a tuning dial take the place of specified sounds. A selected position may yield a broadcast, static or silence. Cage accepts what occurs there. The chart can determine a setting while the broadcasting environment supplies what that setting produces. His account identifies the operation clearly enough to show how the composition engages a situation beyond the score. [CRE-W022, pp. 58–59]

<!-- PDF page 473 -->

Music for Piano 21–52 begins with imperfections in paper. Cage prepares a master page containing musical systems, then uses chance operations to determine how many sounds a page will contain. On a transparent sheet, he marks the corresponding number of imperfections. Registering that sheet against the master allows the points to be converted into musical notation. Further operations determine clefs and characteristics of the tones. A material feature that would ordinarily be ignored becomes an input to composition. [CRE-W022, pp. 60–61]

The procedure combines incidental material with deliberate conventions. The paper supplies points, but the master page supplies their musical interpretation. Decisions about notation and playing methods turn those points into something a pianist can use. Chance operations also work within ranges related to performance difficulty. The process is therefore describable as a sequence: prepare the field, select and mark points, map them onto notation, and determine further features through specified operations. [CRE-W022, pp. 60–61]

Cage also states what remains open for performers. The pieces may be played alone or together, with or without other pieces, and with possible overlap. Durations and dynamics remain free within the conditions described. A programmed concert length can still be maintained through advance calculation and a stopwatch. Determination during composition and freedom during performance occupy different places in this account. Cage's stated aim of freeing continuity from personal taste is expressed through these particular arrangements of choice, material and performance. [CRE-W022, pp. 60–61]

### Different purposes for teaching improvisation

Different purposes for teaching improvisation

Eeva Siljamäki and Panagiotis Kanellopoulos review music-education research to ask what improvisation is understood to be for. Their analysis of seventy-seven selected articles identifies five visions and eleven approaches. They examine how those views inform an educator's immediate response to learners. A teaching decision about an improvised sound can depend on whether the aim is expression, musical understanding, stylistic accomplishment or the generation of material. [CRE-W024, Method; Results, research question 2]

One vision encourages an open relationship to sound and questions inherited criteria about what counts as music. Another treats improvisation as a way to cultivate expression and social relationships. A third uses it to learn musical structures and skills. In that setting, manipulating tonal and rhythmic material can help learners understand conventions through use, rather than encounter them only as an explanation. The same broad word, improvisation, can therefore identify activities with different educational directions. [CRE-W024, Results, visions I–III]

A fourth vision emphasizes expertise within a musical tradition. Students learn building blocks and stylistic conventions and acquire the capacity to vary them fluently. A fifth emphasizes invention, giving improvisation a place in discovering material for composition. Faithfulness to a tradition and discovery of unfamiliar material can each organize an exercise, but they do not ask the teacher or learner to attend to precisely the same thing. The review makes those purposes available for examination through its map of the literature. [CRE-W024, Results, visions IV–V]

The performing practices in these accounts include setting a problem, sustaining attention, generating movement, preparing a compositional field and choosing how a learner will participate. S41 develops other aspects of shared skilled practice and ensemble coordination. Here the games, rehearsals and scores show how particular working conditions become part of making the performance itself.

## S114 Public speaking, rhetoric and audience judgment

S114   Public speaking, rhetoric and audience judgment

### What a speaker can furnish

What a speaker can furnish

In the Greek text of the Rhetoric, Aristotle distinguishes evidence already available from means of persuasion a speaker can construct. He differentiates the character the speaker conveys, the hearer’s disposition and demonstration or apparent demonstration in the speech. This last distinction makes room for an address to affect judgment without settling whether its case is true. The University of Geneva’s historical account places instruction in these arts in settings such as advocacy, where the speaker has to address a particular audience about a disputed matter. [T16-W001] [T16-W004]

### Preparing speech for an occasion

Preparing speech for an occasion

Quintilian’s eleventh book treats suitability as a property of speech in its circumstances. Elaborate language can be unsuitable to a small case, just as a light manner can be wrong for a grave one. The account of delivery treats voice and gesture as parts of the speaker’s practice. A written draft can establish the words available to the speaker. How a voice is used or a gesture timed belongs to the performance for which the author offers instruction. [T16-W002]

The received Chinese text of the Guiguzi describes opening and closing in persuasive exchange. Its opening chapter considers when to encourage another person to disclose something and when to close or withhold. The interlocutor’s words give the speaker material from which to consider intent. The chapter develops its own questions about exchange and disclosure. Its traditional attribution and the dating of the received text require separate historical judgment. [T16-W003]

### An address in manuscript and circulation

An address in manuscript and circulation

Helen Dalrymple distinguishes an early draft of the Gettysburg Address from the manuscript prepared for publication in Autograph Leaves in 1864. The Library of Congress describes the occasion as the dedication of a military cemetery on 19 November 1863. Edward Everett had been invited to deliver the main oration. Lincoln was asked to follow him with brief remarks formally setting apart the grounds. [T16-W005] [T16-W006]

In the Hay manuscript, the passage that begins by referring to the dedication of part of the battlefield turns to the soldiers who fought there. Lincoln says their actions have already consecrated the ground beyond the speakers’ power to add to it. He ends by asking the living to dedicate themselves to the unfinished work. Within the text, the object of dedication shifts from the burial ground to the work left to the living. [T16-W006]

The next day Everett wrote to Lincoln that the short remarks had come closer to the central idea of the occasion than he felt his own long oration had. He singled out their simplicity and fitness to the occasion. His letter records the judgment of the speaker who preceded Lincoln. [T16-W007]
