## S67 Incubation attention and bodily activity

S67   Incubation attention and bodily activity

Setting a problem aside can be part of working on it. The interval may contain rest, an undemanding activity or another demanding task, and the return can concern the same problem or a new one. Walking changes another condition of thinking: what the body is doing while a person generates a response. The studies in this section make these arrangements explicit and examine what changes in the resulting work. Poincaré's account in S64 supplies an earlier history of preparation, interruption and renewed mathematical effort.

### Sio and Ormerod and the structure of an incubation interval

Sio and Ormerod and the structure of an incubation interval

Ut Na Sio and Thomas Ormerod's 2009 meta-analysis examines experiments in which people return to a problem after an interval. Their selection contains twenty-nine publications, many reporting several experiments or conditions. The analysis constructs 117 comparisons between an incubation condition and a control condition, adjusting the allocation of shared controls. [CRE-W026, Method]

The review finds a positive average effect of incubation and asks how the arrangement of work relates to it. Preparation matters because the person has already encountered a particular problem before leaving it. The intervening task then occupies the interval in a particular way. A return to that problem is the occasion on which an incubation effect can be observed. [CRE-W026, Results]

Problem type, preparation and the demands of the intervening task differentiate the results. Highly demanding intervening activity tends to be associated with smaller benefits. The relation between low-demand activity and rest varies with the tasks being examined, and preparation time is related to  outcomes differently across problem types. The review gives the interval contents and the earlier work a substantive place in the explanation. [CRE-W026, moderator analyses]

Incubation is consequently studied as a sequence, not simply as the passage of time. A task is attempted, an interval changes the person's activity, and performance is examined on return. This structure allows different explanations to be compared and makes it possible to ask which part of the arrangement contributes to an improvement. [CRE-W026, Results and Discussion]

### Baird and colleagues and returning to the same material

Baird and colleagues and returning to the same material

Benjamin Baird and colleagues investigate the contents of the interval through an unusual-uses task. Participants first generate uses for objects. The intervening conditions include a demanding task, an undemanding task and rest, alongside a no-break comparison. The break lasts twelve minutes in the interval conditions. Participants subsequently work on previously encountered objects and on new ones. [CRE-W025, Method]

The undemanding condition uses a simple response task, while the demanding condition requires maintaining and updating information. Both occupy participants with something other than the creative problem. They nevertheless make different demands on attention. Including new objects in the later task also helps separate an effect on material already encountered from a general improvement in generating responses to anything. [CRE-W025, Method]

The undemanding task leads to greater improvement in uniqueness on the previously encountered problems than the other conditions. The same advantage does not appear for new problems, and the finding is distinct from simply producing more responses. What changes is connected to returning to material on which work has already begun. [CRE-W025, Results]

<!-- PDF page 476 -->

Participants in the undemanding condition also report more mind wandering, without reporting more explicitly directed thought about the unusual-uses problems. The authors connect that pattern with their incubation result. The study gives a concrete example of an interval that helps creative work while attention is engaged in a modest external task. It distinguishes the condition that was assigned from the mental activity participants later describe. [CRE-W025, Results and Discussion]

### Ritter and Dijksterhuis and explanations of what happens during a break

Ritter and Dijksterhuis and explanations of what happens during a break

Simone Ritter and Ap Dijksterhuis review several explanations of incubation. A break can allow recovery from fatigue, weaken misleading associations, change a mental set or create an opportunity to encounter a useful environmental cue. Their own argument also gives active unconscious processing a role. These accounts describe different changes that could occur while direct attention is elsewhere. [CRE-W027, “Mechanisms Underlying Incubation Effects”]

The review examines studies that vary whether people expect to return to a problem. In one arrangement, participants receive a task and then perform another activity before making a later response. In a comparison condition, participants believe the original task has ended. Both groups can be distracted, but only one retains an active problem-solving goal. The contrast asks whether having a goal during the interval contributes something beyond distraction itself. [CRE-W027, mechanisms section]

The authors also distinguish generating ideas from selecting among ideas. A period without direct deliberation could affect one of those activities differently from the other. Their discussion of studies with and without misleading cues likewise bears on an explanation through forgetting: an improvement where no misleading cue was supplied requires further explanation. These are ways to give competing accounts different empirical implications. [CRE-W027, mechanisms section]

Ritter and Dijksterhuis favour an active contribution from unconscious processes. Their review makes that position part of a developed argument about goals, association, selection and the contents of the interval. The earlier finding that a break helped is a starting point for those questions. The proposed mechanism is presented through the comparisons on which the authors rely. [CRE-W027]

### Oppezzo and Schwartz and thinking while walking

Oppezzo and Schwartz and thinking while walking

Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz's fourth experiment separates walking from moving through an outdoor setting. Forty adults are assigned to sitting indoors, walking on a treadmill indoors, being pushed outdoors in a wheelchair or walking outdoors. The moving-wheelchair condition supplies changing outdoor stimulation without requiring the participant to walk. [CRE-W028, Experiment 4]

The task asks participants to generate symbolic analogies for three prompts within five minutes. An appropriate response must express an analogy rather than merely restate the prompt or identify a surface feature. The scoring then distinguishes novelty from quality. High-quality analogies are specific, reach a relatively distant domain and preserve the relevant relational structure. [CRE-W028, Experiment 4, Method]

Walking produces more novel high-quality analogies whether it occurs indoors or outdoors. Ninety-five percent of those who walk produce at least one such analogy, compared with fifty percent of those who sit in the conditions combined. When lower-quality novel analogies are included, outdoor movement also contributes to novelty. The different measures reveal different relationships with bodily activity and surroundings. [CRE-W028, Experiment 4, Results]

The paper's earlier experiments distinguish divergent production from a convergent association task. Its developed account therefore concerns particular kinds of creative response, rather than an undifferentiated improvement in thought. The analogy experiment gives a particularly clear case: a

<!-- PDF page 477 -->

person receives the same kind of prompt while the body and environment are arranged differently, and the resulting relations among ideas are assessed. [CRE-W028, Experiments 1–4]

These accounts develop several ways of examining activity around a problem. Preparation and return organize work over time; the intervening task changes attention; bodily movement changes a condition under which responses are generated. Their detailed comparisons give substance to the intervals and activities that a brief description of inspiration can leave unexplained.

<!-- PDF page 478 -->

## S83 Serendipity and the cultivation of unexpected discovery

S83   Serendipity and the cultivation of unexpected discovery

### Accident, sagacity and an unexpected finding

Accident, sagacity and an unexpected finding

Walpole introduced serendipity in his letter to Horace Mann of 28 January 1754 while recounting a heraldic discovery associated with a portrait. His explanation joins accidental encounter to sagacity. The princes’ inference about an animal from traces illustrates interpretive ability: what matters is recognizing what an incidental observation may reveal. Walpole explicitly excludes finding what one was already seeking, giving his usage a boundary that later accounts do not all retain. [NC-W024]

Merton places unexpected observations within a larger argument about the functions of empirical research. Research can initiate, reformulate, redirect and clarify theory as well as test a hypothesis. His serendipity pattern concerns an observation that is unexpected, anomalous relative to an existing expectation, and strategic for a broader theoretical question. Strategic value depends partly on what an observer recognizes in a particular discrepancy. [NC-W025]

In the Craftown inquiry, parents reported easier access to adolescent child minders and greater participation in community organizations. Yet the housing community had fewer adolescents relative to young children than the places residents had left. The numerical discrepancy prevented an apparently satisfactory explanation from closing the inquiry. Further interviews suggested that more adolescents were known and trusted in the new community. They were therefore available as usable helpers within the parents’ social relations. [NC-W025]

Merton uses the sequence to develop an account of perception shaped by social relationships. The useful observation is not simply that parents made a surprising statement. Their statement, the conflicting demographic comparison and the renewed interviews together support a different interpretation of what availability means in the community. The developed account shows an empirical finding redirecting a theoretical question. [NC-W025]

### What was being sought, and what was found?

What was being sought, and what was found?

Yaqub’s taxonomy separates the initial intent of inquiry from the eventual role of a result. Walpolian serendipity occurs when targeted search answers a different problem. Mertonian serendipity reaches the intended goal by an unexpected route. Bushian serendipity involves untargeted inquiry serving an existing need, while Stephanian serendipity concerns a solution whose useful problem emerges later. These are different relations between search and use, rather than degrees of good fortune. [NC-W028]

The mechanisms he considers are a separate set of distinctions. Theory-led expectations can make an anomaly conspicuous; observer-led tools and routines can make it visible; an error can expose an unfamiliar effect; and a network can supply information, collaborators or resources. These mechanisms can occur together. Networks can also sustain expectations that make a new interpretation harder to entertain. [NC-W028]

His archival exercise assembled 118 examples to develop ideal types using historical plausibility. The time window matters to the resulting classification. An episode can appear untargeted when preceding years of inquiry are omitted, and one result can acquire several uses much later. His retrospective discussion of Goodyear illustrates how the account changes with the period and purpose considered. The taxonomy therefore asks both what was being sought and when the relation between a result and a problem is recognized. [NC-W028]

<!-- PDF page 479 -->

### Informed attention and freedom of inquiry

Informed attention and freedom of inquiry

Catellin and Loty argue that reducing serendipity to chance conceals the activity of attending to a surprising fact and imagining an interpretation. Knowledge and receptivity, reason and imagination work together in their account. Their broad claim is that every scientific discovery has this character, including the imaginative formation of a hypothesis that later guides a deliberate search. Their neutrino illustration separates an imaginative response to an anomaly from subsequent detection of what the hypothesis predicts. [NC-W029]

Indisciplinarity starts from a person’s question and the needs of inquiry rather than a problem’s assigned location within a discipline. It draws on disciplined knowledge and self-discipline while resisting conceptual or institutional authority that obstructs investigation. The term consequently concerns the relation between inquiry and its governing frames, rather than merely an organization containing several departments. [NC-W029]

The relation works in both directions. A surprising observation can make departure from an accepted frame necessary, while freedom to reconsider the frame can make an observation surprising in the first place. Their broad argument about discovery differs from Walpole’s exclusion of finding a sought result. Preserving those positions separately shows what each author is trying to explain. [NC-W029]

### From an encounter to a useful connection

From an encounter to a useful connection

Makri and Blandford interviewed 28 researchers without first prescribing a definition of serendipity. Their model connects a need to something encountered, projects possible value, follows the connection and reflects on what results. Encounter and recognition need not coincide. Perceived usefulness can change during pursuit, and unexpectedness, insight and value can be matters of degree. [NC-W027]

A researcher struggling to frame a thesis on digital music encoding encountered Latour’s account of inscriptions during a broad search. Days later, a connection with the findings became apparent. Close reading then helped develop the argument that supplied the thesis’s narrative structure. The episode joins exposure, delayed recognition, interpretation and drafting: the useful result is achieved through those later activities as well as the encounter. [NC-W027]

Another researcher first found a website about internal child trafficking, then unexpectedly sat beside its author at a conference lunch. The earlier encounter made the person relevant. Continued discussion and a subsequent meeting helped refine a PhD subject and produced collaboration and further contacts. The chain would be incompletely described as either a fortunate search result or a lucky seating arrangement on its own. [NC-W027]

The two histories give the model different temporal forms. In one, an encountered idea becomes useful after an interval and is developed through writing. In the other, prior information prepares a later personal encounter, which becomes productive through follow-up. The participants’ accounts supply the activities through which the authors explain a useful connection taking shape. [NC-W027]

### Practices for making one’s own luck

Practices for making one’s own luck

Makri, Blandford, Woods, Sharples and Maxwell asked fourteen creative professionals about practices they believed encouraged unexpected useful connections. Reported activities include varying routines, observing, making mental space, relaxing boundaries, drawing on previous experience, looking for patterns and acting on opportunities. The study distinguishes these reported practices from the researchers’ proposals for digital support. [NC-W030]

<!-- PDF page 480 -->

The composer’s Fallen Angel episode starts with an intended piece about Lucifer. During a journey from Angel to Highgate, an advertisement showing an eye recalls peacock-feather imagery. The descent and station names connect with the story. The journey subsequently becomes a structure for the work, including film recorded along the route. The piece is performed, and the composer reports strong responses. Preparation, imagery and the encountered route develop into a particular artistic form. [NC-W030]

The authors’ design suggestions support activities within such histories. Capture and revisiting can preserve material before its possible use is understood. Exploratory displays can help someone form patterns, while follow-up facilities can support development of an idea or contact. The connection with external memory is practical: something encountered now may matter when another problem or interpretation becomes available later. [NC-W030]

### An unexpected model for a library service

An unexpected model for a library service

Trindade and Vechiato combine questionnaire responses from 51 librarians with one returned diary record. A respondent describes watching television images of Black Friday crowds and adapting the promotional form to a library offer: one-month loans for all categories of user. The service is announced online, and the respondent finds a crowded library at opening. The reported episode connects an observed activity in another setting with a specific change in a lending offer. [NC-W032]

The diary exercise asked for a problem, encounter, trigger and possible discovery. Its returned record instead mainly described benchmarking, sketches and discussions in redesigning communication and online registration. The authors observe that it did not identify a distinct unexpected discovery. The distinction is informative because useful service development can be reported in detail without exhibiting the unexpected trigger that the instrument sought. Their proposed relation between serendipity, creativity and innovation is an interpretation developed alongside those observations. [NC-W032]

### Recognizing and developing a possibility in an organization

Recognizing and developing a possibility in an organization

Busch’s systematic review proposes agency, surprise and value as necessary conditions for serendipity. In his model, an unplanned trigger becomes meaningful through association; materialization enacts a valuable possibility. The trigger and the association may occur together or develop over time. The account gives pursuit a role alongside noticing, and treats the process and its related outcome together. [NC-W026]

His potato-washing-machine illustration follows a customer complaint into a different interpretation. Washing potatoes damages ordinary machines. Employees recognize a possible application, and a dirt filter helps develop a product for that use. The complaint changes from an account of misuse into information about an activity a machine could be redesigned to support. Interpretation is followed by a construction that makes the newly perceived use practicable. [NC-W026]

Organizational conditions can support different parts of this development. Interaction across perspectives makes unfamiliar interpretations available. A meaningful but not excessively narrow problem formulation leaves room for them. Permission to express an incomplete idea and access to people or resources can help a possibility be pursued after it is noticed. These conditions concern encounters, interpretation and development through different activities. [NC-W026]

Busch combines sensemaking and event-based theory with a quantum-inspired vocabulary of potentiality and materialization. That vocabulary belongs to his conceptual account of possibilities and their realization. His theory stands alongside the other definitions and histories as an ambitious source contribution, with its own proposed boundary around agency, surprise and value. [NC-W026]

<!-- PDF page 481 -->

### A community in which needs and partners emerge

A community in which needs and partners emerge

Busch and Barkema’s longitudinal study examines the Nairobi incubator they call T-Hub. Fifty-one months of interviews, observation and documents follow a setting in which entrepreneurs’ needs, markets and potential collaborators change. A fixed matching service cannot specify every useful connection in advance. The authors examine how a community can make emerging needs and relationships easier to recognize and develop. [NC-W031]

Cultivating reframing legitimizes changing an idea in response to information. Elevating commitment develops trust and reasons to help other members. Agile platform design adjusts seating, shared places and events. Elevating emerging opportunities adapts partnerships and support as possibilities become clearer. Community-enabling leadership listens and lets members contribute to shaping the community. These named conditions are concrete parts of the authors’ process interpretation. [NC-W031]

One reported encounter places a person with relevant health software near a social enterprise communicating with mothers, opening an application in day-care settings. Other accounts concern finding a collaborator before recognizing that one was needed. Introductions, training and user-research support can then help develop the relationship; some histories also involve investment. The shared place supplies encounters, while the surrounding activity supports what follows them. [NC-W031]

The process includes entrepreneurial agency and feedback. Members interpret what a contact may make possible, and the community can change its support as their needs develop. The authors’ account therefore concerns both emerging relations and an organization capable of responding to them, rather than the presence of a social space alone. [NC-W031]

### Learning to arrange flexible matches

Learning to arrange flexible matches

张颖颖 and 王进富 study three orchestration events at 中科创星: project roadshows, an ecosystem-strategy event and industrial matchmaking. Interviews, documents and participation support their  account of how an entrepreneurial platform develops alertness to connections between enterprises and resources. Need and value may become clearer during the activity rather than being fully specified beforehand. [NC-W033]

In the roadshow case, staff examine other practices and elicit members’ needs. They circulate and interpret possible forms with stakeholders, judge them against investment conditions and the platform’s own capabilities, and create an organizational structure and procedures. Search, interpretation, judgment and institutionalization name connected activities through which a possible arrangement becomes an operating one. [NC-W033]

The relations also feed back. Interpretation can redirect the search, and an institutionalized practice shapes later searches. The study’s process explains the formation of an organizational capacity to arrange flexible matches. Its events and learning activities provide a different unit of analysis from an individual noticing an unfamiliar item, while keeping the development of a possibility visible. [NC-W033]

### Making overlooked possibilities visible

Making overlooked possibilities visible

高橋菜奈子 and colleagues compare five virtual bookshelf configurations through gaze measures and the choice of unfamiliar books participants would like to read. Twenty-five people participate across the experiments, with only three taking part in all environments. The configurations change vertical placement, show covers lower down, or use very tall and cylindrical shelves. The arrangement changes what a visitor encounters within the same collection. [NC-W034]

<!-- PDF page 482 -->

Reversing positions changes the books selected. Showing covers lower down draws attention to an otherwise less-noticed region. Tall and cylindrical arrangements do not distribute attention uniformly. Subject interest and visibility both contribute to selection, so a display feature can change exposure without producing a single even pattern of browsing. [NC-W034]

The measured outcomes are gaze and immediate unfamiliar-book choice. Those observations locate a concrete point at which an interface can affect an encounter: what becomes visible, noticed and selected for possible reading. They complement the histories of interpretation and pursuit by examining how the field of available possibilities is presented. [NC-W034]

<!-- PDF page 483 -->

## S52 Generating alternatives and organizing exploration

S52   Generating alternatives and organizing exploration

Engineering often requires discovering a possible response before its merits can be assessed. The work includes recognizing a problem differently, producing genuinely different candidates, testing them and deciding when to commit. The sources in this section examine how examples, discussion, representations, feedback and organizational learning affect that work. Their procedures range from short individual design tasks to the allocation of resources across an organization.

Several neighboring accounts address different parts of the problem. Alexander's treatment in S08 preserves the inventive work of general design; TRIZ and facilitated problem-structuring methods appear in S44. Ashby's selection and regulatory variety are developed in S03. Baldwin's modular options in S07 and the flexibility accounts in S34 concern retaining choices that can be exercised later. Here the emphasis is on how alternatives arise and how exploration is organized before a choice becomes settled.

### Jansson and Smith: an example can constrain designs without reducing their number

Jansson and Smith: an example can constrain designs without reducing their number

David Jansson and Steven Smith's 1991 experiments examine design fixation: adherence to a limited set of ideas that constrains conceptual design. They ask whether an example supplied with a task can restrict the designs people produce, even when they have been asked for many possible solutions. Their procedure compares participants who receive a problem alone with participants who receive the same problem and an illustrative design. Similarity to selected features of that example supplies a way to observe restriction that a simple count of sketches might miss. [OI-W015, pp. 3–4]

In the bicycle-rack experiment, 25 senior mechanical-engineering students were randomly divided between these conditions. The task called for a rack that would be easy to mount, avoid damage and accommodate different bicycles and cars. The example showed a roof-mounted design with suction cups and rails supporting the tires. Students who saw it produced approximately the same number of designs as the control group, but used its characteristic features more often. Suction cups appeared in 54 percent of their designs, compared with 6 percent in the control condition. The quantity of output concealed a substantial difference in the kinds of solution considered. [OI-W015, pp. 5–6, table 1]

Other tasks introduced clearly undesirable features. In the measuring-device task, the example failed to offer continuous adjustment or protection against overflow, both pertinent to the requirements. In a spill-proof cup task, the sample used a straw and mouthpiece despite instructions excluding them, and its  construction could leak. The groups shown examples again reproduced more of their features, including defects. The cup experiment also assessed flexibility across approaches and originality relative to other participants' designs; both measures were lower in the example condition. Merely asking for multiple designs did not ensure that the underlying approach changed. [OI-W015, pp. 6–9, tables 2–3]

The fourth experiment involved thirteen professional engineers and a device for taking measurements and samples along the intestinal tract. The example used a cable and control box, with an opening at the front of the device. Engineers exposed to it incorporated those features more often than the comparison group. This small professional sample extended the investigation beyond students, while remaining a brief task with a deliberately limited problem. [OI-W015, pp. 9–10, table 4]

Jansson and Smith retain a difficulty important to the interpretation of their experiment: prior knowledge is indispensable to design. Learning from an earlier design and becoming unable to consider a relevant alternative are different things. They ask about useful features, long-term experience and more complex tasks, leaving the conditions of beneficial and harmful influence open. The work demonstrates a barrier under specified conditions and provides a method for examining it; the discussion does not supply a validated general procedure for eliminating it. [OI-W015, p. 10]

<!-- PDF page 484 -->

### Ritchey: organize combinations through dimensions and consistency judgments

Ritchey: organize combinations through dimensions and consistency judgments

Tom Ritchey's account of general morphological analysis begins by identifying dimensions of a problem and possible conditions within each dimension. A configuration combines one condition from each. The dimensions can concern technical properties, financial arrangements, policy aims or ethical commitments, so the representation does not require every difference to be expressed as a numerical quantity. The first work is therefore defining what matters and specifying meaningful alternatives within each dimension. The account first appeared in 2002 and was revised in 2013. [OI-W014, pp. 1–4]

The resulting morphological field can contain many combinations that nobody would have listed unaided. In Ritchey's reduced teaching example, six dimensions contain four, four, four, three, three and four conditions, producing 2,304 formal configurations. This is a count of combinations inside the defined field. It does not mean that 2,304 policies were implemented, evaluated or found workable. Defining a field makes a particular range of possibilities explicit while retaining the judgment that selected its dimensions and conditions. [OI-W014, pp. 4–5]

Cross-consistency assessment reduces that range. Participants consider pairs of conditions from different dimensions and judge whether they can coexist. A configuration containing a rejected pair can then be excluded. The procedure records the judgments used to obtain the remaining configurations, allowing later inspection of how the result arose. Ritchey distinguishes logical contradiction, empirical incompatibility and normative objections, arguing that judgments about what is possible should not be silently collapsed into judgments about what is desirable. The assessments still require people with relevant knowledge and the ability to make disagreements explicit. [OI-W014, pp. 5–7]

His shelter-policy example concerns Sweden's reconsideration of a civil-defense system after the Cold War. The field includes geographical priorities, functional priorities, crowding, new construction, maintenance and the general philosophy governing provision. A policy of equal shelter quality for everyone conflicts, in the illustrated assessment, with selectively prioritizing some geographical areas. Selecting a condition as an input lets participants inspect which other conditions remain consistent with it. The representation supports investigation of the implications of a commitment, as well as the discovery of previously unlisted combinations. [OI-W014, pp. 4–7, figs. 2–5]

The method's operative result is a set of configurations consistent with recorded judgments. It does not simulate their consequences or resolve political choices through arithmetic. Software helps manage combinations and display the implications of selected conditions, while the definition of the problem and the consistency assessments remain substantive work. Ritchey's claims about traceability and the value of the method are methodological arguments illustrated through applications. They do not amount to a controlled comparison showing that the resulting policies outperform alternatives. [OI-W014, pp. 6–8]

### Diehl and Stroebe: giving everyone a chance to speak is a production constraint

Diehl and Stroebe: giving everyone a chance to speak is a production constraint

Michael Diehl and Wolfgang Stroebe's 1987 study investigates why interacting brainstorming groups can produce fewer ideas than an equivalent number of people working independently. Their comparison is between an actual group and a nominal group constructed by pooling independent contributions and removing duplicates. A four-person nominal group's output is not the output of one person. Holding the session length constant gives both arrangements the same total person-time, making the organization of interaction a possible explanation for the difference. [OI-W012, pp. 497–501]

Four experiments examine proposed explanations including reduced effort when assessment is collective, fear of evaluation and production blocking. Blocking occurs when one person's opportunity to express an idea depends on somebody else finishing. The first experiments varied assessment and evaluation conditions. These changes affected productivity, but did not remove the large difference between actual

<!-- PDF page 485 -->

and nominal groups. The findings therefore required an explanation beyond attributing all losses to unwillingness to contribute or fear of criticism. [OI-W012, pp. 499–505]

The fourth experiment made the turn-taking restriction explicit. People in separate rooms used microphones and a light display indicating whether another person was speaking. In blocking conditions, they were to wait until the lights permitted them to speak. One condition retained the restriction while preventing participants from hearing others' ideas. Another allowed participants to ignore the lights and speak whenever they had an idea. Individual assessment was retained across the conditions. This arrangement separated the opportunity to speak from exposure to another person's contribution. [OI-W012, pp. 505–506]

The restricted conditions produced fewer ideas even when participants could not hear one another. Removing the restriction brought output close to the independent control. In that experiment, the mean pooled output of four people working independently was 106 nonredundant ideas, compared with about 56 for an actual four-person group. The result supports production blocking as an important mechanism in those short sessions. It does not by itself identify whether a waiting person's difficulty arose from memory, disrupted development of an idea, motivation or some combination of processes. [OI-W012, pp. 506–508, table 5]

The resources in the comparison matter. Giving an interacting group several times longer would increase its total person-time. Moreover, idea counts, the number of good ideas and average quality are different measures; the later experiments concentrated on counts. The authors suggest independent generation followed by discussion and evaluation, but that combined procedure was not the treatment tested in these experiments. Their participants and brief prompts also differ from an established expert team working over months. The paper identifies a cost of organizing generation around one shared speaking channel and supplies controlled ways to examine it. [OI-W012, pp. 501, 507–508]

### Nemeth and colleagues: criticism and generation need not be separate stages

Nemeth and colleagues: criticism and generation need not be separate stages

Charlan Nemeth, Marie Personnaz, Bernard Personnaz and Jack Goncalo's 2003 working paper tests an instruction frequently associated with brainstorming: participants should avoid criticizing one another's ideas. The authors contrast it with instructions encouraging debate and criticism, and with a minimal condition giving only the task. Their question is whether the attempt to remove evaluation can also remove an interaction that stimulates new thinking. The manipulated object is the instruction governing a discussion, rather than whether every participant agrees with the others. [OI-W008, printed pp. 10–12]

Groups worked on reducing traffic congestion, with one participant recording ideas while the others discussed them. The discussion lasted twenty minutes. Afterward, people separately recorded ideas they had considered but not expressed and new ideas occurring after the discussion. This extended the observation beyond the public record of the meeting. An idea absent from that record could have been withheld, crowded out or developed only afterward; the two individual questions attempted to distinguish those possibilities in the participants' reports. [OI-W008, printed pp. 11–14]

The study used samples in Berkeley and Paris. Debate instructions produced more group ideas than minimal instructions in each sample. A direct comparison between debate and conventional brainstorming instructions was less decisive for ideas spoken during the session. In the combined analysis, debate was superior on the authors' total-production measure, which combined a share of the group output with the individual's subsequent contributions. The pattern therefore depends on which output is counted. It is stronger evidence for attending to discussion and its aftermath than for claiming that every instance of criticism improves every measure of creativity. [OI-W008, printed pp. 13–19]

The authors interpret their findings through the stimulating effects of dissent and competing views. Their procedure encouraged criticism of ideas within a short task; it did not manipulate retaliation by a

<!-- PDF page 486 -->

superior or the consequences of challenging an established organizational commitment. This makes its relevance different from the silence and voice accounts in S51. Its substantive contribution concerns how the terms of discussion can affect the production of ideas, including ideas that become available after the discussion has ended. [OI-W008, printed pp. 17–19]

### Dow and colleagues: make several prototypes before receiving feedback

Dow and colleagues: make several prototypes before receiving feedback

Steven Dow and colleagues' 2010 journal article compares two ways of distributing the same amount of prototyping and critique. In the serial condition, a designer made one prototype, received feedback and continued to the next. In the parallel condition, a designer first made three alternatives and received feedback on them, then made two more and received another round of feedback. Both conditions produced five prototypes followed by a final design, with equal creation time and the same amount of descriptive critique. Parallel here means developing several alternatives before feedback; it does not mean assigning different prototypes to a team of workers. [OI-W013, pp. 18:5–18:10]

Thirty-three participants completed the task of designing graphic advertisements for the same client. They were nonprofessional designers using a common unfamiliar tool, with assignment balanced for prior experience and gender. The final advertisements were assessed through a live online campaign and by independent client and professional judges. Other raters assessed similarity among each participant's designs. The study thus separated several outcomes: response to the advertisement, judged quality, variation among prototypes and the designer's confidence in performing the task. [OI-W013, pp. 18:5– 18:13]

The parallel condition performed better on click-through rate and expert ratings. Exposure must be included in reading the campaign results because the advertising system changed how often advertisements appeared. During the first five days, when aggregate exposure was approximately balanced, the parallel advertisements received 44 clicks from 79,800 impressions and the serial advertisements 26 clicks from 79,658 impressions. The paper also reports higher expert ratings and greater design diversity in the parallel condition. The live response and the expert ratings were distinct criteria and did not simply reproduce one ranking. [OI-W013, pp. 18:11–18:14]

The authors propose several explanations. Seeing alternatives can make the differences among criticisms easier to understand, while attachment to any one prototype may be reduced when several are available. Serial refinement can instead preserve the assumptions of an early design through successive improvements. The experimental comparison changed the schedule of work and feedback as a package. It did not independently establish the causal contribution of each proposed psychological mechanism. Nor did it show that greater diversity necessarily produced higher quality: more experienced participants could produce less diverse work while achieving better results. [OI-W013, pp. 18:14–18:18]

The task was short, inexpensive and allowed consequences to be measured relatively quickly. The authors discuss the need to investigate longer design processes and teams. Maintaining several expensive prototypes could allocate effort differently from the banner-ad task, and the experimenter administering the conditions was not blind to assignment. The equal time and prototype count nevertheless make the demonstrated comparison informative: the observed advantage cannot simply be attributed to the parallel condition receiving more opportunities to build or more feedback. [OI-W013, pp. 18:18–18:19]

### Nutt: searching for a result rather than defending a ready-made solution

Nutt: searching for a result rather than defending a ready-made solution

Paul Nutt's 1999 article examines how organizations establish a direction, identify possible responses and implement a decision. Its cases distinguish defining a desired result from beginning with a solution that somebody already favors. His heat-pump example makes the distinction concrete. A firm spent years trying to make a particular heat-wheel technology work, although its broader opportunity concerned

<!-- PDF page 487 -->

economical heating. Once that solution supplied the definition of the problem, technical effort went into repairing it rather than examining other ways to obtain the desired result. The example concerns how a commitment organizes subsequent search. [OI-W009, pp. 78–81]

Nutt distinguishes several ways of finding options. Copying a single comparison organization imports a package that may fit a different setting. Integrated benchmarking instead examines several organizations and combines pertinent features. A search can also occur in stages: an initial request for proposals teaches the buyer what suppliers can offer, and a later request uses that knowledge to specify a more informed demand. Designing a custom option is another route, requiring design skill, attention to users and the capacity to put the result into operation. His categories describe different work, rather than identifying all search with asking for a longer list. [OI-W009, pp. 81–85]

The underlying evidence is a retrospectively reconstructed collection of decisions in medium and large organizations in the United States and Canada. Interviews and documents were used to establish the process, with subsequent checks of implementation. Success was assessed through such measures as sustained use and full use after two years. Those measures distinguish adoption from abandonment or partial use; they do not by themselves establish profitability, public benefit or the absence of harmful effects. Managers were not randomly assigned to search methods. [OI-W009, pp. 76–77, 89, note 5]

Nutt associates the development of multiple options with more successful implementation and argues that discovering alternatives can reduce later repair work. The multiple-search category contained nine cases, all sustained and fully used after two years. Additional search requires time, access to comparison cases and the ability to combine what is learned. The article also treats participation and implementation separately, so discovering an attractive response does not complete the task of securing its acceptance and use. [OI-W009, pp. 83–89]

### March: learning can consume the differences from which it learns

March: learning can consume the differences from which it learns

James March's 1991 article examines exploration and exploitation in organizational learning. Exploration includes experimentation with new alternatives, while exploitation develops and uses established capabilities. Both consume resources, but their returns can arrive at different times and benefit different people or parts of an organization. Procedures for setting targets, rewarding work, allocating spare capacity and choosing investments therefore affect the balance even when nobody explicitly makes a decision called exploration versus exploitation. [OI-W010, p. 71]

March explains why ordinary adaptation can favor existing activities. Greater competence produces more reliable rewards, which make that activity more attractive and support further competence. A less familiar alternative can perform poorly while people learn how to use it, even if its potential is greater. Feedback about established work is often faster, clearer and closer to the people doing it than feedback about exploration. A process that improves short-term performance can consequently narrow the experience from which later possibilities would be discovered. This is the argument developed through the paper's models. [OI-W010, p. 73]

In the mutual-learning model, individuals hold beliefs about an external reality and an organizational code holds accepted beliefs. Individuals can adopt the code's beliefs; the code can learn from a group of individuals stipulated by the model to be more accurate than itself. The model specifies reality so that accuracy can be measured. Individuals do not directly experience that reality or teach one another outside the code. Those simplifications make it possible to study how two learning processes interact, with rates of socialization and code revision treated separately. [OI-W010, pp. 74–75]

Rapid socialization removes differences between individuals and the code. That can improve an individual's knowledge in the short term while reducing the variation from which the code can learn. In the simulations, slower socialization can preserve useful differences long enough for the organization to

<!-- PDF page 488 -->

absorb them. Mixtures of fast and slow learners can also improve the eventual code relative to a population with a uniform learning rate. The benefits are distributed unevenly: fast learners can acquire knowledge whose development depended disproportionately on people who remained different longer. [OI-W010, pp. 75–77]

Turnover provides another source of variation in the model. A newcomer has less knowledge on average but may hold beliefs that are less redundant with the code. Moderate turnover can therefore improve the code under some learning-rate conditions, while excessive turnover or turnover combined with already slow socialization can undermine the exploitation of what has been learned. When the external reality changes, a population that has fully converged can cease to adapt. Introducing newcomers can prevent that degeneration in the modeled system. [OI-W010, pp. 78–80]

March also distinguishes improvement in average performance from competition to finish first. Reducing variability can make outcomes more reliable while reducing the chance of an unusually good result at the upper end of a distribution. Whether that trade-off matters depends on the competitive objective and the distributions being compared. He uses it to question the assumption that more reliable knowledge necessarily improves every kind of competitive position. The discussion is a model-based argument about the conditions of performance, not an observed comparison of a particular firm's management practices. [OI-W010, pp. 84–85]

The article does not determine one optimal allocation between exploration and exploitation for every organization. Its models explain particular ways that learning rates, recruitment, time horizons and competitive criteria can change the consequences of an allocation. Too much exploration can leave ideas undeveloped and competence insufficient; too little can leave an organization highly practiced at an inferior activity. The work makes those choices and their distribution of costs explicit. It extends the discussion beyond generating candidates during one decision to sustaining the capacity to encounter and develop alternatives over time. [OI-W010, pp. 71, 73, 85]

## S68 Collaborative generation and material methods

S68   Collaborative generation and material methods

An observation written on a card can be moved beside another observation, given a new heading and connected to a larger account. A workshop can supply pictures of technologies, invite children to explain their schoolbags to imaginary visitors, or let designers build a proposal from physical pieces. These procedures give participants something to work on together. Their histories show how the preparation of material, the framing of a task and the opportunities for rearrangement enter into creative work.

### Kawakita's field cards and the KJ method

Kawakita's field cards and the KJ method

In a 2003 interview with Tetsuro Matsuzawa and Yoko Yamada, Jiro Kawakita recalled the fieldwork behind the KJ method. He described transferring observations from a notebook to separate cards, a practice he traced to his field investigations in 1946. A notebook preserves a sequence of recording. Cards allow observations to be read in different sequences and assembled according to relationships that become apparent later. The interview presents this development through Kawakita's recollections of his own research. [CRE-W030, pp. 14–16]

The movable statement retained information about its circumstances: time, place, source and recorder. Rearrangement did not require stripping the observation of its origin. Kawakita emphasized repeated reading of the cards and attention to what they actually said. Statements that seemed close in meaning could be brought together, and a heading could express the message emerging from their association. The heading was preferably a sentence conveying something substantive, rather than a noun that merely named a subject. [CRE-W030, pp. 14–16]

Successive groupings made larger patterns available for consideration. Arranging the material could also expose a gap: an apparent relationship might require information the researcher did not yet possess. The work could therefore lead back to inquiry. Kawakita's account joins the manipulation of records, the interpretation of their relationships and further observation within an ongoing investigation. [CRE-W030, pp. 14–16]

Hiroaki Tanaka's 2013 quick manual specifies a sequence for carrying out KJ work, based on Kawakita's later exposition. It begins by putting one message on each label. Labels are numbered so that they can be related to the underlying data. They are spread out and read before grouping begins. The initial groups are small and arise from similarities of meaning in the statements. A classification prepared in advance would bypass the interpretive work the procedure is intended to support. [CRE-W029, pp. 102–104]

Each small group receives a heading expressing what its labels say together. A label that does not fit can remain on its own. The headings can then be treated as material for another round of grouping, producing larger groups without requiring every statement to enter the same hierarchy. Different colors and the retention of the lower-level labels help participants keep track of these successive operations. The emerging account can be traced through its headings to the statements from which it was developed. [CRE-W029, pp. 103–105]

The groups are next placed spatially to make their relationships intelligible. Positioning comes before an elaborate network of lines; the manual recommends using relations economically rather than connecting everything to everything. A diagram gives the arrangement a visible form, and prose develops an explicit account of what it means. Writing is thus a further operation on the material, requiring the interpreter to state relationships that a suggestive diagram might leave implicit. [CRE-W029, pp. 105–106]

The sequence gives several distinct tasks their own working forms: a label states a message, a heading expresses a group's meaning, a diagram displays relationships, and prose articulates an interpretation. Their combination is what makes Tanaka's account more useful than the instruction to sort observations

<!-- PDF page 490 -->

into clusters. It explains both how the material is transformed and how earlier statements remain available during that transformation. [CRE-W029, pp. 102–106]

### Preparing cards and inventing a workshop situation

Preparing cards and inventing a workshop situation

Michael Mose Biskjaer, Peter Dalsgaard and Kim Halskov examined creativity methods in design through nine components: process structure, materials, tools, combination, metaphor, analogy, framing, divergence and convergence. Their 2017 analysis grouped these into concrete, conceptual and design-space aspects. A workshop's instructions become more intelligible when considered with the material  supplied, the situation participants are asked to imagine and the forms of development expected from them. [CRE-W031]

Their account of the Inspiration Card Workshop begins before participants assemble. Organizers prepare Domain Cards representing knowledge of the setting, often obtained through field studies, and Technology Cards representing technologies or particular applications. Each card carries an image and may include a short text. Selecting familiar technologies can make the workshop easier to enter; selecting unfamiliar or provocative ones can unsettle established expectations. Preparation helps determine the possibilities participants will encounter. [CRE-W031, analysis of Inspiration Card Workshops]

In the workshop, the cards are introduced and then combined to develop design concepts. Participants record emerging ideas on notes and collect them on poster-sized sheets. The main creative phase has room for different ways of working rather than prescribing every operation. Concepts are presented and discussed, but this procedure does not require reducing them to a winning selection. Afterwards, posters can be scanned and distributed. The physical combination of prepared cards, discussion around a developing concept and preservation of its representation occupy different parts of the sequence. [CRE-W031, analysis of Inspiration Card Workshops]

Fictional Inquiry changes the social situation in which participants contribute. In one case described by Biskjaer and colleagues, designers acted as Martians visiting Earth, and primary-school children explained their schoolbags to them. Children could no longer assume that their adult interlocutors already understood an ordinary bag or its use. The fictional visitors gave them a reason to articulate familiar experiences and imagine alternatives while contributing to the design of digitally enhanced schoolbags. [CRE-W031, analysis of Fictional Inquiry]

Another workshop asked participants to help the king of Atlantis understand what humans found extraordinary. Seashells, a scepter and other props supported exploration of interactive aquarium exhibits. The fictional situation supplied roles and objects through which participants could develop ideas; those ideas then had to be related to the real aquarium. The authors describe a method that adapts its narrative to a particular design setting, with the connection back to that setting as an important part of the work. [CRE-W031, analysis of Fictional Inquiry]

Their third example, Extreme Characters, exaggerates the people imagined in a design scenario. A proposed appointment manager might be explored through an unconventional character whose jewelry becomes a temporary stand-in for the device. Touching a ring can suggest an interaction such as moving between appointments. The procedure uses role, appearance, action and props together to provoke a different view of a user group. Biskjaer and colleagues treat such methods as combinations of interacting features, and their examples explain why a label such as analogy alone would leave much of the workshop undescribed. [CRE-W031, analysis of Extreme Characters and discussion]

<!-- PDF page 491 -->

### What analogue tools supply

What analogue tools supply

Dorian Peters, Lian Loke and Naseem Ahmadpour reviewed analogue tools for collaborative ideation. Their review selected 76 tools from research and commercial sources and illustrated a smaller set in the article. They distinguished seven types: methods, prompts, components, concepts, stories, embodiment and construction. A card explaining a method, a question that provokes a response and a physical component to assemble offer different forms of assistance, even when all are described as creativity tools. [CRE-W032, §§4–5]

These distinctions concern what a participant can do with the supplied material. Prompts stimulate responses; components can be combined into a developing proposal; concepts make potentially relevant knowledge available. Stories give participants situations or sequences to develop. The format alone does not determine the activity: two decks of cards may support substantially different kinds of work. The review records features such as a tool's focus, availability and supporting studies alongside its type. [CRE-W032, §§5.1–5.3]

Embodiment and construction extend the account beyond printed cards. Reduced-visibility glasses and reduced-mobility gloves in an inclusive-design toolkit let designers experience particular difficulties while handling a product. Construction materials allow participants to make and discuss a representation. The authors distinguish generic building pieces from LEGO Serious Play's combination of a prescribed method and a purpose-made kit. In each case, the activity depends on the relation between the object and its use. [CRE-W032, §§5.3.5–5.3.6]

The review also draws attention to participation itself. Equipment for simulating an impairment serves a different purpose from tools that enable people with disabilities to participate in design. Peters and colleagues describe examples addressing such participation when discussing gaps and related tools. Their survey makes both material variety and the intended participants visible; it does not rank the 76 tools as though they had all undergone a common effectiveness trial. [CRE-W032, §§5.4.1, 6.2.2]

### Working spaces and the continuing design cycle

Working spaces and the continuing design cycle

Scarlett R. Herring, Brett R. Jones and Brian P. Bailey interviewed ten designers about idea generation throughout their work. Seven interviews took place in project spaces, where the researchers could inspect artifacts, and three took place by telephone. The study identified nineteen techniques and placed them within an account of the design cycle, including implementation and evaluation as well as initial concept generation. [CRE-W033, §§3–5]

Their IR3 model describes research, representation and refinement within an encompassing search for inspiration. Research can produce several concepts; sketches or other external representations let a designer inspect and discuss them; refinement can change what further information is needed. These movements need not occur in long, neatly separated phases. A quick sketch may be evaluated and discarded almost immediately. A concept can concern the definition of the problem as well as a potential solution. [CRE-W033, §4.1]

The techniques reported by the designers include seeking examples, consulting others, acting out situations, manipulating concrete stimuli, documenting ideas and criticizing developing proposals. A critique can generate further ideas by drawing attention to a defect that needs a response. Work on a representation can similarly reveal something that was not apparent when an idea remained verbal. The study presents these activities as recurring parts of professional work rather than as exercises confined to a single introductory meeting. [CRE-W033, §5]

Project spaces make this recurrence tangible. Photographs, notes, comparable products and prototypes can remain spread out, visible and available to handle. A designer can return to an earlier representation

<!-- PDF page 492 -->

while developing another one, and colleagues can refer to the same material. Herring and colleagues use these observations to discuss requirements for computer support, including access to the working environment when a person or dispersed team is elsewhere. Their proposal for support grows out of observed practices and interview accounts. [CRE-W033, discussion]

### Collaborative generation for accessible websites

Collaborative generation for accessible websites

Daniela Satomi Saito and colleagues considered how a shared web environment could support creative collaboration in developing accessible websites. The proposed participants include people with different professional knowledge and users whose experiences matter to accessibility. The chapter examines techniques together with the functions a platform would need to make them available in a collaborative design process. [CRE-W034, pp. 170–203]

The authors consider written circulation of ideas, role-based generation, mind maps and evaluation. Circulating contributions offers a way for a multidisciplinary group to add to and develop proposals. Role-based exercises ask participants to approach the problem from another identity or perspective. A mind  map can make requirements and their associations visible for further discussion. The chapter connects these operations to the task of eliciting and developing accessible interfaces, where the knowledge required is distributed among different participants. [CRE-W034, pp. 184–186]

This is a design and instructional proposal for bringing established techniques into a shared environment. Its account explains how participation, representation of requirements and generation of interface ideas could be supported together. The general written-exchange procedures discussed in Systematic accounts of methods for generating ideas provide another route into this material; Saito and colleagues develop their application to a specific collaborative task. [CRE-W034]

<!-- PDF page 493 -->

## S69 Computer-supported and human–AI co-creation

S69   Computer-supported and human–AI co-creation

Computer support for creative work includes preserving alternatives, sharing developing representations, exchanging ideas and generating candidates. These activities have different histories. Work on creativity-support interfaces and electronic brainstorming provides a setting for later studies of human–AI collaboration, whose interventions range from an initial suggestion to continuing participation in a shared performance or design.

### Shneiderman's creativity-support tools

Shneiderman's creativity-support tools

Ben Shneiderman's 2007 account places exploration at the center of creativity-support design. A person looking for an answer may need to inspect distributions, relationships, gaps and unusual cases before knowing exactly what to ask. Faceted search and dynamic queries allow incremental changes to a view. Rapid, reversible responses help users learn from successive attempts rather than commit to one query and receive a final answer. [CRE-W035, pp. 25–27]

Rich history-keeping supports this extended activity. A record of alternatives lets users compare what they have tried, return to an earlier state and modify it. A promising case can be sent to a colleague, and an investigation can resume without reconstructing its previous path. Shneiderman connects such facilities to both systematic and relatively free exploration. His design proposals concern the working relationship between successive attempts, their representations and the people who may develop them. [CRE-W035, pp. 26–27]

The familiar combination of a low threshold, a high ceiling and wide walls expresses another part of his argument. Beginners should be able to start, experienced users should be able to attempt ambitious work, and the environment should permit different kinds of activity. A tool that supports only a narrow demonstration may be easy to learn while offering little room to develop. Movement among exploration, representation, analysis and communication is therefore part of the design problem. [CRE-W035, design principles]

Collaboration also changes over a project's life. Early exchanges concern problem definition and goals; later ones may involve information, refinement, validation and dissemination. Shneiderman discusses trust, records of contributions and opportunities to expose uncertainty safely. He argues for evaluating creativity-support tools through observation of serious work over extended periods, alongside shorter studies. The article supplies an account of computer support in which a useful intervention can preserve, connect or expose work without generating the central idea itself. [CRE-W035, pp. 26–31]

### Electronic brainstorming and time to use others' ideas

Electronic brainstorming and time to use others' ideas

Hamit Coşkun's 2011 study varied group size, memory instructions and session length in three electronic-brainstorming experiments. Participants worked at separate computers and completed a typing-speed  test before the exercise. Tasks included imagining the consequences of children being born with an extra thumb and proposing improvements to a university. Electronic exchange made other participants' contributions available while people generated their own. [CRE-W036, pp. 91–94]

Across the experiments, larger groups generated more ideas in total and more unique and original ideas. The corresponding individual-output analyses did not show that each participant produced more merely by belonging to a larger group. The results describe an enlarged collective pool alongside a different finding about its individual contributors. Both are useful for understanding what the electronic arrangement accomplished. [CRE-W036, results and general discussion]

<!-- PDF page 494 -->

The memory instruction asked participants to remember ideas because they would later be tested. It reduced production in a fifteen-minute session but improved production in a twenty-five-minute session. In the longer exercise, participants had more time in which attention to the shared material could contribute to further generation. Coşkun presents this interaction as a way of understanding inconsistent findings about such instructions. The same request can have a different effect when the period available for using it changes. [CRE-W036, experiment 3]

Typing speed affected total and unique production, while the study did not find corresponding effects on originality and feasibility. The experiments thus bring the interface, attention to others' ideas and session duration into the account of the exercise. The earlier discussion of group idea generation in this volume provides the broader background; Coşkun's contribution concerns these particular arrangements for electronic participation. [CRE-W036, general discussion]

### COFI and the design of a creative partnership

COFI and the design of a creative partnership

Jeba Rezwana and Mary Lou Maher developed COFI to describe interaction in human–AI co-creative systems. Their framework considers collaboration style, communication, creative process and creative product. Partners can work on a shared task or divide the work, take turns or act in parallel, and follow a plan or respond spontaneously. These choices describe how participation unfolds, beyond identifying what kind of output the system produces. [CRE-W037, framework]

Communication receives particular attention. A person can intentionally instruct a system through text, voice, gesture or direct manipulation. A system may also collect consequential information that the person gives off without making it an explicit instruction, such as gaze, bodily movement or facial expression. Communication from the AI to the person can provide feedback, reveal a contribution's status or support a response. The framework separates these channels so that the presence of an input facility is not mistaken for a complete two-way exchange. [CRE-W037, communication components]

The creative process and product provide further distinctions. A partner may contribute to generating a new element, evaluating an existing one or changing material already present. A shared dance, drawing or narrative presents different opportunities for timing and response. COFI asks how the contributions relate to the evolving product and to one another, making interaction itself an object of analysis. [CRE-W037, creative-process and product components]

The authors applied the framework to 92 systems across thirteen creative domains. Two coders independently examined a quarter of the systems, discussed differences and established a coding basis for the remainder. Their analysis identifies recurring interaction designs in the described systems. Its contribution is a structured account of creative participation, grounded in those designs, rather than an effectiveness ranking of every possible form of partnership. [CRE-W037, §§4–5]

### Suggested beginnings and the stories people write

Suggested beginnings and the stories people write

Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser studied access to AI-generated ideas in a short-story task. The 293 writers were asked to produce an eight-sentence story suitable for a teenage and young-adult audience. They were assigned to write without AI assistance, with access to one generated idea, or with access to as many as five. A generated idea consisted of three sentences offered as starting material; the writer composed the story. [CRE-W038, experimental design]

The second phase obtained evaluations of the stories from a separate group of participants. Evaluators first judged the work without being told about its AI assistance. In the condition allowing five ideas, average novelty ratings were 8.1 percent higher and usefulness ratings 9 percent higher than in the

<!-- PDF page 495 -->

unassisted condition. The study therefore found an improvement in judged individual work under this specific form of assistance. [CRE-W038, results]

The authors also compared stories with one another and with their generated starting ideas. AI-assisted stories were more similar across writers. Access to a pool of suggestions could improve a writer's evaluated result while drawing the collection toward more similar content. These analyses concern different objects: the quality attributed to one story and the relationships among many stories. [CRE-W038, collective-diversity analysis]

The intervention's sequence is important to understanding the result. The model supplied a possible beginning, and a person interpreted and developed it within a tightly bounded writing task. Doshi and Hauser's study makes this early contribution visible as part of the subsequent human work. It also provides a concrete case in which an individual's benefit and the variety of the resulting collection can be assessed separately. [CRE-W038]

### Comparing a language model with oblique prompts

Comparing a language model with oblique prompts

Barrett R. Anderson, Jash Hemant Shah and Max Kreminski compared ChatGPT with the Oblique Strategies prompt deck. Thirty-three participants were included in the analysis. Each worked with both forms of assistance on timed tasks involving product improvements and improbable consequences. Examples included making a jigsaw puzzle more engaging and imagining a world in which only people's feet could be seen. [CRE-W039, §3]

The deck offers brief provocations that a participant must interpret in relation to the task. A language model can provide developed candidates and respond to further requests. The experiment gave these two kinds of assistance a common set of ideation tasks and an eight-minute period for each session. It thereby compared an established prompt device with conversational model support, rather than comparing assistance with no intervention at all. [CRE-W039, materials and procedure]

With ChatGPT, participants produced approximately 15 percent more ideas and covered 27 percent more categories in the reported analysis. Their ideas were also more homogeneous across participants. The analyses did not detect the same change in diversity within an individual's collection, and the unique-idea measure did not show a significant improvement. More output and more represented categories can therefore coexist with greater similarity among the collections produced by different people. [CRE-W039, results]

The authors discuss the interpretive distance between an oblique prompt and the current task, compared with the more developed material a model can supply. This is their interpretation of how the forms of assistance may shape ideation. Together with the task and outcome distinctions, it gives the comparison more explanatory value than a single judgment that one tool makes people more creative. [CRE-W039, discussion]

### Generating a pool of product concepts

Generating a pool of product concepts

Karan Girotra, Lennart Meincke, Christian Terwiesch and Karl T. Ulrich's 2023 working paper compared student product concepts with concepts generated using GPT-4. The task was to propose a physical product for college students that could retail for less than fifty dollars. The comparison used 200 student ideas from a 2021 course, 100 model-generated ideas and another 100 generated with examples of highly rated student concepts in the prompt. [CRE-W040, approach]

The researchers requested descriptions of forty to eighty words in batches of ten, using GPT-4-0314 with a temperature setting of 0.7. To continue generating a large pool within the available context, they had the model compress its previous ideas into shorter summaries. Those summaries accompanied subsequent

<!-- PDF page 496 -->

requests for ideas different from the preceding ones. The candidate pool was thus constructed through repeated generation with a representation of what had already been proposed. [CRE-W040, approach]

The example-seeded condition supplied seven highly rated student ideas from a separate set. It made examples part of the intervention while retaining the same product challenge. The paper compares distributions of evaluated concepts as well as their averages, reflecting the innovation-tournament setting in which a large pool is generated and then selected. [CRE-W040, approach and evaluation]

Survey respondents rated purchase intent for the descriptions. Average ratings were higher for both generated pools, and AI-generated ideas occupied 35 of the best-rated forty places in the combined collection. The human ideas received higher novelty ratings. These results describe judgments of proposed concepts, including the promising end of their distribution; the study did not observe the products being launched and purchased. [CRE-W040, results]

This account connects prompt construction, repeated generation, retention of prior candidates and evaluation of a pool. Its particular contribution differs from the story-writing studies: the generated descriptions are themselves the concepts being screened, rather than starting ideas that participants subsequently turn into finished stories. The procedures and assessed outcomes make those differences intelligible. [CRE-W040]
