## S70 Learning and practising creative methods

S70   Learning and practising creative methods

A creative procedure can be taught as a sequence of actions, practised in a particular setting and assessed through the work that follows. Training studies examine these connections at several levels. Their accounts range from the effects measured across many programmes to the placement of an exercise within a proposed course, and from a learner's personally meaningful discovery to professional achievement.

### What creativity training improves

What creativity training improves

Ut Na Sio and Hugues Lortie-Forgues reviewed five decades of creativity-training research in 2024. Their principal meta-analysis included 169 studies, 844 effect sizes and 18,486 participants. The authors distinguished cognitive content, such as idea-generation skills, from content directed at motivation, emotion or personality, with a further category for combined programmes. Outcomes included divergent-thinking tasks, problem solving and creative products. [CRE-W041, method and results]

The unadjusted average training effect was 0.53 standard deviations. The review also found evidence consistent with publication bias and applied several corrections. PEESE, trim-and-fill, robust Bayesian meta-analysis and the top-ten-percent approach produced estimates around 0.29 to 0.32 standard deviations. The PET estimate was smaller and statistically uncertain. The authors report a positive average effect under several adjustments while showing how substantially its estimated size depends on accounting for the evidence available. [CRE-W041, publication-bias analyses]

The review examined the contents and duration of training as well as average effects. Cognitive and combined programmes compared favorably with the smaller non-cognitive category; the analysis did not establish a difference between cognitive and combined content. A positive association with duration in the simpler analysis weakened when other characteristics were considered together. These findings give more information than an undifferentiated claim that creativity can be taught. [CRE-W041, moderator analyses]

Sio and Lortie-Forgues also examined study quality and the concentration of outcomes in particular kinds of task. Their account treats measured improvement, the content of instruction and the quality of its evaluation as connected questions. A programme teaching generation skills and assessed with a divergent-thinking task supplies evidence about that accomplishment. Its result is most informative when the reader knows what was practised and what the assessment asked participants to do. [CRE-W041, discussion]

### Arranging interventions for children

Arranging interventions for children

Patrícia Alves-Oliveira and colleagues' review of children's creativity interventions organized programmes at eight levels: cognitive processing skill, training technique, delivery medium, practice exercise, target, setting, administrator and dimension of creativity. A skill such as flexibility is distinct from a technique used to develop it, and that technique is distinct from its delivery through discussion, programmed instruction or a digital environment. The classification allows these parts of an intervention to be examined together. [CRE-W042, taxonomy]

The reviewed programmes include imaginative exercises, expressive activity, elaboration, cooperative learning and movement. A teacher can give sequential instructions, arrange discussion or ask learners to work together; an activity can use familiar materials or a computer or robotic partner. These are accounts of the programmes assembled in the review. Their arrangement makes the people conducting the

<!-- PDF page 498 -->

teaching and the circumstances of practice visible alongside the named creative technique. [CRE-W042, results and discussion]

The review distinguishes the dimension assessed from the activity used for teaching. In its classification, assessments concentrated on the person, commonly through tests: approximately 83 percent, compared with 9 percent directed at process and 8 percent at product. An intervention may involve producing something together while its evaluation chiefly measures individual performance on another task. This distinction helps explain what the accumulated evidence describes. [CRE-W042, assessment of creativity]

The authors' eight-level account also allows a method to be adapted without treating every adaptation as an entirely new technique. Delivery, exercises and teaching personnel can change while a programme continues to address a related skill. The review provides a way of describing these arrangements and their diversity across children's interventions. [CRE-W042]

### Placing exercises within an online course

Placing exercises within an online course

Viviane Kuntz and colleagues proposed an arrangement of creative techniques for massive open online courses in 2015. They related particular operations to occasions in a course: welcoming participants, introducing people and the platform, forming groups, establishing plans and working on content. The chapter's procedure is to ask what an activity could contribute at each point, rather than add an isolated creativity exercise to an otherwise unchanged course. [CRE-W043, pp. 217–227]

An opening combinatorial activity asks learners to imagine another form or structure for the subject. Unusual questions can change an introductory exchange. Exploring the positive, negative and interesting aspects of a platform gives participants an activity through which to consider the environment they will use. Profile-based games can help form groups. These proposals connect generating alternatives with the practical work of entering a shared course. Word-based recreation can explore another organization of the course content. [CRE-W043, table 7]

For planning, the chapter brings a desired future into comparison with the current situation and considers inviting someone unfamiliar with the subject to introduce another perspective. For work on content, a mind map can support individual interpretation, inversion can break down and rearrange a logical structure, and unusual analogy can connect material that initially seems unrelated. Each technique is assigned a teaching occasion and an intended contribution. [CRE-W043, tables 4 and 7]

The chapter concludes by proposing a pilot course to examine this arrangement. It is therefore an instructional design and rationale, with concrete adaptations available to inspect. Its historical contribution lies in the proposed connection between established creative operations and the structure of an online course. [CRE-W043, conclusion]

### Different levels of creative accomplishment

Different levels of creative accomplishment

Agustín Tristán López and Liliana Mendoza González's 2016 review of creativity taxonomies considers the range of accomplishments that education and assessment can address. Their account of the four-C model distinguishes personally meaningful discovery, everyday creativity, professional creativity and historically influential achievement. These levels give a place to work that is creative for the learner without requiring it to transform a field. [CRE-W044, four-C model]

Their examples make the distinctions concrete. A preschool child's drawing can embody a personally significant discovery. A child with some instruction in sculpture may produce an independent work worth displaying. An engineer's product can solve a client's problem and receive recognition within professional practice. A major work in music, art, technology or science can alter a domain much more widely. The

<!-- PDF page 499 -->

review uses these cases to explain why the expectations appropriate to one achievement need not fit another. [CRE-W044]

The authors also distinguish an unfolding process from a finished product. Observation and recorded sessions can help reconstruct how an activity developed; expert judgment can address qualities of completed work. Choreography, a technical device and a mathematical contribution pose different problems of description and evaluation. The review examines such differences while seeking more explicit accounts of creative qualities. [CRE-W044, assessment and creative-process taxonomies]

These distinctions give learning and practice several legitimate objects. A programme can develop a person's ways of approaching material, improve performance on a task or support a valued product. The studies and proposals in this section specify these accomplishments in different ways, providing historical accounts of what people have tried to teach and how they have recognized a result. [CRE-W041; CRE-W042; CRE-W043; CRE-W044]

<!-- PDF page 500 -->

## S45 Praxeology, economy of knowledge and philosophies of action

S45   Praxeology, economy of knowledge and philosophies of action

### Several different accounts of prepared action

Several different accounts of prepared action

The sources here examine effective action, economical representation, division of intellectual work, habit and institutions. Some describe how a favorable situation or prepared arrangement supports an action; others ask how people interpret conduct and its purposes.

### Kotarbiński: a favorable position relative to a requirement

Kotarbiński: a favorable position relative to a requirement

Sprawność i błąd includes a chapter on praxeology, the study of effective action. The chapter examines minimizing intervention by finding or creating a favorable situation. A plant requiring moisture is in a positive position with respect to that requirement when its site already supplies the moisture. In a dry site, the gardener must act to provide it. The favorable relation is to a specified property at a later time, not an assertion that the plant is generally independent of conditions. [W019, pp. 100–101]

The example is informative because it identifies the work supplied by the situation. The gardener's reduced action depends on a continuing environmental provision. A condition relevant to one demand can be favorable while other demands remain.

The selected chapter also distinguishes intervention from surveillance or monitoring, alongside potentialization, mechanization and organization as ways of improving action. Reducing the frequency of direct action is different from abandoning readiness to notice and respond. The proposed categories organize possible improvements. [W019, selected chapter, pp. 97–111]

Kotarbiński developed praxeology in Traktat o dobrej robocie (1955) and Sprawność i błąd (first published in 1956 and subsequently expanded). [W018; W019]

### Babbage: distribute the intellectual work of calculation

Babbage: distribute the intellectual work of calculation

Babbage's selected chapter on mental labor reports the organization of de Prony's calculation of mathematical tables. It distinguishes people who determine analytical methods, those who translate them into executable arrangements and those carrying out large quantities of elementary arithmetic. The report's interest is not simply that a calculation becomes shorter for everyone. The required knowledge is distributed across roles, with substantial repetitive labor assigned to people who need not know the complete analysis. [W086, chapter XIX, §§183 and 187–193]

The manufacturing analogy retains the intermediate role. An inventor or designer prepares the machinery; operative engineers construct it and understand the relevant processes; other workers use it. Babbage explicitly says that the work and performance of the machines still require supervision by the second group. Less knowledge demanded of an individual operator is not disappearance of the knowledge needed by the undertaking. [W086, §188, first-edition printed p. 158]

The difference-table explanation gives an actual computational mechanism. Successive squares have first differences increasing by a constant second difference. Once appropriate starting values and differences are known, repeated additions can extend the table. The prepared mathematical arrangement changes the later operations required; it does not make their correctness independent of the initial setup and execution. [W086, §§189–193]

Babbage connects the scheme to the possibility of a calculating engine replacing routine arithmetic. In the text that is a proposed development. His account of the French tables is historical author testimony. [W086]

<!-- PDF page 501 -->

### Mach: economical thought represents more than it repeats

Mach: economical thought represents more than it repeats

In the opening of his 1882 lecture, Mach starts from thought's limited resources in relation to the richness of experience. Scientific concepts and organized representations can let thought handle relationships without repeating every encounter. The relevant economy concerns representing experience and using thought to anticipate it, rather than possessing an exhaustive duplicate of the world. [W021, chapter XIII, selected opening]

The account treats scientific formulae and conceptual organization as intellectual instruments. Its pertinent claim is about what a representation can spare a thinker from separately retaining or rehearsing. The economy of a description and the operation described remain distinct.

### Dewey: habit incorporates an environment

Dewey: habit incorporates an environment

The discussion of habit in Human Nature and Conduct argues against locating habit wholly inside an isolated person. Walking implicates ground as well as legs, and speech requires air and other people as well as vocal organs. Dewey describes habits as organized skills involving materials, tools and surroundings. An acquired disposition operates in relation to a world that supports and resists it. [GL-W093, selected printed pp. 14–17 and 25–26]

This is more specific than saying that a repeated action becomes automatic. A craft can depend on external implements and arrangements, and moral or social conduct can likewise depend on institutions and other people. The selected account treats habit as a way of using and incorporating an environment. It does not make the environment an inert background or the person irrelevant to action.

The discussion of deliberation examines how habits and impulses enter inquiry when action is unsettled. Considering consequences and possible courses can revise conduct, rather than merely applying a ready-made end to neutral means. Established habits make action possible but can also require change. [GL-W093, selected printed pp. 172–184 and revised-habits passage]

Anderson's selected reconstruction of Dewey's moral philosophy adds the relation between means, ends and social ethics. Ends are examined through the activity and consequences of pursuing them, rather than assumed permanently fixed outside inquiry. The reader can therefore study a philosophy of organized conduct without turning every stable habit into a justified institution. [GL-W007]

### Institutional and technical relief

Institutional and technical relief

Turner reads Gehlen's Der Mensch as an account of human beings whose conduct is only partly directed by instinct. Institutions and habits provide a relatively stable cultural setting, reducing repeated demands for motivation and control. Turner presents Entlastung as relief supplied through a taken-for-granted background that permits more focused foreground activity. [UX-W032, introduction, printed pp. 9–11] [UX-W033, through Turner]

The same reconstruction connects Gehlen's account to a conservative criticism of modernity: persistent reflection can destabilize the institutional background on which action relies. This is a controversial philosophical position as presented by Turner. Stability of a background does not settle who benefits from it or bears its costs.

In Die Seele im technischen Zeitalter (1957), Gehlen distinguishes tools that substitute for a bodily capacity, amplify it or relieve people of exerting it. A microscope amplifies sight. A wheeled wagon relieves people of dragging the load themselves. He relates these functions to the ways humans change their surroundings to make action possible. [UX-W039, ch. I, §1]

<!-- PDF page 502 -->

Spinner gives relief a different setting in his account of scientific institutions. He argues that the separation of inquiry from practice gives researchers room to pursue questions without an immediate obligation to act on the answers or assume responsibility for their use. In his account this separation becomes harder to sustain as research moves into technologies that have to be built, financed and operated. [UX-W034, §§III, V]

### Historical time: a persistent structure is not necessarily beneficial

Historical time: a persistent structure is not necessarily beneficial

The selected passages of Braudel's La longue durée direct attention to structures and temporal scales that differ from a short event sequence. A slowly changing arrangement can condition what is possible over many events, without being immediately visible in an event-centered narrative. The relevant contribution is a perspective on duration and constraint. [GL-W051, printed p. 726 and discussion of structure]

Daniel Little's Philosophy of History entry, first published in 2007 and revised in 2025, examines causal mechanisms, contingency and the selectivity of historical explanation as methodological questions. A broad pattern needs evidence about particular processes and contexts. [GL-W050]

### Daoism through Hansen: guidance and normative autonomy

Daoism through Hansen: guidance and normative autonomy

Hansen's selected interpretive account distinguishes strands associated with Laozi and Zhuangzi and examines natural possibilities, guidance and normative autonomy. Its relevance is a philosophical question about how action relates to an order or path without every step being imposed through an explicit command. [GL-W098]

Hansen’s discussion of wuwei concerns guidance and normative autonomy. Mechanical passivity and the absence of effort describe different questions from those philosophical distinctions.

### Effective action, representation and institutions

Effective action, representation and institutions

The sources provide distinct information about favorable conditions, delegated calculation, economical representation, environmentally supported habits, institutional relief and philosophical action.

<!-- PDF page 503 -->

## S49 Stigmergy, emergent patterns and distributed collective action

S49   Stigmergy, emergent patterns and distributed collective action

This section reports selected explanations of coordination through local interactions, a modified environment, and expectations about others. It also includes an important adverse case: local choices can produce an aggregate pattern unlike the mixture the participants would tolerate. “Emergent” identifies a relation between interactions and a pattern.

### Grassé: the product of work stimulates subsequent work

Grassé: the product of work stimulates subsequent work

In the selected passages of his 1959 termite article, Grassé describes a mechanism in which construction changes a material product, and that changed product becomes a stimulus for subsequent activity by the same or other workers. The environment is consequently involved in the sequence of coordination. The next act need not be directed by a central representation of the completed nest or an instruction exchanged between each pair of workers. A worker can encounter a physically altered situation and act in relation to it. [W031, printed pp. 62–63, 71–75]

The selected §V also supplies boundaries. Grassé does not treat this construction mechanism as an exhaustive explanation of every social-insect behavior, or eliminate all possible roles for communication. [W031]

### Heylighen: a broader trace-mediated proposal

Heylighen: a broader trace-mediated proposal

Heylighen’s selected definitions and components generalize stigmergy as indirect coordination mediated by traces left in an environment. An activity changes the medium; a later activity responds to the change. This description can cover more than insect building and need not require every participant to represent the whole collective process. It also makes the medium operationally important: the relevant change must persist sufficiently, be perceivable, and support a response appropriate to the activity. An uninterpretable mark is not a coordination mechanism merely because it is a trace. [W073, §§2–3]

The example and conclusion present Heylighen's broader explanatory proposal. The account acknowledges imperfect use of the available workforce. A trace can guide selection without ensuring that work is evenly distributed, that obsolete information disappears in time, or that all required tasks are covered. [W073]

### Multi-robot coordination retains an engineered organization

Multi-robot coordination retains an engineered organization

Gil, Aguilar, Rivas and Dapena’s article proposes an architecture for emergent coordination in multi-robot systems. In the selected architecture and communication passages, robots do not simply follow unsupported local rules. The design retains sensing, knowledge management, collective memory, and both direct and indirect communication. These layers provide the conditions under which local acts can become relevant to a collective task. The account therefore makes the supporting organization visible within a proposal described as emergent. [W067, §§2–4, printed pp. 76–79]

### Schelling: tolerable local mixtures can produce segregation

Schelling: tolerable local mixtures can produce segregation

Schelling’s selected opening and model passages distinguish individual neighborhood rules from the collective pattern produced by movements under those rules. A person may tolerate some unlike neighbors without requiring the final population to be segregated. Yet moves made in response to locally unsatisfactory mixtures can change other neighborhoods, trigger further moves, and produce substantial separation. An aggregate pattern can therefore be different from the pattern one would infer by treating

<!-- PDF page 504 -->

each participant’s preference as a direct preference for the final collective outcome. [W070, printed pp. 147, 158–161]

The result depends on the model’s population ratios, neighborhood definition, thresholds and movement rules. Schelling explicitly limits quantitative generalization from an artificial board. Even describing the resulting arrangement as undesirable requires a stated social goal; the model does not derive that goal from its updating rules. This is relevant adverse material for a study of structural arrangements: local responses and successful individual adjustment need not establish an acceptable collective outcome. [W070]

### Distributed intelligence as a research landscape

Distributed intelligence as a research landscape

JST CRDS’s 2026 landscape section on autonomous distributed intelligence maps questions across material, bodily and collective scales, including design theory, prediction, oversight and implementation. [W100, S2.03, selected pp. 1–6]

### Double and multi-contingency: order between two agents may not scale

Double and multi-contingency: order between two agents may not scale

Dittrich, Kron and Banzhaf reconstruct a problem associated with Parsons and Luhmann: agents form expectations about how others will respond, including expectations about others’ expectations. The article contrasts shared-culture explanations with the development of expectations through interaction history. The selected abstract and paragraphs 1.1–2.5 introduce their own simulation framework. [SG-W042]

In the dyadic model, two agents alternately display one of a finite set of messages. There is no prior semantic relation among the messages. Each agent’s selection is influenced by wanting to meet the other’s expectations and wanting the other’s response to be predictable. Those two motives can conflict. The model thus specifies a selection problem rather than assuming that “communication” automatically produces a common understanding. Memory and information about the other’s response are part of the arrangement that can produce regularities. [SG-W042, §§2.1–2.5]

The authors report that order achieved between two agents often fails to scale to a larger setting and that observation and the proliferation of information matter. That reported finding belongs to their model. The contribution is a specified obstacle to generalization: a mechanism that produces a stable relation in a pair need not organize many participants under changed information conditions. [SG-W042]

### Leydesdorff: present decisions using a representation of a future

Leydesdorff: present decisions using a representation of a future

Leydesdorff’s 2005 article relates Rosen’s account of anticipation to Dubois’s incursive formulations and to social meaning. In the selected introduction, a system can use an internal representation to consider alternatives and alter present behavior. This differs from describing every adjustment as a reaction only to a past disturbance. The selected derivation then proposes a mathematical treatment and distinguishes an observing system from the system under observation. The quality of observation and the difference between interacting observers and interacting observations become explicit modeling choices. [SG-W055, introductory definitions]

The proposal retains the work of constructing, evaluating and updating the model, selecting among possibilities and making a decision. For Leydesdorff’s later double-contingency exposition, see S47. [SG-W055; WME-W021]

<!-- PDF page 505 -->

### Environmental traces and expectations in collective action

Environmental traces and expectations in collective action

The material distinguishes a physical stimulus, a readable environmental trace, an engineered memory and communication architecture, a neighborhood updating rule, an institutional research agenda, and formal models of expectations. These descriptions make different commitments.

<!-- PDF page 506 -->

### The historical accounts

The historical accounts

The historical accounts examine capabilities produced by physical structures, computational representations, learned practices and institutions. They describe how these capabilities developed, how they were investigated and where their explanations remain disputed.

The source accounts differ in their quantities, mechanisms, aims and evidence. The reading routes and indexes support comparison among them.

<!-- PDF page 507 -->

### Source specific terminology guide

Source specific terminology guide

Variety in Ashby counts distinguishable possibilities in a specified set, or uses the base-two logarithm of that count. Actual state, possible states and observed sequences are different objects. See S03.

Selection in Tektology is a deliberately generalized account of persistence and elimination under conditions, not necessarily biological reproduction and heredity. Egression concerns concentrated influence; degression concerns fixation and protection of more plastic activity. See S17.

Autonomy in the reconstructed viable-system model remains related to coordination, resources, audit, intelligence, policy and communication. Relational autonomy in the selected philosophical account asks a different normative question. See S22 and S48.

Invariant confluence concerns merges of valid reachable states with a common ancestor under specified transactions and invariants. Idempotence says repeating a merge adds no further change; it does not establish arbitrary application validity. See S10 and S11.

Lineage in lineage-driven fault injection describes dependencies explaining a known successful outcome, which guide candidate disruptions that must still be checked by execution. See S30.

Concretization in Simondon concerns development toward compatible functional relations within a technical object and its milieu. See S39.

Closure refers to different specified relations in the biological and chemical sources. These relations coexist with exchanges of matter and energy. See S26 and S40.

Resilience in Holling’s selected account differs from return-rate stability. In the ecological-information articles an overhead measure receives a related interpretation that requires separate empirical support. See S43 and S47.

Free energy denotes different quantities in the thermodynamic lecture and variational probabilistic account. See S46.

Burden in the administrative account includes learning, psychological and compliance costs in citizen– state interactions. See S48.
